en: Śrī: In the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra, the fourth part:
An Exposition of the Rasavat Ornament and Others.
Thus, having thoroughly examined the opinions of both ancient and modern scholars according to my own understanding,
more than a hundred ornaments have been fully described.
Based on rasa, bhāva, their semblances (tadābhāsa), and the subsidence of emotion (bhāvaśānti),
there are those known as Rasavat, Preyas, Ūrjasvin, and Samāhita.

Those four exceedingly beautiful varieties of suggestion not subordinate to other elements (aparāṅgavyaṅgya), which were previously described by ancient scholars, have now attained the status of poetic figures (alaṃkāra).
The conjunction of two states, and variegation—these three [are the remaining varieties].
Thus, seven figures of speech have been defined; others will now be described.

Here, this manual on the principles of rasa is presented in its broad outlines for the instruction of beginners. Nine specific modifications of the mind—namely love, mirth, sorrow, anger, energy, fear, disgust, wonder, and resignation—exist eternally as latent impressions (*vāsanā*). These exist in the form of the prior stages of the sprout of bliss;
whether they are contradictory or non-contradictory, they are unable to suppress that which [is the ultimate state].
This "bhāva" (emotional state), which is the bulbous root of the sprout of bliss, is the locus of the term "sthāyin" (the permanent).

Thus, the permanent moods (*sthāyibhāvas*) have been defined by the sage Bharata as subtle states of bliss that are not eclipsed by other emotions—whether contradictory, non-contradictory, of the same class, or of a different class. The specific modifications of the mind that constitute these [permanent moods] are presented in poetry and drama through the terms *vibhāva*, *anubhāva*, and *vyabhicāribhāva*, which denote their causes, effects, and auxiliary factors.

For example, there is a permanent emotion (sthāyībhāva) called *rati* (love). The causes of this love are well-known in the world: a youthful hero, a beautiful location, the song of the cuckoo, the *mākanda* tree, a gentle breeze, the rising of the moon, bees, a bower of creepers, a lotus pond, the thundering of clouds, and so forth. Its effects are looking, touching, embracing, kissing, writhing of the arms, and so on. Its auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) number thirty-three, categorized as *nirveda* (disgust) and the rest; namely:
disgust, languor, apprehension, envy, intoxication, fatigue, indolence, dejection, anxiety, delusion, memory, and fortitude.
Shame, fickleness, joy, agitation, as well as dullness,
pride, despondency, longing, sleep, and epilepsy;
Sleep, awakening, joy, dissimulation, and ferocity;
as well as thought, disease, madness, and even death.
Terror and mental agitation are to be known as transitory states;
these thirty-three emotions have thus been enumerated by name.

Thus they have been characterized by the Sage. And these, as far as possible, are the concomitants (*sahakārin*) of all nine permanent emotions (*sthāyin*). In the present context, for the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) whose permanent emotion is love (*rati*), the concomitants are eagerness, wonder, agitation, joy, fickleness, and so forth; the excitants (*vibhāva*) for the comic sentiment (*hāsya*) whose permanent emotion is laughter are the sight of deformed objects and the like; the ensuants (*anubhāva*) are the opening of the mouth, the showing of teeth, and so forth; and the transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*) are fickleness, fear, and so forth.

In this same manner, the excitants (*vibhāva*), ensuants (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicārin*) of other aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) should also be inferred by those who have studied works such as the *Rasārṇavasudhākara*. Thus, when these excitants, ensuants, and transitory states are manifested—through their perception in poetry via the contemplation of verses, and in drama through the vocal, physical, and other types of acting perfected by practice—the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) such as love, which resides in the spectator, becomes the aesthetic sentiment (*rasa*). As it was stated by the Sage (Bharata): "The production of aesthetic sentiment results from the conjunction of the excitants, ensuants, and transitory states. This is the summary.
Now, the section on the *rasavat* ornament:
"The wise call this *rasavat* when there is a *rasa*, or when there is a subordinate *rasa* (*rasāṅga*), or even when there is a subordinate emotion (*bhāvāṅga*).

Where a *rasa* becomes a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of another *rasa* or of an emotion (*bhāva*), there is the ornament named *rasavat*. However, when a *rasa* or an emotion is the primary element (*prādhānya*), it is simply considered *dhvani* (suggestive poetry). For this very reason, the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* [states]:
In that poem where rasa and the like are subordinate to another sentence-meaning (vākyārtha),
it is my view that rasa and the like constitute a mere ornament (alaṃkāra).

Thus: *bhāva* (emotional state) is that which is manifested by the *vibhāvas* (determinants) and *anubhāvas* (consequents), consisting of thirty-three varieties beginning with despondency (*nirveda*), as well as *rati* (love) when it is manifested toward objects such as a deity, a guru, a disciple, the son of a brahmin, or a king. As it is stated in the *Darpaṇa*:
"Love directed toward deities and the like, when manifested, is called *bhāva*. Likewise, the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) are to be understood as *bhāvas* when they are manifested."

In Janasthāna, the daughter of the Earth, her body bristling with horripilation, embraced the son of Raghu, who had shaken off the host of demons by the falling showers of arrows released from the string of his strung bow.
In this passage, the heroic sentiment (vīrarasa) residing in Sītā is subordinate to the erotic sentiment of union (saṃbhoga-śṛṅgāra) directed toward Śrī Raghunandana.
Just as Sītā, with her face bowed and her eyes trembling, gazed upon the son of Raghu, whose mighty arms were renowned for shattering the bow of Śiva, which was difficult for others to bend. 2002.

Here, the *adbhuta-rasa* (the marvelous sentiment) arises from the full development of the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of wonder, produced by the shattering of the bows of the gods and asuras—archers otherwise difficult to overcome. And this [marvelous sentiment] serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the *śṛṅgāra-rasa* (the erotic sentiment) residing in Jānaki, which is directed toward the illustrious descendant of Raghu.
Or, for example:
"Upon seeing the son of Bhīṣmaka trembling with his hair disheveled, as if shaken by Hari who was exultant in battle, Balabhadra’s face became smiling. (2003)

In this case, the heroic rasa (vīrarasa) directed toward the Lord, which is manifested through the pride of battle, is subordinate to the fearful rasa (bhayānakarasa) residing in Rukmiṇī, which is manifested by the words "trembling" and so forth; and that [fearful rasa] is in turn subordinate to the comic rasa (hāsyarasa) residing in Balabhadra. This constitutes a specific aesthetic distinction from the previous example.
An example of a *bhāva* (transitory emotion) serving as a constituent of the *rasa* (flavor) is as follows:

"May the couple who are the householders of the Bull Mountain, their limbs entwined with one another, rendered helpless by mutual amorous play, and gazing at each other, sport within the pure inner apartments of our own hearts. (2004)

In this case, the rasa of love-in-union (śṛṅgāra) residing in the divine couple, as perceived by the poet, is subordinate to the dominant emotion (bhāva) directed toward that same divine couple. Although it is argued that once a rasa has attained the status of a bhāva—being a counterpart to the bliss of the indivisible Brahman and having its very life dependent on the perception of the excitants (vibhāva) and so forth—it cannot possibly be subordinate; nevertheless, they maintain that because the permanent emotion (sthāyibhāva) underlying the rasa is subordinate, the term "subordinate to the rasa" is used figuratively.
O Sun of the Raghu dynasty, with the impetuous force of drawing back your great bow, you shattered by the millions the heads of the night-stalkers like so many large clods of earth. (2005)

O Sun of the Raghu dynasty! In the matter of drawing near—that is, bringing close—the exceedingly great battle (*āji*) of enemies and foes, [your arms] were puffed up with impetuosity, whether by speed or by joy; they were arrogant or uplifted. In the alternative sense: by the impetuosity of dragging the exceedingly great, vast earth (*jyāyāḥ kṣiteḥ*), that is, by the force of furrowing with the tip of a ploughshare, they were tossed up, raised high, immense and vast, numbering in the millions (*koṭiśaḥ*). [The suffix] *śas* is used here according to the rule "after words meaning 'much' or 'few'... (Pāṇini 5.4.42).

The heads of the night-stalkers—the nocturnal wanderers such as Daśānana and others—were shattered by the millions, like clods of earth, by [the Lord] who possesses a "million-fold clod-crusher" (a specific type of mallet); according to Amara, *koṭiśo loṣṭabhedanaḥ* means one who crushes clods by the millions. The suffix *śa* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) because the word belongs to the *loman*-class. You shattered them, you tore them apart, as if they were mere fragments of clay. Here, the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) residing in the Blessed One serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the poet’s own state of aesthetic emotion (*rasa*) consisting of love (*rati*) directed toward Him.
O Lord, when you had thus pacified the assembly of the Ten-faced one— who was causing such havoc to the world— the drum of the gods resounded, filled with an excessive and wondrous clamor.

"O God" is the form of address. Here, the heroic rasa (*vīrarasa*) residing in Śrī Raghunandana is the subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the emotion of love (*ratibhāva*) directed toward him that resides in the gods.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter in the *Alaṃkāramaṇihāra*, the figure of speech known as *rasavat*. Now begins the chapter on the figure of speech *preyas*:
if a *bhāva* (emotional state) is desired as *preyas* when it serves as a subordinate element to another *bhāva* or a *rasa* (sentiment), [then it is so defined].

When a *bhāva* (emotional state) serves as a subordinate element to another *bhāva*, it constitutes the *preya* ornament in two forms; this very same figure is designated by some as the *bhāva-alaṃkāra*.
In that regard, as for the state of one thing being an auxiliary to another state:
"May that mass of splendors whose abode is the lotus reside in my mind—that very mass by which the sovereignty of Śrī Veṅkaṭeśvara has indeed been eternally established. (2007)
In this instance, the sentiment of love directed toward Śrīnivāsa is the subordinate element (aṅga) of the sentiment of love directed toward Śrī.
An example of *bhāva* (emotional state) serving as a constituent of *rasa* (aesthetic flavor):
"O Lord of Lakṣmī, when shall I adorn with Your lotus-feet that supreme sky—the abode of auspiciousness, which transcends the sphere of speech and mind of Brahmā, Sanaka, and the other sages? (2008)

Here, the transitory mental state (*vyabhicāribhāva*) called "reflection" (*cintā*), indicated by the phrase "when might it be," is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the poet's dominant sentiment of tranquility (*śāntarasa*).
Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, the *Preyas-sara*, in the *Alaṃkāra-maṇi-hāra*.
Now begins the *Urjasvi-sara*:
either a semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*) or a semblance of emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*) attains the status of being a subordinate element to an emotion (*bhāvāṅgatā*).
When that occurs, this is called the ornament known as Ūrjasvinī (the Energetic).

Where either a semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa) or a semblance of emotion (bhāvābhāsa) attains the status of a subordinate element to the dominant emotion (bhāva), in both those cases there is the ornament named Ūrjasvin. A semblance of rasa is defined as the manifestation of love and other emotions through impropriety, according to the stated definition: "A semblance of rasa, however, is the improper arousal of love and the like."
O Lord who supports the earth like Nārāyaṇa, may my intellect dissolve into you alone; may it never be defiled by a fondness for many objects, as is the case with the minds of ordinary people.

Here, by the power of *samāsokti* (condensed expression), the realization of the wanton woman (*svairiṇī*) within the mind of an ordinary person leads to the emergence of a semblance of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasābhāsa*) residing therein; this, in turn, serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the poet’s own emotion (*bhāva*) directed toward the Blessed Lord. In this case, the erotic sentiment is termed a "semblance" (*ābhāsa*) because it proceeds in an improper manner toward many lovers.
As they have said:
"If the passion is fixed on only one [person], even if that person is an animal or a barbarian..."
"If there is excessive attachment toward women, it is considered a semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa) of three kinds. Thus [it is said].
O Lord, just as many celestial maidens each chose individually numerous heroes who had been severed by your discus in battle and had attained divine bodies in heaven, even so was she chosen by them.
Here too, as before, the woman—who is the semblance of the beauty of touch and taste—is subordinate to the emotion directed toward the Lord residing in the poet's mind.
May the moon-like lord of the Kosala dynasty obtain for a long time such victory and beauty, beholding which even the sages in the Daṇḍaka forest became as agitated by passion as women.

In this passage, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*) regarding Śrī Raghunandana is merely apparent (*ābhāsatva*), as its manifestation among the sages is improper; furthermore, it serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the poet’s own aesthetic emotion (*bhāva*) directed toward the beauty of the Blessed Lord.
Or for example:

"Where are you, the self-controlled and delicate one, and where is the fierce Śūrpaṇakhā, so excessively lustful? O son of Daśaratha, having encountered you who were unwilling, she attained disfigurement [from silver]. (2012)

*Rūpyaḥ* means "one whose form is praiseworthy" (*praśasta-rūpa*); the suffix *yap* is applied according to the rule *rūpād āhatapraśaṃsayor yap*. Amara states: *rūpyam api praśastarūpe*. Here, because Śūrpaṇakhā possesses passion for only one [Rāvaṇa] at a time, or because of her engagement in what is improper, there is the status of a semblance (*ābhāsatva*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*). Furthermore, that [semblance] serves as a constituent element (*aṅga*) of the poet’s own emotion of love (*ratibhāva*) directed toward her. A specific excellence (*vicchitti*) consisting in the commingling with the figure of speech *viṣama* (the incongruous) should be observed here.

All of this is an illustration of a semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*) serving as a subordinate element to a transitory emotion (*bhāvāṅga*). An example of a semblance of emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*) serving as a subordinate element to a transitory emotion is as follows:
"O Lord of the Mountain of Serpents, I have laid the entire burden of the earth upon you. If you protect it, let me protect it; if you abandon it, let me abandon it—I am never weary of this. (2013)

"I do not feel revulsion; I do not attain revulsion. Here, the state of pride is an "appearance" (ābhāsa) because its manifestation is improper. And that appearance serves as a subordinate limb to the emotion directed toward the Blessed One.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, the Ūrjasvi-sara, in the Alaṃkāramaṇihāra. Now begins the Samāhita-sara:
"Samāhita [is the name of] a state of tranquility (bhāvaśānti); however, when it serves as a subordinate element to another emotion (bhāva), it is an ornament (alaṃkṛti)."

Where there is the subsidence of emotion (*bhāvaśānti*)—as defined by the statement "the subsidence of emotions occurs when [other] transitory states (*vyabhicārin*) have manifested"—and this subsidence functions as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to another emotion, there it is included within *samāhita*.
Just as Śiva—

whose forehead is terrifying with his crooked frown and who is difficult even for Brahmā and others to propitiate— became gracious merely upon seeing Prahlāda, how great indeed must be your affection!

The word "O Blessed One" (*bhagavan*) is to be supplied [as the vocative]. Here, the subsidence of the emotion called "fierceness" (*ugratā*), characterized as "inflicting harshness, severity, threats, and so forth upon those who have done harm"—which resides in the Blessed One—is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the emotion of "love" (*rati*) toward that same object which resides in the poet. Some, however, maintain that when a semblance of an emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*) serves as a subordinate element to an emotion, it is termed "composed emotion" (*samāhita*); whereas they say that when the subsidence of an emotion (*bhāvaśānti*) serves as a subordinate element to an emotion, it is termed "subsidence of emotion" (*bhāvaśānti*).
Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, the Samāhita-sara, in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Bhāvodaya-sara:
when the emergence of a *bhāva* (emotional state) serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to another *bhāva*, it is considered *bhāvodaya* (the arising of an emotion).

When the "emergence of emotion" (*bhāvodaya*), defined as "the emergence of emotions [other than the primary one] in the case of both production and manifestation," serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the primary emotion (*bhāva*), there is the poetic figure named *bhāvodaya*.

Just as when the bowstring of Śauri’s Śārṅga bow resounded with a depth like a rain-cloud, alas, even while the heat of his arms blazed forth, the lords of the Daityas were seized with trembling. (2015)

In this instance, the emergence of the emotion (bhāva) consisting of fear arising in the lord of the Daityas serves as a subordinate element (aṅga) to the poet’s own emotion of love directed toward the Blessed One.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, the Lake of the Emergence of Emotion (*bhavodayasara*), in the *Alaṃkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Lake of the Conjunction of Emotions (*bhāvasandhisara*):
when emotions serve as subordinate elements, the conjunction of emotions (*bhāvasandhi*) constitutes the figure of speech known as *bhāvasandhi*.

When the "conjunction of emotions" (*bhāvasaṃdhi*), defined as "the simultaneous manifestation of equal [opposing] emotions," serves as a subordinate element to a primary emotion (*bhāva*), it constitutes the figure of speech known as *bhāvasaṃdhi*.

Victorious is the hero of the Yadu clan, whose pair of eyes blossomed at the sight of the face of Bhīṣmaka’s daughter won by the strength of his arms, and who now wields the Śārṅga bow due to the assault of Śiśupāla and others. || 2016 ||

Here, by the verse beginning with "bhujabalahr̥ta" (seized by the strength of his arms), there occurs a *bhāvasaṃdhi* (conjunction of emotions) through the simultaneous occurrence of joy—a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) of the erotic sentiment (*śr̥ṅgārarasa*)—and agitation, indignation, and so forth—transitory emotions of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*)—arising from the Lord's seizing of the Śārṅga bow due to the assault by Caidya and others. Furthermore, this [conjunction] is subordinate to the poet’s own emotion of love directed toward the Blessed One.
Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, the Chapter on the Conjunction of Emotions (bhāvasaṃdhi), in the Alaṃkāramaṇihāra.

Now begins the Chapter on the Ornament of the Mixture of Emotions (bhāvaśabalatā): when there is a mixture of emotions within the constituent parts of an emotion, that is called the ornament of the mixture of emotions (bhāvaśābalya).

Where there is the predominance of the agitation of emotions (*bhāva-śabalatā*), there exists the poetic figure named *bhāva-śabalatva*. The "agitation" (*śabalatā*) of emotions refers to their occurrence through the successive suppression of each preceding one. As it has been said: "The agitation of those [emotions] is considered to be by means of the successive suppression of each preceding one. This means "of those emotions."
"Just as I shall surely go, what could a person see of me in the darkness? What indeed could he know? If he were to see me and say, 'O Kṛṣṇa, she is enamored,' then I would truly be blessed. (2017)
May Kṛṣṇa be victorious—he who, rushing impetuously toward her as she moved slowly through the dense darkness, closely embraced that dark-lotus-eyed girl of Vraja.

In this context, there is longing (*autsukya*) in the thought "I shall surely go here"; apprehension (*śaṅkā*) in the thought "What if people should see me?"; fortitude (*dhṛti*) in the thought "What indeed would he know in the darkness?"; deliberation (*vitarka*) in the thought "If he should see me"; resolve (*mati*) in the thought "O Kṛṣṇa, what if he should say I am in love with him?"; and joy (*harṣa*) in the thought "Then I would truly be blessed. Through the successive suppression of each preceding state by the succeeding one, there arises a "complexity of emotion" (*bhāva-śabalatā*). And this is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the poet’s own emotion of love (*rati*) directed toward the Blessed Lord.
Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh necklace, the *Bhāvaśabalatāsara*, in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now, regarding the ornaments of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇālaṅkāra*):
if the means of valid cognition, such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the rest, were to possess aesthetic charm (*camatkāritā*), [they would constitute figures of speech].
At that time, other wise scholars spoke of eight ornaments of the means of valid cognition.
In that regard, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is as follows:
they say that the knowledge which arises from the contact of objects and the sense faculties is perception; and if it is beautiful, that constitutes its ornamentation.
If knowledge arising from the contact of the sense organs with their objects is described as being beautiful, it is the poetic figure named *Pratyakṣa* (Direct Perception).

O Lord, just as all the senses of the beautiful-eyed women of Vraja find happiness in you—who possess charming speech, who hold the nectar of life, who are handsome, exceedingly delicate, and the source of every fragrance—so it is with them. (2019)

Here, by means of the first qualification, the object of the sense of hearing; by the second, the object of the gustatory faculty; by the third, the object of the eye; by the fourth, the object of the tactile faculty; by the fifth, the object of the olfactory faculty; and by the phrase "rendered happy," the pleasure born from the experience of the objects of all the senses is presented. Thus, because the perception produced by the direct contact of all the senses is characterized by aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*), this is the figure of speech named *Pratyakṣa* (Direct Perception).
In this regard, the scriptural passage, "He who is all-fragrance, all-taste," should be reflected upon.
Having served Your most divine mind, Your sweet holy water,
Your fragrant *tulasi*, Your exceedingly soft feet, and Your conduct, our collection of senses has attained its purpose.

Here, by means of "the cognition of your body" and so forth—which function as the objects of repeated experience—and by the word "to be enjoyed," there is the presentation of the five sense-objects of the eyes, tongue, nose, skin, and ears, namely form, taste, smell, touch, and sound, as well as the experience thereof; thus, this too is the figure of speech *pratyakṣa* (perception), as previously described.
Just as I have now brought my Lord here before the path of my vision, so too was He, the lover of Śrī, who possesses immeasurable luster, formerly brought to the range of my hearing.

Here, upon this serpent-bearer (Śiva), I have now brought my lord into the path of light—that is, I beheld him. In the alternative sense, "I have brought him to the path of the world" means I have brought him to the range of memory; for the word *loka* signifies "memory," as seen in the statement, "Therefore, I am in the *loka* and in the Veda," where the meaning of "*loke*" in the phrase "*vede*" is explained as being in the *smṛti*.

The meaning is this: He whose splendor was immeasurable and radiant, who was formerly the beloved of Śrī and had been brought to the path of the Vedas—the way of hearing and the course of scripture—and who was previously made an object of auditory perception, has now been brought within the range of our visual perception. In the secondary sense (pakṣa), the meaning is that he who is celebrated in the Vedas as the Lord of Śrī and of immeasurable luster is likewise described as such in the Smṛtis of Manu and others; thus, "I have come to know him. Here, there is a description of the Blessed One as an object of both auditory and visual perception.
Just as one might wonder on the peak of the Cintāmaṇi mountain, "Is this perhaps a flash of lightning amidst the clouds?"— so did I, through my steadfastness, slowly discern Lakṣmī within Acyuta.

The meaning is: "By reason of its stability (*sthemnā*), that is, by way of its constancy, I have determined that this Lakṣmī resides in the Infallible One; I have concluded that this is not lightning in a cloud, but rather Śrī in the Abode of Śrī. The distinction is that in the former case there was merely perception, whereas here it is a perception following a doubt produced by the observation of specific characteristics.
Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth chapter, the Chapter on the Ornament of Direct Perception (*pratyakṣālaṃkāra*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*;
now begins the Chapter on the Ornament of Inference (*anumānālaṃkāra*).
Inference is defined as the knowledge of the probandum (liṅgin) produced by the logical mark (liṅga).

The *liṅga* is the probans (*hetu*), such as smoke; the *liṅgin* is the probandum (*sādhya*), such as fire. Thus, the meaning is that inference (*anumiti*) is the cognition of the probandum produced by the probans. This is inference in its general form. And because this [particular instance] is brought forth by the creative intuition (*pratibhā*) of a poet, it possesses poetic beauty and thus constitutes a figure of speech (*kāvyālaṃkāra*).

O Blessed One, abode of glory, just as the cool-rayed moon, cooling the surface of the world, causes its own cause—the supreme mind—to manifest, so too does your compassion, cool as frost, cause your own mind, the abode of glory, to shine forth supremely. || 2023 ||

Illumination (*prakāśana*) is clear cognition, and that [cognition] consists of inference (*anumiti*). Here, there is the figure of speech *anumānālaṅkāra* (poetic inference), because the subject—the Lord’s mind—is characterized by coolness, and this is produced by a mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the cooling of the surface of the world through the agency of the cool-rayed moon. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "The Lord’s mind is cooled by compassion, because it is the locus of birth for the cool-rayed moon, which is skilled in cooling the surface of the world. Or, for example:
"With floods of tears full of fragrance, with horripilation abounding in the rise of love... [bha].
O Lord, people who have taken up residence among your followers know [only] devotion.
The formal argument is as follows: these people possess devotion toward the Blessed One, because they are characterized by such things as tears of joy and outbursts of laughter.
Just as sprouts of joy flourish when a field is irrigated with the water of Dharma, I believe that the lake of her heart must be filled with the essence of love for Śauri.

The expression "the field itself is the field" is a *śliṣṭarūpaka* (a punning metaphor), meaning the field in the form of her limbs; for the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *kṣetra* refers to the body and a field. Here, by means of the reason—namely, the state of having sprouts of horripilation (*pulaka*) flourishing upon the locus of the field drenched with the water of perspiration—the inference is made that the heart-lake of the young women of Vraja is completely filled with the essence of passion (*anurāga-rasa*) directed toward the Blessed One.

The formal argument (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: "This [heroine] has a lake-like heart filled with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of passion for Śauri, because she possesses sprouts of horripilation (*pulaka*) whose locus is her own joyful body drenched in the water of perspiration," and so forth. The distinction is that in the first two verses the mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) are pure, whereas here they are vitalized by metaphor (*rūpaka*). That this is brought forth by the poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*) is quite evident.

In this context, the distinction is as follows: where there is the presence of both the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*), words such as "I know," "I think," "I suspect," "I am certain," or "I perceive" convey an inference; however, where there is the existence of a cause such as similarity (*sādṛśya*) and the like, those same words convey a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). For example:
"As the dullness departs and the great splendor of the *aśoka* tree manifests, I suspect that Mādhava is indeed surging within these virtuous ones. (2026)

*Jaḍimā* means coldness and ignorance. *Śrī* refers to the excellence of blossoming in the case of the *aśoka* trees—a specific species of tree—or, alternatively, it refers to prosperity (*śrī*) characterized by the absence of sorrow (*aśoka*), meaning a wealth devoid of the qualities of grief and other defects. *Mādhava* refers to the spring season and also to Śrīnivāsa (Viṣṇu). Regarding the phrase "as if" (*yathā tathā*), the commentary on the list of particles states: "The indeclinables *yathā* and *tathā* signify cause. Thus, the meaning is "since" (*yathā*) and "therefore" (*tathā*). Alternatively, according to the *Viśvakośa*: "The word *yathā* is indicated [to mean] equality and inference," it may here function as a term denoting inference.

Here, there is an inference of Mādhava’s manifestation based on signs such as the departure of dullness; the formal argument is: "These virtuous ones possess Mādhava shining within them, because they exhibit the departure of dullness and so forth."

Or rather, O Veṅkaṭanātha, I think that the moon, having stolen the splendor of your face and appearing with its own form only at night within [the sky], remains filled with nothing but apprehension. 2027.

O Veṅkaṭanātha! The moon (śaśāṅka) and the word *śaśāṅka*—there is identity between these two. Having stolen the splendor of your face, [the moon] remains only within the night (*antaḥ-niśam eva*)—that is, only during the night; in the other sense, it means "having its dark form (*śāka*) turned inward" or "having its syllable *śā* removed. It is neuter because it functions as an adverb. The short vowel occurs by the rule: *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya*.

He whose own form (*nijarūpa*)—his very nature—is visible [only at night] is thus described; I believe he is merely filled with apprehension (*śaṅkānvita*), that is, terrified. Otherwise, why would his own form manifest only at night? This is the intended meaning. In the alternative sense (the pun), when the letter *śā* in the middle of the word *śaśāṅka* is elided, it becomes *śaṅkānvita*, meaning it is composed of only those two syllables, *śaṅ-ka*. Here, there is an inference based on the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of having a form visible only at night within the moon (*śaśāṅka*), which gives rise to the inferred property (*liṅgin*) of being "filled with apprehension."
Or rather, I know that this distributor of light [the sun], having been overwhelmed by Your splendor, O Śauri,
has its internal radiance suppressed; it subsequently casts its rays downward and remains forever turned away.

"O Śauri! This Vibhākara, the sun, has been surpassed by your splendor; therefore, its light is internalized, its radiance submerged. In the other sense, the word 'Vibhākara' has its light—the letter *bhā*—internalized, meaning situated within its middle portion. In this latter case, because the word *bhā* ending in the vowel *ā* refers to a phoneme (*varṇa*), it lacks the feminine suffix, and thus there is no shortening of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*)."

"He by whom the hands are placed behind" is the literal meaning; this is a description of his physical state, indicating a lack of energy due to the loss of manliness, as his hands are pressed against the rear part of his body. Alternatively, "he by whom the hands (the letters *ka* and *ra*) are placed at the end (the letter *pa*)" means that his face is always turned away, humiliated by contempt—this is the intended sense. In another sense, it means "one whose face (*mukha*) has undergone a transformation (*vikāra*)," because the word *vibhākara* consists of the syllables shown [in the previous interpretation].

"This Vibhākara has been surpassed by the Blessed One's splendor" is the formal structure of the inference, based on reasons such as his light being internalized. And this, like the previous case, is intensified by a *śleṣa* (punning double entendre) permeated by the identity between the word and its meaning in the manner described. The same should be inferred for what follows as well.
Just as the king of elephants was surpassed by your gait and the king of birds by your face, O young woman of greenish hue, I think those two must have been overtaken by old age in the interval.

O Haritaruṇi! This [address] is intended to highlight her superior power in defeating the king of elephants and others. "In the midst" (antarā) means within her youth; the actual state of affairs is that it refers to the middle portion of her life. "Seized by old age" (jarālīḍhau) means pervaded by old age or senility. The sense is that, due to the mental anguish caused by the defeat inflicted by you, they became withered very quickly. In the alternative sense, the words *gajarāja* and *dvijarāja* are pervaded in their middle by the two syllables *ja-ra*.

In this instance, the state of being licked by fire (jarālīḍhatva) of both the king of elephants and the king of birds is established by the reason that they have been surpassed by the arrival at the face of Śrī.

Or, for example: "O man, I consider the fame of your enemies to have been destroyed by your prowess, since it first found a woman, then was withered, and finally became impotent of its own accord. (2030)
"O Puruṣa, denoted by the term 'Puruṣa' without limiting adjuncts!"— this means "O Blessed One.
For this word "Bhagavān" as well as the word "Puruṣa," both apply to the eternal Vāsudeva when he is without limiting adjuncts.

This is because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*). By this, His causality is also indicated, based on the etymological derivation: "Because 'I was here even before,' that is the Puruṣatva (the state of being Puruṣa) of the Puruṣa. And by that [causality], which implies omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth, His invincibility and other such qualities are illuminated. The sense is: "of You who are of such a nature. By *pauruṣeṇa*—meaning by a disposition or action appropriate to a Puruṣa, or by splendor such as invincibility—the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *pauruṣa* may refer to the state of a Puruṣa, to his action, or to his splendor."

I consider the fame of your enemies—those who hate you—to have been disregarded; for this fame and this deed [have done so]. That is to say, the glory of your foes was first (ādau) withered away—that is, reduced to a woman—and thereafter, at a later time, it was further withered—that is, deprived of its femininity—and I perceived it to be naturally (svataḥ) neuter (klība).

The meaning is this: that I previously recognized you as a woman, as one emaciated, and as a eunuch—that, I believe, has been utterly disregarded by your manliness. The sense is that for the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), it is an easy matter to humble a eunuch who was formerly a woman and is by nature emaciated, through the exercise of his prowess.

In reality, however, the word *yaśaḥ* (fame): first, it is "that in which the letter *ya* resides" (*yoṣitam*); then, immediately after, it is "that in which the letter *śa* resides" (*śoṣitam*), being neuter (*klība*) in gender. The meaning is that I recognized the word *yaśas* to be of such a form. There is an identity between the word and its meaning. Here, the fame of enemies was necessarily disregarded.

The probandum (*sādhya*) is its true nature; the probans (*sādhana*) is the state of being known as such through its femininity and so forth. Thus, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "This fame of enemies has been disregarded by the prowess of Puruṣottama, because it was initially known as feminine, as withered, and as neuter."
Or rather,
it was surely struck by your discus that Vivasvat, his rival, turned away with the sun submerged within him, having reached a state of supreme destruction.

"O Blessed One"—this is understood from the context. Vivasvat, the radiant sun, is a rival to your discus; therefore, he has surely been struck or assailed by it. For, because he has turned his face away (vimukha), with his internal treasures—his rays—submerged within him, and being toothless (adanta), with his teeth fallen out, he has suffered extreme calamity and injury. Thus, I consider that he has been struck; such is the construction of the verse.

In this context, the word *vivasvān* is "turned away" (*vimukha*), meaning that which has a modification (*vikāra*) at its beginning. It "attains" (*prāpta*) the suffix *śas*—the accusative plural ending—which exists "beyond" (*para*) it. It is "ending in *at*" (*adanta*), meaning that the two phonemes *a* and *t* are at its end. The particle *vai* is used for emphasis (*prasiddhau*). This description applies when followed by *śas*, as the form remains as *vivasvat*. The mention of *śas* is illustrative and includes the *ṭā*-case endings and others as well.

Because the presence of the suffix *num* is prescribed only when followed by a *sarvanāmasthāna* case-ending, the state of having a final short *a* (*adantatā*) is not heard [in that context]; therefore, it is stated that [the word] has a final short *a* when followed by the accusative plural suffix *śas*. Here, the fact that Vivasvat was struck by the Lord’s discus is established through reasons such as his turning away [from the Lord].

In this regard, the following should be noted: when words such as "they know" (jānanti) or "I think" (manye) are employed, the expressed meaning is inference (*anumāna*), as in the examples beginning with "with floods of fragrant tears" (*sāmodabāṣpapūraiḥ*). When words that are indicative (*lakṣaka*) such as "he reveals" (*prakāśayati*) are employed, the indicated meaning is [inference], as in the first example beginning with "the surface of the world" (*bhuvanatalam*). When neither of these is employed, it is the suggested meaning in an inference where the probandum (*sādhya*) is implied.

O Hari, just as coral, when placed upon the scale of the brilliance of your feet, was cast out; for though it may be prominent or occupy a central position, it ultimately possesses only the quality of being discarded at the end. 2032.

Here, because the inference is suggested through the exclusion [of coral] from comparison with the splendor of Hari’s feet—which is the *sādhya* (the thing to be proven)—it possesses the quality of being "implied" (*pratīyamānatva*). O Hari! Coral (*pravāla*) has been excluded from comparison with the luster of your feet; for although this coral is "foremost"—meaning it is counted by all as being at the head—it is nonetheless "middling" (*madhya*), that is, inferior due to some base action. According to the *Viśvakośa*: "The word *madhya* refers to what is just, an opening, a waist-band, a fastening, or something base."

Therefore, at the end, in the conclusion, or at a distance, it attains *alaṃ*—that is, the state of being excessively released (*visarga*) by all. In the alternative sense, the word *pravāla* has the letter *pra* at its beginning, and is "with *va* in the middle," meaning that which has the letter *va* as its medial; thus, it possesses the letter *laṃ* at the end and the *visarga* as well. This is the meaning.
O Mother, surely this cuckoo, rivaling the nectar-like essence of your words, has been understood as not merely a forest-dweller; for it shines forth from here, filled with joy to the very end.

O Mother! Is it not so that the "vanapriya" (the cuckoo), which rivals the nectar-like essence of your words, is understood—indeed, ascertained—to be *napriya* (not dear), being outside the sphere of affection? For this reason—that is, even upon thorough investigation in the end—no person who is pleased or satisfied by this [cuckoo] appears; the meaning is that no one is seen anywhere to be gratified by him. Therefore, the sense is that he is merely fond of the forest (*vanapriya*), but not dear to people (*janapriya*).
In another sense, the word "vanapriya" is understood (*vagata*)—that is, it has acquired the letter 'v' (*vakāra*)—and thus it is not [the same].

It is so called because it "becomes" (*bhavati*); that is to say, when the letter *va* is elided from *napriya*, only *napriya* remains. Furthermore, it is "not this" (*na itaḥ*), meaning it is joined with the letter *na*; it is "joined with the group of syllables *pri*" (*prītaḥ*); and finally, it is "from which" (*yataḥ*), meaning it is joined with the letter *ya*. The sense is that the word *vanapriya* (the forest-lover) possesses such characteristics. Here, as before, the suggested nature (*pratīyamānatvam*) is understood through the implication (*ākṣepāt*) of an inference: "The forest-lover is not a lover (*napriyaḥ*)," because, by virtue of its association with the essence of the word for Śrī (Goddess Lakṣmī), it does not produce affection in anyone. The same applies in what follows.

Or as the Śruti says: "The woman who has excellent offspring [becomes] a man here, having become subordinate. Thus, the woman of good intellect shines like a man; for these two, the state of dependence is equal.

The scripture states: "To Viṣṇu, who has a beautiful wife" (*sumajjānaye viṣṇave*). This scripture refers to the Supreme Person, Śrī Viṣṇu, as one who has a "beautiful wife" (*sumatī*); that is to say, he possesses a consort endowed with auspicious qualities, namely Śrī, his co-practitioner (*sahadharmiṇī*). It says: here, between these two—Śrī and Śrīnivāsa—the "beautiful wife," Śrī, though subordinate as a qualifier of the Lord, is celebrated *puṃvat*, that is, just like the Supreme Person; she is renowned for such attributes as being the Sovereign of All and the Pervader of All.

For just as the Blessed Lord is described in such passages as "He is the ruler of what has been and what is to be; He is the Lord of all," Śrī also is heard to possess universal lordship in such passages as "She is the mistress of this world" and "The sovereign of all beings."
"In my view, pervasion by way of qualities and by way of essential nature is considered common [to both]. Just as the universe is pervaded by her in her essential nature and by her very being,
so too is all this pervaded by her, and she is likewise the sovereign controller."
"And by you and by Viṣṇu, O Mother, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is pervaded."

Furthermore, because [terms] such as *iyā* and others describe the pervasiveness of both over the world; or rather, the meaning is that this [Goddess] is also well-known primarily in the same manner as the Blessed Lord (Bhagavān). As in: "To the one of beautiful majesty," "The beloved of Śrī, the Infinite," and "In Brahman, the abode of Śrī"—just as [these epithets apply] to the Blessed Lord.

Because the preeminence of Śrī is also heard in the scriptural statement, "the wife of Viṣṇu," therefore, for both of these—Śrī and the Lord of Śrī—the state of being dependent and mutual subordination is equal. The sense is that this is according to such statements as: "In you, O Murāri, there is a distinction within yourselves regarding womanhood, gentleness, subservience to a husband, compassion, and forbearance; seeing whose face, [you] perform everything entirely subject to her gestures, and whose knitting of the eyebrows is the standard for the gradations in the arrangement of all moving and unmoving things."
Overwhelmed by that [notion], the referent "I" (ahamartha) is established;
and that which arises from the referent "I" is proclaimed as the ego-sense (ahantā).
Know that the relationship between me and my Lord is one of identity, because of their mutual inseparability and their mutual concomitance.
Thus, what is stated in the Lakṣmītantra and other sources is also favorable here.

In this context, the Vedic scripture speaks of a male person—that is, one who is masculine—using the word *sumajjāni*. Here, although the compound *sumajjāni* is technically a *bahuvrīhi*, the word *sumatī* (the feminine form of *sumati*), having become subordinate (*upasarjana*) by attaining the status of a qualifier, manifests in the masculine form (*puṃvat*). Thus, it appears having attained the masculine transformation prescribed by the rule beginning with "A feminine [word] becomes like the masculine when [the word] has been previously used in the masculine" (*striyāḥ puṃvad bhāṣitapuṃskād*).

Therefore, the meaning is that the dependence (*pāratantrya*) of these two words, *sumat* and *jani*, is equal to their being dominated by the meaning of another word (*anyapadārthapradhānatva*), because of the rule: "A *bahuvrīhi* compound is dominated by the meaning of another word. According to Amara, *tantra* means "the primary" or "the established doctrine. Here, the mutual dependence of Śrī and the Lord of Śrī (Viṣṇu) is what is to be proven. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is: "These two, Śrī and the Lord of Śrī, possess mutual dependence, because they possess the pervasion of sovereignty and other qualities where both are equally primary. In this case as well, since no explicit expressive word is employed, it is an inference based on what is implied (*pratīyamāna-anumāna*).

O lady of supreme and excellent complexion, just as the night, desiring to attain your color, was led before you and attained tranquility, so too did Śrī become hopeless regarding the attainment of that intermediate complexion [between yours and the night's].

O *uttamavaravarṇini*! [The term] *varavarṇinī* means one who possesses a *varaḥ* (excellent) *varṇaḥ* (complexion); the suffix *-in* is used here in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*). Amara states: "The most excellent woman is called *uttamā varavarṇinī*. She is both *uttamā* (supreme) and *varavarṇinī*; thus, the compound is formed according to the rule beginning with "sanmahatparamottama... This is her vocative case. The meaning is: "the most excellent even among them. One should recall here the verse: "Sītā is the supreme wife among women."

O Śrī! Since the night (niśā)—that is, turmeric (haridrā), for Amara states: "The one called niśā is golden-yellow; turmeric is of excellent color"—being desirous of attaining your complexion, that is, wishing to obtain it, [the night] desires to attain your most excellent complexion, which is described in the Śruti as "golden-hued" and "sun-hued," by means of its own status as a mere *varavarṇinī*—an excellent woman. This is the intended meaning.

The sense is that she was brought right before you, having been delivered into your very presence, but not yet one who is exerting herself for the sake of attaining her own desired object. "Possessing tranquility" (*śāntimat*)—as in the phrase "the fulfillment of autumn," where the neuter gender is used in a general sense—the state of being so is *śāntimatva*, meaning the quality of being tranquil (*śāntatva*). Behind the scenes, she has merely formed a wish, which is easily obtained upon gaining the sight of you.

The meaning is this: that [the yellow pigment] which is heard of in scripture as being like the sun in its brilliance or as having the very form of the sun (in the mantra *sūryāṃ hiraṇmayīm*) has become lusterless in your presence. For it is well known that turmeric loses its luster when licked by the rays of the sun. Therefore, *antarā*—meaning between your desire to obtain your own complexion and your bringing [the pigment] before you. As Amara states: "Now, *antara*, *antarā*, and *antareṇa* may signify 'in the middle'. The sense is: of the complexion (*varṇa*), namely your complexion which she desired for herself.
The meaning is: "I think that when an object is attained—that is, reached—it is indeed devoid of hope, being one whose thirst has completely vanished."

In the alternative sense, the word *niśā* (night) has the syllable *ni* at its beginning (*purataḥ*, i.e., the first part), and the syllable *śā* as its final (*jaghanya*) element; thus, it attained the state of being "possessed of tranquility" (*śāntimattvam*), because the word *niśā* consists of those two aforementioned syllables. At the end, within the interval between the syllables forming the word *niśā*, [the letter] *rā* [is placed]; according to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *antaḥ* is not feminine; it means certainty, destruction, essential nature, front, proximity, and interior. *Rā*.

The meaning—that upon the attainment of such a complexion (varṇa), there would surely be hopelessness (nirāśā)—is also striking. Here, the form of an inference is perceived: that upon the attainment of the complexion of the Goddess Śrī, the night (niśā) becomes truly hopeless (nirāśā), because by her mere presence, the state of possessing tranquility (śāntimat-tva) is attained.

Or rather, because even the sun shines by the light of your feet, O Blessed One, it is indeed a thief; for its hand—bound by its rays—is directed toward another’s body and has been sent away from the presence of the virtuous.

O Blessed One! Because it is illuminated by the splendor of your feet—the beauty of your feet—even the sun (*bhāskara*) is merely a thief (*taskara*). The sense is that otherwise, it would be impossible for him to be illuminated by the splendor of your feet. Furthermore, he states another reason for his being a thief: "since" (*yat*), because this sun has his rays (*karāḥ*, meaning hands) bound with a rope (*guṇena*, meaning a cord) upon his other limb, namely his back.

For it is observed that those who commit theft of another's property have their hands bound with ropes by having their arms dragged behind them; this refers specifically to the wicked, the unrighteous, and indeed to such thieves—this is the sense. And he was sent "into the midst" (antare); the locative case is used here because the action is intended to express the locus of the activity. Alternatively, there is a word-break as *satām* [instead of *asatām*]; the meaning is "of the wise" (*viduṣām*). "Into the midst" means in the outer region; the sense is that he was cast out by the virtuous.
The word *antara* is used in the senses of interval, space, limit, clothing, disappearance, division, purpose,
hole, one's own, absence, exterior, opportunity, middle, and inner self.

Thus says Amara: "The term *antara* [is used] in the sense of being outside (*bahiryoga*) or as an undergarment (*upasaṃvyāna*). Since the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāma-saṃjñā*) is optional for the nine words beginning with *pūrva* when meaning "being outside," the substitution of *smin* for the locative suffix *ṅi* does not occur here.

Elsewhere, the word *bhāskara* (the sun) becomes *taskara* (a thief). This is because the letter *bhā* is [replaced by] the letter *ta*; having removed the letter *bhā*, the letter *ta* is placed in its very stead. The analysis of the compound is as follows: "of her who has a longing for words" (*padarucyāḥ*)—that is to say, of her who delights in the variety of the transformation of words (*padaparivṛtti*), such as their metrical or syntactic shifts. Thus, for you, O Noble Lady, the word *bhāskara* becomes the word *taskara*.

Furthermore, because this word *bhāskara*—which has attained the status of the word *taskara*—is joined (*saṃdānita*) in its posterior member (*aparāṅge*), that is, its latter part, by the quality (*guṇa*) caused by the *ṭa* suffix prescribed for *ārddhadhātuka* affixes by rules such as *divāvibhāniśāprabhābhasaḥ karaṇe*, resulting in the form *kara* derived from the root *kṛ*; thus it is called "one whose *kara* [latter part] is so constituted. The word *antaresatām* is a compound. The indeclinable *antare* ending in *-e* means "in the middle" (*madhye*).

Regarding the phrase "athāntare'ntarāḥ antareṇa ca madhye syuḥ," Amara states that these are indeclinables (*avyaya*). [The word] *antare* means "in the middle. That which possesses the letter *s* prescribed by the rule *kaskādiṣu ca*, as well as the letter *s* belonging to the augment *suṭ* prescribed by the rule *tadbṛhatoḥ*, is described as such. The state of being that is *antaresatā*; "made to attain" (*gamita*) means "brought to" (*prāpita*). This too is merely an implied inference (*ākṣiptānumāna*).
O Lord of the Serpent Hill, this moon is but a single drop from the ocean of the nectar of your fame; for it is by its very nature that the wise refer to it as a "spray" (śīkara). || 2037 ||

O Lord of Phaṇigiri! This moon is but a drop from the nectar-ocean of your fame; this is what is to be established. The reason for this is "since" (yataḥ). Since this moon is designated as "śīkara" by the wise simply because of its own nature—though in reality, the word "śītakara" (the cool-rayed one) is here used as "śīkara" with the letter *ta* having fallen away (*vigalita*) of its own accord (*svataḥ*), meaning it is perfectly (*suṣṭhu*) without the letter *ta*. Thus, the meaning is that the word "śītakara" is conventionally treated as "śīkara."
Just as all afflictions reach dissolution and all darknesses utterly vanish, so does the moon always shine within the pure sky of the hearts of these virtuous ones.

In this case, because the probandum (sādhya) is implied through the mention of the moon’s shining, it is considered "implied" (pratīyamāna). The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: "The virtuous possess a moon shining in the sky of their hearts, because they are free from the heat [of passion] and because darkness [of ignorance] has dissolved. This is a blend of paronomasia (śleṣa) and metaphor (rūpaka). Where the probandum itself is not explicitly stated, but is inferred through the presentation of the logical mark (liṅga) alone, that is "inference by suggestion" (dhvanyanumāna).
Just as herds of elephants trumpet, alas, the steeds neigh incessantly, and many chariots move with great speed, sporting in the courtyards of the houses of the great. (2039)
Here, the inference of the state of being the object of the side-glances of the Fortune of the great ones is suggested (dhvanita).
Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, the Chapter on Inference (*anumāna*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*. Now begins the Chapter on Analogy (*upamāna*):
"That which is the instrument for the knowledge of similarity, whereby there arises the cognition of the relationship between a name and the object named, is called analogy (*upamāna*)."

Comparison (*upamāna*) is the cognition of the relationship between a name and the object named, produced by the instrument of knowledge consisting of the awareness of similarity. That same [cognition], when it is strikingly beautiful, is the figure of speech known as comparison (*upamānālaṅkāra*).

Know that to be the Kaustubha gem among the multitude of heart-jewels of the Lord of Veṅkaṭagiri; for here, O friend, it has the form of the moon situated amidst the cluster of stars within the sky. 2040.
We know the Lord who dwells on Mount Vṛṣācala to be as delicate as the god of love, as eternally noble as the celestial tree, and as profound as the ocean. 2041.

In this first example, because there is the cognition of a simile—namely, "this object is denotable by the term *kaustubha* maṇi"—arising from the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence introduced as the source of the extended application (*atideśavākya*), which states that the object situated in the midst of the collection of gems within the heart of the Lord of Veṅkaṭagiri possesses a form similar to the moon situated among the clusters of stars in the midst of the sky, this is the figure of speech known as *upamāna*.

In the second example, however, through sentences such as "like Kāma" (*sumaśaramiva*) and so forth, the qualities of possessing beauty like that of Kandarpa, possessing generosity like that of the celestial tree (*surataru*), and possessing depth like that of the ocean—which consist of similarity (*sādṛśya*) that is the meaning of the sentence of transfer—are presented. Since this establishes the fruit of the cognition of the word's power (*tatpadaśaktigraha*)—namely, the simile (*upamiti*) denoted by the word "Vidā" (the Lord) residing on the Vṛṣācala mountain—the means of knowledge (*upamāna*) consisting of the perception of similarity, which is the meaning of the sentence of transfer, is shown along with its result; this is the distinction.
Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, the Chapter on Simile (Upamāna), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on Verbal Authority (Śabdapramāṇa):
that which is the proclamation of a word as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is verbal authority.
Sound is said to consist of the forms of Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and so forth.

The presentation of the Vedas and other authorities as evidence for one's own stated point is the figure of speech known as *śabdapramāṇālaṃkāra*. He states the meaning of the word "śabda" [in this context] with the words "śrutīti. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), there is an inclusion of the Purāṇas, proverbs, common worldly sayings, and the like.
In this regard, an example of a word in the form of *śruti* is:

"O Lord, if you do not descend upon the mountain of the serpent-king (Śrīparvata), how indeed shall we behold you—you whom the Veda, difficult to grasp, declared cannot be seen by the eye," and so forth. (2042)

In this context, the scriptural passage beginning with "It is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech" is adduced as an authority for the fact that the Blessed One, the Supreme Brahman, cannot be apprehended by the sense organs such as the eyes; by the word "etcetera," passages such as "That which is invisible and ungraspable" are included.
Just as you know my devotion toward you, O Savior, why do you nevertheless disregard me? O Lord of All, the Śruti indeed declares you to be omniscient and omnipotent.

In this context, having raised the alternatives—whether there is indifference toward you on my part, or a lack of knowledge regarding my devotion, or perhaps an inability to protect me—the author presents the scriptural authority consisting of the Śruti texts, "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," and "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold," in order to demonstrate that neither of these two possibilities is possible.
O Nārāyaṇa, he who knows you as being truly without a second becomes one destined for liberation; the Upaniṣads describe him as being like you,
and they declare him to be Viṣṇu.

O Nārāyaṇa! By this, it is indicated that the subject matter about to be described is contained within the *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad*. That person who knows—that is, realizes—you as "without a second" (*advitīya*) and "without a rival" (*apratidvaṃdva*), becomes prosperous (*bhaviṣṇu*) and flourishing (*vardhiṣṇu*), meaning he comes to possess ever-increasing excellence. You extend yourself (*ātanuṣe*) to that man who thus knows you, making him like yourself (*tvannibha*); the meaning is that you grant him *sāyujya* (union with you).

In the alternative [reading], regarding the word *bhaviṣṇu* in the phrase *tvannibham*, the word division is *tvaṃ nibham*. By the rule *vā padantasya*, there is an optional substitution of the *parasavarṇa* for the *anusvāra*. The meaning is that *tvaṃ nibham* means "you are devoid of the letter *bha*" (*bhakāra-śūnyam*). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound preceded by the prefix *ni*. [The verse says] "you spread it out" (*ātanuṣe*). Therefore, the end of the *Nigama*—that is, the *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad*—declares that he is the Person, Viṣṇu.

As it is recorded there, beginning with "Now, Nārāyaṇa is eternal," it continues: "The stainless, untainted, changeless, ineffable, pure, divine, and unique Nārāyaṇa—there is no second whatsoever. He who knows thus becomes Viṣṇu himself. In this context, the word *bhaviṣṇu* (one who is about to become) becomes *viṣṇu* upon the elision of the letter *bha*; such is the meaning. Here, the Upaniṣad is brought forward as authoritative evidence for the aesthetic charm of the author’s own stated point.
In this passage, the Upaniṣad is made to recognize its own identity through the words "Nārāyaṇa" and "becomes non-dual through knowledge of the Veda."
In some cases, there is a great excellence in presenting a scriptural passage as authoritative by interpreting its meaning in a different way. For example:
"O Lord, I do not consider that Guru who leads you to Brahman to be a mere human being; for here, the statement of the Upanishad, 'His person is non-human,' is the authority. (2045)

In this context, there is a particular stylistic peculiarity: the citation of the Śruti text, "That superhuman person leads them to Brahman," as an authoritative proof for the author's intended meaning—the possibility of the Teacher being superhuman—by means of the reason that he is the one who causes [the souls] to go to Brahman (*brahmagamayitṛtva*).
Or rather, I know that the Brahman residing on the Bull-hued Mountain (Vṛṣagiri) is indeed the merit of the worlds; for the Śruti says, "That is called merit," which belongs to the Taittirīyas. 2046.

In this context, the Taittirīya Śruti—by accepting the Self alone as the material cause through the statement, "It made itself its own Self; therefore it is called 'well-made' (sukṛta)"—establishes that Brahman is denoted by the term *sukṛta* on the basis of the causal motivation consisting in the activity of skillfully fashioning the manifold of created things (*prapañca*). Thus, the scripture is brought forward as an authority for the Lord’s nature as the well-made form of the world, which is our intended meaning.

O jewel of the immovable serpent-king, we understand that Vedic passage which declares, "The sacrificer who worships another while You, the Inner Self of all, exist, is a mere beast," to be directed toward You alone. || 2047 ||

O delighter of the Yadus, I believe that the Vedic scripture stating "the sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ) is intended precisely for one such as you, who—though ignorant of it—sacrifices to you, the enjoyer of all sacrifices. || 2048 ||

In the phrase "in You, the innermost Self of all," the locative case is used in the sense of a condition (*bhāvalakṣaṇa*) to indicate an excess of disregard [toward others]. A *prastara* is a handful of *darbha* grass or a stone. The intention is that You are the enjoyer of all sacrifices, as stated in the Gītā: "For I am indeed the enjoyer and the Lord of all sacrifices. For this very reason, the address "O Delight of the Yadus" (*yadunandana*) is significant. Here, in the first verse, the state of being a sacrificial animal (*paśutva*), which was figuratively represented by the Vedic scripture for another purpose, is [attributed] to the sacrificer on the grounds of his ignorance.

The metaphorical identification (*rūpaṇa*) is imagined. However, in the second case, one should understand that there is an imagination of a different object in the form of a stone for the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*), which has been metaphorically identified as such because it performs the function of the grass-bundle for the sacrificer.
Or rather: "O Lord, may I not be visible to you; may I remain only invisible. In that case, I shall be dear to you, for the Veda says that the gods are fond of what is out of sight. (2049)

In this regard, the Śruti passage—"They call him who is thus present by the name 'Indra' indirectly; for the gods indeed love what is indirect"—establishes that the gods take pleasure in the use of indirect names, and thereby serves as authoritative evidence for the sense of one's own desire for the state of being beloved on account of being indirect.
People who describe you as the lord of merely the Veṅkaṭa mountain are utterly deluded; for even Gaurjarī says that Viṣṇu is the sovereign of all mountains. (2050)

"Even an old cow is Viṣṇu; even some worn-out animal is Viṣṇu; he is the sovereign lord of all mountains"—so they say. In reality, however, the "old cow" refers to the Vedic text: "May Viṣṇu, the lord of mountains, protect me. Here, the word *hi* (for/indeed) denotes well-known tradition. In this context, the cited scripture has been brought forward as an authoritative support (*upodbalaka*) for the purpose of demonstrating the foolishness of those people who claim that the Lord’s consciousness is restricted solely to Veṅkaṭagiri, as stated in the first half-verse. Or, as it is said: "Do you not know us, the wretched ones? Why [is this] here? etc.
"The Śruti says of you, 'He stands firm like a tree'; so what is the use of further deliberation? (2051)
Or rather,
since these men on the path of worldly existence cry out even while clinging to you, O Hari, the Upanishads now declare that you are beyond both sight and hearing.

In the previous examples cited, scripture (*śruti*) was presented as an authority for the intended meaning. However, in these two present examples, the scriptural passages—"Like a tree, He stands alone, steadfast in heaven; He is without eyes or ears, without hands or feet"—have been brought forward as authorities by one who is weary of the path of worldly existence and intent on censuring the Lord regarding an unintended meaning. This is the distinction. "Stabdha" means inert or dull. But the actual meaning is that, due to the absence of any object to be bowed before, His nature is like a tree, being unbending.
O Lord of Kamalā, by making even those Brahmins who were once clad in rags possessors of splendor, you rendered the Vedic injunction— "Fortune does not delight in a Brāhmaṇa"— a speaker of falsehood.

In this context, the distinction from the previous [case] is that the Vedic scripture stating, "Prosperity indeed does not delight in a Brāhmaṇa," which serves as the authority for the Brāhmaṇas' lack of prosperity, is cited here to reveal their propounding of a false meaning by negating their possession of prosperity.
The authority of the word in the form of memory is as follows:

"O Lord of Śrī, take refuge in my pure, soft, and immovable heart-lotus, which is supported by the king of serpents; do not abandon it, for the mountain does not remain there for long"—such indeed is the recollection. (2054)

"Smaraṇaṃ smṛtiḥ varvṛtīti" means that it occurs through the repetition of an action. Here, regarding the desired object of the prayer for the Lord Śrīnivāsa to abandon his exceedingly harsh mountain abode in order to take refuge in the extremely tender heart of [the Goddess], the Smṛti of Manu—"One should not dwell long on a mountain"—was accepted as authoritative evidence.

Just as one who bows down seeks to conquer a host of enemies by taking refuge in the mountain fastnesses of the king of beasts—for indeed, among all types of fortresses, they remember the mountain fortress alone to be the most excellent—so too [do you]. (2055)

For those who have come for refuge, in order to conquer the group of enemies related to them—the sixfold group of foes beginning with desire—one may understand "mountain fortress" (*giridurga*) to refer to the mountain fortress of Śeṣādri, which is inhabited by lions and other fierce creatures. Here, regarding the matter of taking refuge in the mountain fortress of Mṛgendragiri—which is conceived as having the fruit of victory over the group of enemies related to those who have sought refuge in the Blessed Lord Śrīnivāsa—it is said that one should take shelter in a mountain fortress with every effort;
for a mountain fortress is distinguished by its many excellent qualities.
Thus, the Smṛti of Manu itself has been presented as the authoritative source.

Or rather, how could one lacking discernment attain the Imperishable, which is difficult to reach and beyond the visual range, as Manu has said: "For that which is difficult of access and outside the scope of the eyes can never be attained"? (1056)

It is difficult to traverse, as the Śruti declares: "The edge of a razor is sharp and hard to pass over; the wise call that a difficult path. This is also supported by the recitation of the *Thousand Names*: "He is difficult to attain, difficult to traverse, and difficult [to reach]. It is beyond the eye, not within the range of vision, according to the Śruti: "It is not grasped by the eye. Such is Acyuta—the one from whom those who have attained Him do not fall, according to the etymological definition—and Śrīnivāsa, the Supreme Brahman. [The verse continues: "The ignorant, the evil-doers, the deluded, the lowest of men, do not take refuge in Me;
their wisdom has been carried away by Māyā, and they have resorted to a demonic nature."

In the manner thus described, let the deluded person—whose knowledge has been stolen away by *māyā*—not attain [Me]; that is to say, let him not become one who has taken refuge. Regarding this stated meaning:

The statement from Manu regarding the duties of a *snātaka*—"One should never enter a difficult place that is beyond the range of sight"—which means one should never enter a wilderness (*kāntāra*) that is out of the range of vision, was cited as authoritative by means of a metaphorical identification based on a common substratum (*śleṣabhittikābhedādhyavasāya*). Previously, a Smṛti text was presented as authority for a desired meaning; here, however, the distinction is that it is used for an undesired meaning by one intent upon censuring those who have not taken refuge in the Lord.
The authority of verbal testimony in the form of history (itihāsa) is as follows:

"Though seized by the crocodiles of the senses in the ocean of worldly objects, he has now reached you, the island, and while still alive, he beholds auspicious things"—this is according to the principle [of such a statement]. (2057)

"O Blessed One"—this is understood from the context. Now, at this opportune moment when my past merits have reached their fruition, I have at last found you alone as my island of refuge. Having endured many hardships here, I have sustained my life; regarding this attainment of the fortune of taking refuge at the feet of the Blessed One after a long time—an attainment that is itself indestructible—it is stated that there are many advantages in remaining alive, for "as long as one lives, one beholds auspicious things. Thus, the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa* is cited as authoritative evidence.
As it is said: [The verse follows...]

"O Lord, you have taken this collection of ornaments from me, and I too have given them to you; for one who has been helped must repay that kindness—this is the eternal dharma," so said the *Rāmāyaṇa*. (2058)

O Lord! This collection of instruments—that is, the group of sense organs—is for the purpose of worshipping You; this is the intended meaning. You have given me *alam*, which means "sufficiently" or "adequately," and I too have given to You. In this interpretation, the word *alaṅkaraṇam* is a compound; its meaning is "this composition (*prabandha*) which sets forth ornaments. Here, [it refers] to the meaning intended by [the author] himself.

‘When a favor has been done, one must repay it; this is the eternal dharma. This is a description of the authoritative status of the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa*. This [verse] is enlivened by paronomasia (*śleṣa*), whereas the preceding one was intermingled with metaphor (*rūpaka*).

Just as, although you are omniscient, you nevertheless perceive the faults of those who offer devotion; thus, the best of sages recite "the one who does not know" (*avijñāta*) among your thousand names. (2059)

In this regard, as proof for the determination that even the omniscient Śrīnivāsa does not perceive the faults of his devotees, the statement from the *Sahasranāma* hymn within the *Śrī Bhārata*, "The thousand-rayed one is unperceived," has been set forth.

O Vāsudeva, how could loss have befallen even one who maintains meditation upon You, given that the authority of the Purāṇas and the Śabda-pramāṇa has declared: "That loss occurs if You are not meditated upon for even a single moment"? (2060)

O King! O Mādhava! O Vāsudeva! Even for one who is a "bearer of meditation upon You" (*tvaddhyānabhṛt*)—that is, even for one who contemplates You incessantly—how has loss, the loss of what is desired, come to pass? This is the sense: it is a matter of wonder. To the question of how such a loss could possibly occur, he says: "It is said...
"That moment, or even that instant, during which Vāsudeva is not meditated upon—that is a loss; that is a great void; that is delusion; and that is a calamity. (Bhagavadgītā 1.19)

Thus [ends] the Purāṇa. As for the statement that "you (bhavān) are not to be thought of even for a moment (kṣaṇam api)," meaning even for an extremely short time—that is what constitutes a loss (hāniḥ). But the resolution is as follows: in the first half-verse, the word division is *hā niḥsamāṃ janim āpa*. A person filled with meditation on you (*tvad-dhyānena bhṛtaḥ*)—the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the object of the root *bhṛ* (to fill)—attains a birth (*janim*) that is "without equal" (*niḥsamām*), meaning peerless. The intended meaning is that this birth consists in being a knower of the science of Brahman (*brahma-vidyā-vettṛtva-rūpam*), according to the scriptural dictum: "For he indeed brings him forth from knowledge; that is the best of births. Alternatively, having begun with the words "devoted to the conduct of caste and stage of life" (*varṇāśramācāra-paraḥ*).
By that great merit, he shall attain the status of a Vaiṣṇava;
likewise, for seven births, that man shall be devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu.
A Brahmin who sacrifices solely for the Blessed One within the lineage of the Bhāgavatas then obtains a birth that is extremely difficult even for the gods to attain.

Thus, the meaning is that he attained a birth that is transcendent (lokottara), as stated in the *Vārāha-purāṇa*. He "attained" (āpa) it. The use of the past tense (bhūtanirdeśa) is treated as an established fact (*siddhavatkāreṇa*), in order to illuminate that his attainment was indeed beyond doubt, according to the manner expressed in the passage: "The illustrious Grandfather declared, 'The task is accomplished. The exclamation "Hā! expresses wonder. Here, there is an illustration of the authority of the word (*śabda-pramāṇa*) in the form of the Purāṇa cited above, which serves to determine the impossibility of the loss of the Lord’s contemplator—the very thing intended by the author—by means of a superimposition (*abhedādhyavasāya*) based on a foundation of double entendre (*śleṣa*).

The authority of words according to grammar is as follows: "O Lord, by the word *san* (being) being joined with *mahat* (great), there would be a state of preeminence in its totality; this is what the *sanmahat* rule declares. (2061)

O Deva! [This was said] by you, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who are worthy of worship, and therefore supreme and most excellent, to a certain knower of Brahman who is likewise great, worthy of worship, and a person of excellence.

"By you" means when there is totality—that is, when there is completeness or connection. "Preeminence" (agryatva) would mean being counted as foremost among all the worlds. "This"—meaning this action—is stated by the *sūtra* "sanmahat" (Pāṇini 2.1.61) as the agent. It says, it declares; that is to say, the aforementioned *sūtra* expresses this meaning. In the case of the *sūtra*, when there is totality—that is, when there is a compound (*samāsa*)—of the word "mahat" (great) with the word "sat" (being), which is being honored by the word "puruṣa" (person).

The meaning is that there would be the requirement of being placed first (pūrvaprayojyatva). According to the rule *sanmahatparamottamotkṛṣṭāḥ pūjyamānaiḥ*, which prescribes the formation of a compound with words such as *sat* and others when they are joined with words denoting those who are honored, these [words] receive the technical designation *upasarjana* by the rule *prathamānirdiṣṭaṃ samāsa upasarjanam*. Consequently, by the rule *upasarjanaṃ pūrvam*, the meaning is that they would have to be placed at the beginning [of the compound].

In this context, regarding the determination that the intended knower of Brahman is to be reckoned as foremost among all the worlds by virtue of his connection with the Blessed One, the word in the form of a Pāṇinian sūtra was brought to the status of a valid authority through an identification based on the established foundation of *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

Or, for example, in the battle at the abduction of Pārijāta, Maghavat was greatly exhausted by you, O Hari; even today he is still "Maghavān"—the rule *bahulam* (in various ways) is the authority here. 1062.

O hare! Maghavā Indra was defeated by you at the forefront of the battle for the Pārijāta tree; for this very reason, even today he remains frequently and excessively exhausted and weary. Regarding this matter, the rule *maghavā bahulam* is the authority. The meaning is that the stated rule is the proof for Maghavat’s frequent state of exhaustion even today. The sense is that since the substitution of *tṛc* for the end of the word *maghavan* is prescribed "frequently" (*bahulam*) by the aforementioned rule, that rule serves as the authority for its frequent occurrence in the form ending in *tānta*.

In this context, for the purpose of establishing the meaning thus established, there is a demonstration of the authority of the aforementioned sūtra by means of support from a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) rooted in the identity between word and meaning.
Or rather, if there were a desire to create the world, then repetition would not be required here; for this very reason, O Acyuta, Pāṇini has prescribed the elision of repetition in this case. (2063)

"O Acyuta!"—the sense is: "of you, the sole cause of the universe. If there were a desire to create (*nirmitsā*), that is, a wish to bring forth, then this world (*jagat*) would have already existed, being fully accomplished; there would not be even a moment's delay in its production. This is based on the scriptural statement: "The creation of the Lord is merely His will. Here, repetition (*abhyāsa*) or frequency in the desire to create is not intended. The sense is that since the creation of the world occurs from the mere flash of a single desire, such repetition is not required.
