Therefore, because repetition is not required for the desire to create (*nirmitsā*), Pāṇini states—in this context of the sense "to split" (*nirbhitsā*), and optionally regarding the word *nirmitsā* itself—the elision (*lopa*) of repetition, that is, its non-appearance (*adarśana*), elsewhere [as] reduplication (*dvirvacana*). The point is that since the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is prescribed by the rule "In this case, there is elision of the reduplicated syllable" (*atra lopo'bhyāsasya*), which applies to what was stated starting from "In the case of *san*, for *mī* and *mā*" (*sani mī mā*) following the root *mā* preceded by the prefix *nir*.

In this context, regarding the matter that the Blessed One’s creation of the world does not depend upon the practice of volition, the *Pāṇini-sūtra* has been cited as authoritative, as previously, by relying on a hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) based on paronomasia (*śleṣa*).

Just as [the word] *samrāṭ* becomes *sama*, so too does *puruṣatvam* belong to that very same [word]; for the Sage has stated in the sūtra, "When *mo* follows *rāji*, it becomes *samaḥ* before the locative suffix *kvau*," [and the root *vraśc* undergoes substitution by *bhrasj*]. (2064)

One who exists together with Śrī is *samaḥ*; he alone, being possessed of *lakṣmī*, becomes the sovereign emperor (*samrāṭ*), the Lord of the Universe. This is known from such scriptural and traditional texts as: "This is the world of Brahman, O Emperor; the king, the supreme ruler, Viṣṇu, the great one consisting of Brahman," and from the *Ācārya-Śrīsūkta*: "The imperial sovereignty of one possessed of *lakṣmī* is well-established in every way. The sense is that the imperial sovereignty of those devoid of *lakṣmī* can never come to pass.

That very Being, together with Lakṣmī, possesses both manhood (*puruṣatva*) and the status of being denoted by the word "Puruṣa"—which, according to the *Nirukta*, reveals His causality of all things and His immanence in all—as expressed in the passage, "I was here before; that is the Puruṣa's manhood. This is because He is the husband of Lakṣmī, as stated in "Hrī and Lakṣmī are Your two wives," and because His manhood is heard of in the scriptural text, "I know this great Puruṣa."

Thus, having established his intended meaning through the authority of the Vedas (*śruti*), he also validates the traditional rule (*smṛti*) of Pāṇini’s sūtras by means of a pun, using the word *yat*. The meaning of the first half-verse is as follows: because the word *samrāṭ* would indeed contain the letter *m*—that is, it would be *sama* [ending] with *m*—since, according to the rule "mo rāji samaḥ kvau," when the suffix *kvip* is applied, and the root *rāj* follows, the *m* of *sama* is prescribed to remain as *m*. It does not, however, contain the *anusvāra* prescribed by the rule "mo'nusvāraḥ."

The word *samrāṭ* itself is derived from *puru*, meaning "most abundant" (*bhūyiṣṭha*)—as Amara states: "*puru-bhūḥ* means most abundant. The change to *ṣ* occurs according to the rule "*vraśca-bhrasja-sṛja-mṛja-yaja-rāja-bhrāja-cha-śāṃ ṣaḥ*," whereby the sound replaces the position of the *j* (jaśtva). The sense is that the word *samrāṭ* is thus produced through the aforementioned grammatical process.

Or rather, the suffix *cha* would apply here according to the rule for words ending in *vṛddhi*, and there is no doubt about this; for the Blessed Pāṇini indeed remembered this meaning, O crest-jewel of the Śeṣa mountain. (2065)

O crest-jewel of the Śeṣa mountain! He becomes yours—meaning, he belongs to you—being "aged" (vṛddhaḥ), that is, fully matured; "clear" (acchaḥ), meaning pure because it is uninterrupted by heterogeneous cognitions, like a continuous stream of oil; and whose cognition consists of meditation upon You. As it has been said: "For I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge, and he is dear to Me."

The sense is that, by this manner [of devotion], one would become an object of your unsurpassed affection; of this there is no doubt. Alternatively, the term *vṛddhācchapratyayaḥ* means one whose conviction (*pratyaya*)—that is, trust—is "grown" (*vṛddha*, i.e., increased) and "clear" (*accha*, i.e., pure) because it is far removed from even a scent of connection with other deities; thus, he is one possessed of great faith. The phrase *tvadīyaḥ pumān vṛddhācchapratyayaḥ* should be construed by repeating [the latter part]: "a person belonging to you, having sole refuge in you, is one whose conviction is grown and clear. Such a person possesses fully developed, stainless knowledge, as it is said: "The seer sees everything."

The meaning is that, according to the stated principle "and he is fit for infinity," one becomes possessed of eternal and uncontracted knowledge. The underlying sense is that by performing the surrender of the burden of self-protection—characterized by great faith in You—one becomes liberated. Herein lies the distinction: in the first sense, there is *upāsanā* (meditative worship), while in the second, there is *nyāsa* (surrender).

The word "anyatra" (elsewhere) is to be construed with the locative ending as "anyatra vṛddhācchapratyaye" (except when the suffix *cha* follows a *vṛddha* [stem]). This should be applied by way of repetition (*āvṛtti*) as follows: when the suffix *cha* is applied according to the rule "vṛddhācchaḥ," the form "tvadīya" is produced. The meaning is that since the word *yuṣmad* is designated as *vṛddha* by the rule "tyadādīni ca," the suffix *cha* is prescribed by the rule "vṛddhācchaḥ," whereby the form "tvadīya" is established. The second half of the verse is easy to understand. Here, the authority of Pāṇini’s traditional teaching (*smṛti*) is introduced as proof for the point he intends to establish.

Just as this word *śrī* assumes the designation *ajādi* (beginning with a vowel) even when followed by a nominal suffix (*sup*), so too does it become devoid of its *il* [augment] in this context; the word of the Sage of Grammarians (*Śābdika-muni*) is the authority for this meaning. (2066)

O Śrī! You who have approached Ilā—that is, you who have come near and taken refuge with Bhūdevī (the Earth-goddess)—for the sense is that Bhūdevī is heard to have Śrī as her friend, as in the phrase "the dear friend of Lakṣmī. You, this highly renowned lady, are present in Ājādyā—the first-born, such as Brahmā—who is the cause even of the four-faced one; or rather, this is an epithet of the Supreme Self alone. In the term *supratyaye*, *sup* refers to auspicious knowledge (*suprajñāna*), while *pratyaya* is an elliptical expression for the sixfold divine attributes (*ṣāḍguṇya*) such as power (*śakti*), strength (*bala*), and so forth, including perfect knowledge and the rest.

This is the meaning. *Para* refers to the Blessed One as well; according to the *Viśvakośa*, "the word *para* denotes both 'enemy' and 'Supreme Self'. He "bears" (dhatte)—that is, nourishes—his "command" (*ādeśa*), his teaching. This is because of such statements as: "The entire world, both mobile and immobile, rests upon His sidelong glance; the movements of His eyebrows constitute the very life-force in the varying gradations of the arrangement of all stable and moving things, O Murāri."

In the alternative view (*pakṣe*), when the word *śrī*—that is, the word *śrī*—is followed by a *sup* suffix beginning with a vowel (such as *au*, *jas*, etc., which are members of the *sup*-pratyāhāra), the word takes the substitute *iy*. The particle *api* is displaced and connects with the subsequent clause. It undergoes the substitution *iy* (the form *iy*). The analysis is: "even though it has reached the elision of *ī*" (*īlopagatā*). Although it has reached (*gatā*) the elision of *ī* (*īlopa*), meaning the non-appearance of the vowel *ī*; the particle *api* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*). The verb *bhavati* is derived from the root *bhū* in the present tense (*laṭ*).

In this matter, the word of the sage Pāṇini, the grammarian, is the authority. The sense is that when the word *śrī* is followed by a case-ending beginning with a vowel (such as the nominative singular), the rule "aci śnudhātubhruvāṃ yvoriyaṅuvaṅau" prescribes the substitution of *iyaṅ* for the *y* [of *śri-yaḥ*]. Because this *iyaṅ* is marked with the *ṅ*-sign (*ṅit*), the rule "ṅicca" dictates that the substitute takes the place of the final letter, which is the vowel *ī*. Thus, the *ī* disappears because it is superseded by *iyaṅ*. Here too, the statement of Pāṇini is presented as an authority through a superimposition of identity based on the established pun (*śleṣa*), in order to support the intended meaning—namely, the state of being devoted to Śrī—which is established by the Veda and other sources.

Just as Viṣṇu, whose body comprises the three worlds, eternally abides with Śrī in the supreme state, so too is that [compound] most appropriate for the *tatpuruṣa* when the latter member is a word expressing eternal union (*nityasamāsa*). (2067)

"Trilokatanuḥ" means having the three worlds as his body, that is, having the entire universe as his body, based on such scriptural authority as: "The entire world is your body. Regarding the term *triloka*, since the rule "In the case of a direction or a number, when forming a proper name" would otherwise apply for compounding, the compound is formed by the rule: "In the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), with a subsequent member, or in a collective (*samāhāra*). Having first formed a three-word *bahuvrīhi*—"one whose body (*tanu*) consists of the three worlds (*trayo lokāḥ*)"—there is then a *tatpuruṣa* of the two preceding members [to form *triloka*] when the word *tanu* stands as the subsequent member. In this context, the intermediate *tatpuruṣa*...

Since an option would otherwise have arisen, the compound is a mandatory (nitya) *tatpuruṣa* according to the rule: "In the case of a *dvandva* or a *tatpuruṣa*, when there is a final member [of the compound], it is stated that the compound is mandatory. Viṣṇu, the Blessed One, is together with Śrī, Lakṣmī; because of the grammatical usage "an elder [is compounded] with a youth," the third case ending is used even without the employment of the word *saha*. He dwells—that is, he sits—in the supreme abode, Vaikuṇṭha, which is possessed of Śrī. Therefore, "that person" (*tatpuruṣa*) means that very Person previously mentioned, the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*).

In the northern, most excellent station or place, he always dwells together with Śrī; thus, *sama* means "seated" (*āsa*), derived from the root *ās* with the suffix *ghañ*. Alternatively, it means "always seated" (*nityasamam*) in whatever manner. His speech—his utterance regarding her cohabitation with Lakṣmī—is most appropriate. In the alternative sense, according to the method established, the statement that a *tatpuruṣa* compound is necessarily formed when followed by a subsequent word (*uttarapada*) is highly appropriate. Herein: "In the supreme world of Vaikuṇṭha, the Lord of the Universe dwells together with Śrī."

In accordance with the statement, "Viṣṇu, whose nature is inconceivable, abides," the propriety [of the meaning] established by himself is supported through a hyperbole (atiśayokti) based on a pun (śleṣa), and by citing as an authority the grammatical vārtika stated as "in the case of dvandva and tatpuruṣa compounds."
Or for example:

"That very one who quickly intoxicates the person who serves her is the beloved of Hari; she is also called 'Suva-cā' (well-spoken) and 'Hali-priyā' (beloved of the elephant), for the learned accept the identity between the letters *ra* and *la*. (2068)

She who is beloved by Hari gladdens—making one joyful (*harṣavant*) and intoxicated (*madavant*)—himself, his own servant, who worships her and tastes [her favor]; for Amara states, "In the sense of joy, *mada* is like *āmoda*. She is also appropriately called *Halipriyā* (beloved of Hali), since Hari and Hali are non-different; *Hali* refers to Balabhadra. Alternatively, by the very reason established, she may also be called *Halipriyā* as Kādambarī; for Amara states, "Wine is *halipriyā*."

He further supports the point already established by the maxim of "driving in a pillar" (sthūṇānikhananyāya) with the verse beginning *ralayoḥ*. For (*hi*) the non-distinction (*abhidā*), that is, the identity (*abheda*), between the two phonemes *r* and *l* is accepted by the learned grammarians (*viduṣām vaiyākaraṇānām*).

Therefore, the sense is that the word *haripriyā* can also be easily explained as *halipriyā*. One must not forget the identity between word and meaning (*śabdārthatādātmya*). Here, the statement of the grammarian serves as the authoritative proof (*pramāṇatā*) for determining that the beloved of Hari is indeed the beloved of the plowman (*halipriyā*), which was his intended meaning.

Just as that one Brahman is ageless, we know no other deity that is ageless; for the Sage declared that even though all [beings] beginning with Brahmā are ageless, they nevertheless undergo transformation through aging. (2069)

That Brahman is indeed one, undecaying (*ajara*), being devoid of all modifications characterized by decay, according to such scriptural passages as, "It is free from old age and death," and "That which is peaceful, undecaying, the supreme Brahman. We do not know any other deity to be undecaying, because every other deity is subject to old age, death, and so forth. For this reason, the sage Pāṇini stated that even in the case of the entire group of undecaying deities beginning with Brahmā (the four-faced one), there is modification through old age. Alternatively, the particle *hi* is used in the sense of what is well-known.

In the alternative view (*pakṣe*), even when the word *nirjara*—meaning "one free from old age"—is a compound (*samasta*) and has attained the status of a compound, [the author] states its transformation by means of the substitution *jaras* prescribed by the rule *jarāyā jaras anyatarasyām* when followed by a case-ending beginning with a vowel (*ajādi*). The expression "even when it is a compound" is stated for the purpose of making known the principle: "In matters concerning words or their constituent parts (*padāṅga-adhikāre*), [an operation applies] to that [word] and to what ends in it. Here, the statement of the grammarians (*śābdika*) serves as the authority for determining that [the Lord] is not subject to the decay of old age, as he is distinct from other deities.

O Supreme Self, generally the characteristic of those who have attained You belongs to You alone; for the Lord of Sages, the Grammarian, declared that the gender of a Tatpuruṣa compound follows that of the final member. (2070)

O Supreme Self! For those who have attained You—that is, for the liberated—Your mark, such as having four arms and so forth, generally manifests. By the word "generally," it is indicated that attributes such as being the cause of the universe or being the Lord of Śrī are excluded. For indeed, the great grammarian Pāṇini stated: "The compound [tatpuruṣa] takes the gender of the other [the final member]," meaning that for such a person of Yours—the liberated one—the mark or sign becomes like that of the Supreme Self (para). In reality, however, by the rule "the gender of a dvandva and a tatpuruṣa is that of the final member," he stated that the gender of a *tatpuruṣa* compound is determined solely by its final member.

Here, regarding the attainment of the marks of the Lord by the liberated devotees (bhāgavatas) as intended by [the author], Pāṇini’s sūtra has been cited as authoritative by resorting to paronomasia (śleṣa).

Indeed, since the entire universe has its single abode in Him, what else could there be besides that Supreme Person? The seer who knows the meaning of words clearly stated in the *Viśvambhara* [Upaniṣad] that [the universe] is attached to the Mother (Umā). (2071)

In whom indeed—this entire universe, this whole world—is contained; that is to say, in whom alone [it resides]. The word *nanu* is used here for emphasis. "Having a single nest" (*ekanīḍam*) means having an undivided location; the sense is that they share a common substratum (*aikādhikaraṇya*). Is he other than Puruṣottama—that is, other than Nārāyaṇa, who is distinct from the inner self (*pratyagātman*) in its three states of bound, liberated, and both? What could he possibly be? The word *kim* is used here in a derogatory sense (to imply impossibility). The meaning is: he can never be anything else. By the construction of the words "in whom the universe has a single nest," [it is shown that] "where... [the rest follows].

The Śruti text, “the universe has its single nest,” is thus made known through recognition. This traditional authority (āgama) present in the intellect—the Śruti cited as beginning with “wherein the universe”—is fixed upon and devoted to Viśvambhara Nārāyaṇa himself. The word *śabdavit* here refers to one who knows the Veda; for the term *śabda* in this context signifies the Veda, as in passages such as “and because of the [Vedic] word regarding the non-performance of what is desired. This is the meaning of “knower of the Veda” (*vedavit*), based on the statement: “I am indeed the knower of Vedānta and the knower of the Veda.”

The meaning is that the *ṛṣi* who has descended as Vāsudeva is Nārāyaṇa, the ascetic of Badarikāśrama. Furthermore, the word *ṛṣi* is heard as a designation for the Blessed Lord in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*: "Faithfully sacrificing to the one *ṛṣi* themselves... This is explained in the *Upaniṣadbhāṣya* as: "'The one *ṛṣi*' means the principal *ṛṣi*, the Supreme Self. The scriptural passage, "Who are those *ṛṣis*? The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) indeed are the *ṛṣis*," is also favorable here. That the word *ṛṣi*, though ending in the plural form *ṛṣayaḥ*, refers to the Supreme Self was stated in the *Prāṇādhikaraṇa*. [The term] *āha* means "he speaks."
There are these two persons in the world: the perishable and the imperishable.
All beings are the perishable; the one who stands at the peak (the immutable) is called the imperishable.
But there is another, the Supreme Person, who is declared to be the Supreme Self;
the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them.
Since I have transcended the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable,
therefore I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).

Thus, by the phrase "the Blessed Lord sustains," the meaning is that he declares the Śruti passage, "Wherein the universe becomes a single nest," to have Nārāyaṇa alone as its ultimate referent. For likewise, in this very commentary (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), by the statement "designated as the Supreme Self," the Śruti passage, "In the middle of that crest the Supreme Self is established," is recalled. And by the phrase "He who, having entered the three worlds," the passage beginning with "Whatever there is" is explained.

"That which is perceived is the world (*loka*); these three constitute the triple-world (*triloka*). They are: the insentient, the sentient conjoined with it, and the liberated [sentient]. These three, which are known through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), He who, having entered them as their very Self, sustains—He is therefore distinct from that which pervades and that which is to be sustained. Thus says the *Śrīmad-Gītā-Bhāṣya*. By the statement "He sustains," which expresses His nature as the substratum (*ādhāratva*), the meaning of such passages as "That wherein the universe has its single nest; that which is the desirable glory of the Sun; the firm, immovable, immortal abode named Viṣṇu, the support of all"—is explained.

By the mention of the word "immutable" (*avyaya*), there is a summary of what was stated in passages such as "eternal, auspicious, and infallible. Here, the word "Lord" (*īśvara*) intends both the quality of being characterized by the governance of all things—following from the pervasion mentioned in "Nārāyaṇa stands pervading [all]" and "He has entered within as the Ruler"—and the state of not being governed by another, as expressed in "the Self, the Lord. Thus, regarding the question "Who is the Supreme Person? the *Śrīmat Stotrabhāṣya* provides the answer.
Therefore, it is well said that the Teacher of the Gītā declares the Śruti passage, "Where the universe becomes a single nest," to refer to Nārāyaṇa, who is none other than Himself.

However, the seer Pāṇini, an expert in words and grammar, clearly stated the addition of the augment *mum*—that is, the augment consisting of the letter *m*—to the word *viśvaṃbhara*, by means of the rule beginning with "In the sense of a name, after [roots] *bhṛ*, *vṛ*, and *vṛj*," etc.; for he applied the *mum* augment to the root *bhṛ* when preceded by the word *viśva* in the *khac* suffix, according to the rule "The augment *mum* is added to [a word] ending in *ar*, *dviṣat*, or a short vowel."

In this instance, the distinction from the previous examples is that, in order to determine that the status of being the substratum of the entire universe—proclaimed by such scriptural passages as "Wherein the universe [rests]"—resides exclusively in Puruṣottama alone, both the Smṛti passage beginning with "He who, having entered the three worlds," which is favored by the author himself, and the Vyākaraṇa Smṛti (grammatical authority) cited through the identification based on the foundation of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), are presented as authoritative evidence.

Furthermore: "He who knows Brahman as non-existent, the dull-witted, they indeed call him non-existent. Let scripture remain the authority here; for is it not the case that the Sūtra states, "The eternal is not capable [of being perceived]? (2072)

The one who is "of dull intellect" (*durmedhāḥ*) is he who knows that Brahman is "non-existent" (*asat*); the meaning is that he does not know that it "exists" (*sat*). Here, the particle *a-* is an indeclinable having the same sense as the negative particle *na*, according to the Amarakośa’s list of indeclinables: "*na*, *ahi*, *anaḥ*, and *nāpi* [are used] in the sense of non-existence. Alternatively, the word *asat* may be taken as a compound, to be construed exactly as heard; the meaning is: "he who knows that Brahman does not exist. The rest is the same.

Regarding this, the first interpretation is in accordance with the purport of the Śrībhāṣya as situated within the Great Siddhānta, which describes the meaning of the scriptural text "He becomes non-existent indeed" as stating that through the presence or absence of knowledge whose object is Brahman, one speaks of the destruction of the self or the existence of the self. The second, however, is in accordance with the commentary on the Upaniṣad (the Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣya), which describes the meaning of the present scriptural passage as: "Liberation and transmigratory existence result from the knowledge of the existence or non-existence of the one consisting of bliss."

They say that he who is dull-witted and evil-minded is [referred to by] the word *durmedhaḥ*; and they say that the word *asan* means only "non-existent" or "unrighteous," with the letter *as* being merely the final syllable. In this regard, let the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) serve as our authority (*mānam*): "He becomes non-existent indeed, if he knows Brahman as non-existent. This is the scriptural proof.

The name [is justified]. For there is the sūtra *nityamasic* (Pāṇini 5.4.122); the word *hi* is used for emphasis. The meaning is that it is precisely the sūtra *nityamasic prajāmedhayoḥ*. Is it not sufficient? Is it not adequate? The implication is: "Since this alone suffices for the derivation, why pursue the matter all the way to the Veda? This is the actual state of affairs, because by the aforementioned sūtra, the suffix *as* is prescribed as a compound-final affix (*samāsāntapratyaya*) for the word *medhā* when preceded by the prefix *dur-* in a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

Here too, for the purpose of establishing the stated meaning, the means of valid cognition consisting of the recollection of words—which is enlivened by the identification based on the wall of *śleṣa* (punning) with the notion that [the object] is non-existent—is employed alongside the means of valid cognition consisting of direct audition (*śruti*).

Just as you are omniscient by means of that [knowledge], there exists a very great power within that awakening (*bodha*). O Blessed One, let there be no quality in any other quality; however, that [power] does exist in awakening, according to the principle of verbal expression (*śabdanaya*). (2073)

The Blessed One is fully endowed with the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and other qualities; thus, O Blessed One, by that quality of awakening (*bodha-guṇa*), which is the foremost of the six divine attributes (*ṣāḍguṇya*), you are "all-knowing" (*sarvavit*). According to the scriptural expression, "He who is all-knowing is all-perceiving," your status as the omniscient one arises precisely from possessing an eternally uncontracted awakening. Within that awakening—knowledge consisting of the direct perception of everything—there exists a very great power (*śakti*), which is a specific attribute included among the six divine attributes.

And that [cognition], which appears as if unaccomplished because it cannot be achieved by others, consists in the capacity to effect such an accomplishment. Its true nature, however, is the capacity for the realization of omniscience. It "exists" or "is present. According to the principle stated in the scripture, "His supreme power," since your own omniscience has been brought to fulfillment by this [cognition], the sense is that there exists a power even greater than yours within this awakening. Now, one might object: how can this statement be consistent, given that a quality is not admitted to reside in another quality?

Since both [the qualities] are indeed powers of cognition (*bodha*), he says "let it not be. The sense is: let there be no other quality in a quality other than cognition, or rather, let it be or not; however, in cognition—that is, in the quality whose nature is cognition—there exists that quality consisting of the aforementioned power. To the question, "What is the proof for such a determination? he replies, "From the perspective of the *śabdanaya*. The sense is that the existence of the quality in cognition is stated according to the system of grammar (*vyākaraṇanaya*). In that view, since the word *bodha* is derived from the root *budh* with the suffix *ghañ*, the rule "apugantalaghūpadhasya ca" prescribes the presence of the *guṇa* (vowel strengthening), and thus the quality exists.

In this context, regarding the presence of the quality of "possessing great power" within the quality of "the nature of consciousness" intended by the author himself, the authority of the grammatical procedure is established through an identification based on the pun inherent in the word *śakti*, which conveys both qualities.

Just as the radiance of your limbs, O Lotus-like One, surpasses the beauty of the color of gold, so too does the multitude of grammarians declare that "a suffix is stronger than its constituent phoneme" (*vārṇād āṅgaṃ balīyaḥ*). 2074.

The distinction here is that, while asserting the greater strength of the operation pertaining to the *aṅga* over the operation pertaining to the phoneme (*varṇa*), the *paribhāṣā* "an operation pertaining to the *aṅga* [prevails] over one pertaining to a phoneme" (*vārṇād āṅgam*) is presented as an authority for its intended meaning by means of an identification based on the conflation of the two meanings conveyed by the words *aṅga* and *varṇa*.

O Acyuta, just as that which is internal (*antaraṅga*) always subverts what is external even when it serves its own purpose, so too has the Muni of Grammar declared that which is internal is stronger than even that which is eternal (*nitya*). (2075)

O Acyuta! You are eternal, according to the Vedic revelation: "The eternal among the eternals. And you are supreme, according to the Vedic revelation: "The highest among the high. My *antaraṅga*—that is, my internal organ, the mind—acting as the agent, obstructs or afflicts you (meaning it causes you pain) regarding its own purpose (*svārtha*), that is, its desired objective. The underlying sentiment is: "Surely the world, intent on its own self-interest, does not know the distress of another. In another sense, the *para* (supreme) and *nitya* (eternal) scripture (*śāstra*)—specifically the *antaraṅga-śāstra* acting as the agent—obstructs you regarding its own purpose; the meaning is that it becomes an obstacle to your activity. He cites the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) of the Grammarians as authority for his own stated point with the words "the Grammarian" (*śābdika*). The meaning is that the Sage of the Grammarians, Patañjali, states that an *antaraṅga* [rule] possesses greater force even than a subsequent (*para*) or obligatory (*nitya*) [rule], based on the technical rule: "Among subsequent, obligatory, *antaraṅga*, and exceptional (*apavāda*) rules, each succeeding one is stronger."

Or rather, O Acyuta, by your grace, my sin—which is now on the verge of being destroyed—may I not commit it even while under its influence; for those who have not mastered the grammatical system would surely be like followers of Pāṇini [who still make errors].

O Acyuta! By Your grace, all my karma is on the verge of destruction; for that reason, even though I am subject to it—though under the sway of karma—I shall not commit further sin (agham). For the followers of Pāṇini do not perform an operation when the cause [of its application] is seen to be on the verge of destruction, because of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating, "The followers of Pāṇini do not perform an operation when the cause is on the verge of destruction" (*akṛtavyūhāḥ pāṇinīyāḥ*). This is the meaning of the rule: "Having perceived that the cause is about to perish, they do not carry out the effect produced by it."

In this context, by taking recourse to a Pāṇinian paribhāṣā regarding the non-performance of subsequent sins prompted by an action that is on the verge of destruction, the poet’s mastery of Pāṇini’s grammar is also revealed.

Alternatively, O Blessed One, how could those with whom you have a connection possess similarity to yourself? For here, those who know words say that dissimilarity is not produced by mere connection. (2077)

O Blessed One! For those people who have a continuous connection or relationship with You—the meaning being that they attain the state of being a *bhāgavata*—or rather, the meaning being that they achieve union in the supreme ether (*parame vyoman*) preceded by the complete cessation of ignorance; for such people, how could there be a lack of similarity to You (*asārūpyam*), that is, a dissimilarity to Your form? Since they are accepted by You as Your own remains (*śeṣatvena parigṛhītānām*) and meditate upon You alone, they will certainly possess similarity to You, such as having four arms and so forth. Just as:

The sense is that this is due to the guidance of grammatical rules (*kratunaya*). Here, the scriptural passage, "The stainless one attains supreme equality" (*nirañjanaḥ paramaṃ sāmyamupaiti*), should be kept in mind. For this reason, those who know words—experts in grammar—state that the lack of similarity (*asārūpya*) caused by an *anubandha* (such as the letter *ṇ*, which serves the purpose of technical designation [*itsaṃjñā*] in rules like *ṛhalorṇyat*) does not result in a lack of similarity for the suffix *ya* prescribed by rules such as *poradupadhāt*; this is because of the metarule (*paribhāṣā*) stating, "A lack of similarity is not caused by an *anubandha*. This is the underlying intention.

Thus, in examples such as *śapyam* and *labhyam*, the suffix *yat* prescribed by the rule *poradupadhāt* serves as an absolute sublater (*bādhaka*) of the suffix *ṇyat* prescribed by the rule *ṛhalorṇyat*. It should be noted, however, that it does not acquire an optional status of sublation based on dissimilarity (*asārūpya*) according to the rule *vā sarūpo'striyām*.

Here, despite the existence of hundreds of authorities in the form of Śruti and Smṛti, another meaning is constructed through a pun upon the grammatical maxim (*paribhāṣā*) *nānubandhakṛtamasārūpyam* (dissimilarity is not caused by an indicatory letter), and this is employed for the sake of producing an excellence of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*).

O Murāri, one who speaks of you and another as being equally supreme and inferior does not commit an offense, for Pāṇini stated in the *Pūrvāparāvara-sūtra* that the terms "para" and "avara" are synonymous.

The citation of the Pāṇinian smṛti—“*pūrvāparāvaradakṣiṇottara...*”—is presented as an authority for the point that there is no fault in speaking of you, who are supreme, as being equal to another deity who is inferior to you. In the previous examples, the Pāṇinian smṛti was established as an authority for the intended meaning; here, however, [the following is cited]:
“But he who regards the Lord Nārāyaṇa as merely ordinary goes to a terrible hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.”
He who regards the god Nārāyaṇa as being equal to deities such as Brahmā and Rudra is called a heretic.

Thus, according to the manner stated above, there is a distinct difference [in this work], as it has been taken as authoritative for an unintended meaning—one that is intent upon censuring people by describing the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa as being on an equal footing with other deities.

Just as that imperishable state of Viṣṇu is traditionally taught to be imperishable, yet begins with a vowel; so it being the case, how did Pāṇini declare the word *svarādi* (beginning with a vowel) to be an indeclinable (*avyaya*)? 2079.

That station of Viṣṇu—the place traditionally known as "that supreme station of Viṣṇu"—is imperishable and undecaying, as established by such scriptural passages as "in that imperishable, supreme heaven. However, the station or place beginning with heaven (svarādyam), such as the celestial realm and so forth, is not imperishable; thus it is traditionally known as non-imperishable (anavyayam), meaning it is perishable.

This being so, and this being the case, how did Pāṇini declare—in the rule "svarādinipātamavyayam"—that a word such as *svarga* (heaven) and the like belongs to the *svarādi* group, and that such a word is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), meaning it is imperishable (*anaśvara*) and designated as an indeclinable? This is the intended meaning.

"O Lord, how could there be a fall for you who possess such sovereignty? Or where, by whom, has such a thing ever been seen?"—while this was being said, Pāṇini uttered the term *nipāta* (particle); thus arose the reflection: "How indeed [is this]? (2080).

O Master, O Lord of All! Regarding sovereignty—that state of being the Lord of the Universe—has the fall, the ruin, of Your supreme majesty ever been seen by any person anywhere? It has not been seen, for Your supreme sovereignty has been heard in the scripture: "He is the Lord of all; He is the sovereign of all beings."

The meaning is "thus. This being the case regarding the nature of reality, and this being the state of affairs, Pāṇini—[referring to] you who possess such sovereignty (or, in the alternative sense, [referring to] the word *svāmin* itself)—how indeed could he have uttered the *nipāta* (irregular form) *svāmin*, given that there is no etymological derivation (*lakṣaṇā*) for the meaning of sovereignty? The point is that, according to the rule *svāminnaiśvarye*, the word *svāmin* is established as an irregular form (*nipātita*) specifically for the sense of sovereignty; therefore, how could he have used it merely for the sake of phonetic correctness (*śabdasādhutva*) when its conventional meaning was absent? Such is our reflection.
Just as the first Person beheld all names and forms on every side, so the Śruti declares; how then does the sage Pāṇini state that same thing only in certain instances? (2081)

The Śruti says: "Entering by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), let me manifest names and forms. This Śruti [indicates] that the first person—the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) who is the Supreme Brahman—manifests all names and forms everywhere; that is, the collection of both the name and the form of all things. Elsewhere, the word "first" (prathamaḥ)—referring to the masculine gender—is used in all case-endings (vibhaktiḥ) which serve as the locus for the functions associated with the status of a pronoun (sarvanāmatā); thus, it refers to the form of the pronoun-word itself.

"He revealed" means he made manifest; thus he says. But it is a matter of wonder how the sage Pāṇini stated that this manifestation of all names and forms by that first Person occurs only "somewhere," that is, in only one part [of grammar]. This objection—that the neuter pronoun *tad* (this) refers to the entire manifestation—is resolved by the fact that he declared the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*) for the masculine word *prathama* (first) only in the case of the nominative plural (*jas*), according to the rule: "The words *prathama*, *carama*, *tayaP*, *alpa*, *ardha*, *katipaya*, and *nema* are also [pronouns]. Thus, the objection is answered.

In these three verses, the specific point is that the jester, having imagined through punning (*śleṣa*) that the Sūtra is intended to reveal a meaning contrary to its universally accepted sense, presents it as an authority for the purpose of censuring its author by means of identifying the two as non-different.

O Lord of the Serpents and Leader of the Mountain, how can those learned in the scriptures speak of a violation of policy (*naya*) on Your part when You, who delight in the straight path of upholding the Vedas—the subject matter of all principles—adopt the form of the fish? (2082)

O Lord of the Mountain (Śiva), who is like the king of serpents! Since You took delight in the recovery—that is, the preservation—of the *Nigama*, the Veda, which is the subject matter of all systems of thought (*naya*) and the principles of Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya, how can the knowers of words (the grammarians) speak of a "loss of system" (*nayalopa*) regarding Your incarnation in the form of the Fish (*Matsya*)? The sense is that it is inconsistent for them to speak of a loss of system in an incarnation so preeminent for its recovery of the Veda, which is the locus of all systems of thought.

Regarding the form *mātsya*, which ends in the suffix *aṇ* and has the appearance of the word *matsya*, the objection that there would be no elision of *ya* (i.e., the absence of *yalopa*)—since the elision of *ya* prescribed by the rule *sūryatiṣyāgatsyamatsyānāṃ ya upadhāyāḥ* is precluded by the restrictive rule *matsyasya ṅyām*—is the solution offered. Alternatively, the phrase *phaṇīndragiri* may be treated as a separate word; thus, O Leader, O Lord (*netaḥ svāmin*), the meaning "on the mountain of the Lord of Serpents" (*phaṇīndragiri*)—that is, on the *Bhāṣya* of Patañjali—should also be supplied as an embellishment.

In that context, the meaning of the phrase "those who employ the rope for the purpose of rescuing the Vedas, which are the objects of all systems of thought" is precisely what has been stated; the underlying intention is that the *Vyākaraṇa-bhāṣya* was composed for the purpose of instructing upon the words of the Veda. Here, having attributed to the statement of the grammarian a quality contrary to his own intended meaning through a pun (*śleṣa*), this [statement] is cited as an authoritative source (*pramāṇa*) for the sake of censuring him. The same should be inferred for what follows as well.

Just as when "Viśvaṃbhara" (the Earth) is mentioned alongside [another], it is Viśvaṃbhara alone who assumes the state of being the subordinate (*śeṣatā*); yet, when it is stated that "she alone is his subordinate," one who knows only the individual words falls into doubt. (2083)

In the context of a "sahokti" (mention together) with the Earth-goddess Viśvambharā—on the occasion of their simultaneous discourse—it is the Lord Viśvambhara alone who assumes the state of being the "remainder," that is, subservience to her. Alternatively, in the case of a "sahokti"—meaning a simultaneous verbal expression—with the word *viśvambharā*, the word *viśvambhara* alone remains as the remainder. The sense is that because there exists only the distinction of gender (female and male), the rule "the masculine [remains] after the feminine" (*pumān striyā*) prescribes the remainderhood of the single masculine term alone.

In the statement that "that very Earth, the supporter of the universe (viśvaṃbharā), is the remnant (śeṣabhūtā) of this," as in the Lord’s own words, "Likewise, the earth and Nīlā are considered by me to be the remnants (śeṣabhūte),"—in that case, when it is said that the word *viśvaṃbharā* itself is the remnant (*śeṣabhūtā*), meaning the remaining part of this word *viśvaṃbhara*, what [is it like]?

One who knows the grammatical rule (*lapada-jña*) but not the supreme state (*paramapada-jña*), meaning a dry grammarian who has not even caught the scent of the Lord’s scriptures or the true tradition (*satsampradāya*), and whose gaze is fixed solely upon the grammar he has studied—such a person doubts. The sense is that he hesitates, thinking: "Since by the rule *pumān striyā* (Pāṇini 1.2.67), when there is a difference in gender between two co-referents, the masculine alone is ordained to remain, how can the feminine form of the word *viśvambharā* be what remains? This is the intended meaning.

The distinction here is that this composition of the meaning of the words of the Blessed One’s scripture is intended to demonstrate the contradiction with grammar in a matter established by a certain mere grammarian; however, its being supported by paronomasia (śleṣa) remains as before.

Or rather, the statement that "the universal is one, follows after many, and is eternal" is false; for Brahman is indeed one, follows after many, and is eternal, yet it is not a universal at all. (2084)

That entity which is one, which is pervasive and inherent in many individuals such as cows and the like, which is eternal, and which is not subject to destruction—that is *sāmānya* (the universal); this is the meaning of *jāti* (the genus). As Amara states: "The genus (*jāti*) and that which is born (*jāta*) are the universal (*sāmānya*). Thus, the statement of the Naiyāyikas—"the universal is eternal, one, and inherent in many"—is false. Why? To this he says: because Brahman, though one, inherent in many, and eternal, is nonetheless not a universal and is indeed not a genus.

In the ultimate sense, however, it is one, peerless, and pervading—having entered into and permeated the many sentient and insentient beings—as stated in such scriptural passages as: "He who dwells in the earth," "He who dwells in the self," and "Having entered within, He is the teacher of all people. It is eternal, because of the revelation: "The eternal among the eternals. It is unique and without equal, because of the scripture: "Neither its equal nor its superior is seen. Alternatively, "asāmānyam" means that it is unsurpassed.

In passages such as, "But those who are devoted to exertion for the sake of others, provided it does not conflict with their own interest," the word *sāmānya* is employed in the sense of being devoid of both excellence (*utkarṣa*) and deficiency (*apakarṣa*). Here, however, there is a distinction from previous instances: having imagined, through a pun (*śleṣa*), that the statement of the logician (*nyāyavid*) is contrary to one's own intended meaning, this [verse] cites that very statement as an authoritative source (*pramāṇa*) in order to censure it. Thus, it differs from earlier examples.

Or rather, when there is no contradiction, it is indeed logical that the Veda should be supplemented by the Smṛti; yet, O Śauri, it is the Veda itself that supplements the Smṛti regarding Your qualities—alas, how wonderful this is for us! 2085.

O Śauri! When there is no contradiction—that is, when there is no conflict with direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*)—it is proper to supplement the Veda (*śruti*) by means of *smṛti*, the legal compendium composed by Manu and others, in order to clarify its indistinct meanings; this is consistent with the principles of Mīmāṃsā. The particle *kila* indicates that this is a traditional teaching of the scriptures. However, when there is indeed a contradiction with the *śruti*, the *smṛti* must simply be disregarded.

The sense is that this is like the contradiction between the scriptural injunction (śruti), "One should chant the udgītha while touching the audumbarī post," and the traditional rule (smṛti), "The entire audumbarī post must be wrapped [with cloth]," which is set aside by the former. This has been aphorized by the Great Sage [Jaimini]: "But in case of contradiction, it [the smṛti] should be disregarded; for there is no inference [of its validity] when such a contradiction exists. Such being the case, he states that in the system of the Śāstra, this is the opposite: "It is the Śruti [that prevails]."

Regarding "the Veda itself": the Veda alone—specifically those scriptural passages that set forth Your auspicious qualities such as truthfulness and knowledge, beginning with "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" and "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving"—is what is meant. In this context, "mere hearing" refers to our own *smṛti* (recollection) concerning Your auspicious qualities and so forth; that is, the *smṛti* of Parāśara and others, beginning with "All-knowing, all-seeing, omnipotent, possessed of the perfection of knowledge and power. In the other sense, it means the continuous flow of remembrance (*smaraṇa*) of You.

It nourishes and increases [the meaning]. "Hanta" expresses the wonder produced by the contemplation of a paradoxical situation. Herein lies the distinction from the previous [section]: the presentation of verbal authority (*śabdapramāṇa*) in the form of the principles of the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā, intended to further enrich the variety of the author's own stated meaning through the inclusion of wordplay (*śleṣa*).
Or rather, O Blessed One, even those who are light and cling at your feet possess dignity; I do not speak falsely, for those well-versed in the meters indeed declare this.

O Blessed One! At the tips of Your feet—that is, at the very front of Your feet—those who are attached or bound elsewhere, even those who are light, meaning devoid of greatness derived from their genus, qualities, and so forth; or, in the alternative sense, the word "those" (*te*) functions as an adjective for "light" (*laghavaḥ*). Those "lights" are the phonemes taught by the rule *hrasvaṃ laghu* ("a short vowel is light"). [They] possess dignity (*gauravaṃ*), that is, venerability; or, in the alternative sense, the word "or" (*vā*) connects with "dignity" (*gauravam*), such that they "possess dignity optionally," meaning they possess the status of being a heavy (*guru*) phoneme.

Regarding what they say: "A long *la* [phoneme] accompanied by an anusvāra, ending in a visarga, followed by a conjunct consonant, or standing at the end of a quarter-verse (*pāda*), may [optionally] be short. The distinction here is that an authoritative statement from those learned in the science of prosody (*chandaśśāstra*) has been cited as a proof in order to establish the aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*) of his own composition. Furthermore, the term *chandobhijñāḥ* can also be understood to mean "those who know the Vedas"; through this, an exceeding degree of authority (*prāmāṇya*) is conveyed.

Just as those who are devoted to you are indeed upright while others, being light, are crooked; so it is that the followers of Vedic grammar, alas, declare the "heavy" (guru) syllable to be "crooked" (vakra) and the "light" (laghu) to be "upright" (ṛju). || 2087 ||

The word "O Blessed One" (*bhagavan*) is to be supplied here. Your devotees are venerable teachers (*guravaḥ pūjyāḥ*), according to the statement: "In whomsoever this eightfold devotion exists, even if he be a barbarian (*mleccha*), he is to be honored just as I am. They are upright (*ṛjavaḥ*), possessing a conformity of the three instruments (mind, speech, and body). Others, however—those who are not your devotees—are insignificant (*laghavaḥ*), trivial, crooked (*vakrāḥ*), and of a deceitful nature. This being the case, it should also be understood that they are "students of the Veda" (*chāndasāḥ*), meaning those who know the science of metrics (*chandaśśāstra*) and those who follow the Vedic tradition.

The term *chāndasa* is used here to indicate dull-wittedness, in accordance with the saying: “O King, like that of a dull and unlearned *śrotriya*, your intellect is destroyed by mere rote recitation (*anuvāka*). They say that a long syllable (*guru*) is crooked (*vakra*) and a short syllable (*laghu*) is straight (*ṛju*). The word *batā* expresses the distress felt upon hearing such a contradictory statement.

Here, the citation of the statement of those learned in the science of prosody—“That [long vowel] is to be known as crooked, while the other [short one] consisting of a single measure (*mātrika*) is straight”—is introduced for the purpose of censuring them, as it contradicts his own intended meaning; thus, this constitutes a specific kind of poetic charm (*vicchitti*) distinct from the previous one.

Just as the moon, O Hari, bestowing friendship upon you, becomes a friend to Budha and an enemy to no one; so too, O Lord who are a treasury of splendor, you are equal to all in this world—this is the testimony of the science of astronomy.

O Treasure of Abodes, O Treasure of Splendor, O Hari, O Blessed One! (In the alternative sense: O Radiant One!—this is the meaning. "Friendship" (*maitrī*) toward you, the Blessed One, and toward the Sun, refers to taking refuge; for in the passage, “For he who knows the Dharma is compassionate toward those who have sought refuge; let there be friendship with you,” the word *maitrī* is explained as having the sense of seeking refuge. Elsewhere, [the term] denotes friendship. The "King of the Twice-born" (*dvijarāja*) is both the foremost of Brahmins and the Moon.

The sense is that he is "luminous" because of his friendship with the moon (Candramas). He is a friend of Mercury (Budha), possessing affection for those who know Brahman, and is a friend of the gentle planet (Saumya), because the moon is its friend. He is "without enemies" (anariḥ), being free from the group of adversaries such as desire (kāma) and the like; in the case of the moon, the sense is that he is devoid of enemies, as the moon lacks inimical planets. In this world, he is "equal toward all" (aśeṣeṣu samaḥ), meaning he perceives everyone equally everywhere according to the stated principle that "one is equal toward the factions of friend and foe"; elsewhere, the reading is "equal to Śeṣa."

Regarding the "remaining" planets—meaning those other than the ones already mentioned—the meaning is that he becomes equal [to them all], because he is equal toward all others. In this matter, the authority (*pramāṇa*) is the science of astronomy (*jyotiṣa*); the sense is that the statement of Varāhamihira and others—"The Sun and the Moon are friends, while the remaining [planets] are neutral toward the Moon"—is the authority. Here, by means of the power of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), the authority of the Smṛti in the form of astronomy is established to support his own stated point; this is the distinction from the previous [instance].

Just as the sun, which has golden rays, is a swan, is endowed with great radiance and honor, and gradually ascends to a high position—so too, if the science of astronomy were an authoritative means of knowledge here, like the Vedas. (2089)

He who is the *haṃsa*—a particular type of ascetic—and the Sun; one whose vision is fixed upon Lord Hari, meaning one whose knowledge consists of devotional worship (*upāsanā*), is so described. In the alternative sense, it means one whose gaze is directed toward Leo (*hari*), that is, one situated in Aquarius, for it is only while stationed there that a gaze upon Leo—the seventh sign—is possible; as the astrologers say: "All [planets] aspect the seventh."

That distinguished ascetic, honored by the hospitable reception of the Great Radiance—the fire that is non-material and consists of the *ātivāhika* [guiding] light—will, through that honor and service, proceed in due order according to the sequence beginning with "from the light to the day, from the day to the waxing fortnight," and so forth, until he reaches a high station and abides in the Supreme State.

In that fortnight, the Sun, having moved through the sign of Aquarius (Kumbha) in due order and preceded by his arrival at the sign of Pisces (Mīna), reaches the sign of Aries (Kriya)—for the astronomers have stated that the names of the signs beginning with Aries are given in sequence as "Kriya, Tābu, Urubja, Tuma, Kulīya, Leya, Pāthona, Jūka, Kaurpya. Having reached that [sign], he is "añcita," meaning situated in his exaltation (ucca); for by the rule "Aja, Vṛṣabha," and so forth, Aries is declared to be his place of exaltation. Thus, he is established in his high position (uccasthāna).

Therefore, he will possess great radiance and great brilliance, according to the statement of Vidyāmādhava: "A planet is 'blazing' when in its exaltation. The rest is clear. Here too, astrology serves as authoritative proof for the intended meaning.
Just as poets describe your two comparisons—the emerald and the sapphire—there is no difference in their color; that which is said, O Kṛṣṇa, is certainly not false.

"O Kṛṣṇa!"—the sense is that you are dark like a deep blue rain-cloud. Poets declare the emerald (*harinmaṇi*) and the sapphire (*indranīla*) to be the similes for you, whose color has been described as such. Anticipating the objection—"How can there be a relationship of simile and object of comparison between these two gems of green and blue hues and you, who are dark-colored?"—he resolves it with the words "of these two. The ellipsis is to be supplied as follows: "The difference in color between these two—the emerald and the sapphire—is not [as great] as is asserted by poets."

Thus, it is indeed not false that between these two spoken words there is a distinction only by the letter *na* and not by other letters; this further meaning is also striking. Here, for the purpose of describing the similarity between the Lord—who is as blue as a dark rain-cloud—and both the emerald (*harinmaṇi*) and the sapphire (*harimaṇi*), the statement of the Alamkārikas beginning with "Of Lakṣmī and Saṃpat, of Kṛṣṇa and Hari, of Nāga and Sarpa," and ending with "The identity of Dānava, Asura, and Daitya is intended," has been brought to bear as authoritative evidence for the intended sense, which consists in the description of the absence of difference in their color.

In this manner, other forms of verbal testimony found in different treatises and in common worldly speech may also be cited as examples of the means of knowledge known as *śabda*. Furthermore, regarding the conduct of the virtuous (*sādhūnām ācāra*) and self-satisfaction (*ātmanas tuṣṭi*), which are established as means of knowledge by the statement "And also the conduct of the virtuous, and self-satisfaction," these two—conduct and self-satisfaction—are included within the very category of *śabda*, since they lead to the inference of Vedic words, which are the primary means of knowing Dharma according to the Mīmāṃsakas.
In this regard, conduct is the authority:

"O Lord of the Mountain, how could that Sun be wicked? For whatever day people perform [rites] for your pleasure, here, the distinction between the good and the evil is always discerned through right conduct. (2091)

O Lord of Ahicchatra! How can that Śauri, Śani (Saturn), be sinful? For it is impossible for his sinfulness, as declared in the *Jyotiṣa*, to be true; such is the thought [of the author]. Intending to state the reason for this, he says: "Of whom" (*yasya*). On the day (*vāre*) of that Śani, virtuous people perform an immeasurable vow (*vrata*), consisting of restraints such as fasting, for your pleasure—the word "people" being understood from the context. To the question, "How can his sinlessness be determined merely from such conduct?", he replies: "Being good" (*sad-iti*).

In this world, whether something is good or bad, virtuous or non-virtuous, it must indeed be discerned and determined solely by the conduct of the virtuous. The sense is that, since on Saturday one observes the conduct of the virtuous—such as the performance of vows and rites for the propitiation of Śrīnivāsa—it is improper to assert that Saturn (Sauri) is inherently sinful. Here, in determining that Saturn is not sinful, the virtuous conduct consisting of the observance of vows on that day is presented as the authoritative proof. As stated in the Mādhavīya: "Conduct (ācāra) is a specific mode of behavior favored by the learned, characterized by compassion, courtesy, and so forth."

Just as devotion or surrender is remembered as a means for attaining You, so too is self-satisfaction considered a valid authority; yet, O Lord of Vṛṣādri, for people like us, it is specifically through surrender that complete satisfaction arises.
O great sage, I am attainable here either through supreme devotion or through surrender;
I am not attainable in any other way by those who desire my service.

Thus, between the two options of devotion (*bhakti*) and surrender (*prapatti*), it has been established that for people like us, the authority (*pramāṇa*) for engaging in surrender alone is the satisfaction of one's own self (*ātmatuṣṭi*).
In this way, other means of valid cognition such as direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth, as described by the Mīmāṃsakas, may also be cited here as possible examples.
In this regard, the direct statement (*śruti*) is as follows:

"By your very name you are Hari; you take away misfortune—what need is there here for an indicative mark? Indeed, there is no requirement for a mirror when one is looking at the bracelet on one's own forearm. (2093)

Here, by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) that the name of Śrīnivāsa is "Hari," his quality of removing all evils is established. Those learned in the systems of philosophy say: "A *śruti* is a word that is independent [of other means of knowledge]."

Or rather, O Hari, since you bear the gesture of fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*) and are heard of as "Brahman is fearlessness," once the Supreme Reality has been determined by the Vedas, who indeed would pay heed to a mere physical mark? (2094)

O Śrīnivāsa! You do not bear—that is, you do not hold—the *abhayamudrā*, which consists in displaying the palm of the hand with the fingers pointing upward and serves as a signifier of fearlessness; rather, by bearing the *varadamudrā*—which consists in displaying the palm of the hand with the fingers pointing downward and serves as a signifier of the granting of boons—you [confer protection].

The expression is used in that way because you bear such a mudrā of fearlessness; for you are heard of in the Śruti as "fearless Brahman" in the passages, "This is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman," and "Brahman is indeed fearless. This is a *pañcamī-bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that from which fear is non-existent."

For instance, when the true nature of reality—the supreme and most excellent truth—has been determined by scripture itself, that is, by the direct statement (abhidhāna-śruti), who would take heed of an indicative mark (liṅga) that merely infers it through its capacity? The point is that once the meaning has been ascertained by scripture alone, no regard is ever paid to a weaker indicative mark.

Furthermore, since the status of Nārāyaṇa alone as the supreme reality has been determined by such scriptural passages as "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the highest truth," who indeed would honor the *liṅga*—that is, the Śiva-liṅga? It is also understood that one who knows the true nature of the meaning of the Vedas does not honor Rudra or any other deity as the supreme reality. In this context, the necessity of bearing the *liṅga* in the form of the "fearless" (*abhaya*) mudrā is established for Śrīnivāsa by the scriptural passage "abhayam."

Or rather, since the Śruti declares me to be the Lord of Śrī (Śrīpati), why did you previously cast aside the conch and discus? O Lord of Mountains, have you forgotten this scriptural meaning? Indeed, in matters based on Śruti, no other mark is taken into account.

O Lord of Ahicchatra! The Śruti, in passages such as "Hrī and Lakṣmī are your two wives," declares me to be the Lord of Śrī (Śrīpati). Since the status of being the Lord of Śrī is already determined by the Śruti itself, what purpose is served by these two, the conch and the discus? What need is there for the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the wearing of the conch and discus once the matter is established by the Śruti alone? Thus, there is the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*): why did you previously abandon and cast away the conch and discus? For indeed, according to the Tantrikas, a mark (*liṅga*) is not respected when the matter has been established by an independent statement of the Śruti.

The rest follows. Here too, by means of the cited scripture, the non-obligatory nature of bearing the conch and discus is established. In this context, the abandonment of the conch and discus due to other causes is considered possible for one who possesses the aforementioned cause. Here, the Puranic narrative is recalled, wherein Lord Śrīnivāsa bestowed the conch and discus upon a certain king for the sake of victory over his enemies.

O Blessed One, just as Your manifestation exists for the sake of benefiting the world, not even a single one of Your activities is for Your own purpose; rather, I believe it is Your very nature as the body of all that speaks thus. (2096)

In this context, the Lord Śrīnivāsa’s exclusive dedication to His own purpose is established by the mark (liṅga) of His being the embodied one of all things that benefit all beings, as well-known from such scriptural passages as "He whose body is the earth," and so forth. This is because His activity proceeds from that very nature.

[Objection: But surely, since *liṅga*—which consists of semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*)—falls outside the category of verbal testimony (*śabda-pramāṇa*), how can it be cited as an example in the context of discussing verbal testimony? [Reply: This is not so; because it lacks intrinsic validity (*pramāṇatā*), its status as a means of knowledge exists only by way of inferring the Veda, and thus it is included within verbal testimony itself. Likewise, even worldly *liṅgas* are included within worldly verbal testimony itself, as they lead to the inference of worldly words. Such a *liṅga* should also be cited in this very manner.

As for the statement: "O Mother, having determined your word to be powerful in the context of the expiation for sin, I choose you as my refuge; for, according to the context, the statement itself is indeed more authoritative. (2097)
In the section on the removal of sins, when the occasion for expiation arises, your own statement is as follows: "But when the occasion for expiation occurs due to the emergence of all sins,
one should go for refuge to me alone, the queen of the God of gods."

Having thus determined that your statement as declared in the *Lakṣmītantra* is more powerful, O Mother Śrī, I take refuge in you. For, according to the context—characterized by mutual expectancy—they say that a sentence, characterized by syntactic proximity (*samabhivyāhāra*), is stronger and more powerful; this is the understood conclusion of the Tantrikas. And so it is stated in the aphorism of the Great Sage (Jaimini): “In the case of a conflict between direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactic unity (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*), each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding in terms of its meaning.”

"By way of preeminence": "Direct statement (śruti) is an independent word; indicative power (liṅga) is semantic capacity; syntactical connection (vākya) is co-utterance; context (prakaraṇa) is mutual expectancy; position (sthāna) is common location; and name (samākhyā) is a derivative term"—this is the summary. Here, the stated meaning is supported by a syntactical connection (vākya), which is stronger than context (prakaraṇa), and which is bolstered by an identification based on paronomasia between the two meanings conveyed by the words in the forms of context and syntactical connection.
Or for example:

"Who would believe the statement that 'this boy is you, Mādhava,' when you have already seized the enemy? For a syntactical connection (*vākya*) is weaker than both direct assertion (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*). (2098)

O Blessed One! The sense is that [the Lord] is indeed called Mādhava by name alone, according to the scriptural statement: "Mādhava on Veṅkaṭagiri. By this, the direct scriptural declaration (*abhidhāna-śruti*) is shown. Furthermore, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is present in the phrase "in Him who has taken up the conch and discus" from the venerable teacher Śrī Bhagavad Rāmānujācārya. As for the statement of certain fools, "This boy is Skanda," who would believe it? For, since both direct scripture (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*) are present, a mere sentence (*vākya*) is weaker than those two.

In the previous example, the superiority of syntactical connection (*vākya*) over context (*prakaraṇa*) was demonstrated; here, however, the distinction is that its inferiority to direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*) is shown. Everything else is the same.
As for the context:
wherever it may be, it is that very context of the narration of your virtues which is honored by the virtuous; for no other location possesses greater power than that context. (2099)

O Blessed One! Let there be an occasion, a context, or a discourse concerning Your qualities—let it occur anywhere, even in an unworthy place; such is the meaning. That very discourse on Your qualities alone is held in high esteem by virtuous people, the devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas), while even the highest station or the supreme state itself is not so esteemed by them, because for them, the narrative of the Blessed One is their sole object of enjoyment; this is the underlying sense. That...

The "supreme place" (*paraṃ sthānam*) mentioned as such in the Sūtra refers to a location characterized by commonality of region; and this is indeed weaker—meaning less powerful—than both context (*prakaraṇa*) and occasion (*prastāva*), because of the weakness of the latter being established by the Sūtra itself. This is the intended meaning. Here, the intended sense is supported by means of the context, which employs a superimposition (*adhyavasāya*) based on a pun (*śleṣa*) between the two meanings denoted by the words *prakaraṇa* and *sthāna* according to the aforementioned method.
O Veṅkaṭeśa, even your designation shines forth as being defined by its position, just as Jaimini has stated that position is more powerful than designation. (2100)

O Veṅkaṭeśa! The sense is that Your majesty is celebrated by hundreds of Śrutis. Even Your designation—that is, Your very name—is designated by Your location, namely the mountain Veṅkaṭādri which serves as Your abode; it has attained renown through such designation, just as in the expression "those designated as Vasiṣṭhas. The implication is that Your title "Veṅkaṭeśa" is indeed preceded by the mention of the place in the form of Mount Veṅkaṭa.

Since Jaimini stated—in the *Paradaurbalyasūtra*—that among the means of proof, the designation (*samākhyā*), which consists of a derivative word or a name, is weaker than its correlate, namely "place" (*sthāna*)—which takes the form of a common location or an abode—it follows that place alone is stronger. Therefore, the construction is as follows: even your own designation appears to be designated by place.

Here, the fact that the Lord’s designation is to be designated by place is established through the identification [of the two], based on the pun (*śleṣa*) between the two meanings conveyed by the words "designation" and "place," which are fused into a state of non-difference and extreme unity.
O Viśvātman, just as You are designated by names such as Vedhas, Kṛttivāsas, Śānta, and Vṛddhaśravas, so too there is no other measure here than Your own self-designation. 2101.

"O Viśvātman!"—this is the indicator of the recognition of the word *viśvātman* found in the passage that is about to be cited here. The pronoun *saḥ* (he) is to be supplied to all [the epithets], beginning with *vedhāḥ*. He is *vedhāḥ*, the four-faced one, renowned as the creator of the worlds; he is *kṛttivāsāḥ pinākī*, the one clad in animal hide who wields the Pināka bow, celebrated as the destroyer of the universe; and he is *vṛddhaśravāḥ*, Indra, famed as the lord of the immortals. They are called "with their ends" (*sāntāḥ*), meaning they exist together with their final syllables.

The meaning is "perishable. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), the meaning is that all the words mentioned end in the letter *s*. He [the Self] is "undecaying, immortal, free from old age, free from death, truth, knowledge, infinite"—thus proclaimed by hundreds of scriptural passages (*śruti*). You are not an end (*anta*); you are infinite (*ananta*). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound preceded by the negative particle *na*. The meaning is "eternal. In the alternative sense, the word "O Soul of the Universe" (*viśvātman*) ends in the letter *n*.

In this context, *mānam* means "authority" (*pramāṇa*). Regarding the phrase "you and they" (*te ca tvam ca yūyam*), there is a "retention of the last" (*para-ekaśeṣa*) according to the rule: "When pronouns beginning with *tyad* (i.e., *tyad*, *tad*, etc. are used together, that which follows remains. *Samākhyā* means "name" itself.

Here, when Brahmā and the others have dissolved, when the world of moving and non-moving beings has perished, and when the dissolution of all beings (*ābhūtasaṃplava*) has occurred, [the universe] is dissolved into primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and the Great Principle (*mahat*) [remains].
The one who remains is the Soul of the Universe; he is indeed the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
Thus says the venerable Mahābhārata:
"Brahmā, Śambhu, as well as the Sun, the Moon, and Śatakratu—
these and others likewise are indeed joined with the splendor of Viṣṇu."
At the conclusion of their worldly activities, they are deprived of their own splendor; and being thus divested of their luster, they all undergo dissolution into the five elements.
Thus, the statement from the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara* is also made known by its meaning; here, the name (*samākhyā*) serves as the authority for the intended sense.
Just as the Discus-bearer (Viṣṇu) was purchased by the multitude of bowing devotees through their intensely kindled devotion,
his very name "Cakrī" (the Discus-bearer) clearly declares his state of being purchased.

The designation *cakrī* is merely the name of this Blessed One; its "purchased-ness" (*krītatva*) consists in being the object of the act of purchase (*krayaṇakarmatva*), or, in another sense, its being endowed with the phoneme *i* which has the form of the root *krī* (to buy). Here too, regarding the intended meaning of "purchased-ness," the designation itself is made to serve as the authority by means of the power of *śleṣa* (punning wordplay), based on the identity between the word and its referent. In this context, the meaning of the scriptural authority, "Janārdana is purchased by devotion," should be reflected upon.

O Blessed One, just as the sun, having been shaken from its place by you, became the foremost among those wandering in the sky, so too it is understood that even one who is distracted is surely known by his very name. 2103.
O Blessed One! Ravi, Bhānu, and the word Ravi [are names for you]. By the word "your" (tvat-padena), it refers to you.

"By the luster of his feet"—meaning, he was shaken; therefore, among the *kheṭas* (the base), for Amara states, "*kheṭa*, *garhya*, and *aṇaka* are synonyms. The true meaning is that he was the foremost among the sky-traveling planets (*gaganacārigrahas*). Elsewhere, "foremost" (*agresaraḥ*) means excellent; by the identity of the word's meaning, it implies "possessing the letter *ra*" (*repha-viśiṣṭaḥ*), being at the beginning (*agre*). Being thus, even though he was *vyagra* (disturbed or busy), he became so. And he was one whose *vi-* (colorless) was at the *agra* (end); for "the word *agra* denotes 'in front,' 'above,' and also the measure of a *pala*."

According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *abhyudaya* may be neuter when it means an object (*ālambana*), a collection (*samūha*), or a limit (*prānta*); it is also used in the sense of being superior (*adhika*), preeminent (*pradhāna*), or first (*prathama*), according to its referent. It became [so]. The word *nūnam* expresses probability (*sambhāvanā*). Here, this meaning is understood through the very name [of the work] itself. The sense is that such a meaning is obtained through the name in the manner described above. In this case as well, the name itself is established as the authority for the intended meaning by virtue of the power of *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

O Lord, just as the moon here, having been eclipsed by your face, was shaken off and subsequently attained friendship with it; does not its very name itself declare this fact—what need is there for further deliberation? (2104)

O All-pervading Lord! Here, the moon—the *vidhu* or *indu*—has become *vipratipanna* (disputant) with Your face; that is to say, it has reached a state of contradiction or opposition. For this very reason, the suffix *tasi* is used here in the sense of all case endings (*sārvavibhaktika*), meaning "by that face. It is thus "shaken" or, in other words, "disregarded. The word *tataḥ* connects with both [the preceding and following clauses] according to the maxim of the central gem (*madhyamaṇinyāya*).

Then, he entered into friendship and affection with him; the sense is that for one of inferior intellect who has been slighted by a superior, it is fitting to seek refuge immediately. This very point—that which has been stated—this name itself of the moon (*vidhu*) declares and reveals. The sense is that regarding this matter, there is no need for further deliberation or other investigation. However, in the case of the name, the analysis of *vidhu* is: *vibho* (O Lord) + *abhavat* (he became).

In the first part of the word, at the beginning of the mouth [of speech], he became—that is, he was—resorted to by the syllable *vi*. Immediately after that, "dhutaḥ" (the suffix *tasi* used in all cases) means friendship, that is to say, association, with the letter *dhu*. He attained it; the meaning is that the word *vidhu* was thus produced. The rest is as before.
Just as at the beginning Indra was propitiated by him, and though he was terrified in the middle, O Śrīdhara, he was favored by him at the end; for this very reason, he bears that name. (2105)

O Śrīdhara! *Sutrāmā* refers to Indra, and the word *sutrāmā* [is derived from] *sutra*. He is *svā*, meaning one for whom *svaḥ*—that is, heaven (*svarga*)—was *rāddham*, or accomplished, prior to the calamity caused by the curse of Durvāsas.

*Śvārāddhaḥ*: "Accomplished in heaven" (*svarge rāddhaḥ*) or "perfected" (*saṃsiddhaḥ*). The meaning is that he is fully endowed with all sovereign powers (*sarvaiśvaryaparipūrṇaḥ*). By the rule *ro ri*, the *repha* is elided, and by the rule *ḍhralope*, the preceding vowel is lengthened. In the alternative interpretation regarding the word *sva*, he is *svārāddhaḥ*—one by whom the syllable *su* was first attained. Furthermore, even though he was terrified during the interval between receiving the curse of Durvāsas and obtaining the glance of Lakṣmī—that is, when he was threatened by Vairocana and others through the loss of his position and other such means—he remained steadfast.

In another sense, "in the middle" (*madhye*) means between the two syllables *su* and *mā*; he is "terrified" (*trāsitaḥ*), meaning the collection of syllables *trā* has been made to sit (*āsitaḥ*) or seated there. By the cluster of syllables *ca*, he is "bound" (*sitaḥ*) or "tied" (*saṃbaddhaḥ*). The particle *api* here functions as a conjunction; thus the meaning is "and terrified. "At the end" (*ante*) means at the conclusion, signifying that he is "graced by Mā" (*mānugṛhītaḥ*), i.e., made the object of Lakṣmī’s sidelong glance. In another sense, "at the end" (*ante*) refers to the final portion, meaning he is "composed of the syllable *mā*" (*mānugṛhītaḥ*).

It was so. This very meaning is stated by the name of this Sutrāman himself; the sense is that once this matter has been understood through the name "Sutrāman" alone, there is no need to pursue citations from the Purāṇas to the end. Thus, the authority of the name is established here for the purpose he intends to demonstrate.
Just as the Lord of Umā carries the moon within himself, so too does this [world] exist dependent upon Him; if this point is difficult to grasp, let its very name be properly considered.
Śiva, the Lord of Umā, bears Śrīnātha within himself, holding him as his inner self. "My inner self, yours, and those others who are designated as embodied beings—
the Blessed Viṣṇu is the self of Bhava, the one of immeasurable splendor."

The sense is: "from such scriptural authority as this. For this very reason, this Lord of Umā (Umāpati) has his existence dependent upon Him; that is to say, the distinctions of His nature, subsistence, and activity are subject to Him. This meaning—the meaning established by the evidence presented in accordance with the purport of the Antaryāmin Brāhmaṇa—is difficult to grasp.

If it is difficult to understand for those of little wisdom, then let its very name—indeed, the name *Umāpati* itself—be reflected upon; through such reflection, this meaning will become clear even to those of limited knowledge. This is the intended sense. Regarding the alternative interpretation based on the name: *Umāpati* (the word *Umāpati*) "bears" (*bibharti*) the "māpa" within—that is, in the middle between the first and last syllables—the combination of *mā* and *pa*. Such is the collection of phonemes it contains.

Therefore, this term "Umāpati" has its existence dependent on her; its own status is contingent upon the color (varṇa) of Umā. The sense is that in the absence of the aforementioned color of Umā, the existence of the term "Umāpati" would be impossible. Here, the designation "Umāpati" is employed as a proof for the intended meaning that Umāpati is the inner self (antarātman) of the Lord.
O Blessed One, just as when there is something to be enjoyed, one who desires other meat becomes like a crow for that particular object; thus he speaks, and his very name signifies this. (2107)

O Blessed One!
