Even when there exists that which is to be enjoyed by all, in every way, by everyone—that is, other flesh (*āmiṣa*) or other objects of enjoyment (the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *āmiṣa* is masculine and neuter; it refers to an object of enjoyment, sexual union, a bribe, and also to meat"; the term *anyamāṃsa*, "flesh of another," should also be supplied)—he who is a *kāmuka*, a seeker of pleasure.

Because the prohibition of the genitive case characterized by its connection with *kṛt*-suffixes—as in the rule "not in *loka*" and so forth—is set aside by the exception "there is no prohibition for *kāmin*," the word *itarāmiṣa* takes only the genitive when in construction with the word *kāmuka*. Thus: *saḥ amukaḥ*, "that such-and-such desirer. This undeclined word *amuka* has the same meaning as the pronoun *adas*. As in: *amukagotrasyāmukaśarmaṇaḥ* ("of one of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such name"), and *jñātassvareṇāmukaḥ* ("the person known by his voice as such-and-such").

This is because we observe such usage [in the rule *adaso 'ser dādū*]. However, the word *adaḥ* does not possess the augment *sak* (i.e., it is not *adasak*). If that were the case, the form would have to be *asuk*; or rather, *kāka* would simply be *vāyasa*. The sense is that, due to its greed for meat (*āmiṣagṛdhnutva*), it is exactly like that [vulture]. In the alternative view, the word *kāmuka*, deprived of the letter *m*, would simply be *kāka*—that is, the word *kāka* itself. Here, in order to determine the intended meaning, the designation *kāmuka* with one syllable displaced is presented as the authority;
thus, this example possesses a particular elegance (*vicchitti*) distinct from the previous examples of designations where no syllables are displaced.
Or rather, since you possess a nature contrary [to that of a swan], you surely appear as a lion; for the very word "lion" is sufficient proof in this matter. (2108)

"O Lion! O Narasiṃha! If you were to possess a hostile disposition—that is, if you were to act with hostility toward me—it would surely appear as if you were a *haṃsī* (a female swan); the meaning is that it appears to me as if you were destroying a person who harbors hostility. In the alternative sense, 'O Lion' is an address using the word *siṃha* itself; when a state of hostility (*pratikūlabhāva*) is reached—meaning when the word is reversed—you appear as a *haṃsī*, that is, you manifest in the sequence *haṃsī*."

In this matter, regarding the stated meaning and such a state of inverse order (*prātilomya*), the word "siṃha" itself—which results from the formation of "haṃsī"—is sufficient as the proof (*māna*) or authority (*pramāṇa*). The sense is: what is the use of searching for any other proof? Here, in the stated meaning, the vocative designation "siṃha" in its aforementioned form is presented as the authority; thus, this possesses a specific distinction from the preceding [example].
Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, the Chapter on Verbal Authority (Śabdapramāṇasara), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on Presumption (Arthāpattisara):
That which is postulated as some meaning because it cannot otherwise be accounted for is presumption.
The wise describe that presumption as having a different meaning.
The poetic figure named *arthāpatti* (presumption) consists in the postulation of another fact based on the impossibility of a given fact being otherwise accounted for.
Just as the mass of luster from the young elephant Nanda’s trunk completely eclipsed the kunda flower— otherwise, how could even that which grows in the forest possess such self-restraint?

The flower of the *kunda* tree is called *kunda*; because of the inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahula*) in the rule *puṣpamūleṣu bahulam*, there is the elision of the suffix *-ika* (indicating a product). According to the rule *dvihīnaṃ prasave sarvam*, it is neuter. This [subject], meaning the *mādhya* flower, stole—that is, it emulated—the multitude of splendors of the rays from the hands of Nanda’s youth (Kṛṣṇa), which is the object.

If there were no such theft, how could the "dāntatā"—that is, the connection with the teeth—of this *kunda* flower, which grows in the forest (*vipina*), be established? It is not established in any way whatsoever; this is the meaning. Since the word *kunda* ends in the letter *da*, its state of being "dānta" (ending in *da*) is well-established. Here, because the state of the *kunda* being "dānta" is otherwise inexplicable, there arises the figure of speech *arthāpatti* (presumption), based on the determination that it has stolen the multitude of lusters from the teeth of the Blessed One.

O Mother, I believe that the elephant who hated the path of Your feet incurred such grief from that act that he became an outcaste (caṇḍāla); otherwise, how else could he have attained the state of a mātaṅga? 2110.

O Mother! This elephant (*śuṇḍālaḥ*) is a hater of the path to your feet—that is, one who hates going to your feet; and since "your feet" refers to your station, the supreme heaven (*paramavyoma*), it is a hater of attaining that. Therefore, having incurred grief (*śucam*) due to that hatred—[in another sense, the word *aśu* is split as *a-śu*]: being devoid of the letter *śu* (*aśu*), and according to the maxim "not with every utterance," having obtained the letter *ca* in place of that *śu*, it became a *caṇḍāla*.
The sense is that this is the fruit of hating the state of Lakṣmī’s feet, just as in the saying: "One who hates Nārāyaṇa should be known as one whose semen flows at the end. [The word] *śuṇḍāla*...

The meaning is that the word *caṇḍāla* is formed by first removing the letter *śu* from the word *śuṇḍāla* and then placing the letter *ca* in its place. Otherwise, if *caṇḍālatva* (the state of being an outcaste) were not attained in the manner described, how could this *śuṇḍāla*—being a *mātaṅga*—not be denotable by the word *mātaṅga*? This is the intended sense. According to the *Medinīkośa*, "mātaṅga" refers to both a dog-eater (outcaste) and an elephant. Here, since the conventional usage of the term *mātaṅga* for an elephant would otherwise be inexplicable, his status as a *caṇḍāla* is inferred through the power of *śleṣa* (punning).

Or rather, I think that the moon’s face has turned pale because it was outshone by the luster of Hari’s mouth; otherwise, how could it come to such extreme paleness, waning, and numbness at every step? (2111)

I think that the moon (vidhu), Indu, has been surpassed by the face of the Blessed Lord Hari; otherwise, in the absence of such a defeat, this moon would not be so excessively pale (*atipāṇḍuru*), as if afflicted by the disease of extreme palor—according to Amara, *strī rug rujā* [means "woman" and "disease"]; for this very reason, he has a discolored face (*vivarṇamukha*), a countenance devoid of luster. Alternatively, he possesses an exceedingly bright radiance (*ativiśadadīpti*)—according to Amara, *prabhā rug ruciḥ* [mean "splendor," "disease," and "beauty"]—and thus his face has a "vi" color [the color white] at its tip (*agra-bhāga*). This is the meaning.

It would undergo decline—meaning both the wasting away known as the disease *rājayakṣman* and, in another sense, the loss of its digits—as well as coldness (or dullness). For it is said in the *Medinī*: "The word *kṣaya* refers to a type of disease, a house, the end of an aeon (*kalpānta*), and decay. Thus, the meaning is that it would also become cold. From what cause could this happen? Here, because the moon's having a discolored face and so forth cannot otherwise be accounted for, its being humiliated by Hari’s face is inferred. The reinforcement through *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is as before.

O Mother, because of the abundance of your exquisite delicacy, even butter has its loftiness diminished; otherwise, how could it be so utterly bowed from beginning to end as it is when nestled within the hollow of a forest?

O Mother! Your butter (*navanīta*) has its height diminished by the abundance of your own exquisite tenderness, and its own tender loftiness contracted; otherwise, this very butter would be "nata" from beginning to end—that is to say, perpetually bent or curved. For what reason would it otherwise go to the "vanīgarbhaga"—that which goes to the interior or womb of the forest? The sense is: in the absence of your tenderness causing its own tenderness to be dwarfed, how could it enter the heart of the forest in the manner described?

In this context, the word *navanītam* (butter) is so described because it has the letters *na* and *ta* at its beginning and end (*ādyantayoḥ natau*), and the syllables *vanī* are situated within its interior (*garbhagau*). The sense is that the very nature of the word *navanīta* is such. Here, by the fact that the presence of *vanī* within the interior and the bending (*bhugnatva*) at the beginning and end of *navanīta* would otherwise be inexplicable, the extreme delicacy of Śrī’s form—which has rendered her natural height dwarfed—is suggested.

I think that the glories of the lightning bolts, desiring to seize your splendor, were struck down firmly by you; otherwise, how could they have failed to cast off their exhaustion even though their heads were bent downward?

O Śrī! Those flashes of lightning—truly desirous of seizing your splendor, that is, wishing to steal your beauty—and therefore struck by you most severely—otherwise, as the popular saying goes, "even those whose heads are cast down" (meaning those who undergo excessive exertion)—did not abandon their exhaustion or weariness. This statement is made because even when the word *taṭitaḥ* is reversed, it remains in its original state, and thus does not lose its final letter *t*.

There is a superimposition upon the word of a multiplicity that resides in the meaning. Here, although the head has been cut off, the fact that the suffix -tā remains cannot otherwise be explained; therefore, it is inferred that Lakṣmī must have struck them with great force.
Or rather, Mother, if Makaranda had not stolen this very essence of your words,
how could he have attained such expulsion from his status as a son?

"In the *sūnā* of this *makaranda*": for *sūnā* means a place of violence (*hiṃsāsthāna*). However, the true meaning [here] is "flower" (*kusuma*), because of its established usage; as the *Medinī* states: "The word *sūna* refers to a blossom or a flower; *sūnā* is feminine and refers to a daughter, a slaughterhouse, or the uvula. "The attainment of *udvāsana*" means crushing (*pramathana*); as Amara says in the list of synonyms for killing: "*udvāsana*, *pramathana*, *prathana*, and *ujjāsana*. This is derived from the root *vas* (meaning "affection," "cutting," or "taking away") belonging to the *curādika* class, with the suffix *lyuṭ* added after the prefix *ut*.

The "perfume" (parimala) is the excellent latent impression (vāsanā); its "attainment" (avāpti) is the true meaning [of the term]. Here, because the presence of the flower and the attainment of its removal (udvāsana)—established through the application of puns (*śleṣa*) regarding *makaranda*—would otherwise be inexplicable, it is inferred that he is a thief of the essence of the words of the Mother of the World.

Or rather: If this cow's milk, which was held by your word, had indeed been placed before us, why would it have fallen into the hands of a hunter at the very end, when a great danger had arrived in the midst? 2115.

O Blessed One! If this cow’s milk (*gavyam*) has not already been shaken off—that is, discarded—by Your word, then it must have first mounted a mountain (*agam adrim ārūḍham sat*); for it is well known in the world that those who have been driven away by their adversaries take refuge in the fastnesses of mountains. This is the intended meaning.

In the midst of the journey through the mountain region, when an extreme terror was reached due to the remembrance of your words which had become an adversary, and when an absolute fear was attained—at the very end, [the deer] became "one who has contracted a disease," a compound formed according to the rule *dvitīyā-śrita* etc., meaning one who has acquired a malady. The sense is that for those utterly bewildered by excessive fear, even physical illness can arise. From what cause would this occur? The sense is that the cow attained such a state solely because it was shaken by your words.

In the alternative interpretation, however, "śabda" (sound) is the primary referent. In this view, the word division is: *puraḥ*, *gaṃ*, *atibhaye*, *avāpteḥ*. Regarding the first meaning, in the analysis where "avāpte" ends in the locative case, there is the optional doubling of the letter *ś* of the word *śrī* situated later [in the compound], according to the rule "anaci ca. O *atibha*, O one of exceeding splendor (*atitejasvin*), O *śrīman*! The word *gavyaṃ gavyam* has *gaṃ*—the letter *ga*—placed before it, i.e., attained at the beginning, because the letter *ga* is heard at its opening.

Because of the occurrence—due to the application—of the *vaikārika* suffix beginning with *y* prescribed by the rule *ye ‘gopayasoryat*, and because of the application—due to the attainment—of the *av*-substitute in place of *o* prescribed by the rule *vānto yi pratyaye* between the letters *ga* and *ya* in the middle, [the word] would ultimately (*antataḥ*) at the end (*ante*) result in reaching the collection of phonemes beginning with *vy* (i.e., *vyeti*).

The point is that, according to the method already stated, it is only when the suffix *yat* is applied to the word *go* and the substitution of *ava* for *o* has occurred that the word *gavya* achieves its status as having a vowel (*ya*) at its end; it cannot be established otherwise. Here too, because the word *gavya* appears in the preceding verse, one must assume—on the grounds that it would otherwise be inexplicable—that the Lord’s speech possesses a sweetness won through a pun rooted in the identity between the word and its meaning. However, another distinct charm (or poetic figure) is quite evident.

Just as Dantavakra, who vied with the beauty of your arm, was struck by your hand upon his own mouth—I believe that otherwise, how could the lord of the mountain have become double-tongued like a serpent? (2116)

In the phrase "abhūddviradatvam," the word division is *viradatvam*. This means "the state of having lost one's tusks" (*vi-ra-da-nyaṃ vibhraṃśita-dantatvam*). "The state of being a double-tusked elephant" (*dviradatvam*) is the resolution [of the pun].

Or rather, O Hari, when you struck him hard on the mouth, the teeth of that fire which rivaled your splendor vanished under the guise of sparks; otherwise, how could he be a consumer of sacrificial oblations?

The analysis of the compound is *eṣaḥ ha viradanaḥ* (this is indeed the consumer of oblations). The indeclinable *ha* is used in the sense of well-knownness (*prasiddhi*), according to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *ha* is used in address and in the sense of well-knownness. Alternatively, *haviradana* is a single compound word, meaning "the consumer of oblations" (*hutāśana*). In these two examples as well, because the state of being a consumer of oblations (*viradatva*) or not being a consumer of oblations (*aviradanatva*) would otherwise be untenable, there is the conceptualization of the striking of the mouth by both the elephant and the fire, brought about through the superimposition of non-difference based on the foundation of paronomasia (*śleṣa*).

Just as the Blessed One, the son of Vasudeva, was born as a charioteer and a man of Pārada descent—this is indeed fitting; otherwise, how could the Vedic statement, "He is indeed the essence (rasa)," attain its meaningfulness? (2118)

It is logical that the Blessed One, the son of Vasudeva, was called Sūta and Pārada. In reality, however, "Sūta" means the charioteer of Arjuna. "Janipārada" is a compound word; he is "Pārada" because he grants the "pāram" (the further shore) of "janer" (birth). The meaning is that he bestows the supreme liberation (*niḥśreyasa*) which constitutes the further shore of the succession of births.
He who knows in truth thus my divine birth and action, upon leaving the body, does not take rebirth; he comes to Me, O Arjuna.
Thus it is sung:
"For those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, whose minds are assailed by sense-objects,
there is no other refuge whatsoever except for Viṣṇu as their boat."
For those rushing toward the shoreless wilderness of saṃsāra, which is so difficult to traverse,
the single prostration to Kṛṣṇa is the sole guide to the ford of liberation.

This and more are being recalled. Otherwise, if there were no such qualities as being mercury (*sūta*) and being quicksilver (*pārada*), how could the scriptural statement, "He is indeed *rasa*," be meaningful? The point is that its status as *rasa* alone makes its being mercury and quicksilver logical; for the traditional teaching (*anuśāsana*) states that the three words—*rasa*, *sūta*, and *pārada*—have identical meanings. The established fact is that *rasa* consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*). Here, the Lord’s nature as mercury and quicksilver is inferred from the impossibility of his being *rasa* otherwise.
Or, for example:
I believe that this [lotus] has stolen away the exquisite beauty of collyrium and Mount Añjana; otherwise, how could it have appeared as something stuck to the eyes of beautiful women? || 2119 ||

"Entering the eyes" (*akṣigata*) means being loathed by those with good vision, by the learned, and by women; as Amara states: "The term *akṣigata* refers to one who is loathed. Here, because the application of collyrium would otherwise be inexplicable for those with good vision, there arises the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that the Lord’s form possesses the defect of stealing away their splendor.

Or rather, I think that the rain-cloud has taken away from its own body the luster of your braided hair; otherwise, how could this lotus produce the infamy of being the abode of all the stationary beings within the world? (2120)

O Kamalā! I believe that this rain-cloud (ghanāghana), by means of its own body, has stolen—that is, taken away—the beauty of your braided hair from its own form. Otherwise, how could there be for this rain-cloud such a birth as one devoid of fame (apakīrti) within the world? That is to say, a birth characterized by infamy; the meaning is that his birth would be ignoble due to his state as a stationary being (sthāvara). The sense is that, owing to the fault of bodily actions of the aforementioned kind, he has obtained this birth as a stationary being.
Through defects of action born of the body, a man goes to the state of an immobile being;
through those of speech, to the state of birds or beasts; and through those of the mind, to the state of a low-born caste.

This is because of the traditional teaching of Manu. In this context, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of a general relationship; the meaning is "from this rain-cloud" (*ghanāghana*). [The compound] *varāpakīrtijani* is analyzed as follows: a collection of waters is *āpaṃ*; "excellent" is *vara*; thus, that which is both excellent and water is *varāpa*. *Kīrti* means mud (*kardama*). *Jani* means birth or origin. Thus, it is the origin of both [water and mud]. It is situated within the world, meaning it stands in the midst of the universe. The underlying idea is that from the rain-cloud alone does the production of water and mud arise in the world.

Here, the attribution of a physical defect in the form of the theft of the luster of Lakṣmī’s hair-tuft is based on the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the birth and acquisition of ill-repute among the stationary beings within the world by the rain-cloud (*ghanāghana*). As before, however, this is supported by *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
I believe that the multitude of stars was defiled by your toenails;
for otherwise, how could even this [moon], though called "the virtuous," attain its course through the sky?

O Mother! I believe that the multitude of stars—understood here as those who deliver one from the distress of calamities and the like—has defiled, or rather continues to defile, your nails by means of their rays, which are both words and beams of light. Otherwise, this multitude of stars, though possessing the name *sat* (meaning "good" or "existent"), would not truly deserve that appellation; for the actual state of things is such that, according to the rule "the asterism, the star, and the existent are called *sat*," the term *sat* is applied to them.

The sense is: how could one obtain the "vaihāyasī" state—the destiny associated with birds, which is the fruit of karma? For, according to the authority shown in the immediately preceding example, "through vocal [karma] one attains the state of birds or wild animals," this aerial state is established as the fruit of the defect of vocal action; thus, how could it possibly occur even for one perceived as a sentient being (*satva*)? The reality is that *vaihāyasī* refers to a state or movement existing in the atmosphere (*antarikṣa*). As the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *vihāyas* denotes a bird in the masculine, and the sky in both masculine and neuter."

Here, by the fact that the movement of the multitude of stars through the sky is otherwise inexplicable, it is inferred that they are being defiled by the speech of the agent whose instrument is the toe-nails of Lakṣmī’s feet.
Surely the stainless swan, having stolen the wealth of your smile, took up residence in your mind; otherwise, how could it dwell with the water-fowls while approaching the state of being a fish?

It is understood that he is a stainless twice-born one (*dvija*), a swan (*haṃsa*), and a pure Brahmin (*vipra*). He was surely a "stealer of the wealth of your smile" (*smitavasuhārī*) because he carried away the riches—the treasures—of your smile within your mind (*mānase*). Alternatively, he was captivating like the ray (*vasu*) of a smile; the meaning is that he was as charming as a smile and as bright as a smile. The construction is: "He attained existence (*abhavat sattām alabhata*) in the *Mānasa*," that is, in the lake of that name. The implication is that swans reside in the *Mānasa* lake.
Otherwise, even in the absence of such faults of mental action, [the state of] being an outcaste (*antyajatvam*)...

"Attaining the state of an outcaste through mental [sins]" refers to attaining the status of an outcaste as the fruit of the fault of mental action, as established by the previously cited statement; however, the true meaning is "possessing the letter *ka* at the end" (i.e., being a *kāpālika*). How could one dwell together with *plavas*—namely, *caṇḍālas*, or birds called *kāraṇḍavas*? Amara states: "Caṇḍāla, plava, mātaṅga, divākīrti, and janaṃgama [are synonyms for an outcaste]; and *madgu*, *kāraṇḍava*, and *plava* [are synonyms for a water-fowl]."

In passages such as "crowded with *haṃsa* and *kāraṇḍava* [birds]," the constant association of the *haṃsa* with the *kāraṇḍava* is described everywhere. Furthermore, the *Medinī* lexicon, beginning with "the word *plava* may mean swimming, a water-fowl, a frog, a dog-cooker (outcaste), or a beast," concludes by stating it refers to "the bird named *kāraṇḍava*. Thus, through the three examples shown here, the fruits of the defects of action produced by the three instruments (body, speech, and mind) are demonstrated in sequence.

In this case, the possession of the defect consisting of the theft of Lakṣmī’s smile and wealth—which is mental—is postulated because it would otherwise be impossible for the stainless twice-born man to attain the status of an outcaste.
Just as it appears here, I think that the bracelet placed upon your hand has turned into a crab; otherwise, how could this lotus possess both the face of a lion and the quality of pure luster? (2123)

O Mother! I think that the bracelet (*kaṭaka*) placed upon—that is, set upon—your *agrakara* (the hand-tip; meaning *karāgra*, the tip of the hand)—where the part and the whole are non-different according to the rule "hand-tip, tip-of-hand, etc., [are used] because of the difference-in-identity between quality and the possessor of the quality"—has attained the state of a crab (*karkaṭaka*), the state of being the Crab asterism (*karkaṭakarāśi*). For Amara says, "It may be *kulīra* or *karkaṭaka*," and Vidyāmādhava, in his list of synonyms for the Crab asterism, states, "It may be *karkaṭa*, *karkaṭaka*, or *karkī*."

In the alternative sense, the word *kaṭaka* (bracelet) attains the state of being a *karkaṭaka* (crab); that is, it acquires the nature of a crab. Otherwise, if its connection to the state of a crab were impossible, how could this *kaṭaka* possess a lion’s face or be counted as preceding the sign of Leo (*siṃharāśi*)? The point is that the sign of Leo follows immediately after the sign of Cancer (*karkaṭakarāśi*). [The compound] *siṃhamukha* means "that which has a face like the face of a lion."

That which is so described is called "tattva" (the true state of affairs), meaning the actual condition of things. It is well known that the bracelet possesses the form of a lion's face, as it is commonly referred to by people as a "lion-forehead-bracelet" (*siṃhalalāṭakaṭaka*). How could the station or the true nature of the pure-rayed moon be that of a crab (*karkaṭaka*)? The sense is that the lunar mansion was actually the domain of the crab, as indicated by the statement: "The Moon is the lord of the Crab. (Karkaṭa).

In reality, however, the meaning is that it is the "pada"—the place or support—of *śuci* (purity) and *dyuti* (splendor). Alternatively, it means it is the *pada* of *śucidyuti*, meaning it possesses a brilliance equal to fire (*agni*), and is thus exceedingly radiant. Here, the nature of the bracelet as a *karkaṭaka* (crab-claw) is inferred because its lion-mouthed shape would otherwise be inexplicable. Or, for example: "I believe the moon was crushed in a clash of weapons by the multitude of your fingernails; otherwise, how could the Lord of the Serpent Mountain (Śiva) bear a form so softly marked? (2124)

Why does that moon bear a form that is soft, tender, scarred, and mangled? For it is precisely because of being crushed by weapons and missiles that the form possesses softness and a state of being cut; this is the intended meaning. The term *mṛdulāñchitām* means "that which is both soft and marked" (*mṛduś cāsau lāñchitā ca mṛdulāñchitā*, feminine accusative singular); thus, it means "soft and stained. The rest is clear. Here, from the fact that it is stated "why does he bear a form that is soft and marked," and since this statement would otherwise be inexplicable, one infers that the moon’s state of being crushed by weapons and missiles was caused by friction with the Lord’s fingernails.
Or as it is said:
"O King, surely the two suns, having vied with your majesty and fame, have been struck upon their faces; otherwise, how could they have reached such an end and such exhaustion? (2125)

The term *puṣpavantau* refers to the sun and the moon. It possesses both the state of ending in a dental (*adantatvam*)—meaning the absence of a dental—and the state of ending in a *ta*-sound (*tāntatvam*), as well as the state of being weary (*klāntatvam*). In another sense, it has the state of ending in the vowel *a* and the state of ending in the letter *ta*. As Amarasimha states: "By a single expression, they are called *puṣpavantau*. They *aitām*, meaning they went. This word exists both as ending in a dental and as ending in a *ta*-sound, since we observe its usage in both ways: in the line, "The increase and decrease of the friend of the night-lotus [the moon] occurred during the eclipse of the *puṣpavantau*," and in the line, "The two eyes of that Lord are renowned for their possession of flowers (*puṣpavat-tayā*). In all these instances, the degree of being enlivened by *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is equal.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, the Chapter on Presumption (Arthāpatti), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on Non-apprehension (Anupalabdhi):
"If the determination of non-existence arises from the non-apprehension of something perceptible, the wise know that charming non-apprehension to be a poetic ornament."

The determination of non-existence produced by the non-apprehension of the perceptible is the figure of speech called *anupalabdhi* (non-apprehension); however, loveliness (*ramyatva*) is indeed inherent in all figures of speech.

If even a mere atom of fault were present in you, it would surely be perceived by those with clear vision; for indeed, a blemish is perceived upon the full moon, which is the sole treasury of auspicious qualities.

In this context, if even a trace of fault were to exist in the Blessed One, then it would certainly be perceived by those possessing the eyes of the Śrutis and Smṛtis—according to the statement, "The Śruti and Smṛti are the two eyes fashioned for the Brahmins. Since there is no such perception, and because this non-perception determines that there is no possibility for even a scent of fault, this is the figure of speech known as *anupalabdhi* (non-perception). The address "O sole treasure-house of auspicious qualities" contains the intention of the absolute absence of faults. "In the full moon" means in the complete orb of the moon.
A stain is perceived. Its perception occurs precisely because it exists; for if it were not present, it would certainly not be perceived—this is the negative example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*).
Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, the Lake of Non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Lake of Possibility (*saṃbhava*):
possibility is the determination of a lesser state due to the presence of something greater.
Possibility (*saṃbhava*) is the determination of the existence of the lesser when there is the existence of the greater, according to the principle that fifty exists within a hundred.

Just as your compassion, however many times it may be exercised, does not fail to attain eternal glory, by that very same principle, O Knower of Glory, tell me: could such glory not also arise for me? 2127.
By that very same [means], namely by compassion alone; she is eternal glory.
Just as when you, O dark cloud, rain down the most divine nectar for the prosperity of the world, how could I, who subsist like a cātaka bird, not also obtain it? (2128)

In both examples, the *sambhavapramāṇa* (the means of proof based on possibility), which consists in the ascertainment of the existence of the lesser given the existence of the greater, has been demonstrated. For example:

"O you who have long been tossed about in the great ocean of worldly existence, if you forcibly remember [the Lord] while trembling, then, upon attaining the Supreme, you shall abandon all torment; this same [attainment] shall be yours as well. (2129)
In this matter,
whether through knowledge or even through ignorance, by the glorification of Vāsudeva,
all that [evil] goes to dissolution, just like salt in water.
Even when remembered but once, Govinda quickly burns away the heap of sins accumulated by men over hundreds of years, just as fire consumes a pile of cotton.
When his name is uttered, even by one who is unwilling, a person is instantly liberated from all sins, just as deer are freed when terrified by a lion.
Hari removes sins even when remembered by those with wicked minds;
even when touched by chance, fire indeed burns.

By the aforementioned method, even for those who forcibly remember Śrī Hari, the attainment of the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra is possible; thus, this [attainment] shall also be yours—this is a demonstration of the proof of possibility (*saṃbhavapramāṇa*). In the word *paratāra*, the substitution of *tāra* for the word *tīra* occurs according to the rule: "In place of *tīra* following words denoting direction, the form *tāra* may optionally be expressed."
Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, the Chapter on Probability (*saṃbhava*), in the *Alaṃkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on Tradition (*aitihya*):

Where there is a traditional report such as "so they say" (*itihocuh*) and so forth, whose original speaker is not specified—that succession of oral report is the figure of speech known as Tradition (*aitihya*).
*Aitihya* (tradition) is the succession of oral reports such as "so they say" (*itihocuḥ*), whose original speaker is not specified.

Just as a tree, having been straight during the stage of its grain-like growth, bends down—why should this be so? A wise person, remembering this worldly maxim, should serve Hari from childhood. (2130)

In this context, for the wise person who recalls the worldly verse beginning with "During the ripening of the crops... and so forth, the meaning is that Hari should be served from childhood onwards, according to the principle stated: "A prudent man should practice the Bhāgavata duties here in this world from his youth. By the phrase "worldly verse" (*laukikagādhām*), it is shown that this is a traditional oral transmission (*pravādapāraṃparya*) whose original speaker is unspecified.
"O Śauri, as long as my memory does not perish, so long indeed shall karma not exist for me; for why would one apply collyrium to the eye until the eye itself perishes?"—so they say. (2131)

In this context as well, it should be understood that by the phrase "they say" (āhuḥ), a traditional succession of teachings from unspecified speakers is indicated, which serves as a reflection of the worldly verse beginning with "For what purpose is collyrium applied? (atrāpi tāvat kimartham añjanam).

Although these eight figures based on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇālaṃkāra*) have not been individually distinguished by those prior to Dīkṣita, nevertheless, since the figure of inference (*anumānālaṃkāra*) has been defined by everyone, the figures based on perception and the other means of valid cognition are also essentially defined. For there is no difference between perception and the others in their status as means of valid cognition, nor is there any distinction created by the presence or absence of aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*).

Therefore, with the intention that the mention of the figure of speech *anumāna* (inference) by the ancients is an illustration for all other figures based on the other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), Dīkṣita has examined and demonstrated all of them in the *Kuvalayānanda*; for this reason, we too have demonstrated them here.
Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, the Chapter on Tradition (Aitihya), in the *Alaṃkāramaṇihāra*. Now begins the Chapter on Conjunction (*Saṃsṛṣṭi*):
[it occurs] when all the figures of speech (*alaṃkṛti*) are combined as far as possible.
For, from the observation of their excellence in beauty, they appear like those of the worldly realm.
The status of *alaṃkāra* (poetic figure) shines forth as distinct through the method of Narasiṃha;
therefore, we shall here state its determination according to the opinion of the ancients.

Now, one might ask: when several of the aforementioned figures of speech coexist in a single instance, is it merely each individual figure of speech, or is it a distinct figure of speech produced by their combination according to the analogy of Narasiṃha (the man-lion)?

To this, some say that it is not proper to admit a separate figure of speech, because there is neither a new name nor a specific aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) beyond the respective individual figures of speech themselves. Others, however, maintain that it is indeed a distinct figure of speech according to the analogy of Narasiṃha; for it is unproven that there is an absence of both a new name and a specific aesthetic charm.

Just as in the case of worldly ornaments—such as gold, pearls, coral, sapphires, emeralds, and so forth—which possess distinct beauties that mutually enhance one another, there is an excellence of beauty produced by their combination; likewise, here too, the presence of a specific aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) in their conjunction is witnessed solely by the hearts of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*). Therefore, this combination in the form of Narasiṃha (the Man-Lion) is indeed a distinct figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*). It is with reference to this view that it was stated: "The status of being a figure of speech shines forth separately."
When figures of speech are blended with one another to such an extent that they are intermingled like sesame seeds and rice grains, that is called *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture).
The meaning is that *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling) occurs when figures of speech are combined such that their distinction is clearly perceivable, according to the analogy of sesame seeds and rice grains.
The commingling (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of two figures of sound with each other, of two figures of sense with each other,
and of both together— this is considered to be threefold.
Among these, the first is as follows:

"O Destroyer of Madhu, having spent my life in service to kings whose minds were stained by the impurities of the Kali age, I shall now, through your conduct, shake off the burden of my weariness. (2132)

Here, there is a *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture) of the two sound-figures (*śabdālaṅkāra*)—alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and yamaka—which are to be described later and which reside respectively in the first and second halves [of the verse] independently of one another.
May that one named Śrī Vāsana— whose face has attained victory over the blue lotus, who possesses the moon as his crest-jewel like a bull-bearing mountain,
and who is the auspicious fortune of the worlds— protect us.

Here, there is a combination (saṃsṛṣṭi) of the poetic figures—successive metaphor (paraṃparitarūpaka), simile (upamā), and feigned denial (kaitavāpahnuti)—which are mutually independent of one another.

Just as the beauty of the Tamāla and Sāla trees shines amidst rows of forests purifying the serpent-mountain (Girivraja), may that Supreme Person, whose mind is captivated by Ramā, protect me, who am afflicted by sin and distressed.

He who shines in the royal row of those purifying forests belonging to the mountain of serpents (Pannaganaga); he whose splendor is like the splendor of the Tamāla tree; he whose mind is captivated by Ramā (Śrī)—may that Supreme Person (Paramapuruṣa) protect me, who am afflicted by sins, may He protect me intensely. [The suffix *yaṅ* is elided.

Here, there is a commingling (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of the verbal ornaments of alliteration (*chekānuprāsa*), *vṛttyanuprāsa*, and *yamaka*, along with the semantic ornaments of simile (*upamā*) and indirect expression (*paryāyokti*).

Just as we take refuge in Him alone, so let us worship Him with delight—Him who is embraced by the golden-hued Bhaya; O Vāmadeva, even in the midst of great calamity, let us call out to You, "O Refuge! || 2135 ||

We take refuge in—that is, we surrender to—that very same glorious Nārāyaṇa, who is embraced by Ramā; that is to say, he whose radiance and splendor are born of gold, meaning he is golden-hued. O Vāmadeva, O Virūpākṣa! Even in the face of great calamity, shall we call upon you as our refuge? The meaning is: we shall certainly not call upon you. One should not even entertain the possibility of addressing you as a refuge.

The sense is: "How much more so regarding the discourse on seeking refuge? Following the principle stated in the saying, "When a great calamity has arrived, the Lord Hari must be remembered," we worship that very Lord of Śrī alone; we do not even utter a word of "protect me" directed toward you. The sense is: "O sir, we are those who are steadfast in the vow of Ambarīṣa, [saying], 'I do not worship anyone else, having abandoned Govinda. By the phrase "embraced by Ramā," the [Lord's] majesty... (Note: The provided source text appears to be incomplete at the end.)

By the word "vāmadeva," its essence as water (*vāta-sarasatva*) is indicated, and its deviation from that—its curvature—is also suggested. Here, the verbal ornaments (*śabdālaṅkāra*) characterized by the forward and reverse order (*anuloma-prātilomya*) of five syllables in the first and second halves of the verse are combined (*saṃsṛṣṭa*) with the semantic ornament (*arthālaṅkāra*) of *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification).
Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, the Section on Conjunction (*saṃsṛṣṭi*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*. Now begins the Section on Commixture (*saṃkara*):
wherein these ornaments [blend] with one another like milk and water.
Those who know poetry understand that if these were to be mixed, it would constitute this defect known as *saṃkara* (confusion).
The meaning is that *saṃkara* (commixture) occurs when figures of speech with indistinct boundaries are combined, according to the analogy of milk and water.
Thus, this [combination] occurs through the relationship of subordinate and principal, through equal primacy,
through doubt, and likewise through the entry into a single expressive word.
The fourth is declared by the illustrious Appayadīkṣita to be *saṃkara* (admixture);
thus, five types of figures (*alaṃkāra*) are considered to have the form of Nṛsiṃha.
Thus, the five ornaments beginning with *saṃsṛṣṭi* have the sense of being like the form of Narasiṃha.
If the primary ornament is revitalized by means of a subordinate ornament,
then that is accepted as a commingling (*saṃkara*) based on the relationship between the subordinate and the principal.

Just as the young elephant-calf of the flower-arrowed god (Kāma) has raised its trunk-tip from the nectar-ocean of the moon’s face, so does the musk-tilaka shine upon the serpent-mountain moon (Śiva).

Just as in my own *Prapannānanda-stuti*, I surely meditate upon the pearl of the Goddess, which was spat out by the great king of fish—her eyes—as they sported in the lake of her face’s luster, and which has now become lodged in the cavity of her nostrils. (2137)

In both of these examples, the *paraṃparita-rūpaka* (successive metaphor) in "the nectar-ocean of the beauty of the face" (*vadanasuṣamāsudhāmbudhi*) and so forth, and the [metaphor] in "the lake of the splendor of the face" (*vadanarucihrada*) and so forth, serve as the subordinate elements (*aṅga*) for the two *utprekṣās* (poetic fancies), because they give life to them; for such *utprekṣās* do not arise in the absence of the metaphors. Therefore, there is a *saṃkara* (commixture) between these two, characterized by the relationship of subordinate and principal.

Just as one who does not open their eye—soiled by the film of non-discrimination—with the probe of the collyrium of perfect discrimination, becomes blind from birth; who indeed could be more wretched than such a person? (2138)

For those lacking discrimination and knowledge, the "film" (paṭala) is indeed a film—a specific disease that covers the faculty of sight; by this, the eye is rendered turbid. "Excellent discrimination" (suviveka) is the discernment of the true nature of the three principles (tattvas). The rest is clear. Here, because the determination of being blind from birth is established through the metaphor (rūpaka) beginning with "the film of non-discrimination," there is a commingling (saṃkara) of these two figures based on a relationship of primary and subordinate (aṅgāṅgibhāva), specifically the figure of "poetic indication" (kāvyaliṅga).

O delighter of the Yadus, just as a fresh ornament made of peacock feathers was placed by you upon your head, so too did it seek to serve as a crest-ornament for the capture of the doe-like young women of Vraja.

A fresh, new, and beautiful ear-ornament (*vataṃsa*) was fashioned and placed [upon her]; it attained the state of a *vitaṃsa*—that is, the state of being a snare for binding deer. In the alternative sense, the word *vataṃsa* is "new" (*navaḥ*), meaning it is devoid of the letter *va*.

It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound preceded by the negative particle *na*. Being "fashioned" (*vihitaḥ*)—meaning that which has had the modification (*viḥ*) consisting of the letter *ha* placed (*hitaḥ*) precisely in the position of the letter *va*—it thus attained the state of being the word *vitaṃsa*. Here, the metaphor (*rūpaka*) "the young women of Vraja as does” is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the *nidarśanā* (illustrative simile) based on the meaning of the word *vitaṃsatām*.
Just as lightning exists within a dark cloud, so may it be with you who abide within the crest of the Self; yet how could you, O Supreme Self, be like lightning within a dark cloud? (2140)

O Supreme Self! By this, the term "Supreme Self" (paramātman) heard in the scripture, "In the middle of that crest-lock the Supreme Self is situated," is recognized. The "crest-lock of the Self" (ātma-śikhā), described as "in its middle is the flame of fire," is a flame in the form of the inner self (pratyagātman); for the commentary on the Upaniṣad states, "The flame of fire is the flame of the Self, the radiance of the Self. The sense is: [I bow] to You, whose divine form is dark like a blue rain-cloud.

When the letter *antastha* is present, according to the manner stated in the phrase "of that crest-lock" (*tasyāśśikhāyāḥ*), she is one whose crest-lock has a dark cloud within; thus she is described as being like lightning, in accordance with the Śruti: "Resplendent like a streak of lightning standing in the midst of a dark cloud. The meaning is that she resembles lightning within a dark cloud because she rests upon the Lord’s body, which is dark like a dark cloud.

The author of the *Upaniṣadbhāṣya* remarked: "The absence of the prior placement of the qualifier 'nīlatoyada' (dark cloud) in the word 'madhyastha' is a Vedic [archaism]. This is an *abhūtopamā* (impossible simile). How indeed can you be "the lightning within the dark cloud"? Since you reside in the midst of the "dark-cloud-like" crest of the Self (*ātma-śikhā*), you may well be called "the lightning within the dark cloud"; however, the point is that such a manifestation of yours is astonishing because of the absence of any [external] cause for it.

In reality, however, the resolution is as follows: the word *nīlatoyada* (dark cloud) is situated within [the compound] of which the word *vidyut* (lightning) is a part; that is to say, when the word *nīlatoyada* is inserted into the middle of the syllables of *vidyut*, the resulting form is *vinīlato yadadyutiḥ* (shining like a dark cloud). Thus, it is so described because it shines like a dark-blue water-bearing cloud. Here, the simile (*upamā*) expressed in the first half-verse is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the aesthetic emotion (*vibhāva*) expressed in the second half-verse, and it is embellished by the figure of speech *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
O lotus-eyed one, those who have been delivered by you never again experience the transformations of *prakṛti* due to delusion; yet even they remain bound by that very [delusion]. (2141)

O lotus-eyed one! Those people who have been delivered—meaning liberated—from *bhava* (existence) by You, those people never at any time experience the transformation of *prakṛti*, that is, the world of material nature, due to reversal—that is to say, because of returning again. This is because of such scriptural declarations as, "This is the path of the gods, the path of Brahman; those who proceed by this do not return to this human whirlpool," and because of the traditional teaching, "But having come to Me, O son of Kuntī, rebirth does not exist," and because of the Sūtra, "Non-return [is established] from the word. This is the intended meaning.

In this context, the word *tāritāḥ* never undergoes a change or alteration (*anyadhābhāva*) from its original form (*prakṛti*) due to reversal or inversion; that is to say, it remains exactly as it was before. Nevertheless, despite being "crossed over" (*tārita*) through such a connection with the original form, the sense is that they remain "as before. Thus, there is a contradiction (*virodha*), for those who are "exhausted" (*tāntāḥ*)—meaning possessed of the weariness caused by hunger, thirst, and so forth—are [here described as] "crossed over."

The resolution is that the word *tāritāḥ*, even when there is a reversal [of meaning], is established as *tāritāḥ* just as before; thus, it ends precisely in the letter *t*. Here, the poetic figure *kāvyaliṅga*, embellished by *śleṣa* (paronomasia), serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the *pūrvarūpa* (prior form) consisting in the persistence of the previous state, namely, that they again end in *t*.
Or rather:

O Acyuta, the submarine fire (Āurva), desiring to conquer your splendor but defeated by it and unable to offer resistance, has plunged into the ocean while consuming poison; such is the fate of the Vāḍava fire.

O Acyuta! Aurva, the submarine fire of the mare’s mouth (*baḍabāmukhāgni*), consuming poison and drinking water—such is the course and the state of both the Brāhmaṇa Aurva and the submarine fire: namely, that they fall into the ocean by consuming poison due to their inability to avenge an insult from one who disregards them. In the other sense (the literal meaning), it refers to dwelling in the ocean by drying up its waters. The rest is clear. Here, there is a relationship of principal and subordinate between the *viṣama* (incongruity) and the *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration), both of which are permeated by *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

Just as one who has experienced the power of a small spark might wish to weigh it against Your great majesty, O Blessed One, fire is surely insufficient for that task; therefore, they call it "Anala" (the Insufficient).

"Kṛśānubhāvaḥ" means one by whom a diminished majesty or power has been attained; he is so called because he possesses the state of being a "kṛśānu" (fire). According to Amara, "anubhāva" refers to both majesty and power; "prabhāva" refers to prowess, and "dhāma" means splendor or brilliance—meaning his prowess and splendor. He is certainly unable to equal [the other]. Therefore, they say that this fire, this "anala," is "aparyāpta," meaning incompetent; the truth is that it is merely a name desired for the sake of the word "anala. They speak thus.

Herein, the distinction is that the etymological analysis of the word *anala* ("fire") serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) for the poetic figure *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic cause), which consists in establishing the insufficiency of the comparison; this *kāvyaliṅga* is based upon a superimposition of non-difference (*abhedādhyavasāna*) supported by the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) of the two meanings conveyed by the word *kṛśānubhāva*.

However, some maintain that such a commingling (saṃkara) exists not only between figures of sense (arthālaṃkāra), but also between figures of sound (śabdālaṃkāra); thus they speak of the commingling of the two sound-figures *yamaka* and *anulomapratiloma*. An example of this is as follows:

"O Lord, renowned in various Vedas, may she—who is ever established in devotion, who protects those who bow [to her], who is the ocean of grace, and who is the consort of the God who has no enemies—protect me as well. (Deve nānāvede prathite nityaṃ sthitā natānavitum | Deve'nā'vede vaiṣā mām api ramā kṣamā-jaladhiḥ ||) In this verse, the sound-figure *yamaka* is commingled with the sound-figure *anulomapratiloma*. This is because the first half-verse reads identically when its syllables are reversed, while the second half-verse reads identically when its syllables are read forward and backward. Thus, both figures coexist within the same metrical unit.

"In various Vedas" (*nānāvede*) means "in various kinds of scriptural revelation" (*nānāvidhaśrutau*), where the singular number is used by way of genus (*jātyekavacanam*). "In the well-known God" (*pratithe deve*) means in the Blessed Lord Śrīnivāsa, who is the Lord of All and is propounded by all the Vedas. "To protect" (*avitum*) means to save those who have bowed down and sought refuge. She is "constantly present" (*nityaṃ sthitā*); the sense is that if she were absent from this state for even a moment, the Lord—becoming heated with anger born from perceiving the offenses of those who bow before him—would no longer be inclined toward their protection.

*Ānā* means she who brings [beings] and causes them to breathe; it is formed with the suffix *ac* from the root *ān*. She is the *inā*—the sovereign power—of the *devas*, namely the world-protectors such as Indra and others; thus, she is the *ānā*, the one who sustains the life-force of those gods. This refers to the Ocean of Forgiveness (*kṣamā-jaladhi*), meaning she is expert in pardoning the offenses of those like me. The thought is that even for one like me, who is foremost in committing a continuous succession of manifold transgressions, she—*Ramā*—will surely protect me. This is an expression of possibility: "She will surely know [my state], and she will surely protect me."

May she who is the ornament of the Bull-Hill (Śrīśaila), whose navel is like the lotus, who possesses a river-like luster, and who is full of grace, protect you; and may she also be his ornament, she who has a navel like a lotus, whose radiance is like that of the sky, and who is not devoid of essence.

*Sārasanābha* and *padmanābha*: in the rule "ac praty-āṅ-van-vi," the suffix *ac* is applied by means of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of a rule) following the word *aj*; alternatively, its ending in the vowel *a* is to be justified through its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group. *Nadīnabhāna*: the splendor (*bhāna*) of him who possesses a splendor like that of the Lord (*inaḥ*, i.e., the master) of rivers (*nadīnām*), namely the Ocean (*udanvān*).

The meaning is: she whose form is dark like the ocean is *prakāśa* (illuminated). She is *sarasā*—full of passion, full of bliss, or accompanied by the Earth (*Bhū*). She is the ornament of the Vṛṣagiri mountain, that is to say, Śrīnivāsa. "May she protect"—this is the sense of the first half-verse. Furthermore, she who is his ornament—that is, she who serves as the primary adornment for Śrīnivāsa as well—is indeed Śrī herself; such is the intended meaning. May she protect.

The word "tvit" (indeed) is also to be supplied here. She is so called because she shines with a *sārasana*, meaning a girdle or waistband. The goddess Śrī is not one whose splendor (*bhāḥ*)—that is, her light—is "nadīna," meaning meager or small; nor is she "asarasā," meaning sapless; rather, she is indeed "sarasa," full of essence. This is the meaning of the second half of the verse.

In the first verse here, there is a commingling (*saṃkara*) of the subordinate and principal relationship (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) between the two figures of sound (*śabdālaṃkāra*), namely *yamaka* and *anulomapratiloma*, because they stand in mutual dependence—one upon the other—within the first and third quarters and within the second and fourth quarters respectively. However, the author of the *Sarvasva* maintains: "In such a case, since there is no relationship of mutual assistance (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*) between the two figures of sound, a commingling of the subordinate and principal relationship is not appropriate; rather, it is simply a commingling (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of two figures of sound."

Alternatively, he [the author of the *Kāvyapradīpa*] stated here that "two verbal figures of speech have entered into a single expressive word. However, the author of the *Kāvyadarpaṇa* argued: "In such a case, because two verbal figures of speech mutually impart an excellence of charm (*vaicitryātiśaya*) to one another, there is indeed *saṃkara* (commixture) and not *saṃsṛṣṭi* (coexistence); for even in the absence of a relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*), the fact that they serve as causes for mutual excellence of charm remains intact. Furthermore, even when a relationship of primary and subordinate exists, it is precisely this quality of being a cause for mutual excellence of charm that serves as the distinct determinant of *saṃkara*."
A certain ornament is elevated when it contains another ornament as its core;
if, however, it occurs simultaneously with another, there is a commixture (*saṃkara*) of equal prominence.
I praise the crown of the serpent-king, which, like a monarch constantly proclaiming his sovereignty by cherishing it with his own head, bears the golden splendor of Fortune.

He who perpetually—that is, eternally—proclaims his own sovereignty (*sāmrājya*) to those who cherish their own selves with their heads, who bear [the crown], and who offer salutations; a sovereignty defined elsewhere as: "He who has performed the *Rājasūya* sacrifice, who is the lord of the circle of kings, and who rules by command over kings, is a *Samrāṭ*," and in another context as "he becomes self-ruling (*svarāṭ*"), which refers to the liberated state of mastery. The sense is that without the wearing of such a crown, the renown of being a *Samrāṭ* would be impossible. In the alternative sense (of the metaphorical interpretation), it means spreading or extending it extensively, without contraction.

I shall praise Śrīnivāsa—who, like the mountain Śeṣādri (the serpent-mountain) itself, bears the *kāñcanalakṣmī* (the splendor or abundance of gold; alternatively, the goddess Lakṣmī of ineffable majesty)—as the crown of that king who is the mountain of serpents. "I shall praise" (*īḍīya*) is the first person singular of the optative (*liṅ*) of the root *īḍ*, meaning "to praise."

Here, the hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) consisting of the identification of the Lord Śrīnivāsa with a crown—serving as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) rooted in the pun-based hyperbole beginning with "those who fondle him with their heads"—is itself elevated by the metaphor (*rūpaka*) which superimposes the behavior of a great king upon the serpent-king. This occurs because the aforementioned pun-based hyperbole benefits both [the subordinate and the principal figures].

Therefore, since the hyperbole of identification and the metaphor share the same time and possess an equal manifestation of beauty in relation to one another, there is parity of importance (*samaprādhānya*) due to the absence of any decisive factor for preference.
Or for example:
"Alas! The flute, rendered helpless by the touch of your hand, speaks with passion as it surely drinks the exceedingly sweet nectar of your lips—a flavor unattainable by others—O Śauri! (2147)

O Śauri! Your flute, made of a bamboo stalk, has been rendered helpless—subjugated by the touch of Your hand; in one sense, because it is dependent upon You, and in another, through the emergence of *sāttvika* emotions such as paralysis (*stambha*) and fainting (*pralaya*). It is likewise described as having "passionate conversation" (*sarāga-ālāpa*): in one sense, its mutual speech is full of affection; in another sense, it is filled with the intonation of musical modes (*rāgas*) such as Śaṅkarābharaṇa and others as taught in the science of music (*gāndharvaveda*).

It is so called because it exists together [with passion]. "Hanta!"—this exclamation expresses the joy born from contemplating the attainment of such good fortune as this: that she indeed drinks the exceedingly sweet nectar of your lower lip, which is difficult for others to obtain. Here, the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the flute’s tasting of the Lord’s nectar is nourished by the figure of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) based on the identity of the two (the flute and the heroine) through the foundation of punning (*śleṣa*), such as in the word *sarāgā* ("full of passion" / "red"). This fancy is further nourished by the figure of concealed metaphor (*samāsokti*), which consists in the superimposition of the behavior of a heroine upon the flute; for the punning of words like *sarāga* serves to enliven both figures simultaneously.

Therefore, because the suggested metaphor (*utprekṣā*) and the compound expression (*samāsokti*) are established as occurring simultaneously, and because the metaphor of tasting the nectar of her lower lip would lack a basis without the core of the compound expression, there too the two elements possess equal prominence.
Just as this necklace—charming, exceedingly playful, and lustrous—is embraced by the heart of the Lord of Śrī, it seems to move with incessant shimmering as its silken cloth slips away. (2148)

She is charming, lovely, and in the bloom of youth; she is exceedingly graceful, fickle, and restless. Elsewhere, she is intensely devoted to various graceful amorous sports (*vilāsa*), affectionate, and full of tender endearments. This necklace (*hārayaṣṭi*) is perceived as a heroine (*nāyikā*) due to its feminine gender. Being embraced by the heart of the Lord of Śrī, it has rays streaming forth and spreading out, thus it is "galadaṃśukā" (one from whose cloth [or rays] drops [or spreads]); the suffix *kap* is applied here according to the rule *aśeṣād vibhāṣā*.

Elsewhere, she is described as such because her *aṃśuka*—her garment—is slipping and falling away from that very spot. She goes, so it is imagined, to the continuous (*anavarata*) radiance (*ullāsa*) or manifestation; in another sense, she goes to the delight (*ullāsa*) or curiosity (*kutūhala*) in fresh enjoyment (*navarata*), that is, in new sexual union. This is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).

Here, the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*)—consisting in the attainment of incessant splendor caused by the embrace of Śrīnivāsa’s chest, which is based on a metaphor (*atiśayokti*) rooted in the identification [of the necklace] with the heroine through a superimposition (*adhyavasāya*) founded on the pun (*śleṣa*) beginning with "the innocent one" (*mugdha*)—is supported precisely by that [first] metaphor, which is itself supported by the pun beginning with "slipping garment" (*galadaṃśuka*).

This [second] fancy is further infused with the "poetic inclusion" (*samāsokti*) consisting in the attribution of the heroine’s behavior to the necklace-string. Because these two are equal in being supported by the pun, because they occur simultaneously, and because their excellence of beauty depends upon one another, they possess equal prominence (*samapradhānatā*), as in the previous case.

May the Lord whose abode is the Vṛṣācala mountain be victorious— he who is adorned with auspicious qualities, whose splendor surpasses even the foremost of clouds, and who is like the central gem of the three Vedas.

"Unreleased" (*āmukta*) means never separated from, or eternally endowed with, auspicious qualities (*kalyāṇaiḥ guṇaiḥ*) such as good character (*sauśīlya*) and the like; or alternatively, "bound" (*saṃbaddha*). In the other sense, he is "bound" (*āmukta*) by auspicious qualities in the form of golden threads; or else, he is "āmukta" because he has pearls (*muktāḥ*) on all sides (*ā*) which constitute his auspicious qualities. This is a *karmadhāraya* compound where both members function as adjectives. According to the *Ratnamālā*, "kalyāṇa" refers to auspiciousness and heaven.

"Payodharāgresaraḥ" means the foremost among clouds; "ghanāghanaśreṣṭhaḥ" means the best of rain-clouds. "Atiśāyinī" refers to that which surpasses or exceeds them—thus, he whose "śrīḥ," or splendor of his divine form, is such [is so described]. In another sense, "payodharāgre" is analyzed as separate words: it means possessing exceeding beauty upon the necklaces (sareṣu) on the tops of the breasts (payodharayoḥ upari). He stands like the central gem of a necklace (taralaḥ), situated in the midst of the string of the triple Veda (trayyāḥ śruteḥ). The rest is easy to understand.

Here, the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the Lord’s trembling sound, which is sustained by the word-play (*śleṣa*) and hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) on words such as "virtuous qualities" (*kalyāṇaguṇa*), is itself sustained by including within it the metaphorical identification (*samāsokti*) consisting of the superimposition of the behavior of a heroine onto the Veda. Since both [the *utprekṣā* and the *samāsokti*] are equally supported by the word-play, they possess equal prominence (*samaprādhānya*).
O Hari, since you surely desire to liberate the gods, sages, and ancestors from their bonds,
how else could you bear the burden of their deliverance while bestowing prosperity upon them? (2150)

O Hari! This [particle] here serves as an embellishment for the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "from the debts to the gods, sages, and ancestors," specifically "to the ancestors" (pitṛbhyaḥ), there is a long vowel by rule (*savarṇadīrgha*) according to *akassavarṇe*. I surmise that you surely wish to liberate—meaning you intend to release—the humble ones who have come for refuge. Otherwise, how could this be? For these humble ones, the "interest" (*vṛddhi*) refers to the amount to be paid, namely the substance to be taken by the creditor in excess of the principal; that [interest].

In the case of the [other] side, "bestowing" (*vitaran*) means providing *vṛddhi*—that is, prosperity (*abhyudaya*), or abundance in the form of liberated sovereignty. Regarding the word *vṛddhi*, the *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *vṛddhi* occurs in the sense of growth, yoga, a medicinal herb from the group of eight, a future time, prosperity, abundance, and also a woman. Here, the suffix *śatṛ* (present participle) is used according to the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ*; in this context, "cause" (*hetu*) refers to the result. Thus, the meaning is "in order to bestow. Regarding the "burden of debt" (*uddhārabhara*), it refers to the excessive weight of the loan; as the lexicon says: "Debt (*ṛṇa*) is also called *paryudañcana*."

"Uddhāraḥ" (extraction/rescue), according to Amara. In the alternative sense, following the manner stated in the verse, "I am their deliverer from the ocean of death and worldly existence," you bear the burden of rescuing [them] from the sea of *saṃsṛti* (transmigration). Here, because the bearing of the burden of rescue—preceded by the granting of growth—is otherwise inexplicable, the Lord's desire for the discharge of debt (*ṛṇavimocanecchā*) is inferred.

"O King, he who has with his whole being taken refuge in Nārāyaṇa, the worthy refuge and teacher of the world, is neither a servant nor a debtor to the gods, sages, beings, himself, or the ancestors. (Bhagavadgītā 9.22)

Thus, the meaning of the verse is here connected. Here, the presumption of the stated matter (*uktārthāpatti*) is elevated by means of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) based on the identification [of the two meanings] through the medium of paronomasia (*śleṣa*) in the words "interest" (*vṛddhi*) and "recovery" (*uddhāra*). This [presumption] is further elevated when conjoined with the *samāsokti* (condensed expression) characterized by the superimposition of the legal practice of a guarantor upon the Blessed One. Since the assistance provided by the aforementioned paronomasia, the mutual dependence for the manifestation of beauty, and the simultaneity of these two are equal, they possess equal prominence (*samaprādhānya*).
Even in the absence of simultaneity, if two figures of speech are elevated by a single factor,
that too is a "Commixture of Equal Importance" (samaprādhānya-saṃkara).

Just as the Triple Veda weaves together the abundant blossoms of your fame by means of your virtues, so too do the wise, grasping that [fame], fashion it into the braided tresses of the quarters of space.

Here, although there is a difference in time between the two poetic fancies (*utprekṣā*), they possess equal prominence, because they are presented by two distinct sentences that are independent of one another. This is because the first fancy does not depend upon the second, as the latter merely subsists on the metaphor (*rūpaka*) consisting of the collection of the flowers of fame (*kīrti*).

Nor should it be argued that this is merely a *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling) of two metaphors (*utprekṣā*), as in the verse "Darkness seems to smear the limbs; the sky seems to rain collyrium. This is because the present case differs from *saṃsṛṣṭi*: here, the excellence of beauty is brought forth through the sequence of the two metaphors, which follows the sequence of worldly established conventions, ornaments, and temporal priority. Therefore, these two metaphors are of equal importance, like the new moon and other rites, insofar as they are means to a single end. Furthermore, this type of *saṃkara* (blending) is indeed an innovation of Dīkṣita himself.

"But the authors of the *Rasikarañjanī* maintain that the former [type of mixture]—this mixture of equal prominence—is not recognized as a distinct variety by others, on the grounds that the first type is already covered by the relation of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*), while the second is covered by 'commingling' (*saṃsṛṣṭi*). The details of this should be seen in that very work.
Where neither a proof nor a refutation is observed for the inclusion of either one of two alternatives, that is a confusion of doubt.

Where two contradictory figures of speech manifest simultaneously in a single place, and no evidence is seen either to support or to refute the acceptance of one over the other, there occurs the commingling of doubt due to indecision.

O Śauri, alas, those who compose the Kośas, while speaking of Kātyāyanī— who is all-auspiciousness itself and whose auspiciousness never falters due to the granting of boons by you— are themselves nothing but mere cocoon-makers.

The meaning is: she who possesses perpetual auspiciousness, being one whose auspiciousness never falters due to the granting of a boon by you. Here, the narrative from the *Padma Purāṇa* is to be recalled: when Lord Mahādeva was defeated in the battle with Bāṇāsura, Bhavānī, being terrified, made a request to that very Lord, and he granted her a boon characterized by perpetual auspiciousness.

Therefore, the authors of lexicons—referring specifically to those who composed works such as the *Ratnamālā* and the *Liṅgānuśāsana*—state that the Goddess Bhavānī, also known as Kātyāyanī, who is called by that name because she possesses auspiciousness in every way (*sarvaprakāramāṅgalyaśālinī*) and is thus "all-auspicious" (*sarvamaṅgalā*), is indeed Kātyāyanī; for the lexicographer Umā states: "Kātyāyanī is Umā; she who is half-old, clad in saffron robes, and whose husband has departed [is] Kātyāyanī—the one who is half-old, clad in saffron robes, and widowed. Thus, they are indeed the authors of lexicons.

The word *hanta* expresses the sorrow caused by the utterance and contemplation of such a loathsome name. In this context, the definition of a "lexicographer" (*kośakṛt*) provided by lexicographers is subverted by its lack of utility, thereby implying their lack of discernment; thus, there may be the figure of speech *vidhi* (prescription). Alternatively, there may be the first type of *apahnuti* (concealment), based on the superimposition that "lexicographers are merely lexicographers—that is, silkworms—and not authors possessed of discernment. Since no evidence is seen—neither a probative nor a subverting proof—to determine which of these two is the case, there is a commingling of these two figures through doubt (*saṃdehasaṃkara*).

May that tilaka-mark of musk, which sports upon the mountain-like forehead of the Goddess, protect us—[the tilaka] which produces the notion of a boat in the pair of fish-eyes sporting in the ocean of her face’s radiance. 2153.

Here, if there is an intention to convey that "intellect" (dhiyam) is of the nature of an error, the resolution lies in the figure of speech *bhrāntimad* (illusion); if there is an intention to convey it as a supposition, the resolution lies in *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). Due to this indecision between the two, there is a commingling (*saṃkara*) based on doubt.

Just as certain noble-born trees, whose essence is far removed from the springtime and which flourish at the arrival of the clouds, may have fine blossoms yet fall in vain because they do not bear any great fruit; so too are some people. (2154)

Even some wise men (*sumanasaḥ*), though born of noble lineage (*sujātibhavāḥ*) and produced by great scriptures (*ghanair āgamaiḥ*)—being far removed from the nature of Mādhava and remaining at a distance from the arrival (*āgamena*) of great beings—fall away in vain due to the non-attainment of the supreme fruit (*mahāphala*) consisting of liberation (*niḥśreyasa*).

Except for Mādhava (the spring), those beautiful species of *jāti* creepers (*mālatī*) which exist far away, being made to bloom and flourish by the arrival of the clouds (the rainy season)—even though some of these flowers have attained the state of blossoming, they fall away in vain because they do not grasp any great fruit. The sense is that since *jāti* flowers do not open during the time of spring, yet bloom in the rainy season without bearing fruit, their falling away is indeed in vain.

Here, there is a *saṃdehasaṃkara* (blending through doubt) among these three possibilities: either it is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), since the praise of the unstated *jātī* flower culminates in the stated scholars of the aforementioned kind; or it is *samāsokti* (speech of brevity), since from the account of the stated scholars there arises the manifestation of the conduct of the unstated *mālatī* flower; or it is *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the relevant and the irrelevant. Because one cannot determine with certainty which is the case, there is a blending through doubt.
O Lotus, if a young sprout, having long served beneath your feet with its head bowed low, were to become a beautiful cluster of blossoms, it would then be worthy of worshipping your feet. (2155)

O Kamalā! A goat (bastah) has, for a long time—over a vast duration—remained with its head downward, its head bowed in devotion; this is the inner meaning, as it is the natural state of a goat. However, the true reality is that it has been served, worshipped, and consumed. O beloved one! If there is a beautiful cluster (stabakaḥ) of blossoms, let it attain the state of being born from a cluster which is the fruit resulting from tasting the sprouts of your feet.

The intended meaning is: "If it were to go [to its proper place]," then it would be worthy of worship at your feet. The sense is that without being born as a *stabaka* (cluster/bunch), such worthiness would not exist. The word *basta*—the term *basta* itself—is formed as *staba* when it is inverted with its head downward; the factual state is that if, at some point, it were to become beautiful (*kānta*) by having the letter *ka* at the end, it would become the word *stabaka*. Here, there is a poetic possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*): if the *basta* were to become a *stabaka*, it would be worthy of worshipping your feet.
Since it is impossible to determine whether this is "never accomplished" or a "false resolve," there is a commingling of doubt (*saṃdehasaṃkara*) between these two [poetic intensities].
Or, for example:

"O Mādhava, when you bestowed [this] upon me who was about to fall into wretchedness, I believe that at that very moment, out of your supreme excellence, you extended compassion within [my heart]. (2156)
O Mādhava! For me, who desires to attain You and seeks refuge in You, there is wretchedness due to the deficiency of the collection of bodily parts, the incapacity for ritual acts,
the non-attainment of qualification, and the decay of place, time, and quality.
"Indeed, skillful means do not succeed, and likewise obstacles are numerous"—
this loss of self-confidence is called dejection and wretchedness.

When you offered this limb designated as *prapadana* (surrender), which was characterized by wretchedness (*kārpaṇya*), you bestowed it; at that very moment, I believe, you manifested compassion (*kāruṇya*) toward me within your heart, because it is supreme and transcends all else. The sense is that otherwise, you would not have accepted such a collection of limbs from me. In the alternative [pun], when you offer the word *kārpaṇyam*, making it devoid of the letter *r* (i.e., *kāpaṇyam*), then the division of the word is *sa-rvādhikyam*.

The construction is "saḥ tvam" (you, such as that). I think that you, being of such a nature, manifested compassion within [the word] *kārpaṇya* because of the predominance of the letter *r*—that is, due to the predominance of the syllable *ru*. The sense is that by the elision of the syllable *rp* from the word *kārpaṇya* and the insertion of the syllable *ru* in its very place, the word *kāruṇya* (compassion) is produced. Here, there is a doubt: is this an *arthāpatti* (presumption), whereby the Lord’s manifestation of compassion is inferred because the state of wretchedness (*kārpaṇya*) would otherwise be inexplicable; or is it an *anumāna* (inference), whereby this Lord is possessed of supreme compassion toward me because He is the one who causes me to offer up the various limbs of my surrender (*prapadana*)?

O Śauri, it is no wonder that those of clear vision call him— who out of pride says of another, "He is the cause of the worlds even more than you"— the one who possesses the highest vision, yet [still] regard him as a secondary cause.

O Śauri! That man who, out of pride, claims that there is someone other than You—the cause of the worlds—who is "well-eyed" (sudṛk) or "wise" (sudhīḥ), or who is "possessed of sight" (cakṣuṣmān)—those who possess good vision, those who are wise, and those who possess sight, say of that very man who asserts that there is a cause of the worlds other than You: "He is one whose cause is another" (aparakāraṇaḥ). This means he is one for whom there is another [cause], or rather, he is one whose cause is inferior (aparam), meaning non-superior (avaram) or not the best. What wonder is there in this? Such is the common worldly saying.

The sense is this: for one who asserts that there is a cause other than you, it is not surprising that there is another cause; rather, it is entirely logical. Therefore, this is the figure of speech *samālaṅkāra* (simile). Alternatively, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound: "another" (*aparam*) and "that which is a cause" (*kāraṇam*), thus "another-cause" (*aparakāraṇam*). They call him an "other-cause" (*aparakāraṇa*); what is so surprising about this? It is a great wonder—this is the sense. Therefore, this is the figure of speech *virodhābhāsa* (apparent contradiction).

The actual state of affairs is that they call him "one-eyed" (kāṇa) because he is a male person (puṃs) from whom the letter 'ra' (repha) has departed as his cause. Those with keen vision declare that one who propounds a meaning contrary to the Lord’s causality—established by hundreds of Vedic passages such as "Nārāyaṇa alone existed," "the one Nārāyaṇa residing in all beings," and "Brahman, whose form is the cause, beyond the letter 'a'"—is indeed one-eyed and not possessed of sight.

The meaning is that this is because of such statements as: "The Śruti and Smṛti are the two eyes ordained for Brahmins; one who is deprived of one is one-eyed. Here, since the poet’s creative effort does not rest upon either the semblance of contradiction (virodhābhāsa) or the semblance of doubt (sandehe) alone, there is a commingling (saṃkara) of these two based on doubt.

Or rather, O householder of the chariots of the Kuru heroes, I consider that you have taken up either a sickle, a goad, or a cane for the purpose of cutting the enemy; yet, there is this difference between them: a sickle cuts, while a cane merely bends. (2158)

O charioteer of Arjuna, the family-pillar of the Kuru heroes, O Blessed One!
