I consider that staff (*vetra*) or sickle (*dātra*) held by you in your hand for the purpose of urging on the chariot horses—that goad (*todana*), as Amara states: "The goad, the prick, and the driver's whip are synonyms"—or that scythe (*lavitra*) which is the instrument for cutting down the forest of the enemy lineage—as a mere blade (*dātra*). I imagine this; the distinction between these—the blade, the goad, and the scythe—is that the blade has "cut" (*dātaḥ*), derived from the root *do* (to cut) with the suffix *kta* in the passive sense.

The substitution of *ā* for *e* occurs by the rule *ādecaḥ*. According to Amara, “*kṛttaṃ*, *dātaṃ*, *ditaṃ*, *chitaṃ*, *vṛkṇam*” [are synonyms for cut]. The word *avetaḥ* means “understood,” being the past passive participle (*kta*) of the root *iṇ* preceded by the prefix *ava*, used in the sense of the object (*karman*). The meaning is that because these [weapons] possess the common quality of splitting the enemy host, the state of being a divider (*bhedabhāva*) is indeed known. The particle *tu* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), as Amara states: “*tu* may be used for distinction or emphasis. Alternatively, the meaning is: “I consider the sickle to be nothing but a reaper (*lavitra*); I am certain of this. Everything else remains as explained previously.

The reality (*tattva*) of these objects—the sickle and so forth—is this: the distinction between them consists merely in the letters *dā*, *to*, and *ve* respectively; this is the meaning. The suffix *-tas* here functions as a general case ending (*sārvavibhaktika*). Alternatively, I consider or know the sickle (*dātra*) to be like a goad (*totra*) or a cane (*vetra*). However, the distinction among these is only by means of the aforementioned letters, and not in every respect. One must not forget the identity between word and object (*śabdārthatādātmya*).

In this passage, there is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) based on the intention that there is a possibility of identity between the sickle and the goad or the cane; there is *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic cause) based on the intention that the determination of the object as a sickle is supported by the meaning of the subsequent sentence; there is *vyatireka* (distinction) based on the intention that among the equal things—the sickle, the goad, and the cane—there is only a difference of some few phonemes in their respective designating words; and there is *apahnuti* (concealment) based on the intention that the object held in the hand of the Blessed One is indeed a sickle and not a goad or a cane. Since the poet’s creative impulse cannot be restricted to any one of these figures within this single context, there is a *saṃdehasaṃkara* (blending through doubt).

Just as fire is considered pure by name because it is [purified] by your most pure devotees; indeed, alas, even poison, upon being consumed, attains a state of tranquility through the destruction of life. 2159.
He who is pure regarding his purpose through supreme purity is truly pure; one who is purified by earth and water is not truly pure.
For the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), purification is considered supreme through the knowledge of the Lord (īśvara).

The meaning is: by many of your devotees who possess purity of every kind in the manner described; "pure by name" means one who is designated as pure merely by name, but not one who is truly the most pure like them—this is the sense. "Anala" (fire) was surely "avamata" (disregarded). "Aha ha" expresses either grief or wonder. "Upayan viṣāśanam" means consuming food characterized by poison—that is, eating it. Due to the "jīvanabhaṅga" (destruction of life), he has reached "śāntatām" (extinction/destruction).
"Hi" is used for emphasis or to indicate a reason.

As for the actual state of affairs: "aha" is an indeclinable, and "ahaha" has no meaning distinct from it. The instrumental case in "haviṣā" (with the oblation), such as clarified butter and so forth, denotes non-difference; thus, it is an eating that is non-different from the oblation.

"By approaching [the fire], he has gone to tranquility and *nirvāṇa* because of the destruction of his life, like a wave of water. Here, the disregard for devotion to the Blessed One—which is established through the identification (based on *śleṣa*) with the consumption of poison and so forth, whose agent is fire—is not the actual cause. If the intention is to conceive of that non-cause as a cause, then it results in *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). If, however, there is the postulation of his disregard based on the impossibility of the aforementioned consumption of poison otherwise, then it is *arthāpatti* (presumption), by means of the cause consisting of the consumption of poison and so forth.

If the intention lies in establishing the state of being disregarded, then it falls under the figure of speech *anumāna* (inference); thus, because the poet’s creative effort (*saṃrambha*) flows out through various channels, there is a "commingling of doubt" (*saṃdehasaṃkara*) among these figures.

Just as a single, vast mountain that cannot be moved does not undergo even a fraction of transformation even when shaken, who could possibly describe the depth of this Abode of Fortune, whose resolve is so steadfast? (2160)

On the side of the mountain, he is exceedingly vast; on the side of the Blessed One, he is most venerable, for according to its etymology, "mahān" means that which is honored (*māhyate*) or worshipped (*pūjyate*). He is the one unshakeable mountain; on the other hand, he is incapable of being destroyed by others.
Because he forcibly seizes Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Yama, and Varuṇa as well, he is therefore called Hari.

Thus, because the Blessed One himself has declared his power as the destroyer of all; even when subjected to agitation by people desiring flowers, fruits, stones, wood, and other objects, and even when provoked by supplicants seeking their respective desired ends, he does not undergo even a trace of modification—that is, not even a fraction of transformation. [The term] *bhūdhara* means "of the earth," as in the expression *sthirāyā bhuva āśayasya ādhārasya* (the support or receptacle of the firm earth), like the word *jalāśaya* (reservoir of water). Alternatively, it refers to that which possesses firm *āśayas* (mango trees); for the *Medinī* lexicon states: "*Āśaya* may mean intention, as well as a mango tree (*panasa*) or a support (*ādhāra*)."

The meaning is: "of one whose heart is firm toward his own side. The sense is that his heart cannot be shaken even by those close to him who point out the faults in the protection of those who have come for refuge. Thus it is said: "I would never, under any circumstances, abandon one who has approached me with the spirit of friendship. [The term] *śrīdhāmnaḥ* refers to the abode of *sarala* trees or *bilva* trees; as the *Ratnamālā* states: "'Śrī' [is used] for dress, arrangement, beauty, prosperity, and the *sarala* tree; for speech, Lakṣmī, and cloves; and also for poison and the *bilva* fruit."

According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *śrī* denotes the beauty of attire, the goddess Sarasvatī, the *śarala* tree, Lakṣmī, the attainment of the three aims of life (*trivarga*), and the requisites of knowledge. In the alternative sense, it means "of Śrīnivāsa" (the Lord). The "depth" (*gāmbhīrya*) of this mountain and of the Blessed One refers to their impenetrability or imperturbability. In the case of the Blessed One, it refers to the fact that His generosity toward devotees and other qualities are difficult to fathom from the very root, even when faced with the offenses of those who have sought refuge or the inferiority of the recipient.

Alternatively, even though he possesses self-knowledge, it is difficult to grasp because of his concealment of it; for it is with this intention that even the Omniscient One is said to be "one who does not know. Who would be able to speak of or describe his desired [state]?

In this case, since the praise of a certain great mountain—which is not the subject at hand—concludes in the praise of the Lord Śrīnivāsa, who is the actual subject and possesses similar attributes, it is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise). Alternatively, as the account of the current subject, the Vṛṣādri mountain, is being described, because of the similarity of the adjectives, there is the cognition of either the account of a great king who is not the subject, or the account of such an ocean of milk; thus, it may be *samāsokti* (condensed expression).

In this sense, regarding the *Vṛṣagiri* (the Bull Mountain) interpretation, [he] "conducts" (*aniti*) with very great, splendid festivals (*sumahā-śobhinair-mahair-utsavaiḥ*); the form *aniteḥ* is derived from the root *an* with the suffix *kvip*. Regarding the *Mahārāja* (Great King) interpretation, he is one whose kingdom (*rājya*) is "splendid and great" (*śobhanaṃ mahat*); because of the extended application of the *śatṛ*-suffix status by the rule "the present tense [participle] is treated like *pṛṣat*" (*vartamāne pṛṣat*), the *num* augment is applied due to its being marked with *u*. The *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *mahat* occurs in the feminine in the sense of a particular lute (*vallakī-bheda*), but in the neuter it means a kingdom. The *Amara* lexicon also states: "*mahat* [is used for] a great kingdom."

In the case of the ocean, it means that even though it was subjected to an exceedingly great and vast agitation; in the case of the Bull Hill (Vṛṣagiri), it means that even though it was trampled by people desiring to behold the Blessed One through climbing, treading upon its slopes, and so forth; in the case of the Great King, it means that even though he was tormented by the insults and provocations of his enemies; and in the case of the ocean, it means that even though it was churned and stirred by the gods seeking nectar and other treasures—it does not undergo even a trace of transformation.

Regarding *sthirāśayasya*: In the first sense, it refers to one whose *āśaya* (abode/support) consists of firm *sālaparṇī* trees; for the *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *sthirā* [is used] for the earth, *sālaparṇī*, destruction, liberation, strength, and mountains. In the second sense, it means one whose *śaya* (hand/arm) rests upon firm ground—that is, one who has the earth under his own control. In the third sense, *śaya* is derived from the root *śī* with the suffix *ac* (according to Pāṇini 3.1.134), meaning one who lies (*śete*) completely (*samantāt*) upon the firm earth; that is, one who encircles the earth like a girdle. Regarding *śrīdhāmnaḥ*: in the first case, this applies because he possesses the feet of Lakṣmī (*śrīpāda*), because he is the abode of Śrī, and through the power of the word itself (*śabdaśakti*) and its etymological connection (*yoga*).
By common usage, this mountain came to be known by the name Śrīśaila.

Thus, according to the manner stated by Vāroha, the meaning is "of that which is the abode of Lakṣmī. In the second [interpretation], the meaning is "of the locus for the attainment of the three goals of life (trivarga). In the third, the meaning is "of the birthplace of Śrī. "Profundity" means being difficult to enter, being unassailable, and being deep. The rest is as before. Alternatively, since while describing the account of the mountain at hand, the very account of the abode of Śrī (Śrīnivāsa) is illuminated, this is the figure of speech *prastutāṅkura*. Or else, because the expressed subject—the Lord himself—is described through a different turn of phrase, it is the figure of speech *paryāyokta*.

Or rather, regarding the reading *ekohārya*, there is a pun (*śleṣa*) between the non-contextual *arya* (wealthy) or *ārya* (noble), which is *ahārya* (unremovable), and the contextual *śeṣādri* (the mountain Śeṣa), through the splitting of the compound as either *ekaḥ hā aryaḥ* or *ekaḥ hāryaḥ*. Since it is impossible to establish the poet’s intended emphasis on only one of these among those proposed, there is a "blend" (*saṃkara*) based on doubt (*sandeha*). The word *arya* means "master" or "lord," a single sovereign; this is derived from the root *ṛ* ("to go") with the suffix *yat*, according to the rule that *arya* is a nipātana for "master" and "vaiśya."

The meaning is that the *ārya* is one who is to be attained (*prāpya*), which is derived from the aforementioned verbal root by the rule *ṛhalorṇyat*. This is a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) to the sūtra stating "the *arya* is a master" (*svāmin*). The indeclinable *ha* expresses wonder (*vismaya*) induced by the contemplation of his profundity; the supplement is "the particle *ha* is used in wonder and in disgust. In the sense of *arya* as "master," the previously stated meaning should be understood.

But as for one on the side of the Noble Ones (āryapakṣa), even when provoked to agitation, and even when tempted by other means—such as the display of trivial rewards in the manner described by the words "These women, with their chariots and musical instruments"—he does not undergo even a fraction of a transformation, nor even the slightest mental fluctuation caused by attachment to them. The sense is that, having rejected all of that in the manner of saying, "Your horses are yours, your dancing and singing are yours," his mental state remains unshaken, following the principle: "The boon I must choose is this very [state]."

The meaning is: who is capable of describing the profundity of this one—who is the abode of glory (Śrīdhāman), a treasury of knowledge (Vidyānidhi), whose intention (āśaya) is fixed on liberation (sthiramokṣa)—for the meanings of the words "Śrī" and "Sthira" have already been stated; he is one who cannot be led astray (ahārya), who is noble (arya), and who is truly venerable (ārya).

Just as this single emerald gem shines most intensely for the sake of the prosperity of the entire world, those of great fortune alone obtain it as their most excellent object of enjoyment, and no others.

In this regard, is it *rūpakātiśayokti* (hyperbole of metaphor), wherein the Blessed Lord himself is determined to be an emerald; or rather, is it *rūpaka* (metaphor), wherein the Blessed Lord—the subject—is first indicated by the word "this" and the quality of being an emerald is superimposed upon him; or else, is there an implied *vastūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy of a thing), consisting in the imagining of the Blessed Lord as an emerald; or perhaps, is it *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect description), wherein the matter at hand—the account of Śrīnivāsa—is understood through the account of an irrelevant emerald; or finally, [is it the figure of speech] belonging to Śrīnivāsa, who has been determined to be an emerald?

Because it is understood as a distinction from the perspective of the world-renowned Garuḍa—that [the Lord] "shines forth for the sake of the prosperity of the entire world"—there is the figure of speech *vyatireka* (contrast). Alternatively, since this is a description of Śrīnivāsa himself through a different stylistic turn, there is *paryāyokta* (periphrasis). Thus, there is a *saṃdehasaṃkara* (blending by doubt) of many figures of speech.

O Lord of the Serpent Mountain, just as at the break of dawn, when the fault of the dense darkness of accumulated sins has been dispelled by the light of Your sidelong glance, the lotus within my inner heart unfolds and blossoms on all sides.

In this case, because there is an absence of any evidence—either probative or subversive—to determine whether it is a simile (*upamā*) such as "your sidelong glance is like the dawn," "the mass of sins is like deep darkness," or "the inner heart is like a lotus"; or whether it is a metaphor (*rūpaka*) such as "your sidelong glance itself is the dawn," "the mass of sins itself is the deep darkness," or "the inner heart itself is the lotus," there is a commingling (*saṃkara*) by way of doubt (*saṃdeha*). Here, "probative" and "subversive" evidence refer to the forms of logical proof and refutation.

Where there is the application of either a proof or a refutation—characterized by the principles of logic (*nyāya*) and fallacy (*doṣa*)—there is no doubt, because one of the two is ascertained. In some cases, analogy (*upamā*) is the proof for [the presence of] metaphor (*rūpaka*), yet it is neither a proof nor entirely contrary to metaphor. In other cases, however, it is the proof for metaphor, while it is neither a proof nor entirely contrary to analogy. Furthermore, in certain instances, a fallacy may be a refutation of analogy, but remains indifferent (*taṭastha*) toward metaphor.

In some cases, however, [a defect] is a sublater of metaphor (rūpaka) but remains indifferent to simile (upamā). In this manner, the presence of merit or fault regarding two other figures of speech should likewise be inferred.
In this regard, the *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification) stands as an independent principle that establishes the simile, as in:
"May he who bestows upon us that [divine] form which is our very fortune, and who leads away calamity, cause the lotus-feet of that [Lord] to extend our prosperity. (2163)

"Make that prosperity of ours—the wealth of liberation—thin," [saying this] to those people who take refuge in Him, may He who is the Abode of Śrī (Śrīnivāsa) diminish—that is, cause to become thin—the calamity consisting of worldly existence (bhava), and indeed bestow and accomplish that very prosperity they have prayed for. The indeclinable *nu* here is used in the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) to combine the previously mentioned thinning of calamity with the granting of prosperity. As stated by Śeṣa: "The word *nu* is to be known as used in response, in comparison, in dejection, and in poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*); it is also to be understood in the sense of filling a metrical foot (*pādapūraṇa*), in inquiry (*jijñāsā*), and in conjunction (*samuccaya*)."

May the lotus-feet of that Blessed One extend every kind of prosperity and glory. Here, the primary meaning conveyed by the phrase "may they extend prosperity" consists in the bestowing of all forms of splendor; this meaning finds its natural correspondence in the word *bhagavat-pada* (the feet of the Blessed One) itself, thereby supporting the simile (*upamā*) "the foot is like a lotus. However, it does not support the metaphor (*rūpaka*) "the foot is itself a lotus" as directly, because in the case of a lotus, the bestowing of the intended prosperity is not primarily understood.

One might object: "In that case, why should the simile not rather be the sublater of the metaphor? This doubt is raised because it is possible for even the lotus to bestow its primary excellence, such as fragrance and so forth. Therefore, it does not function as a sublater of the metaphor; rather, it remains merely peripheral.
The simile, acting as a neutral witness regarding the proof of the metaphor,
bestows delight upon the eyes like moonlight, which dispels the entire spreading darkness that obstructs the path of the virtuous, belonging to the nectar-moon of Mādhava’s face.

"Excellent" means that which obstructs movement—whether it be wandering elsewhere, proceeding upon the right path, or traveling by way of the *arcirādi* (the path of light) and so forth. The rest is easy to understand. Here, in the metaphor (*rūpaka*) "the face itself is the nectar-rayed moon," the word *jyotsnā* (moonlight) serves as the supporting evidence (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*). Since the primary meaning of the word *jyotsnā* is understood to be favorable only to the "nectar-rayed moon," it acts as the proof for the metaphor "the face-nectar-rayed moon. However, it is not a natural proof for the simile (*upamā*) "the face is like the nectar-rayed moon," because the meaning of *jyotsnā* in its primary sense—namely, moonlight—is not perceived in the face.

Nor should it be argued that, in that case, the *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification) must necessarily be a sublater of the *upamā* (simile). For instance, in the phrase "the face is not like the moon," although there is no actual favorability [of the moon] toward the face as there is for nectar, because favorability can somehow exist through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), it does not constitute opposition to the simile; rather, it should be understood as mere neutrality (*tāṭasthya*).
The acceptance of *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification) over *upamā* (simile) occurs when the latter is precluded by logical inconsistency, as in:

"Like a jewel from the Vṛṣādri mountain, possessing the radiance of the moon risen in autumn, the lotus-eyed Lord whitens our hearts with the nectar of his side-glances, just as [the moon] whitens the interior of the night. (2165)

"Naḥ" means "our"; "svāntam," "niśāntam," and "bhavanam" constitute a *vyastarūpaka* (distributive metaphor). The present participle (*śatṛ*) in "viśadayat" is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*); here, "cause" refers to the result (*phala*). The phrase beginning with "śaradudita" is an adjective for "kaṭākṣasudhayā" (by the nectar of the sidelong glance). In this context, within the simile "the sidelong glance is like nectar," the aforementioned *vyastarūpaka* does not act as an obstacle; however, even the employment of the common attribute in "śaradudita" and so forth acts as an obstacle.

The ancients, however, maintain that [the word *upamā*] is not used [as a separate term], because the rule "that which is compared is compounded with *vyāghra*, etc. prescribes the compound formation precisely when such a word is not employed. We, on the other hand, say that even the employment of a common attribute (*sāmānyadharma*) in certain instances does not preclude the presence of a simile (*upamā*).

Just as one might, through yoga, obtain a noble elephant— a celestial tusker that follows its own will, is beautiful, adorned with lotuses, easy to manage, and possesses a majestic gait and profound, steady temperament— so too [may I attain such a state].

*Vaśā* means one's own; it refers to a female elephant (*kariṇī*), a barren woman (*vandhyā*), a daughterless woman (*asutā yoṣā*), a cow, or a female elephant. In three genders, it denotes that which has come under one's control; as a neuter, it signifies subjection, attainment, or mastery over one's desire.

*Yoḥ*—according to the *Medinī* lexicon, this means "of her" (the earth). His *anucaram* (attendant/companion) refers to his helper. In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), he is an *anucara* by his own power—that is, by his own will. As it is said, "One who goes wherever he desires is self-controlled," the meaning is that he is independent, wandering through all the worlds. To him thus described: *sapadmakam*, meaning "accompanied by *padmaka*" (a cluster of dots); in the alternative sense, "accompanied by *padmā*" (Lakṣmī). Regarding the suffix *kap* used here as a secondary derivative (*śaiṣika*), the shortening of the vowel is optional according to the rule *āpo'nyatarasyām*.

It is easy [to attain] Śrīnivāsa, the best of gods, who possesses a beautiful trunk and lovely hands; who dwells with his retinue in Nāgāgrāma and on the mountain of the serpent (Phaṇiśaila); who is firm and profound like a divine elephant—the analysis being "the god is like an elephant" (devaḥ kuñjara iva); and whom one may find through yoga—meaning through application, preparation, or means—or, in another sense, through meditation. As Amarasimha states: "Yoga refers to armor, means, meditation, union, and application."

May the divine elephant, who wanders the forests of Mount Phāṇagiri, always victorious and accompanied by all his herd, triumph—he who, by bestowing an exceedingly great fragrance, constantly renders the excellent bees helpless! 2167.

He who possesses an exceeding increase of fragrance—meaning, he whose intoxicating fragrance is characterized by such surpassing growth—and who, by the offering of that scent, renders helpless the "best of the rows of the virtuous" (sadāli-varān)—that is, the most excellent among the virtuous knowers of Brahman (satām brahmavidām āleḥ paṅkteḥ ye varāḥ śreṣṭhāḥ)—or, in the other sense, the best of bees (sadā alivarān); and who is endowed with complete splendor (sakalā bhā), as described in such passages as, "By His light all this shines."

May the Lord, the divine elephant (*daivatanāga*)—the best among gods—accompanied by his young elephants (*kalabha*), those specific types of elephants thirty years of age, be victorious! According to Amara: "In the latter member of a compound, words such as *vyāghra*, *puṅgava*, *vṛṣabha*, *kuñjara*, *siṃha*, *śārdūla*, *nāga*, and so forth, when used in the masculine, signify excellence. In both these verses, in the expression *devakuñjaram* (the elephant among gods) and *daivatanāgam* (the divine elephant), the employment of a common attribute (*sāmānyadharma*) based on the assumption of a metaphorical compound (*upamitasamāsa*) does not subvert the simile.
[This is illustrated by] the common attribute in the phrase: "being honored by the *bṛndārakas* (gods) and *kuñjaras* (elephants)."

Since the formation of compounds is established even in the case of usage through the inclusion of "vyāghra" and others in the *ākṛtigaṇa*, this statement is intended for general application; therefore, in this instance, doubt between simile (*upamā*) and metaphor (*rūpaka*) alone is appropriate.
The acceptance of a simile [is established] by the sublation of a metaphorical identification (rūpaka), as in:
"The divine lotus-feet of the Lord of the Mountain of Serpents spread auspiciousness for the worlds, rendered tawny by the mass of rays from the jewels set in the crowns of the bowing gods. (2168)

In this case, qualifiers such as "bowing immortals" (namadamara) and so forth are in no way possible with respect to a lotus; thus, they subvert the identification of the word itself as a lotus, rather than being merely extraneous.
Thus,
while the mountain of Vṛṣabha— the abode of the gods— shines like the Pārijāta tree, the glorious Mañjarī, who bestows fragrance upon the world, triumphs within the enemy of Mura.

On the mountain of Śeṣa (Śeṣādri), the abode of the wise, the learned, or the gods; alternatively, on that which has Indra as its king (vṛṣabhūbhṛt). [She resides] in the enemy of Mura, Śrīnivāsa—who shines like the Pārijāta tree in the abode of the gods (vibudhānām āvāse)—the destroyer of the world's sorrow, joy, and fragrance. [The compound is formed with the genitive case of Śeṣa.]

Victorious is the Śrī-mañjarī, the very creeper of the milk of Fortune! Here, in the expression "Śrī-mañjarī," one must accept only a metaphor (*rūpaka*), because the inclusion of the common attribute "bestowing fragrance upon the world" acts as a sublater of the simile (*upamā*). Nor should it be argued that this is inconsistent with the opening of the comparison, "like the Pārijāta tree"; for even when a sublation exists, the rule that "the opening alone must be followed" is neither a Vedic injunction, nor an injunction on Dharma, nor a royal decree. However, where [no such sublation exists]...

As for the subverting factor (*bādhaka*): for instance, if in this very verse the third quarter were made *jagadamodavidhātari*, then, in accordance with the opening of the passage, let there be an upamita-samāsa (compound of comparison) there as much as one likes.
Thus, may the glorious Mahodara flourish—He who is the bull-bannered Lord, the abode of the gods, the wish-fulfilling tree for Śrīnivāsa, and the bestower of joy upon the world! 2170.

Thus, when the verse previously cited is presented in another manner, although the general attribute (*sāmānyadharma*) is not employed in the phrase "śrīmañjarī," a compound based on simile (*upamāsamāsa*) is not appropriate. Rather, since a compound based on metaphor (*rūpakasamāsa*) is established in the phrase "śrīnivāsapārijāta" by virtue of the employment of the general attribute "jagadāmoda" and so forth, it is more fitting to conform to that [metaphor].

Otherwise, there would be the fault of "falling excellence" (*patatprakarṣa*), wherein one first relies upon a superior metaphor characterized primarily by non-difference (*abheda*), and subsequently resorts to a subordinate simile characterized primarily by both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*).

Just as, upon the breast of the excellent jewel [Viṣṇu] embraced by the Queen of Jewels [Lakṣmī], the lovely pearl necklace of the crest-jewel of the Lord of Serpents shines like a line of beads of perspiration. (2171)

In this instance, the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is that [the pearl necklace] is "like a garland of drops of perspiration," rather than a simile (*upamā*). For if it were a simile, the qualification of the chest as "embraced by the excellent gem" would result in being purposeless; this is because the comparison of the pearl necklace to a garland of sweat-drops is established independently of the aforementioned qualification. Therefore, the qualification of the chest beginning with "by the excellent gem" acts as a sublater of the simile.

If there were various figures of speech (alaṃkāras) with distinct meanings yet expressed by identical words, then that is considered the commingling (saṃkara) resulting from the entry of multiple figures into a single expressive unit.
This [conjunction] is proclaimed to be of three kinds, based on the mutual entry (anupraveśa) of two meanings, two words, or a word and its meaning within a single expressive unit.

The commingling (*saṃkara*) of figures occurs when multiple ornaments enter into a single expressive word (*ekavācaka*), provided that there is no difference in the cognition of the words and no diversity in the ornaments themselves. In this regard, there is a threefold division based on the entry of two semantic ornaments (*arthālaṃkāra*) or two verbal ornaments (*śabdālaṃkāra*) into one expressive word. Dīkṣita maintains that the entry into a single expressive word applies only to two semantic ornaments. The author of the *Sarvasva* holds that it applies to two verbal ornaments as well. The author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, however, asserts that it applies only to two ornaments, whether verbal or semantic.
Among these, the first is as follows:
"O Śauri, if a person were ever to obtain the nectar of immortality by worshipping a deity other than You, he would surely find butter even from a mere churned drink. (2172)

In the expression "manthaudana" (porridge-water), there is an optional substitution of *ud* for the word *udaka* according to the rule "udakasya manthaḥ. Here, the meaning being conveyed takes the form of an illustration (*nidarśana*), characterized by the superimposition of a single unified sentence-meaning upon two [separate] meanings. Furthermore, it takes the form of a poetic fancy (*saṃbhāvana*), as one conjecture serves as the means for another conjecture. Since these two figures of sense (*arthālaṃkāra*) are communicated by a single sequence of phonemes, they constitute a commixture (*saṃkara*) through the entry into a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*).

Just as when the foremost of the gods (Indra) possesses respect within his heart for the *tatpuruṣa* compound in its entirety, he then maintains the status of being a "well-spoken" one (*suśabda*); how indeed could one who is not thus be considered well-spoken? 2173.
The sound of meritorious action touches both heaven and earth;
as long as that good reputation endures, so long is one honored in heaven.

Thus is the application of the *bhārata* [verse]. The meaning is that one becomes a possessor of supreme fame through devotion to the Blessed One (*bhagavat*). How indeed could a person who is not thus—that is, one who would not extend devotion to the Blessed One—be "suśabda," meaning one of good fame? For how could there be such for one who is not a devotee of the Blessed One?

The meaning is that there shall be the attainment of good fame. "Elsewhere" means when there is the intention of forming a *tatpuruṣa* compound. In the word *surapuṃgava*, the division is *surapuṃgava-śabde gauḥ avaṃ*. When the word *gauḥ* (the word "cow") has entered into a compound (*samastaḥ*), it undergoes the substitution of *avaṃ* for its own final constituent, the vowel *o* (in *puṃgava*).

The meaning is that by the rule "gorataddhitaluki" (Pāṇini 5.4.92), when a *taddhita* suffix is elided after a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in "go," the final vowel *o* undergoes the substitution of *ava* according to the rule "eco'yavāyāvaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.78). Then, immediately after this substitution of *ava*, it attains the status of being a correct word (*suśabdatām*), that is, the state of being grammatically standard (*sādhutvam*), because in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, only the word "go" that has undergone the *samāsānta* suffix [elision] is considered standard.

If the word *go* were not present in its entirety as the second member (*uttarapada*) of that *tatpuruṣa* compound, it would not undergo the substitution of *ava* due to the absence of the compound-final suffix *ṭac*; how then could that word *su* be a correct form (*sādhu*)? The sense is: since the aforementioned compound-final suffix is obligatory, in its absence, how could there be correctness for that [form]? Here, there is a single instance of *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of causal indication), because the state of possessing "correctness of speech" (*sauśabdya*) has as its cause the state of possessing devotion to the Lord, which constitutes the meaning of the sentence.

By means of the praise of the effect—the state of possessing excellence in speech (*sauśabdya*)—which belongs to the devotees who are not the subject under discussion (*aprastuta*), there is the apprehension of the excellence of the bestowing of auspiciousness belonging to its cause, namely devotion to the Lord; thus, this is one instance of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect description) based on an effect. Likewise, by means of the praise of the effect—the state of possessing such lack of excellence in speech—which belongs to those who are not the subject under discussion, there is the apprehension of the excellence of the bestowing of misfortune belonging to its cause, namely disrespect for the Lord; thus, this is another instance of *aprastutapraśaṃsā*. Furthermore, there is the figure of speech called *śleṣa* (paronomasia), which involves both the relevant and the irrelevant. These figures of sense (*arthālaṅkāras*) are blended (*saṃkīryante*) because they enter into a single expressive word (*ekavācaka*).
Or as it is said:
"If this form, smooth with the virtues of Hari, is disregarded by the wicked, what of it? If a woman, dense with loveliness, is censured by those blind from birth, what of her? (2174)

In the expression *januṣāndhaḥ*, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the third-case ending due to the specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*): "And [the forms] *puṃsānujaḥ* and *januṣāndhaḥ*. Here, the entire verse consists of the figure of speech *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration). Furthermore, each half-verse (both the first and the second) consists of the figure *avajñā* (disregard), characterized by the non-arising of one defect despite the presence of another. Thus, there is a commingling (*saṃkīrṇa*) through the mutual entry of a single expressive word (*ekāvācaka*).

Or rather, O Blessed One, where indeed has such a hater been seen—one whose nature is struck down by fate and who reviles you? And where has one been seen who is beloved by you—one whose nature is eternally noble and who does not revile you? (2175)

Because it is difficult to describe the extreme nature of his evil deeds, he is referred to as "he" (saḥ). A person who hates you—being one whose very nature has been struck down and destroyed by fate, such that his natural disposition as a subordinate of the Lord has vanished—where could he ever be praised? The sense is that he would be reviled everywhere. On the other hand, one who constantly honors you, being of noble nature and praiseworthy character—where could he not be praised? The sense is that he would be lauded by everyone everywhere.

In the *pakṣa* (alternative view), the word "dveṣṭā" (the hater) always—that is, eternally—has a base (*prakṛti*) that is "nihata," meaning unaccented (*anudātta*), specifically the base of the suffix *tṛc*, which is the form of the root *dviṣ*. This is because the root *dviṣ* is enumerated among the unaccented roots. For this very reason, the rule "ekāca upadeśe'nudāttāt" (Pāṇini 7.2.10), which prohibits the augment *iṭ* for monosyllabic roots that are unaccented in their original instruction (*upadeśa*), applies here. Thus, it is not connected with the augment *iṭ*.

The meaning is as follows: the word *añcitā-añcitā* is always of an inherently acute (udātta) nature; that is, its root-form (*prakṛti*) is the acute-root *añcat*. For this very reason, it cannot be characterized by the augment *iṭ* after the suffix *kvap*, because due to its being acute, the augment *iṭ* would necessarily apply according to the rule *ārdhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ*. Here, the specific sentence-meaning, which takes the form of *samāsokti* (speech-implication), is blended with two other sentence-meanings in the form of *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason), all converging within a single expressive word.
Or rather: O Lord of Śeṣa-giri, since the two best of birds and serpents are under your control, I consider these two—who constantly dwell together—to be without physical bodies.

O Śrīnivāsa, Lord of Śeṣagiri! [In the alternative sense: O master of the *Śeṣagiri* [grammar], you who are capable—this is an address to a certain learned man. The locative case is used according to the rule "the master (*svāmī*), the lord (*īśvara*)," and so forth. Regarding the term *khagabhujagatallajau*: it is a compound formed by the rule "with words expressing praise" (*praśaṃsāvacanaiśca*), meaning Tārkṣya (Garuḍa) and Śeṣa (Ananta). In the alternative sense, it means the two words *khagatallajaḥ* and *bhujagatallajaḥ*.

For this reason, *nityasamāsa* [is so called]: from the root *ās* in the sense of "sitting" (*upaveśane*), with the suffix *ghañ* used in the sense of abstract state (*bhāve*). The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that which is both equal (*sama*) and a sitting (*āsa*)," meaning an equal state of being or co-existence. Alternatively, they are "those that always possess the nature of a compound. Regarding these as *nityasamāsas*, like *kṛṣṇasarpa*, *vāpyaśva*, and so forth, Sudhākara and others have stated this in the commentary on the verse beginning "matallikā macarcikā. Therefore, these two words—*khagatallaja* and *bhujaṅgatallaja*—are *avigraha*, meaning they are devoid of the analytical sentence that makes their derivative meaning understood.

Alternatively, I consider that these two compounds lack a *vigraha* (analytic expansion) using their own constituent words; otherwise, they would not qualify as *nityasamāsa* (eternal compounds). This is the intended meaning. Grammarians state: "A *nityasamāsa* is either one without a *vigraha* or one whose *vigraha* does not employ its own constituent words (*asvapadavigraha*). A *vigraha* is a sentence that makes known the meaning of the compound formation (*vṛtti*). Here, there is a coalescence (*ekavācakānupraveśa*) of the figures of speech *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *anumāna* (inference) within a single expressive word.
Just as one who has transcended the path of the stars and attained the consecration of a new sovereignty,
so too is this best of mountains, the Ahiśaila, worthy of its status, joined with its lofty peaks.

It is so called because it transcends the path of the stars, that is, the atmosphere; elsewhere, the meaning is that it does not overstep the duties of a Kṣatriya (*kṣatradharma*). It has been brought to consecration by a fresh, dense line of clouds; elsewhere, it has been brought to consecration in a kingdom that is fresh, new, and solid. It is joined with, or connected to, lofty peaks, summits, or ridges; or else, it is associated with loftiness through its preeminence or sovereignty.

According to the *Medinī*: "The word *śṛṅga* [denotes] sovereignty, a peak, a mark, a water-fountain for play, a horn, and excellence. And according to the *Amara-kośa*: "*Śṛṅga* [denotes] preeminence and a mountain-summit. Thus, "the best of mountains" (*bhūbhṛdvaraḥ*) refers both to the most excellent king and the finest of peaks. Here, there is a mutual penetration (*ekavācakānupraveśa*) of the two figures of speech—*kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason) and *samāsokti* (speech of brevity)—which are themselves infused by *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
Just as a cat, once defeated by emeralds that surpass its own eyes, would surely be defeated even by Māra if he were to possess a body of sapphire; so too [is the case with the emerald]. (2178)

The word *mārjāra* (cat) refers to the Lord [Viṣṇu] because of the cat's eyes; that is to say, because of the cat's eyes which surpass His own eyes in brilliance—meaning they outshine the luster of His eyes. This is due to the *vaidūryas* (cat's-eye gems), which are held as ornaments by the Blessed One. The term *vaidūrya* is derived from the analysis *vidūrāt prabhavanti vaidūryāṇi* ("they originate from Vidūra"). Under the governing rule "prabhavati," the suffix *ñya* is applied according to the rule *vidūrāññyaḥ*.

‘Vaidūrya is [the gem] born of Vālavāya,’ according to the *Viśva* lexicon. Here, the word *vidūra* is either a substitute (*ādeśa*), a synonym (*paryāya*), or used metaphorically (*upacarita*) for *vālavāya*. By this, the objection—that this gem originates from the mountain Vālavāya and not from the city of Vidūra, but rather is refined there—is answered. As it has been said: "Whether *vālavāya* or *vidūra* is considered a distinct source material (*prakṛti*), if one should say 'it is certainly not there,' one should apply the term as in the case of the word *jitvarī*."

Thus [it is said]. However, other points to be stated have been elaborated by us in the commentary on the *Lakṣmīsahasra-saundarya-stabaka* at the verse beginning with "vaidūryavīkṣābhayodgacchat. The sense is that [the blue lotus] was "conquered" (*nirjita*), meaning it was surpassed; the idea is that it was itself defeated by the defeat of its own luster by her eyes. Regarding the verbal root (*śabdapakṣe*), here the prefix *ni-* ends in *i*, not in *r*. That which has the syllable *rjā* (composed of *r* and *jā*) departed from it is *nirjāḥ*.

The word *nirjita* is derived from the root *ji* (to conquer) with the prefix *nis*, followed by the causative suffix *ṇic* in the sense of "making [something] so," and then the passive past participle suffix *kta*. One should understand that because of the sovereign principle of identity between word and meaning, the very sound of the word *mārjāra* (cat) is "conquered" by the *vaidūrya* gem. Now, the underlying thought is that if he were ever *māra* (the god of love), he would also be a slayer of his enemies (*vidveṣimāraka*), and if he were the crest-jewel of the valiant, he would also be skilled in avenging his enmity. The phrase "if he were even *kāma*" (desire) carries the same sense. Regarding the verbal aspect, the meaning is that if one were to elide the letters *r* and *jā* from the word *mārjāra*, the form *māra* would result.

Regarding the rule "The *liṅ* [optative] occurs after *jātu* and *yadā*," there is a supplementary rule stating that it also occurs after *yadā* and *yadī* when expressing improbability (*anavaklṛpti*). Improbability here means impossibility; the sense is that this is simply inconceivable. Even then, he might have been victorious in the conflict—that is, in battle—with the *harinīla* gems, the sapphire jewels worn by the Lord.

The sense is that even if [the mountain] were previously surpassed by Vaiḍūrya gems, it would still be surpassed by Indranīla gems upon assuming another form; thus, in either case, its state of being defeated by the jewels held by Hari (Viṣṇu) is possible. It should be understood that because Māra is dark-complexioned, he is surpassed by the body of Hari-nīla (Indranīla); the meaning is that he is surpassed by the divine form of the Blessed One. Here, there is a combination of *saṃbhāvanā* (poetic fancy) and *viṣama* (incongruity) within a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*). Furthermore, the reinforcement by *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is just as before.
Just as there is no doubt that both the conscious and the unconscious are lords of the world, so too are the divine couple distinct only by their forms as male and female; indeed, they are one. 2179.

The sense is that both you, the divine couple Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, are young. You are the "best among the conscious and the unconscious" (*cidacid-varau*), meaning you are superior to—and distinct from—the sentient and the insentient by virtue of being free from the transformations characterized by a change in nature or a change in state. For this very reason, you are the lords (*īśvarau*) of the world (*jagatyāḥ*); there is no doubt, for since sovereignty resides in both, one should not entertain any doubt in this matter. Thus, the equality of the two has been stated.

He states the distinction: "But [the difference lies] merely in the forms of woman and man"—that is, they differ only insofar as they possess the forms of female and male, but not in their status as the Lord of the Universe; this is the sense. Here, they say that you are as she is, and Kamalā likewise is your wife; between the two of you, there is not even a scent of difference.
They say that you alone, having assumed a youthful female form through your power of illusion, are both the mother and the youthful father.
Thus, it should be understood as stated in the sections concerning the majesty of Śrī Viṣṇu.

Elsewhere, however, there is the address: "O divine couple, O Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa! In this world, they are the two Lords (īśvarau) designated by the word *īśvara*. They are the best among the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*); that is to say, one is the letter *ca* (representing *cit*), and the other is the letter *ta* (representing *acit*).

The meaning is that *cit* (consciousness) and *acit* (matter) are the two "excellent" (*vara*) things, from which the suffixes *-vara* and *-pratyaya* are derived. They are formed by adding the suffix *-vara*—according to the rule "stheśabhāse" etc.—to the verbal root *īś* (meaning "lordship"), and by adding the suffix *-varaṭ*—according to the rule "aśnoteḥ āśukarmaṇi varaṭ ca"—to the verbal root *aś* (meaning "pervasion"). However, they differ merely in their forms as feminine and masculine, that is, in their feminine and masculine grammatical genders.

The sense is that when the word *īśvara* is derived as feminine (*strīliṅga*) from the base *vara*, the form is *īśvarā* by the addition of the suffix *ṭāp*; however, when derived from the base *varaṭā*, the form is *īśvarī* by the addition of the suffix *ṅīp* according to the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*. In the masculine (*pulliṅga*), however, the form remains *īśvara* regardless of the derivation; thus, this is the distinction between the two. Here, there is a commingling (*saṃkara*) of the figures of speech *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *vyatireka* (distinction), both of which enter into a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*).
Or as it is said:

"O lotus, surely you have been cast aside by the eye of Ramā; you remain as mere life-breath, embraced by the bowstring and with your stalk severed—such is the extent of the existence of one whose vital force is so meager. (2180)

Is it not so? "O lotus! O fish! O deer!"—in this alternative, the word "O lotus" (*rājīva*) itself is the vocative. According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *rājīva* refers to a lotus; in the masculine, it denotes a distinction [of species], as well as a deer and a fish. You have been surpassed and eclipsed by the eye of Ramā (Lakṣmī). This statement of being "surpassed" is made because, according to poetic convention (*kavisamaya*), the fish and the deer are accepted as points of comparison for the eyes of beautiful women. As it is stated in the thirteenth chapter of the *Alaṃkāraśekhara*:
"With the deer, its eye, the lotus, its petals, the fish, and the wagtail;
with the eye, the *cakra-vāka*, its eye, the *ketaka*, its filament, and the arrow of Smara (the god of love)."

The meaning is that similarity (*sādṛśya*) is to be described by poets in this manner. And the formal usage (*prayoga*) is: “In your glance, there is a resemblance to lotuses grown in the forest. In that very same [work], in the fifteenth ray (*marīci*), similarity is established through terms such as *bhṛtaka* (hireling) and *bhṛtya* (servant) which imply the sense of humiliation, as well as through doubt and various specific sentences.

And thus, through such expressions of doubt as "Is it the moon? Is it a lotus? and so forth, as well as through various statements such as "It nourishes its loveliness; it steals its radiance," similarity (*sādṛśya*) is established—this is the meaning [of the verse].

In the case of the word *rājīva*, this prefix *ni-* has been removed; that is to say, it has been made such that the letter *rā* is excluded. Because *rā* does not end in a feminine suffix, there is no shortening of the vowel in a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). That which remains is merely life—that is, the mere maintenance of breath. According to Amara, "life (*jīva*) is the maintenance of breath. The sense is that he performs only the maintenance of those breaths because they are difficult to release when the time ordained by fate has arrived. In the alternative interpretation (the word-play), the meaning is that upon the removal of the letter *rā*, the word *rājīva* remains as *jīva*. Therefore—

*Avāgraḥ* means "bent downwards"; according to Amara, *avāgra-avanata-anatam*. It signifies "with face turned downwards. You are one by whom the earth (*jyā*) has been embraced or clung to; the sense is that you have fallen upon the ground with your face downward and are unable to rise from there. In the alternative [puzzle] interpretation, it means "joined" (*āśliṣṭaḥ*) with the syllable *jī*; the word is split as *vāgra*. That which has the syllable *va* at its beginning (*agre*) is so described.

The sense is that [the word] *rājīva* was thus because only the two syllables "jī" remained. To the question, "This *rājīva* was refuted; why was he not capable of countering it?", he says: "svalpaprāṇa-," meaning one whose body (*ātman*)—that is, his physical form—is of little breath and little power. In the other sense (the verbal play), the word *rājīva* consists of syllables with few breaths (*alpaprāṇa*). This is because it is stated: "The first, third, and fifth letters of the consonant groups, as well as the semi-vowels *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*, are those with few breaths."

The meaning is that his "stay" (sthitih) is merely this much: even though he has been repelled by his enemies, because he lacks the power to retaliate, his stay consists only in lying silent upon the ground with his face turned downwards. In another sense, the meaning is that the "stay" of the word *rājīva*—which consists of few syllables—is only this much.

Here, by describing the effect—the rejection and so forth of the lotus (*rājīva*), which is not the subject at hand—the cause of that effect, the drawing of Ramā [Lakṣmī], which is the actual subject, is perceived through its extraordinary stillness, steadiness, and lack of fickleness; thus, this is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Praise of the Non-Subject) based on an effect. Furthermore, there is *śleṣa* (paronomasia) involving the non-contextual fish, deer, and the word *rājīva*. Since the state of being rejected is the cause for the survival of all living beings, and that survival is the cause for the stringing together of the bowstring and so forth, there is *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of causal indication). Additionally, there is *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle) in the form of supporting a particular instance with a general one. All these figures are merged within a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraviṣṭa*).

O Mother, let alone the coconut, which—because it is inferior to your breasts—is not even capable of conquering them despite being split; such is the movement of those who possess the meager strength of eunuchs.

O Mother! The *nārikela*—the coconut fruit—is expressed in the neuter gender (*klība*) to indicate its lack of manliness (*niṣpauruṣatva*). Its neuter state follows the rule: "In the case of all [fruits], the neuter gender applies when it has produced [its fruit]. Due to its state as an enemy—that is, its state as a foe—even though it is *vibhinna*, meaning its head is split open (a common worldly expression), it was not capable of conquering your two breasts. By using the masculine dual number for *vakṣojau* (breasts), the nature of those two as being like two heroic men is implied. The sense is that it is impossible for a single neuter thing to conquer two heroic men.

In this context, the word *nārikela* (coconut) has its syllable *ri* absent due to the state of being an enemy (*ari*), meaning that the letter *ke*—in which the letter *ri* is distinct—is likewise distinct; that is to say, it has undergone the loss of the letter *ke*. The word *api* is used for conjunction. The sense is that only the two remaining syllables, *nā* and *la*, remain. The point is that such is the condition—the state—of one who is impotent, a eunuch, whose vital breath is meager and whose power is small: namely, the very fact of being beyond the reach of defeat by others.

Elsewhere, the meaning is that there is the persistence of the neuter gender (*napuṃsakaliṅga*), which consists of vowels with few breaths (*alpaprāṇa*). Here, there is a single-locus coalescence (*ekavācakānupraveśa*) of the figure of dissimilitude (*viṣama*) and the corroboration by a different matter (*arthāntaranyāsa*).

Or as it is said: "Just as the coconut fruit, though remaining in the sky and not losing its meaning even when its external form is transformed, falls downward once it reaches ripeness; so too does the thief of the beauty of the breasts of the illustrious [lady]. (2182)

The coconut, which steals the fortune of Śrī’s breasts, remains somewhere in the sky—that is, in heaven—in some unknown region, having undergone a change of disguise (*vyañjanaparivṛtti*), meaning a transformation of dress through the exchange of its own marks. According to the *Ratnamālā*, "disguise" (*vyañjana*) refers to a sauce, a mark, a beard, a limb, or a syllable. It remains there even though it has not relinquished its purpose—that is, its wealth has not been lost. By this, the author expresses the extreme degree of the fault that causes its downfall.

However, regarding the renunciation of wealth acquired through censurable means, the intention is that there would not be an excessive degree of fault, according to the stated principle: "Whether by instruction or by liberation, the thief is released from theft; they are purified by the relinquishment of that which they have acquired through censurable means, as well as by recitation and austerity. For this very reason, at the time of ripening—the fruition of one's own committed evil deeds—one falls downward.

The meaning is that it "finds its course. In the alternative sense, the word *nārikela* (coconut) remains as *nārikela*—possessing the two syllables *nā* and *ke* in an unaltered state. This refers to the remaining letters; that is, even through the transposition of the consonants (*hal*), specifically the reversal of the *repha* and *lakāra* (the letters *r* and *l*) situated therein, yet not even of the vowels (*svara*) consisting of the *a* and *ā* residing therein. The point is that those [vowels] remain exactly in their original positions.

"Amuktārtham" means that its own denoted meaning has not been abandoned; the sense is that, according to the stated method, even when the word *nārikela* assumes the alternative form *nālikeram*, it is observed to possess precisely the same meaning. Here, because the falling of the coconut is supported by the meanings of such phrases as "the theft of the beauty of Śrī’s breasts," there is the figure of speech *kāvyaliṅga*. Furthermore, since the praise of the effect—the falling of the coconut—is the means of understanding the excellence of the beauty of Śrī’s breasts, which serves as its cause, there is also *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Praise of the Unrelated) based on the effect. These two figures are blended (*saṃkīryate*) through their mutual entry into a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśena*).

Just as someone who has attained a certain extraordinary proof established here by the Lord of the Serpent Hill (Śiva) would reach the state of being "jyeṣṭha" (the eldest/best), which is praised in the grammatical rule for the substitution of "jyā," and thus become worthy of praise like those beginning with Aja. || 2183 ||

A certain man is "praśasyaḥ," meaning praiseworthy or worthy of praise—that is, fortunate. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), the word *praśasya* refers to that which causes excellence (*ātiśāyanika*), meaning that which brings about superiority. The suffix *ṭhak* is applied here by the rule "prayojanam. In this context, by the word "prayojana," the cause (*hetu*) is intended, as explained by the statement: "The word *prayojana* signifies both fruit (*phala*) and cause (*kāraṇa*). In the alternative sense, it means that [the suffix] is prescribed for a word denoting excellence by the rule "atiśāyane tamabiṣṭhanau," which applies to words functioning with a qualified sense of preeminence. [The form *praśasya*] is derived from the root *śās* preceded by *ati*, with the suffix *lyuṭ*.

*Atiśāyanam* is simply *atiśayanam*; the lengthening of the vowel occurs due to this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*), and not because it is found in a *sūtra*. Therefore, the long vowel is correct even in common usage. Commentators state: "Irregular derivations (*nipātanas*) do not always invalidate [the general rule]; thus, the short vowel is also correct. For this very reason, [the term applies] even to Brahmā, Rudra, and others who begin with vowels.

"Praiseworthy" (ślāghyam) refers to that which begins with an *ac* vowel—that is, the first letter—which is of the form *aj*. This qualification should be understood so that there may be no doubt as to which suffix (*pratyaya*) is to be taken here, given that both *tamap* and *iṣṭhan* are prescribed for expressing excellence (*atiśāyana*). [The author] was [honored] by the Lord of the Ahiga mountain, Śrī Navāsa.

Elsewhere, in the *Pātañjalabhāṣya* on the *Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā*, the all-pervading Lord, who is adept at discerning the principles (*tattva*), has ordained knowledge in the form of a continuous stream of recollection (*smṛti-saṃtāna*). This is supported by the Vedic scripture: "May that God unite us with auspicious recollection," and by the Smṛti: "I grant that yoga of the intellect (*buddhi-yoga*) by which they come unto Me. This is the intended meaning. In the context of grammar (*śabda-pakṣa*), having attained the technical grammatical suffix (*pratyaya*), he reaches the earth (*jyādeśa*), for the *Amara-kośa* states: "The earth is called *kṣoṇī*, *jyā*, *kāśyapī*, and *kṣiti*."

"He would attain, that is, reach, preeminence (*jyeṣṭhatām*), which is the state of being most praiseworthy. The sense is this: by first attaining purity through the performance of actions without regard for their fruits, a man becomes praiseworthy; yet, upon reaching a state of most transparent conviction obtained through the grace of the Lord, he becomes exceedingly praiseworthy. Regarding the linguistic derivation (*śabdapakṣe*), the word *praśasya* takes the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan*, undergoes the substitution of *jy* for *praśasya*, and thus [becomes] *jyeṣṭha*. (Pāṇini 5.3.60: *praśasyasya śraḥ*).

By the word "jya," the meaning is that through the substitution of "jya," the form "jyeṣṭha"—characterized by the state of being the eldest (jyeṣṭhatām)—should go to, or attain. Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning conjunction) between the word "praśasya" (praiseworthy), which is the subject at hand, and the word "jyeṣṭha" (eldest), which is not the subject at hand. Furthermore, because the attainment of the state of being the eldest is caused by the meaning of the preceding sentence, there is also *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic causality). Thus, both of these figures of speech are subsumed within a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraviṣṭa*).
Just as an exception always subverts even your internal rule, how much more so [would it subvert] the one who ordains the commands of the station for all the gods, beginning with Acyuta? 2184.

O Acyuta! You are the ordainer of the governance and the administrator of the commands of all the abodes of the gods, beginning with the four-faced Brahmā; for as the Śruti declares: "Under the governance of this Imperishable One, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon remain held in their places."

And because it is said, "Viṣṇu is the teacher of the entire [universe]," the term *apavādaḥ* refers to your command—that is, the instruction issued by you—or it means censure; the sense is that it is a reproach directed toward you. According to Amara, "The two meanings of *apavāda* are censure and command. It is *antaraṅgam*, meaning extremely close due to being your own offspring; one should here reflect upon such scriptural passages as, "A son is indeed the heart," and "You are truly the self named 'son'. This [command] constantly agitates—that is, causes to tremble—even the Creator, the four-faced Brahmā.

The sense is that even Brahmā and the other gods tremble out of great fear, wondering what will happen when this command is transgressed. This is known from such scriptural passages as: "Whatever exists in this entire world, having issued forth, vibrates through the Prāṇa; it is a great terror, like a raised thunderbolt. What more need be said about how He agitates others—such as Marut, Taraṇi, Pāvaka, Tridaśanātha, Kāla, and so forth? The point is that if even they tremble at the mere instruction or censure of His own son, what need is there to mention others?

The meaning is this: apart from [this work], there is the instruction—that is, the teaching—of all divine words, that is, Sanskrit words; having made the promise, "Now begins the instruction of words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*), it belongs to the author of the *Mahābhāṣya*. "Your" means belonging to you, that is, determined by you. An exception (*apavāda*)—meaning a rule concerning exceptions—always subverts, that is, sets aside, even an internal (*antaraṅga*) rule or scripture. How much more so does it set aside a subsequent (*para*) rule? This is the sense of the rhetorical question.

The sense is: what wonder is there that an exception (*apavāda*), which is an internal obstacle, should subvert that which is itself to be subverted? For it is a rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "among the subsequent, the permanent, the internal, and the exceptional, each succeeding one is stronger. Here, because the linguistic conventions of grammar are superimposed upon the subject matter of the Vedānta system, there is both *samāsokti* (speech of brevity) and *kāvyārthāpatti* (poetic presumption), in the form of the establishment of a meaning by way of *kaimutya* (a fortiori), both of which are merged within a single expression.

Just as even one of low caste, having entrusted the burden of his soul to you, O Lord whose crest-jewel is sapphire, attains from you a supreme prosperity difficult for others to obtain, O Beloved of Śrī. (2185)

O beloved of Śrī! Though the sapphire on your crest—the crown of Indra-nīla gems—is of an inferior color (or, in another sense, though it is a *śūdra*, for Amara states that "the *śūdras* are of inferior caste"), it has placed its own burden upon you; that is to say, its weight is borne by your head because you wear it (in the other sense, it has entrusted the burden of its protection to you).
The qualification for *prapatti* belongs to anyone of all castes who lacks other means and desires to attain the goal,
provided they possess a sattvic disposition and so forth;
for it bestows the fruit of all desires upon everyone everywhere.

Because it is stated in such passages that *prapatti* (surrender) is accessible to all qualified persons (*sarvādhikārika*), one attains from You—more exalted than before—that which is superior even to the worlds of Brahmā and others; which is difficult for others to obtain, as it is supported by the splendor of the Lord’s divine form and cannot be reached by those who do not wear ornaments sustained by You; and which is hard to attain for those other than the surrendered, according to the saying: "Mukunda does not grant His own abode to anyone other than the surrendered. Thus, one attains *śrī* (prosperity)—in one sense the form of Śyāmala, and in another sense the wealth of supreme liberation (*niḥśreyasa*).

In this context, while the Lord’s sapphire crown is the subject to be described, the story of a man of low caste who has attained a high position is understood through the power of the similarity of epithets; thus, there is *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation). Furthermore, because the attainment of great glory even by one of low caste is caused by the fact that "the burden of his soul has been placed upon You," there is *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of causal indication). And because the excellence of the sapphire’s own natural blackness is described as being enhanced by its proximity to the divine form of the Lord, there is the *anuguṇa* (concordant) ornament. These three figures are thus blended (*saṃkīrṇa*) by their entry into a single expressive word.
If the oath "I shall never abandon Acyuta" is firmly established within the heart, that alone constitutes the true path; any other path that may become fractured is a wrong path. (2186)

The Lord Acyuta is one who never falters in his vow to protect those who have taken refuge in him; according to the maxim that "every statement carries an implicit emphasis," I shall certainly not abandon Him, my sole abode. O Purandara, if your oath—that you are a *viś* (a commoner)—is well-formed and truly firm, then strike me or do not strike me; go back to your city, O Indra!
For I shall never, having abandoned Govinda, worship anyone else, sir.

Thus, according to the manner stated by Aśvārīṣa in the *Viṣṇudharma*, the sense is: "If [one's devotion] is made firmer through exclusive dedication (*aikāntya*) to the Blessed One. This alone is the "good path" (*supatha*), the auspicious way; any other besides this is indeed a "bad path" (*vipatha*), a wrong way. The sense is that whatever oath is broken—that is, loosened—will result in falling away from exclusive dedication.
This is the thornless path upon which Hari is fully honored;
one should recognize that as a wrong path which leads to a destination devoid of Govinda.

This and other such examples are pointed out here for recognition. In both cases—*supathaḥ* and *vipathaḥ*—there is no compound with the word *pathin*, because the suffix for compounds is prohibited by the rule "not after a word denoting worship" (*na pūjanāt*).

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the word being neuter according to the rule *patha-saṃkhyā-vyayādeḥ*. However, there exists a word *patha* derived from the root *path* (meaning "to go") with the suffix *ac* (pacādyac), analyzed as *pathati* (it traverses) or *vyāpnoti* (it pervades). A compound is formed between that [word] and the two prefixes *su* and *vi*. Thus, the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa* states: "Vāṭa, patha, and mārga are synonyms for road. Therefore, there is no inconsistency in the present context. Moreover, Rabhasa says: "Vyadhva, vipatha, and kāpatha [denote bad roads]."

Elsewhere, the word *śapatha* (oath), when the letter *śa* is removed and joined with the letter *su*, becomes the very word *supatha* (good path). Conversely, another word, *vipatha* (bad path), when the letter *śa* is present and joined with the letter *vi*, becomes *viśapatha*. Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning conjunction) between the relevant and irrelevant meanings; furthermore, because the states of being a "good path" and a "bad path" are supported by the preceding and following sentence-meanings respectively, two instances of *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason) and *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) are intertwined through their mutual entry into a single expressive unit.

Just as the letter *r*, being thus addressed by your honor here, became deprived of its form during the stage of grammatical derivation; having entered into a closed position (*saṃvṛta*) and come to possess the sound of a semi-vowel (*antastha*), it was finally released at the end. || 2187 ||

O Blessed One, here "the enemy" (ari) refers to one who has been spoken of by you as an adversary, cast out, and rejected—meaning he has been driven away; for Amara states, "viddha, kṣipta, and īrita are synonyms. Therefore, immediately thereafter (atha), he is separated from his state of authority over the kingdom (prakriyā-daśā); for Amara states, "prakriyā is authority (adhikāra), while daśā means condition (avasthā). The implication is: how could there not be a fall from royal authority for one who has been cast out by you?

Having assumed a concealed and guarded appearance and form, he—driven by the loss of his royal authority and due to an abundance of shame—is hidden and lurking somewhere; such is the sense. He is called *antasthāḥ* because he "stays within" (*antaḥ tiṣṭhati*). The suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *sthā*, as evidenced by the usage in the *Mahābhāṣya*: "the word *śaṃsthā*. Alternatively, the suffix *vic* may be used. Everything that needs to be said on this matter has been elaborated by us in our commentary on the verse beginning with "antasthoṣmoddhārāt" in the *Lakṣmīsahasra-ratnaprakāśikā*.

The meaning is that, possessing such a tone or sound—that is, having a guttural sound—he became one whose voice was submerged by shame and fear; [as Medinī states: "The word *svara* refers to the breath of the nose, to vowels such as 'a', and to musical notes such as *ṣaḍja*. Ultimately, he was released or cast out. The sense is that, due to his lack of manliness, he was excluded from the assembly of the brave.

In this context, *atrabhavate* is a compound word. It means "by the venerable one," that is, by the learned one. *Īritaḥ* means "stated. *Prakriyā-daśayā* means "in the state of grammatical derivation," specifically the stage of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*). *Vidhuraḥ* means "devoid" or "lacking. *Ariḥ* refers to the word *ari*. The point is that at the time of employing the word *ari* alone—as in *ariḥ*—no euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) of the letter *a* with another *a* is observed. In this interpretation, the division of the phrase *bhavatākāram* is *bhavatā akāram*.

The meaning is as follows: having attained the *saṃvṛta* (closed) [articulation], characterized by the effort of being closed and the short form of the vowel *a*—in accordance with the rule stating, "When a short *a*-vowel is employed, it is *saṃvṛta*"—during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*), the short *a* possesses the effort of being *vivṛta* (open). However, when the word *ari* alone is employed, because the stage of derivation no longer exists, the *a* possesses only the effort of being *saṃvṛta*. This fact was indicated by the author of the Sūtras; for instance, in the rule *a a*, the *vivṛta* [quality] is restated and the *saṃvṛta* [quality] is prescribed by this [rule].

Furthermore, because this [substitution] is not established (*asiddha*) with respect to the entire *Aṣṭādhyāyī* from the perspective of the grammatical system (*śāstra-dṛṣṭyā*), its state of being "unveiled" (*vivṛtatva*) certainly exists. Thus, the Sūtra states: "What precedes is unestablished" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*). This is an introductory heading (*adhikāra*); by this, the three chapters (*tripādī*) are unestablished with respect to the seven chapters and a quarter (*sapādasaptādhyāyī*). Within the three chapters as well, a subsequent rule is unestablished with respect to what precedes it. All of this is explicit in the *Kaumudī* treatise. In this view, the word *atha* ("now") connects here [to the preceding context].

Now, immediately after the pronunciation of the vowel *a*, there follows the semivowel (*antastha*) and the vowel (*svara*). According to the usage in the *Pāṇinīya-śikṣā* and other texts—such as "this [word] ends with a semivowel" and "it is joined with semivowels"—the phoneme designated as a semivowel (*antastha*) in the word *ari* is the letter *r*. Then, the vowel is the letter *i* following the *r*. This is based on the grammatical rule: "The letters *y, r, l, v* are the semivowels (*antasthāḥ*); the vowels (*ac*) are the vowels (*svarāḥ*)."

Having become "tadvān" (possessing that), at the end—in the final stage—he became "visṛṣṭaḥ" (emitted/ended); this expression is so stated because the word *ari* is composed of the short vowel *a*, the letter *r*, the letter *i*, and the *visarga*. It should be understood that here there is a *śleṣa* (punning conjunction) between the meaning of the word *ari* as it occurs in the non-contextual (aprakṛta) sense, and the word *ari* itself in its non-contextual form. In the first stage, the excellence of the Lord’s prowess—the contextual subject—is perceived through the account of the enemy who was defeated—the non-contextual subject; thus, this is an instance of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) based on the effect (*kāryanibandhanā*).

Because the deficiency of the ten stages of the creative process has been cast aside by the Blessed One, and because that [process] is established as having a conventional form, a series of poetic figures (kāvyaliṅga) are intermingled through their entry into a single expressive word.

Just as this one Lord is "madhyama" (the middle) because he is not subordinate, while that other is "adaḥ" (that), who else could be "para" (beyond)? For he alone is counted at the very beginning by the most excellent of the wise.

This Blessed One, Śrīnivāsa, is alone because he exists in a state that is not subordinate (*anupasarjanabhāvāt*). According to Amara’s lexicon, *upasarjana* means "subordinate" or "secondary" (*apradhāna*), while that which is other than this is *anupasarjana*; the meaning is that he exists through his primacy. He is "not mediocre" (*amadhyamaḥ*); the intention is that he is the most excellent of all, being the foremost in all the worlds, in accordance with the statement: "Of him, the Lord of the World and Protector of the Earth. *Ato'nyaḥ* means "other than this," i.e., different from this Blessed One.

Who is superior, even the most excellent? The meaning is: none at all. The sense is: what possibility could there even be for another to possess excellence compared to this one? Here, the particle *api* expresses possibility. By the best among the wise—the foremost knowers of Brahman—he, this very Blessed Lord (*bhagavān*), is indeed reckoned as being at the very beginning, ahead of all others including Brahmā and the rest. He is celebrated as the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world. (Amara states: "The word *hi* is used in the senses of cause and emphasis.")

Elsewhere, words such as *eka* and others refer to the word-form itself; "this one" (*ekaḥ*) refers to the Blessed Lord (*bhagavān*) who is not intermediate (*amadhyamaḥ*), meaning devoid of middle vowels (*madhyamavarṇavidhuraḥ*). The word *adaḥ* means "another," and the word *api* is displaced [in the sentence]. Why is this one, "this very word" (*tat eṣo'pi śabdaḥ*), counted at the beginning of the *sarva*-group by the best of scholars, the grammarians, because it does not exist in a subordinate state—that is, because it lacks the status of being subordinate to another? Each of these, beginning with *eka*, is connected with the verb "is counted."

It has been stated that "the words beginning with *sarva* (sarvādi) do not include those that have become subordinate members (*upasarjanībhūta*) of a compound, because they are included in the list only as things consistent with that [definition of being a word], since the name 'Great List' (*mahāsaṃjñā*) was established for that purpose. Thus, it is said that only those *sarvādi* words which are not subordinate members are read in that list. It should be understood that in this verse, the words *eka*, *idam*, *bhavat*, *adas*, *anya*, *kim*, *para*, *tad*, and *etad* are indeed arranged exactly as they appear in the *sarvādi* list. Herein lies a *śleṣa* (punning double entendre) concerning both the subject at hand and that which is not.

In the context of the primary subject matter, because the Lord’s status as being counted among all the *sarva*-class [of numerals] is supported by the meaning of the preceding sentence, there is the figure of speech *kāvyaliṅga*. Furthermore, because words such as *eka* and others—which are well-known to be recited together with the *sarva*-class—are placed [in juxtaposition], there is the figure *ratnāvalī*. These two coalesce through their entry into a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*). It was established during the discussion of those figures of speech below that even when the conventional order is reversed, the *ratnāvalī* still occurs.
O Lord, at the very beginning of this world as it flourishes, you alone were seen; who indeed could there be other than you—neither one superior to you nor one equal to you? (2189)

O Lord! You shine forth at the very beginning of the entire universe; that is to say, You are the cause of the entire world. This should be construed by repeating the phrase "shines forth" (*samullasati*) from this [subject] "from You": [the meaning is] "it shines forth" when You have manifested. In this world, there is nothing else of such a kind—that is to say, nothing other than You who is the cause of the world.

Who indeed is there other than you—whether superior (para) or equal (sama)—other than this very you? Let it be observed; that is to say, let it be reflected upon. The sense is: in this world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, which is an effect of you who are the cause of the entire universe—who else, being devoid of such causality over the universe, could be either superior or equal to you, being merely an effect of yours? This is in accordance with the Śruti: "Neither his equal nor his superior is seen."

Otherwise, O Lord! the word *bhavat* shines forth in this group beginning with *sarva*, being that in which the substitute *smāt*—which takes the place of *ṅasi*—is absent, and likewise that in which the substitute *smin*—which takes the place of *ṅi*—is absent. The sense is this: although the word *bhavat* is listed in the group of pronouns (*sarvanāman*), because it ends in a consonant (*halanta*), the substitutes *smāt* and *smin* prescribed by the rule "for *ṅasi* and *ṅi*, there are *smāt* and *smin*" (Pāṇini 7.1.15)—which are conditioned by [the stem] ending in *at*—do not occur. From here, in this group of pronouns, the suffix *tasi* is used for all case-endings (*sārvavibhaktika*).

The word *paraḥ* [is like] the word *paraḥ*; the word *itaraḥ* [is like] the word *itaraḥ*; the word *samaḥ* [is like] the word *samaḥ*; and the word *kaḥ* [is like] the word *kiṃ*. The meaning is that the word *bhavat*, unlike these, is not devoid of the substitutes *smāt* and *smin*.
