The sense is that since these aforementioned words—listed in the group of pronouns (*sarvanāman*) beginning with *para*—end in a vowel, the substitutes *smāt* and *smin* necessarily apply to them. Here, there is a commingling (*saṃkara*) of two figures of speech through their entry into a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*): the figure of "blending" (*śleṣa*) between the subject at hand and the subject not at hand, and the variety of "lamp" (*pradīpa*) consisting of the statement that the comparison of the Lord, the subject being described, is not fully realized.

Just as You are expressible by all names, situated at the beginning and end of all things, and are indeed the universe itself; so too, O Acyuta, I do not speak of any other being here who is inferior to You. 2190.

O Acyuta! You are expressible by all names; that is, You are expressible by all names, such as Brahmā and others. He states the reason for this: because You abide at the beginning and at the end of the entire universe. In the phrase "abiding at the end," it should also be understood that You abide in the middle as well. Therefore, You are the Viśva; You are the one whose body is the entire universe.

The meaning is that, according to the process described in such scriptural passages as "From which indeed these beings [are born]," you are the source of the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the universe; and because you are the inner self (sarva-śarīraka) of all, words denoting bodies ultimately refer to the embodied self—thus, you are the referent of all words, beginning with "Brahmā."

"Then indeed, the Person Nārāyaṇa desired, 'May I create the worlds,'" beginning thus, and ending with, "They arise from Nārāyaṇa, they proceed toward Nārāyaṇa, and they dissolve into Nārāyaṇa"; and [the scripture] beginning with, "Brahmā is Nārāyaṇa, and Śiva is Nārāyaṇa," and ending with, "All this is indeed Nārāyaṇa"—these [passages], which establish the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between the world and Brahman based on their relationship as effect and cause, are already considered in their sense by the statement: "Having created that... [and so forth].

The scriptural passages beginning with "It entered into that very thing; having entered it, it became the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat)" should also be considered here. That which is "other" (itaraḥ), meaning inferior to you (tvadadharaḥ), is even less than that. Regarding the word *ihatyam*: from the indeclinable *iha*, the suffix *tyap* is applied according to the rule "avyayāttyap," as restricted by the rule "amehakvatasitrebhya eva."

I do not speak of even that aforementioned Brahmā who has arisen in this world which is your own effect, as being like You—namely, as the denotation of all words by virtue of being the cause of all and the body of all. The sense is that he does not possess such qualities. In the alternative (allegorical) sense: *viśvam* is the word *viśva*; *tvat* is the word *tvad*; *adharaḥ* is the word *adhara*; *itaraḥ* is the word *itara*; *yaḥ* is the word *yat*.

The meaning is that *bdaś* is expressed by a pronoun, insofar as it is stated to possess the technical designation (*saṃjñaka*) of a pronoun. He states the reason for this: because it stands at the end or in the middle of the group beginning with *sarva*, according to the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) "those beginning with *sarva* are pronouns" (*sarvādīni sarvanāmāni*). The construction is as follows: in this group beginning with *sarva*, I declare—that is, I recite—the word *nema*; I declare the word *tyam*; and likewise, I declare even the word *kam*, which stands at the end of the group beginning with *sarva*.

Because the word *kiṃ* is listed at the end of the *sarva*-class (the group of pronouns beginning with *sarva*), there is a commingling (*saṃkara*) of the two varieties of *samāsokti* and *pratīpa* through their mutual entry into a single expressive word.
Just as that Brahman first ordained everything, and thereafter protects this entire universe equally, bestowing within itself both the high and the low—what else could there be beyond it? (2191)
In the beginning, at the outset, that Brahman fashioned and created everything; thereafter, following that creation, that Brahman protects and sustains the entire universe together with me, Śrī.
Hṛṣīkeśa, together with Lakṣmī, who is the embodiment of compassion,
is celebrated as the Protector in all the Siddhāntas and even in the Vedāntas.

Because of this statement: at the time of ultimate dissolution (*pralaya*), what else could there be that places—meaning deposits within itself—the entire universe, both the superior (such as the Supreme Brahman) and the inferior (everything else), being the agent of creation and sustenance? What other entity could there be to perform the act of withdrawal? The sense is that, according to such scriptural passages as "from which indeed these beings are born," it is He alone who is established as the cause of the world's birth, maintenance, and dissolution.
In this regard, one should also remember such verses as: "In whose belly is the manifold universe headed by Hara and Viriñci? Who protects it, and from whose navel was it born? and so forth.

In one sense, at the beginning—that is, at the commencement of the entire group of words starting with "sarva"—He established that Brahman as the word *sarva*. Following that, immediately after the placement of the word *sarva*, He protects and establishes the word *viśva*; such is the meaning. [The word] *antaḥ* refers to *viśva*.

Between the two words *kim*, there are the words *sama*, *sva*, *para*, *avara*, and *anya*—that is, from the words *samasvaparāvarānya*; here, no specific sequence is intended. *Ādadhat* means "he placed" (*nyadadhāt*). This is the *laṅ* (imperfect) of the root *dhā* in its *parasmaipada* form. "In the end" (*antataḥ*) means at the conclusion of the list; the word *kim* would be placed there. The sense is that in the *sarvādi* group, after the initial words *sarva* and *viśva*, and between the words *sama*, *para*, *avara*, and *anya*, the word *kim* is seen at the very end.

Here, since the account of the unmentioned verbal sage (*śābdika-muni*) is perceived while the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*) is the subject under discussion, this is *samāsokti* (speech of brevity). Furthermore, because the creation and so forth mentioned in the Vedas and the grammatical derivation of the *sarva*-class of words are respectively presented in sequence, it should be understood as a *ratnāvalī* (jewel-garland) figure mixed with *śleṣa* (punning), wherein both meanings enter into a single expressive word (*ekavācaka*).
O Friend of Śrī, just as the essential nature of either of you two is to be counted here among the entire multitude of faces, so shall it never be for even one among the final few remaining.

O Friend of Śrī! And this [address] is an embellishment for the meaning that is about to be expressed. Regarding the term *bhavadubhayānyatarasya*: "Śrī" and "you" (*bhavān*) are "the two Bhavantas. According to the rule *tyadādīni sarvair nityam*, there is a single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) formation with the word *bhavat*. The sense is: of that pair (*ubhaya*), which is the form of "you," consisting of the two—namely, Śrī and you (*bhavataḥ*)—it is "of either one" (*anyatarasya*). Thus, it means "of Śrī and of you."

The meaning is as follows: His essential nature (svarūpa)—consisting of being the cause of all, the sovereign of all, and so forth—is to be counted upon by the multitude of mouths (mukhagaṇa), that is, the collection of faces, of all people in this world; it is to be propounded everywhere by everyone with their own voices. However, in the end, even among those few who are recent, limited, and inferior—meaning even among the likes of the four-faced Brahmā and others—the essential nature of any one of them whatsoever shall not be thus countable by the multitude of mouths of all. This is because the nature of all of them is not such.
The compound "bhavad-ubhayānyatarasya" is a collective [samāhāra] of these words:
*pakṣe* (in one alternative), *bhavān* (you), *ubhaya-* (both), and *anyatara-* (either one); it refers to the very forms (*svarūpa*) of these words in this science of grammar.

It must be counted among the *sarvādi* group within the *sarva-mukha-gaṇa*, because they are recited therein. The compound of the words *carama*, *alpa*, *katipaya*, and *anyatama*—meaning "one of these"—is formed as before. However, their own forms, like those of *bhavat* and so on, will never be included in the *sarvādi* group; for, since they are not recited there, the rule *prathamacarama* (Pāṇini 1.1.33) specifically prescribes their status as *sarvanāman* only when followed by the suffix *jas*. Here, there is a single-word-entrance (*ekavācakānupraveśa*) of the figures of speech *śleṣa* (paronomasia), *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification), and *parikarāṅkura* (the sprout of poetic embellishment).

Just as the term "right" (dakṣiṇa) is established as denoting both [the south] and [the east], and "left" (uttara) as denoting the north, so too this "other" (para) and "this" (avara) are not established in such a fixed manner.

He is the "Eastern" one, being the cause of the entire universe, according to such scriptural authorities as: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," "I indeed existed here before," and "The cause of effects is prior. He is the "Southern" one, possessing the skill for the creation of the universe and so forth in accordance with His own mere volition, through the process described in such passages as: "It thought: 'May I become many. It should also be understood that He is "most noble" (*mahodāra*).

He is established as the "Teacher who has entered within, the Self of all beings," and so forth; thus, according to the manner described, he has entered into the entire world and is its controller. Furthermore, it should be understood that his resolve is firm because his mind remains unperturbed even by those who point out his internal faults.
The sky might fall, the earth might shatter, and the Himalayas might break into pieces;
the ocean of waters might dry up, O Kṛṣṇa, but my word shall never be in vain.

This is because he himself has stated this. This very one, the Lord Devottara—the best of gods—possesses the nature of being the "All" (sarvanāmatā) and is thus denotable by every word. He is "unrestricted" (avyavasthita), meaning he is devoid of fixed limitations such as being the cause of the universe, entering into it, or acting as its controller. It should also be understood that, due to his fickle-mindedness, he is incapable of fulfilling his own promises.
Furthermore, even the "other" (para)—anyone else such as Brahmā or Rudra—is certainly not like him, for they are "inferior" (avara), being lesser than the Blessed One.
The intended meaning is that it certainly does not partake in being denotable by all names on the basis of such grounds as being the cause of the entire world.

In this context, O Lord: these words—*dakṣiṇa*, *pūrva*, *uttara*, *para*, and *avara*—when they are "established" (*vyavasthita*), that is, having attained a fixed status, do not possess the designation of "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*). They say that "establishment" (*vyavasthā*) is "the restriction of a limit relative to its own denotation. For example, the aforementioned words *dakṣiṇa* and so forth, when they do not possess such establishment—that is, when they have not attained a fixed status—do not bear the designation of "pronoun"; such is the meaning.

Regarding the rule "the words *pūrva*, *para*, *avara*, *dakṣiṇa*, *uttara*, *apara*, and *adhara* are [all] pronouns when used in the sense of relative position (*vyavasthā*) and not as proper names (*asaṃjñā*)," since their status as pronouns is caused by their being in a state of relative position, and their lack of such status is caused by their being non-relative, two instances of *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason) are here merged into a single expression through the blending (*śleṣa*) of the relevant and the irrelevant.
Just as the sun, approaching before you with its own hand in an attempt to steal the luster of your feet, was driven away by her, O Mother; shaken off, this maker of day became a pale-rayed one.

O Mother! This maker of the day, the sun, having approached you—meaning, having come face-to-face, acting as one who advances against an enemy (abhyamitrīṇa)—desires to seize the luster of your feet, that is, the beauty of your feet (and not the beauty of your hands), with his own hand, that is, his ray. By means of that luster, he has been banished right from before you, from your own dwelling, house, or city—according to Amara, *agāra*, *nagara*, and *pura* all mean "city"—just as the banishment of great offenders is well known.

Therefore, the *dhūta* (the shaken one) trembled, wondering what further punishment might come; or rather, he was "expelled" (*nirvāsita*) from the very body before him—that is, withdrawn from it. Alternatively, even having attained another body, the *dhūta* trembled due to the lingering attachment to his former dwelling. [Medinī lexicon: "The word *pura* is neuter when meaning 'house' or 'body']. He became one whose hands were *dhūsara*—slightly pale; the sense is that his luster became exceedingly dull. It is also understood that his hands became leprous (*śvitri*).”

In this context, the word *vāsarakara* (the sun) has its initial portion (*agra-bhāga*)—namely the syllable *vā*—rendered "perfumed" (*vāsita*), meaning it is not [so] perfumed because it is connected with the particle *na* (forming *na-vāsita*). Here, as in the case of *niścala* and similar compounds, the prefix *nis-* has a meaning equivalent to the negative particle *na*. Thus, the meaning is that the syllable *vā* is non-existent. The actual state of affairs is that the syllable *vā* is shaken off (*dhūta*) and, in its very place, the phoneme *dhū* is woven (*ūta*), resulting in the form *dhūsarakara*.

Here, based on the identification [of two things] through the medium of paronomasia (*śleṣa*) starting with the word "in front" (*purataḥ*), there is the figure of the "Uneven" (*viṣama*), characterized by the attainment of an undesirable state—namely, the sun's (*vāsarakara*) having pale rays (*dhūsarakaratva*). Furthermore, since the excellence of the luster of the Goddess’s feet (*śrīcaraṇaruci*), which serves as the cause, is illuminated by the action of the irrelevant sun (*aprastutavāsarakara*) acting as the thief of that very luster, there is also the figure of "Indirect Description" (*aprastutapraśaṃsā*) based on the effect. These two figures, along with the figure of "Poetic Reason" (*kāvyaliṅga*), are mutually interpenetrated within a single expressive word.

O lotus-eyed one, just as it is said that this holy ford, which destroys sins and was brought down from your mountain, is called "Pāpanāśana" (Destroyer of Sins) not only by the Draviḍas, but indeed by everyone, so too [is it known]. 2195.

O Abjekṣaṇa! Regarding that purifying holy site named Pāvanāśana, which has been brought forth—that is, caused to flow—from your mountain Śeṣādri, it is not only the Dramiḍas (those born in the Draviḍa country) who designate it as "Pāvanāśana. Rather, all people, even those born in every other land, designate it as such. The word "batā" expresses wonder. Since the Dramiḍas pronounce the initial letter *pa* as *va* due to their training in the grammar of Agastya, their usage of the term "Pāvanāśana" is entirely appropriate; however, the fact that those born in other lands pronounce it thus is indeed a matter of great wonder—this is the intended meaning.

The apparent contradiction—whether "Pāvanāśana" refers to Śeṣa (the serpent) who feeds on air (*pavana-aśana*) and bears the form of a mountain (*giri-rūpa-dhara*), or whether it belongs to the sages (*pavana-aśana*) who are "air-eaters," or whether it means that his food (*aśana*) or consumption (*prāśana*) is purifying (*pāvana*)—must be resolved. Thus, there is the figure of speech *Nirukti* (etymological analysis). In the alternative sense, the meaning is: even people from all lands call the word "Pāpanāśana" (Destroyer of Sin) by "Pāvanāśana," because it has been diverted (*apavāhita*) from your mountain (*tāvakagiri*)—that is, from your speech; for the letter *va* has been placed in the very position of the letter *pa*, resulting in the word "Pāvanāśana" where there was "Pāpanāśana. (In this case, *apa* means "without *pa*," or "diverted").
Here, there is a mutual interpenetration of the figures *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing) and *nirukti* (etymological interpretation) within a single expressive word.
O Murāri, behold how a man, once favored by you and then restrained by you, dwells together with his queen upon a magnificent throne, radiant as the sun! (2196)

O Murāri! A man favored by you, even if he is one who has been restrained, together with his queen, becomes noble like the sun; for the Amarakośa states: "The word *śubhra* refers to mica (neuter) and to that which is radiant or white (masculine/feminine/neuter)," and the Medinīkośa also states: "'*Śubhra*' is neuter for mica, and masculine/feminine/neuter for the radiant and the white."

The meaning is that he becomes a great king who dwells upon a magnificent golden throne in the form of a vast couch (*subhūriparyaṅka*), enjoying immense power together with queens who have been consecrated. Regarding the word *bhūri*, the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The masculine *bhūri* refers to Vāsudeva, Hari, and Parameṣṭhin; it is neuter for gold, and it is used as an adjective for a wise man. It is fitting that one favored by you should become such a person. However, the phrase "Alas! Even when restrained, he becomes such a person" indicates a sense of wonder.

The resolution [of the apparent contradiction] is as follows: he is so called because he dwells together with female buffalo and female camels; thus, in the phrase *aryamaśubhram*, the word division is *aryam* and *aśubhram*. *Aśubhram* means turbid; *subhūri* means exceedingly vast; *aryam* means devoid of the letter *rya*; and *paryaṅkam* means mud. The sense is that he "inhabits" it, meaning he undergoes rebirth as a buffalo. Here, there is a *saṃkara* (commixture) characterized by the mutual entry of a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*), consisting of the figure of speech *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) enlivened by *śleṣa* (paronomasia), as well as the figures of *samavibhāvanā* (poetic fancy of equal distribution).
O Mukunda, those dull-witted ones for whom reverence toward those prostrate at Your feet always appears as mere poison, will surely find that state of true reverence.

O Mukunda! toward those who have bowed at your feet and taken refuge in your lotus-feet, even that which is hateful appears as mere poison—that is to say, it becomes an object of aversion—to those people for whom you possess honor and great regard; yet those dull-witted and unfortunate ones find the station of Raurava, a particular hell characterized by the experience of thousands of miseries resulting from a continuous succession of terrible sins.

The essential meaning is this: those great devotees (*mahā-bhāgavatas*) who disregard the burden placed upon the feet of the Blessed One fall into the very great hell. Elsewhere, the word *gauravam* (respect) appears as *garatayā*—that is, by the "gar-ness" of the syllable *ga* and the "rat-ness" of the letter *ra*. The word division is *amandāḥ*, meaning "the wise" or "the skillful. Such people understand that the state of *gaurava* (respect) is actually *raurava* (the Raurava hell). Thus is the sense.

The sense is that, according to the stated method, the word *gaura* acquires the state of being *raurava*. Here, the figure of speech *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason), based on the meaning of the sentence; the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the relevant and the irrelevant; and the *ullāsa* (exaltation) alaṃkāra—characterized by the emergence of a defect born of disregard for the *Bhāgavata* due to its greatness and virtues—all three enter into a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraviṣṭa*).
Or rather, O Blessed One, let those who perceive reality as it is declare that you are not eternal; we shall awaken that person by taking your side—what loss is there in that? (2198)

"O Blessed One, O Eternal One!"—the meaning is "O Ancient Person. A person who perceives contrary to reality (*pratīpadṛk*), one whose vision is opposed to the truths established by the scriptures, might say of You, the Eternal One: "At that time," meaning at the time prior to creation, "it was not" (*na tad āsa*), i.e., it did not exist. Thus [the verse begins] "Not non-existent" (*nāsad āsīt*).

One who considers himself omniscient but possesses a crooked intellect might speak thus, being satisfied with the meaning perceived at first glance from the mere fragment of scripture stating, "He was [then] always existing" (*sīnnno sadāsīt tadānīm*). The sense is that such is simply his natural state. The word *āsa* is an indeclinable (avyaya) that resembles a verbal form ending in a *tiṅ* suffix. In the alternative view, for a person who perceives the sequence of syllables as reversed—reading it as *sadātana* rather than *tadānāsa*—it appears as *natadāsa*; the statement is made thus to account for the perception of such a person.

Addressing that person who thus perceives contradictory meanings and observes an inverted sequence, we first show him respect and awaken him, saying, "Do not speak thus"; then, having consoled him, we set forth the meaning of the treatise, saying, "Behold correctly."
But for one who imparts knowledge and instruction in Dharma to a person lacking understanding,
the fruit of that act is not equal to giving away the entire earth.

The sense is that this is because one hears of the great fruitfulness of giving knowledge to one who is ignorant. Therefore, what loss could there be from such contrary speech? The meaning is: even if he is thus enlightened, if he does not abandon his contrary way of speaking, there would be no loss for you at all by his words; on the contrary, [the loss] would be his alone.

Alternatively, the meaning is that he is the *puruṣa*—well-known as eternal, and for that very reason unlimited by time, as indicated by the etymological derivation: "Because 'I was here previously,' that is the *puruṣatva* of the *puruṣa*. This is also an elliptical expression for his being devoid of spatial and substantial limitations. The word division is *tvā ādṛtya*. We address you (*tvā*) with the phrase *tena na tadāsa*.

The meaning is that we address Him with that vocative term, having analyzed the compound as "one whose [servants] are Brahmā, Īśāna, and others," who are bowed down, prostrated, and have become servants—according to the teaching that "all selves are indeed by nature the servants of the Supreme Self. That word "by him" (tena) is repeated; the sense is: what loss is there for you in such contrary speech? There is no loss at all; on the contrary, it would only serve to declare His status as the Lord of All.

Here, the *ullāsa* ornament— which consists in the description of the non-arising of faults in the form of defects— becomes blended (*saṃkīrṇa*) with the *vakrokti* ornament, characterized by the conceptualization of a different meaning for the words spoken by the messenger who speaks against [the intended purpose], through their mutual entry into a single expressive word.

O Eternal One, if one with perverted vision says, "I bow to Natanāsa," let him say it; but who with sound vision would describe You, O Acyuta, as the protector of the lowly and the compassionate? 2199.

O Eternal, Ancient Puruṣa! Let a man of perverted vision—one who perceives things contrary to their actual state—say as he pleases that you possess the entirety of the marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa) as described in the *Sāmudrika* [treatises]; what power is there to restrain him? For those with distorted vision do not accept an object even when it is correctly described by those with clear sight. This is the sense. In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*): [He whose nose is bent down is] *natanāsa*; O *natanāsa*! Let him say as he pleases... [the rest follows as above].

The phrase "like a Yavana" (yavana iva) implies that one who displays a reversed nose-mark (*pratilomavaṇadarśa*) should call out the word "Sanātana" as "Natanāsa"—this is the intended meaning for the sake of producing an extraordinary aesthetic charm (*camatkārātiśaya*). O Acyuta, O You of boundless mercy! What man of true vision (*sudṛk*), a right-seer, would describe You—who possess a prominent nose according to the description "with a prominent nose, a pure smile, and tender cheeks"—as *avanāṭa*, meaning having a sunken or depressed nose? The sense is that no person of true insight would speak in such a manner.

From the word *ava*, which is carried over from the preceding sūtra "ava-kuṭārācca," the suffix *nāṭac* is applied according to the rule "nate nāsikāyāḥ saṃjñāyāṃ ṭīṭac-nāṭac-bhraṭacaḥ. That which is the bending (*nata*) of the nose is *avanāṭa*; by connection with that, the nose is called *avanāṭā*. A person [with such a nose] is *avanāṭaḥ*. Amara states: "The words *avaṭīṭaḥ*, *avanāṭaḥ*, and *avabhraṭaḥ* refer to one with a bent nose. Alternatively, [the term *nāsa* is derived as follows]: from the root *nas* meaning "to bend" (in the sense of "not placing"), with the addition of the causal suffix *ṇic* and then the suffix *ac* (pacādyac), we have *nāsa*; this is then compounded with the negative particle *na*. Thus, *na nāsaḥ* becomes *anāsa*. (Note: The text here appears to be explaining the formation of *anāsa* as part of the etymological derivation of *avanāṭa*.)

"O you whose nose is bent down (natanāsa)—meaning, one who has completely destroyed those who bow before you—address Him thus: O Natanāsa! Speak to Him who is elevated by boundless compassion (anavadhikakṛponna); for Amara states, 'samunnam and uttam mean elevated. O Acyuta, such is the sense that You alone are supremely compassionate. He is called 'Avanāṭa' because He causes [the world] to bend down; the root naṭa is used in the sense of 'avaskandana' (striking down) according to the Curādi class. For avaskandana means injury; from that, the suffix 'ac' is applied (pacādyac).
Thus he explains.

"No one with clear vision calls you, the source of supreme compassion, a 'harm-doer' (hiṃsaka)," so he says. This is the underlying sentiment (*bhāva*). Here, there are two figures of speech (*kāvyaliṅga*): the state of having "perverse vision" (*viparītadṛktva*) serves as the cause for the statement that he has a "drooping nose" (*natanāsa*), and the state of having "clear vision" (*sudṛktva*) serves as the cause for the non-statement that he has a "drooping face" (*avanāṭa*). Furthermore, the figure of speech *avajñā* (disregard)—characterized by the non-arising of the defect of having a drooping face in the Blessed One due to the defect of the ill-spoken words of those with perverse vision—is included within the same expressive word (*ekavācakānupraviṣṭa*).
Or, for instance:
"O Nanda’s youth, because you are intoxicated, this peacock-feather crest, having become a peacock on your face, becomes an armlet and adorns your arm. (2200)

O Nandakiśora! *Māyūram* means "belonging to a peacock"; according to the rule *avayave ca prāṇyoṣadhivṛkṣebhyaḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* (forming *maya*) is used here in the sense of a part (*avayava*). Thus, it means a peacock feather. This [feather], acting as the agent, has been *śekharitam*—meaning made into a crest (*śekhara*), or adorned. Alternatively, *śekharitam* means made into a crest, which is to say it has been brought to the highest pinnacle of excellence. The essential truth is that it has been worn as an ear-ornament (*avataṃsa*).

For this reason: *mādyattvāt* means the state of being intoxicated (*mādyataḥ bhāvaḥ*). This is derived from the root *mad*, ending in the suffix *śatṛ*, with the abstract suffix *tva* added to express the state. When *mādyattvam* is analyzed, it refers precisely to the connection with intoxication, according to the statement of the grammarians: "In the case of primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*), the suffixes *tva* and *tal* denote a relationship. Thus, the meaning is "intoxication brought about by excessive joy. Alternatively, *mādyattvam* may be analyzed as follows: that which has the letter *mā* (the syllable *mā*) as its initial part is *mādya*; the state of that is *mādyattvam*. Here, the doubling of the letter *t* occurs according to the rule *anaci ca*.

The sense is that this is because the word *māyūra* possesses such a nature. The ablative case is used with the elision of the suffix *lyap*; the meaning is "having set aside the initial *m-* and the following vowel. There is an identity between the word and its meaning. "With a cry" (*sakekam*) means "accompanied by a *keka*"—that is, the cry of a peacock; thus, like a peacock which is its own constituent part, it itself also emits the sound *keka* due to being overcome by intoxication. This is a hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). Elsewhere...

The meaning is as follows: in the first part of the word *mukha*, when the letter *ma* is separated, it is "accompanied by the letter *ke*" (*sakekam*), that is to say, it exists together with the letter *ke*. The suffix *kap* is applied here according to the rule *śeṣād vibhāṣā*. Having become a *keyūra*—that is, having turned into an armlet—in the manner described, it becomes the word *keyūra*; this is the sense. It adorns your arm, your *bhuja*. The underlying intention is that it honors [the arm] out of a desire to repay the favor of being made its own crest-ornament; the actual fact, however, is that it merely decorates it.

Through the imaginative identification (*tādātmya-sambhāvanā*) of Keyūra with the peacock’s tail-feathers, his being composed of emerald is illuminated. Here, because the mutual benefit between the Lord and the peacock’s tail-feathers is described, there is the figure of speech *anyonyālaṅkāra* (mutual ornament), which is integrated into a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraviṣṭa*) with the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).

Just as a wood-apple fruit (*mālūra*) there desires to conquer her pair of breasts, having internally assumed a slow rhythm (*laya*), it then becomes a peacock feather (*māyūra*) and sports upon your head, O beautiful woman, daughter of Nanda! (2201)

The word *mālūra* refers to the *bilva* fruit; [the moon], desiring to conquer your pair of breasts, was thus [vanquished] by that very pair of breasts. The sense is that it met its end within [your bosom] itself, remaining unknown to anyone else. Having reached its dissolution, it then became a peacock feather (*māyūra*).

The meaning is as follows: in the *pakṣa* (side/alternative), the letter *la* is "driven out"—that is, removed from the very middle portion—of that word *mālūra*, which is such that its *ya* [is present]; thus, by removing the *la* from the middle and joining it with that very *ya*, the word *māyūra* is produced. It becomes "sportive" (*vilāsi*), meaning characterized by sporting, upon your crest (*tyanmaulau*). The implication is that it ascends your head, being the manifest adversary for the sake of avenging the enmity.

"O wife of Nanda’s son"—this is the address, containing the intention that "just as a peacock feather becomes your crest, so too [the moon] shall become yours. The truth is this: "your head (mauliḥ) is as playful as your braided hair (dhamillaḥ). According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *mauliḥ* is not neuter when it means a crown, braided hair, or a topknot. The sense is that, having reached the state of full growth, it attained equality with your braid. Here, there is a single-word-entrance (*ekavācakānupraveśa*) of the figures of speech *viṣama* (incongruity), *pratyanīka* (counteracting), and *parikara* (poetic elaboration).

O Daughter of the Earth, either your body shines forth as it truly is, or else, through the desire to disparage it, it may become possessed by ornaments; yet, having fallen from its own true purpose, it would merely be a semblance of radiance.

O daughter of the Earth, O daughter of Janaka! And this [epithet] is for the sake of conforming to the meaning that is about to be stated. *Nirbhāsilatā* means a creeper that is exceedingly radiant (*nirbhāsinī*), having the nature of shining intensely. It was "shaken" (*dhutā*)—that is, surpassed—by your body, by your own form. Now, out of a desire to humiliate her, she might have entered Laṅkā; or, for the purpose of your defeat, let her too enter Laṅkā, just as [the demon] Ekākṣa, Ekakarṇa, and others did.

Even by that much, she would be "bereft of luster" (nirbhās), meaning her light would vanish; being like sand or grit (sikatā), she would be deprived of her own purpose—that is, her desired end consisting in the nature of her slight humiliation—and thus her wish would remain unfulfilled and she would encounter what is undesirable. This is the meaning.

In this alternative view, the word *nirbhāsilatā* (shining creeper) would be rendered "useless" (*alam*), meaning it would be as if non-existent. This is because, having been forced into that very [compound] with the syllable *ka* inserted, it becomes *nirbhāsikata*, which has fallen away from its own meaning—that is, from its own denotation, the nature of a "shining creeper. The sense is that the sequence *nirbhāsilatā* cannot convey the same meaning that the sequence *nirbhāsikata* conveys; therefore, they are incompatible. Here, the figures of speech *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) and *viṣama* (the incongruous) are merged within a single expressive word.

O Lord of the Hill of the Serpent (Śrīparvata), because the moon’s beautiful splendor is eclipsed by the luster of Your toe-nails, it becomes utterly devoid of its rays; of this there is no doubt. || 2203 ||

O Lord of Phaṇigiri! Although the moon possesses pure rays and clear beams, it has set its heart upon the theft—the act of stealing—the luster of your toe-nails; thus, having developed such a longing, it becomes utterly devoid of light, its brilliance vanished, due to its base and wretched nature. (As Amara states: *nihīno 'paśado jālmaḥ*). "Mayūkha" means radiance, ray, or flame. (As Amara states: *mayūkhas tviṭ-kara-jvālāsu*). It becomes so.

In this alternative sense, the word *viśadamayūkha* means "one whose *śadau*—the letters *śa* and *da*—have departed due to being *apaśada* (base or fallen). The state of being so is its "nature" (*tattā*), by which the form *vimayūkha* is produced; such is the meaning. Here, the figures of speech *virodhābhāsa* (apparent contradiction), *viṣama* (incongruity), and *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) are merged within a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraviṣṭatā*).

Just as the night, though its syllables are reversed [when read backward], remains pure and possesses the essence of the stars because the entire nectar of the *Bhārata* resides somewhere within your words, O Acyuta, so too does this poem remain pure and possess the very essence of excellence. 2204.

O Acyuta! Even the entire land of Bhāratavarṣa, filled with the essence of the Bhārata people, has become a mixed caste (*saṃkīrṇavarṇa*) through inverse order of castes (*pratilomavarṇa*), such as that described by the rule: "born from a Kṣatriya father upon a Brāhmaṇī mother," and so forth.

Though she is so called because she "frequents" [the night], she is also said to possess a portion of blue color due to the abundance of *tamas* (darkness). The phrase "situated here and there" means that, as expressed by the words "O fortunate one, in some places and in others," they are situated in various locations. Being like the night, with the stars belonging to you—meaning the constellations—she becomes exceedingly pure, faultless, and clear; thus, she is described as having a most excellent and superior luster (*bhā*).

In this instance, the entire sequence of phonemes (*akhilā samagravarṇā*) belonging to the word *bhāratarasa*—even when its syllables are in reverse order (*pratilomavarṇabhāg*) and thus contrary to the original sequence—results in the very form *sāratarabha*. This is the meaning. Here, there is a coalescence of a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*) between a specific type of *vibhāvanā*—characterized by the emergence of the effect "being *sāratarabha*" despite the presence of the obstacle consisting in the reversal of phonemes—and a simile (*upamā*).
Granted that people may call you, the sovereign of the entire world, the Lord of the Vṛṣa Hill; but how could beginningless scripture declare Viṣṇu to be the lord of mountains? (2205)

"Janāḥ" means common folk (pāmarāḥ); as the *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *jana* refers to the world, to Maharloka, to the other world, and also to a commoner. Here, although the Veda proclaims that the Lord Śrīnivāsa—who possesses unbridled sovereignty over the entire universe—possesses lordship over a mere limited mountain, this [claim] is indeed not to be accepted. To refute that, the citation of the Vedic text "Viṣṇu is the lord of mountains" constitutes the figure of speech *Śabdapramāṇa* (Testimony as Word), which enters into the single expressive word (*ekavācaka*) shared by the two figures of speech *Sama* (Similarity) and *Viṣama* (Disparity) propounded in the preceding and following halves [of the verse].

O Acyuta, those who have been hidden within the oyster-shell of the vast ocean of worldly existence are, when drawn forth from it in due time, become excellent jewels endowed with divine qualities; because of their state of liberation, they become Your foremost followers.

O Acyuta! That vast ocean of existence (*bhavāmbhonidhi*), which is the sea of *saṃsāra*, contains "oysters" (*śukti*) related to it—meaning sorrow (*śoka*); this is an elliptical expression for the waves of hunger, thirst, and so forth. [The souls] are "hidden" (*tirohitāḥ*) by that [sorrow], meaning their innate, true nature is veiled. In another sense, there is a vast existing ocean; those oysters (*śukti*) within it are "reddened" (*rohitāḥ*), meaning they are brought forth by drops of rainwater from the self's own showers.

The word *ca* (and) is displaced [in the verse]. Therefore, "at that time" (*tataḥ kālam*) means at the occasion when the ripening of merit—whether accidental or otherwise—has occurred, according to the process described in the statement: "He was observed by him at the time due to the various transformations of destiny. Elsewhere it is said:
"In a river, raindrops resting upon a pearl-oyster shell, when the sun is in its own sign [Cancer], become solidified after six months and are born as pure pearls."

The meaning of this is as follows: "when so spoken" refers to the time of ripening; "there in the Tāmraparṇī river at the place where it meets the ocean" is the specific location. "Uddhṛtāḥ" (drawn out) means they have been raised up by the Teachers, who are oceans of compassion, through the practice of skillful means (*upāya*) and so forth; in another sense, it means they have been lifted up by artisans. This also implies the state of having had holes bored through them. "Because of being liberated" (*muktatvāt*) means because of being separated from the bondage of *prakṛti*; in the other sense, it means because of being pearls (*mauktikatvāt*). The state of being a pearl is "pearl-ness" (*muktatvam*); when the suffix *tva* follows, according to the rule "and *tva*," the vowel *ā* is shortened.

Those who possess divine qualities (*divyā guṇāḥ*) are so described; that is to say, those for whom the Brahmanic qualities such as the manifestation of freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and the like have appeared, and who are woven with beautiful golden threads. The "excellent jewels" (*sanmaṇayaḥ*)—meaning the foremost among the knowers of Brahman (*brahmavid*) and beautiful gems alike—are your "foremost attendants" (*agrasarāḥ*), standing before you and forming the finest necklaces. Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning double entendre) between the relevant [jewels] and the irrelevant [knowers of Brahman]. Because the aforementioned meanings—such as being hidden within the oysters of the vast ocean of worldly existence (*vipulabhavāmbhonidhiśuktirohitatva*) and so forth—occur in succession, this constitutes a "string of jewels" (*ratnāvalī*) integrated into a single sentence.
Or rather:
"O lightning, when you, struck by the splendor of Ramā, fall headlong from the cloud that shines according to her will, only then will you realize that she is indeed Nirmadā. (2207)

*Saudāmanī* is [so called] because it is in the same direction as the mountain *Sudāmā*; thus, by the rule *tenaikadik* (Pāṇini 4.3.112), the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "being in the same direction as that," and by the rule *an* (Pāṇini 6.4.167), there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). Its vocative is *he saudāmani*. The popular saying is: "Out of pride that 'my own luster is supermundane,' you flash in the cloud—that is, in the atmosphere (*abhra*). The reality is: "You flash in the rain-cloud (*jaladhara*). Being struck by the splendor of *Ramā*, you have consequently fallen headlong.

"Thus leaping about, you are 'nimadā'—this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound preceded by a negative particle (*na*), like the word *nivāta*. The meaning is: 'one whose pride in possessing luster has completely vanished. When that [pride] was present, one would have known [the truth]; this is a common proverbial expression. The sense is: 'You will know the fruit of your leaping then; do you know it now? In the other sense, it refers to the lightning (*saudāmanī*)."

The meaning—that the word *saṃbuddhyanta* (ending in the vocative case) results in *nimadāsau* when reversed—is intended for the sake of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*). Here, through the praise of the cessation of the pride of the unmentioned lightning, its cause—the radiance of Lakṣmī (*Ramā*)—is perceived as being far more brilliant than that; thus, this is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Indirect Description) based on the effect. Since the phrase "struck by the radiance of Lakṣmī" serves as the reason for its falling head-first, there is *kāvyaliṅga* (Poetic Reason), and the popular proverb (*lokokti*) is also present; these blend together through their entry into a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*).

O Goddess, if even Śiva himself were to become that [Cupid] who has been conquered by your sidelong glances in order to conquer him back, even then the arrow (śilīmukha) would not be able to conquer him; rather, it would itself turn into a monkey (valīmukha).

O Goddess! Even if [the god of love] were to become Śiva—that is, to possess three eyes—by means of your *apāṅga* (the corner of your eye; by which is also understood "your son Anaṅga"), as Amara states: *śilīmukha*, *rolamba*, or *kalamba* denote a bee or an arrow (*alibāṇau śilīmukhau*). [Regarding *apāṅga*: "The term *apāṅga* may refer to one who is deficient in limbs, the corner of the eye, or even a beauty mark. Even then, he would not be able to conquer you; rather, he would simply become a *valīmukha*—that is, a monkey.

The literal meaning is as follows: if the word *śilīmukha* (bee) were to result from the transformation of the letter *śa* into *va*—that is, by removing the letter *śa* from *śilīmukha* and establishing the presence of the letter *va* there—it would become *valīmukha* (monkey). One must not forget the power of the identity between word and meaning (*śabdārthatādātmya*). Here, there is a commingling of the figures of speech *viṣama* (incongruity) and *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) within a single expressive unit.

O lotus-petal-eyed one, it is wonderful that this [song] which praises your virtues and yet disparages them will become a great boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence, providing ease to those who travel upon it.

It is a marvel that one who speaks ill of your virtues, or those who repeat them, should become a great boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), moving easily across it. [The meaning is: one who repeats your virtues moves easily—that is, possessing the bliss born from reciting your qualities—and shall become a great boat, a rescuer like a massive vessel. However, the one who reviles them shall "not move easily" (*asukhaga*); this is the word division (*cheda*).

In the ocean consisting of worldly existence (*bhavamaya-pārāvāra*), he is a "great boat" (*mahān āplavaḥ*); that is, one for whom there is a great means of crossing, meaning he is eternally submerged [in it]. For this very reason, he is "one who goes to unhappiness" (*asukhagaḥ*), having attained misery. Alternatively, a "great boat" (*mahān plavaḥ*) refers to a *caṇḍāla*; as Amara states: "The *caṇḍāla*, *plava*, *mātaṅga*, *divākīrti*, and *janaṅgama* [are synonyms]. The sense is: "This fruit of censuring the qualities of the Blessed One is not sufficient. For this very reason, he is "one who goes to unhappiness," which has the meaning already explained.

Alternatively, "mahān plavaḥ" refers to a certain beautiful bird named Plava—such as a madgu or kāraṇḍava—and "asukhagaḥ" means one who is not a "sukhaga" (one who moves happily); thus, it will become an unlovely bird. Here, there is a convergence of the figures of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor), *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic cause), and *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing) within a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*).

Just as a lotus flower, by concealing the sun within itself, attains joy from that very act, so too may your eye attain the state of being like the sun by worshipping the eye of Hari; yet, O Mother, it shall not become his eye itself.

O Mother! May they hold within their minds the sun, the lotus (aravinda), as the sun (ravi) holds the lotus; this is the imperative form derived from the root *dhā* (to hold) belonging to the *bhvādigaṇa*. The sense is that they should worship it in order to attain the state of your eyes. From that worship, may they become filled with such joy—that is, possessed of such bliss—as is appropriate for attaining that [state].

Even so, that which is real, good, or praiseworthy—whatever it may be—attains the state of being the Sun (ravitām) while serving Him; for one who worships the Sun according to the principle of "as one intends," there is the inevitable occurrence of becoming permeated by that very nature. O Lord, even with such effort, [the eye] becomes the eye of Hari.

The sense is that it would indeed be his [the Sun's] eye, because he is known to the world and the Vedas as "Bhānu" (the one with rays); but it is not your eye. The sense is that your eye—quivering with waves of gentle, beautiful, and most noble compassion, and the liberator from all suffering—would not be so. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), the word *aravindam* bears a *ravi* (the letter 'ra') within itself; for those two aforementioned letters are heard in the middle of that word. Likewise, there is the division *anandam*.

"Let that which is devoid of 'a' and 'ka'—that is, one for whom the two sounds 'a' and 'ka' (andau) do not exist—be so; yet let it possess the two existing (santau) sounds 'ra' and 'vi' (ravīti). The sense is that when all other letters have departed, only the letters 'ra' and 'vi' remain. Here, the figures of speech *samaviṣama* (the even and the uneven), *saṃbhāvanā* (poetic fancy), and others should be seen as merged within a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*)."

Just as even the emeralds and other gems were cast aside by you because they desired to equal your luster, O Hari—among those whose heads are surpassed by yours, which one could this emerald possibly be? (2211)

O Hare! Those gems—such as the *mahānīla* and others—whose faces are indeed the *harimaṇi*, the sapphire (*indranīla*), [are] understood by their masculine gender to be males and by their plural number to be many. Desiring to attain equality with your luster, they have therefore been cast aside; that is to say, their brilliant darkness has been dispelled by that one woman, your own luster.

Among those [gems], by saying "this is emerald, this is [that]," it is indicated that [emerald] is the faintest blue compared to sapphire and the rest. The common expression "araṃ adharitaśiro'pi" (even with its head turned down excessively) suggests: among sapphire and the others, what kind of thing would this be? It is even too weak to be counted among them; how indeed could such a thing attain the good fortune of resembling Your taste? This is the intended meaning. In the alternative sense, "maratakaṃ adhaśśīrṣamapi araṃ" [means...]

"What is that which, when deprived of the letter *ra*, becomes 'sat' (existent)?"—this is another meaning [of the verse] intended for a particular striking effect (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*). Here, there is a single-locus interpenetration (*ekavācakānupraveśa*) of the figures of Unevenness (*viṣama*), Poetic Fancy (*arthāpatti*), and Indirect Praise (*aprastutapraśaṃsā*).

Or rather, O Acyuta, let even the *kataka* nut, though it has its head turned downward, become an immortal emerald; for it alone can purify the mind of the virtuous, just as [the *kataka* nut] purifies water, but not Your body.

"O Acyuta! May the emerald (marakata) and the lapis lazuli (gārutmata) attain immortality—that is, divinity itself—in their desire for equality with Your divine form; may they indeed obtain divinity. Not only this much, but let them even have their heads turned downward (avākchiro’stu)—this is a common worldly expression. Even so, let them remain as *kataka* fruits. Even in their divinity, because they do not obtain what they truly desire, let them suffer with heads bowed down and remain merely in the form of *kataka* fruits"; thus, the attainment of an intensely undesirable state is expressed.

Even then, the *kataka* fruit, though it may clarify a small amount of water, would not purify the ink-like impurity; likewise, Your divine form—just as Your body is divine—would not purify the "excellent mind" (*sanmānasa*), which is the very mind of the virtuous and is like the exceedingly deep Lake Mānasa. Just as Your divine and auspicious form clarifies the Lake Mānasa despite its extreme depth, the emerald (*marakata*) would not clarify it even with great effort in the manner previously described; rather, it would only clarify a very small amount of foul water. This is the essential meaning.

By this, it is stated that the emerald (*marakata*) is not far from equality with the form of the Lord in every respect. In reality, however, the word *marakata*—having attained "immortality" (*amaratva*), that is, the state of being devoid of the letters *ma* and *ra*—remains as *kataka*; even when inverted, it remains precisely as *kataka*. Here, one should note the convergence of the figures of speech *pratīpa*, *viṣama*, and *vyatireka* within a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*).
Just as many previous successions of births have passed away in vain and gone to delusion,
O Acyuta, by Your grace let even this present birth of mine not turn toward a contrary course.

"O Acyuta! My lineage of births—the succession of my births—is vast; this is the implied meaning. They have become deluded, O Lord, having fallen into confusion by Your māyā; therefore, they have reached a state of futility—that is, a state of uselessness because they have not worshipped the lotus-feet of You. This is the sense. "Prayātā" means they have attained [this state].

The sense is this: "May she—whether she be my own birth or this present birth of mine—not fall into hostility through Your grace; may she not perish, being ignorant of the true nature of the higher and lower realities (parāvara-tattva-yāthātmya) and having failed to practice the means for attaining You, in accordance with the scriptural statement, 'For they are obstructed by untruth' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.2). In this regard, it is said: "A vast succession of births has been undergone by you in vain;
reflecting upon one among them, take refuge [in me] today."
Having placed [all beings] upon the wheel of saṃsāra with the strong ropes of karma,
Time drags along everything that has the nature of both the moving and the stationary.
Alas! A vast and ever-increasing succession of births has passed for me, during which I failed to worship the two lotus feet of Govinda.
She has not tasted the nectar-like essence of virtuous action, knowledge, and devotion;
she has not seen the boat for crossing the ocean of infinite saṃsāra.
The meaning expressed by these and other such passages should be reflected upon.

In this context, the word *mugdha* is a specific verbal form; the compound *agatāmudhābhāvam* is a single word. The vowel *a* in *aga* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). The sense is that the letter *ga* is [retained] after the elision of the mere consonant (*hal*) [following the *a*]. The construction is: "having reached the state of being *mudhā*," that is, having attained the status of the word *mudhā*. Furthermore, the word *nijajaniḥ* is a specific verbal form; let there be no "contrary movement"—even when recited in reverse order, it remains established in its original sequence.

[The word] *bhāvaḥ* [is used]. Since the rule *māṅi luṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.175) is an exception (*apavāda*) to all other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*), the aorist (*luṅ*) is used here in the sense of the present indicative (*laṭ*). Here, the transitory emotion (*saṃcārī bhāva*) of world-weariness (*nirveda*), indicated by the phrase "the succession of births has gone in vain," serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the dominant sentiment (*sthāyibhāva*) of tranquility (*śāntarasa*); thus, there is the figure of speech *preyaḥ*. Furthermore, because the thought expressed in the first half-verse—that the succession of births is fruitless—acts as the cause for the prayer to prevent one's own birth, which is set forth in the second half-verse, there is also the figure of speech *kāvyaliṅga*. These two are blended through the technique of *ekavācakānupraveśa* (coalescence within a single expressive word).

Or rather: Just as that which was initially inhabited by disease and subsequently greatly decayed—how could it possibly endure when struck from above? If your arm, O seeker of victory, were to be attacked by a swarm of serpents, it would surely become utterly agitated.

O hare! First of all, that [forest] was already inhabited by disease—meaning it was seized by pestilence. Furthermore, immediately thereafter, the multitude of beasts of prey (*vyālakula*)—not just a single beast—fell away, having dropped down due to a lack of strength; such is the sense. If they, desiring to conquer your arm, were capable for some reason, why would they fall upon you for the sake of a duel? Such is the sense.

However, the sense is that [the army] would become agitated because of its inability to conquer. In another sense, the word *vyālakulam* (a multitude of serpents) is such that at the beginning there is the letter *vyā* residing in it, and immediately thereafter (*atho*), it is largely (*bahu*) corrupted, meaning the letters *la* and *ra* have fallen away. Then, from which bad letter (*ku-varṇāt*) above, would the letter *la* fall—that is, move—immediately after? (The verb *patati* is transitive here), for the rule "the accusative is used with *śrita*, *atīta*, *patita*, etc. prescribes the formation of the compound.

This is also evident from such usages as: “Fall into hell! Go to heaven! Fly up to the sky! Fall to the earth with your head downward! The meaning is that the phrase *vyālakulapadam* would become disordered; that is to say, it would result in the form *vyākulam*, having merely lost its initial letter *la*. In this interpretation, however, the word *tu* serves to emphasize.
Here, one should observe the coalescence of the figures of speech *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason) and *viṣama* (incongruity) within a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*).

Just as a person belonging to you, upon coming into contact with even a mere drop [of your grace], becomes a milker of the nectar of immortality, so too it is fitting that one who is turned away from you should become like this; O Lord, this is indeed a marvel! (2215)
O Lord! Your devotee, even upon attaining a rare union—a brief association with you—becomes a milker of nectar and an instructor on the path to the supreme good.
Day by day, association with the virtuous is the source of dharma;
indeed, association with the foolish is the source of the net of delusion.

Such points as these should be considered here. This is logical: it is a marvel that even one who is averse to you, having attained such a union with the letter *da*, becomes a "milk-monger of nectar" (*amṛtadogdhā*). The factual state of affairs is that by attaining the union of the forms of the letters *da* and *ra*, he becomes "Amṛtadogdha" (the Nectar-Milker). This is an instance of the coalescence of two figures—Sama (Equal Pairing) and Tulyayogitā (Equal Treatment)—within a single expressive word.

O Moon on the mountain of serpents, are you not indeed generous and exceedingly cool? Yet, by means of *viparītalakṣaṇā* (contrary indication), I consider this "generous one" here to be quite the opposite, like a forest fire.

O Pṛdākuśailendra! Indeed, you alone [are such]. For Amara states: "The particle *nanu* is used in the senses of questioning, ascertaining, granting permission, conciliation, and addressing. Like nectar (*sudhā*), you are exceedingly cool—meaning, cooled by the extreme cold of compassion. In the case of the moon (*indu*), it means exceedingly cool with its nectar. You are generous (*vadānya*); for it is said: "One who is pleasant of speech and disposed toward giving is celebrated as *vadānya*," and from the Śruti: "He who gives himself, who gives strength"—the sense is: who else but you is a great donor of all things, even unto one's own self? As it is stated in the *Śrī Viṣṇudharma*:
"Therefore, O best of Brahmins, you too should be devoted to Nārāyaṇa."
Who else besides him is so magnanimous as to be able to grant what is requested?

Thus [he says]. "Another," meaning someone other than you, whom he considers to be generous—this is the sense. Due to *viparītalakṣaṇā* (indication by contrariety)—that is, from the contrary characteristic of being extremely cool like nectar and so forth, to the characteristic of causing torment—I consider him to be like a forest fire (*dāva*). The sense is that I know him to be difficult to approach and to be avoided from afar. Alternatively, "another" means through *viparītalakṣaṇā*, which is a form of *virodhilakṣaṇā* (contrary indication), and this is specifically *jahatsvārthalakṣaṇā* (indication where the primary meaning is abandoned), by which a meaning contrary to one's own denotation is indicated.

Just as in the phrase "upakṛtaṃ bahunām" (benefit has been done by many), the word *vadānya* means "not generous" (*avadānya*). The meaning of *dāvam* has already been stated. In the alternative sense, I consider *vadānya*—which is devoid of the letter *ny*—to be *dāva*, having perceived it through its characteristic reversal, that is, by reading it in reverse order. In this case, the word *vadānya*, when stripped of the letter *ny*, leaves *vadā*; when read in reverse order, it results in *dāva*. In this interpretation, the particle *iva* serves as a poetic ornament (*vākyālaṃkāra*) for the sentence.

Here, although generosity could apply to both the Blessed One and others, because it is restricted to the Blessed One alone, it constitutes a *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification). Furthermore, since there exists a distinction between those two in the form of dissimilarity—namely, that they are respectively like the moon and a cloud—the figure of *vyatireka* (contrast) is also present; these two figures are thus merged within a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraviṣṭa*).
O Lotus-eyed One, those men who have been beheld by you shine with exquisite grace in the vast halls whose floors are made of sapphires, which are as radiant as rubies and lamps.

The meaning being expounded here consists of a description of a prosperous object, and thus takes the form of the *udātta* (the Exalted) figure of speech; it also takes the form of *atiśayokti* (Hyperbole), as it consists of a statement of a relationship where no such relationship exists. Furthermore, it is not determined that in every instance of *udātta*, there must be the character of stating a relationship where none exists.

It should not be said that there is no coexistence of these two distinct figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*), for in descriptions such as the abundance and prosperity of the divine realms, there is the *udātta* (the Sublime) untouched by *atiśayokti* (Hyperbole), and in descriptions involving hyperbole concerning heroism, magnanimity, poverty, and so forth, there is *atiśayokti* untouched by *udātta*. These two rest upon their mutual distinction. Furthermore, when these two meet here by the force of the subject matter, there is no *saṃkara* (commixture) characterized by the relation of primary and subordinate, because one does not arise from the other.

Furthermore, there is an understanding of the distinction between independence (*svātantrya*) and dependence (*pāratantrya*). Nor is there equal prominence (*samaprādhānya*), because when a thing endowed with excellence is presented by certain words, and that very same thing is presented as having the nature of a relation where no [actual] relation exists, there is no absence of difference in the objects established by the distinct expressive words. Nor is there a commixture of doubt (*saṃdehasaṃkara*), because within the scope of one poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*), there is no rejection of the scope of any other poetic figure.

Therefore, here there is a *saṃkara* (commixture) characterized by the mutual entry into a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*) between the Hyperbole of Excellence (*udāttātiśayokti*) and [the other figure]. Likewise, because the aforementioned prosperity has as its cause being glanced upon by the Blessed One, there is also a *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason), which is likewise entered into the same single expressive word as the aforementioned commixture; thus, there is a particularity of aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*).

And this description of the absence of equal prominence is according to the followers of the *Kuvalayānanda*. However, the author of the *Rasikarañjanī* states: "This is to be considered. For one who accepts the commixture (*saṃkara*) of equal prominence, the distinction of meanings established by different words is the cause of equal prominence; for even when there is a difference in originative injunctions (*utpattividhi*) as in the case of the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices, equal prominence is established in such cases as 'He sacrifices seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati,' where there is no difference in the injunction."

The same applies here as well, because even in the absence of a difference in the expressive words, the possibility of predominance [of one over the other] exists. For this reason too, there is no possibility of a commixture (*saṃkara*) of equal predominance; otherwise, the commixture of "entry into a single expressive word" (*ekavācakānupraveśa*) would become devoid of its proper scope. This is because, when two figures of speech enter into a single expression, their being equally predominant is justified precisely by their serving as the cause of a single type of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*). Thus he spoke; enough of this.

The second type of *saṃkara* (commingling), which is the commingling of word and meaning through their entry into a single expressive unit (*ekavācakānupraveśa*), has already been illustrated on the occasion of defining equal prominence (*samaprādhānya*). The third type of *saṃkara*, the commingling of word and meaning through their entry into a single expressive unit, is as follows: "Indeed, here the suffix, though ending in *t* (the letter *t*), does not abandon its own nature (*satva*); but the nature of one who possesses devotion to you, having approached of its own accord, bestows upon him that very essence (*tat-tva*). (2218)

O Blessed One! In this world, for a person who worships and serves you, there arises *pratyaya*—meaning knowledge (*jñāna*). According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *pratyaya* is used in the senses of dependence, trust, a breach of intellect, a cause, fame, a beginning, and an oath. Even when exhausted, such a person—due to causes such as physical or spiritual suffering (*ādhyātmika-tāpa*)—may himself become weary; yet he never abandons his *sattva*, meaning the quality of goodness or excellence. The meaning is that the knowledge of your devotee does not relinquish its abundance of the quality of *sattva* or its state of excellence, even in a condition of exhaustion. Here, by the word *jñāna*...

O Great Sage, it is said that both knowledge and action are the causes for attaining that [liberation]. Knowledge is likewise said to be twofold: that arising from scripture and that arising from discernment.
The Brahman of Sound consists of scripture, while the Supreme Brahman is born of discernment.

Thus, it has been stated that both types of knowledge regarding Brahman—both mediate (*parokṣa*) and immediate (*aparokṣa*)—are intended. He states the contrast with the knowledge of one who is not a devotee of the Lord by means of the word "tvad" (than You). In the case of a person who does not bear devotion to You—that is, one who does not possess devotion toward You—the term "pratyaya" (cognition) is to be supplied here as well. Cognition, which is knowledge, having itself attained *asattvam*—meaning the absence of the quality of goodness (*sattva-guṇa*) or worthlessness—bestows upon that non-devotee *tāntatvam*, which is exhaustion or dejection.

The sense is this: knowledge derived from ordinary scriptures and the like, when it culminates in non-devotion to You, fails to instill the quality of *sattva* due to its lack of devotion to You; instead, becoming either ineffective or even harmful, it causes exhaustion to its very locus by failing to attain the supreme human goal, which is liberation (*niḥśreyasa*). Elsewhere, the phrase "one who possesses non-devotion to You" (*tvad-abhakti-bhṛt*) refers to both words. In the word "bhajati" (he worships), the suffix is the present participle suffix *śatṛ*, ending in *t*. The word "api" (also/even) is placed out of its logical order and is used in conjunction [with the following].

In the section on *ccaye*: "Even though it possesses the designation *sat*, it does not abandon its lack of *sattva* (the state of being *asat*). The meaning is that the designation *sat* is prescribed for the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* by the rule 'those two are *sat*' (*tau sat*). In the word *tvadabhaktibhṛt*—where there is the suffix *kvip*—the term 'suffix' (*pratyaya*) is to be supplied here as well. The suffix *kvip* itself lacks *sattva*, meaning it lacks the designation *sat*; the meaning is that, like *śatṛ*, *kvip* is not subject to the designation *sat*."

Alternatively, having reached the state of non-existence (*asattvam*) or non-presence (*avidyamānatvam*), the entire *kvip* suffix undergoes elision because the letters *k*, *i*, and *p* receive the designation *it* by the rules "laśakvataddhite," "upadeśe'janunāsika it," and "halantyam," and consequently the letter *v* is subject to elision by the rule "tasya lopaḥ" and "verapṛktasya. The meaning is that this [suffix] bestows the state of ending in *t*—that is, being *takārānta*—upon that word "bearing devotion to you" (*tvadabhaktibhṛt*), because the *kvip* suffix is a *pit* suffix.

The sense is that, by the rule *hṛsvasya piti kṛti tuk*, the suffix *tuk* is added to the root *bhṛ*, whereby it comes to end in the letter *t*. Because the addition of the suffix *tuk* is caused by the presence of the *kvip* suffix, the statement that the ending in *t* is "given" by that [suffix] is made. Here, there is a *śleṣa* (punning conjunction) between the two—the primary subject (*prakṛta*) and the non-primary subject (*aprakṛta*)—namely, knowledge (*jñāna*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*). In the first half-verse, since there is a description of the non-arising of the effect, which is the abandonment of one's being (*sattvaparityāga*), despite the existence of the cause, which is the exhaustion (*glānatā*) of knowledge, within the level of the primary meaning, there is *viśeṣokti* (the figure of speech of specificity).

In the latter half [of the verse], however, because there is a description of the effects—such as the attainment of existence—in accordance with the cause, which is the adornment of general knowledge by means of devotion to the Lord, the figure of speech is *samālaṅkāra* (symmetry).

The meaning of the Great Saying (*mahāvākya*), however, consists of a figure of contrast (*vyatireka*) characterized by the description of the difference between the cognitions of the devotee and the non-devotee of the Blessed One. Furthermore, in the level of the non-contextual meaning, there are two figures of speech (*samālaṅkāra*) due to the description of the two corresponding properties: the suffix *śatṛ* having both the state of being present (*sattva*) and the state of ending in *-ta*, and the suffix *kvip* having the state of being absent (*asattva*) and the bestowal of the state of ending in *-ta*. These are the figures of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*). Additionally, there is the phonetic alliteration (*vṛttyanuprāsa*) characterized by the repetition of the letter *ta*. Since these [figures] enter into a single expressive word (*vācaka*), this is a "commingling" (*saṃkara*) through the mutual entry of multiple figures into one expressive unit.

Nor should it be argued that since a verbal figure of speech (śabdālaṃkāra) cannot reside in a single expressive word (vācaka) because it resides in the expressed meaning (vācya), how can it be said to enter into a single expressive word;

for the meaning of the term "entering into a single expressive word" in this context is simply its being based upon that single expressive word. Nor should it be argued that in this way, a semantic figure of speech (arthālaṃkāra) lacks the status of residing in the expressive word, and thus how could it be a subject of entering into a single expressive word; for they say that even for the latter, this is possible through the relation of being the expressed meaning (vācyatā-sambandha).

Indeed, in this world, for one who knows the six states of existence, a good rebirth occurs when there is diligent application to ritual action; conversely, even if all ritual actions are performed, a bad rebirth results from a lack of such diligence. (2219)

The term *satpadavidām* refers to those who know that "existent" (*sat*) state which is the reality in the form of Brahman; this is the meaning of "reality. As it is said: "The designation of Brahman is traditionally held to be threefold: *Oṃ*, *Tat*, and *Sat*. According to Amarasimha: "The word *pada* [is used] in the senses of determination, protection, place, mark, foot, and reality. Alternatively, it means the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of Brahman, based on the commentary on the verse "That is the supreme *pada* of Viṣṇu," which explains: "*Pada* is so called because it is reached (*padyate*); it is the essential nature. Those who know that are thus described. The genitive case here denotes the agent (*kartari ṣaṣṭhī*).

The meaning is: "for those who worship the Supreme Brahman. Since the identity of meaning among words such as *vedanā*, *upāsanā*, and *dhyāna* was established in the commentary on [Brahmasūtra 4.1.1] beginning with "Repetition [is required], because of the instruction more than once," when there is devotion toward the practice of action (*kriyāyoga*)—that is, the performance of actions without aiming for their fruits—in the yoga of action (*karmayoga*), the attainment of the True Goal (*sadgati*) occurs at the end of the body, namely, the journey by way of the path beginning with light (*arcirādimārga*). Indeed, the word "indeed" (*khalu*) indicates well-known authority in the scriptures.
He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together—
having crossed over death by means of ignorance, he enjoys immortality through knowledge.
"Brahmins desire to know this very Self through the repeated study of the Vedas.
Relying on knowledge, he too performed many sacrifices,
having taken his stand upon the knowledge of Brahman in order to cross over death by means of ignorance.

"In accordance with such scriptural authorities as, 'And those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity, they attain the light (arcis) itself,' [it is established that] even for those who know Brahman, [tapaḥ and so forth function] as auxiliaries to their knowledge."

The sense is that since there is a necessary inclination toward performing actions according to one's capacity, such action is a means for attaining a good state (*sadgati*). Now, it follows that immediately upon reaching the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*), all activity whatsoever becomes an honor performed by the *ātivāhika* deities of the light-path and so forth. By stating "an evil state" (*asadgati*) and so on, he declares the undesirable consequence of the opposite case: when there is disregard for the performance of the aforementioned type of action during its application, an evil state results.

The sense is that even for those who know Brahman, if they neglect the duties of their stage of life (*āśrama-karma*), their internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) becomes defiled; consequently, since the very arising of knowledge (*vidyā*) is impossible, they meet with an evil end. Alternatively, the term refers to those who "find" (*vindanti*)—that is, reach—the feet of the Supreme Brahman Śrīnivāsa (the root *vid* with the suffix *kvip*). This means "of those who have surrendered. The genitive case is used in the sense of a general relationship. When there is application to action—that is, when there is devotion upon obtaining the opportunity for service (*kaiṅkarya*)—there is a "good end" for people (this is the ellipsis). In the absence of such devotion, there is indeed an "evil end."

The underlying sense is that through devotion to, or the absence of devotion for, the service rendered toward those who have taken refuge in the Blessed One, there arises either the attainment of the Blessed One’s grace or its absence. In this regard,
while there may be doubt among the servants of Acyuta as to whether success will be achieved or not,
there is no such doubt for those whose souls delight in the service of His devotees.
A householder does not rejoice in a son who is disrespectful;
likewise, the Blessed One does not rejoice in one whose devotee is unhonored.
Such passages as these should be investigated.

Elsewhere, that which is "sat" (existent) is praised; "pada" refers to the science of words, meaning for those who know it, namely the grammarians (*vyākaraṇa-vedin*). When respect is intended—that is, when the sense of showing reverence is to be expressed—in connection with an action (*kriyā-yoge*).

When there is a connection with a word denoting an action (*kriyā*), the analysis is: "sat gatiḥ. This means that *sat*—the indeclinable (*avyaya*) having the form "sat"—is a *gati*, that is, it receives the technical designation *gati*. Now, [the word] *samastā* has entered into a compound with this *sat*. By intending the substantive *kriyā* (action), the feminine gender is applied; thus, the action becomes a "good action" (*satkriyā*), and the form *satkriyā* is produced. When contempt (*anādara*) is intended—that is, when the sense of contempt is to be expressed in connection with a word denoting an action—the analysis is: "asat gatiḥ. [The word] *asat* is...

The indeclinable *sat* (meaning "good") in this form becomes a *gati*, that is, it receives the designation of *gati*. Furthermore, it should be understood that the phrase "the entire [compound] becomes an action" (*asatkriyā*) is also to be supplied. The sense is this: while the rule "and *gati*" (*gatiśca*) is being carried over, by the rule "in the case of respect and disrespect, *sat* and *asat*" (*ādarānādarayossadasatī*), when the meanings of respect and disrespect are intended, the indeclinables *sat* and *asat* receive the designation of *gati*. Consequently, because the formation of a compound with a *gati* is prescribed by the rule "compounds with *ku*, *gati*, and *prādi* words" (*kugatiprādayaḥ*), [the result follows]. Here, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the relevant and the irrelevant.

In the level of meaning pertaining to the subject matter at hand, there is a single-word-entrance (ekavācakānupraveśa) of the two semantic figures—the two types of *samā* occurring in the first and second halves [of the verse]—and the verbal figure of *yamaka*.
Just as:

"He who is growing seeks refuge in the Bull-Mountain (Vṛṣaśaila), which has attained coolness from the scriptures; he who is not growing seeks refuge in the Bull-Mountain, which has attained coolness from the scriptures. (2220)

He who is ever-expanding (vardhiṣṇu) takes refuge in that Vṛṣa-mountain, whose trees (agāḥ) have attained coolness (śaityam). In the second half [of the verse], he who is not expanding (avardhiṣṇu) has reached the "Vṛṣala" (vṛṣalam)—meaning one by whom there is a loss (tyāgaḥ) of the syllable 'śai'. [As Amara states: "The low-born are called vṛṣalas. Here, the figure of speech based on meaning (samasyārthālaṅkāra) and the figure of speech based on sound characterized as *yāmaka* consisting of the repetition of meaning (*arthāvṛtti*) both enter into a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraviṣṭatā*).

Just as one who is devoted to you, even if situated in the midst of hell, would shine as the crest-jewel of the virtuous; so too one who is not devoted to you, even if situated in heaven, would be feared as a crest-jewel of the wicked. || 2221 ||

O Blessed One! May he who is your devotee—dwelling in the midst of heaven, that is, residing in the celestial realm—shine like a crest-jewel (*mauli*) among the virtuous, such as the divine sages and others present there; that is to say, may he manifest as Indra. He who...

"It is a marvel that even he who is not your devotee should fear [you] in that very same way. The resolution of this is as follows: the word division is *madhye nā ka-sthitimān*. That person (*saḥ nā*; "man"—according to Amara, *puruṣāḥ*, *pūruṣāḥ*, *naraḥ*) has a crest (*mauliḥ*; meaning *maukaliḥ*) situated in the middle (*madhye*), that is, in the interval, which possesses the letter *ka* (*ka-sthitimān*). There is an identity between the word and its meaning. Thus, he would be feared by the virtuous like a crow (*kāka*). The sense is that one who is not a devotee of the Lord should be avoided from afar by the knowers of Brahman, being equal to a crow.

Alternatively, that devotee of yours, situated in the midst of *nāka*—that is, in the middle of the sky (*ākāśa*; cf. Amarakośa: "In the sky, in heaven, [it is called] *nāka*") or in the supreme ether (*parama-vyoman*)—possesses a station.
