The sense is that, by your grace, he has attained a body composed of light, according to the saying: "You have become a star in heaven. The meaning is that he would shine brilliantly in their midst, becoming the crest-jewel (*mauli*) of the virtuous, that is, of the stars or of the liberated souls (*mukta*).

But one who is not devoted to you, like a *maukali*—that is, a crow—is devoid of luster; he stands even lower than common folk and would be struck with fear, meaning he would be terrified. Amara states in his list of synonyms for a crow: “*maukali* means a *pikavardhana* (a crow that raises cuckoos). The author of the *Ṭīkāsarvasva* and others explain: “*Mūkala* is Yama; his offspring is *maukali*. According to the *Śabdārṇava*, *mūkala* may mean the Lord of the Dead (*pretabhartṛ*) or a forest-dweller (*kānanecara*).”

Here, because being a devotee of the Lord and not being a devotee of Him function as causes for "being firmly bound" and "not being firmly bound" respectively through the mediation of their adjectives, there are two instances of *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of causal indication) intermingled with *rūpaka* (metaphor). These, together with the *arthāvṛtti-rūpaka-yamaka*, are unified within a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraviṣṭa*).
Or, for example:

"One who is without a loincloth (*asakaupīna*), yet increased by prosperity (*bhūtyopacita*) and clad in yellow garments (*pītāmbaraśrita*); he might also be one who is without a loincloth (*asakaupīna*), yet increased by ashes (*bhūtyopacita*) and clad in green garments (*haridambaraśrita*). (2222)
He who has taken refuge in Śrīnivāsa, the wearer of yellow garments—by this, the abundance of all prosperity is indicated.
That person (asau) would be [protected]; the word *adaḥ* [is used here]... [of the class of] indeclinables and *sarva-*...

By the rule *nāmnāmakac prāk ṭeḥ*, the suffix *akac* is added; then, by the rule *adasa au sulopaśca*, the vowel *au* replaces the final portion of *adas* when followed by the nominative case-ending *su*, and that *su* is elided. By the rule *tadassassau*, the *d* of *adas* is changed to *s*. [The phrase] "augmented (*upacitaḥ*)"—meaning enriched—by prosperity (*bhūtyā*) consisting of clothing, ornaments, food, drink, and so forth, and therefore "fat" (*pīnaḥ*), meaning having well-nourished limbs; this is to be connected here as well. The literal meaning is: "one whose garment is green" (*haridambaraṃ*)—that is, one whose clothing is green—or "the sky-clad one" (*digambaraṃ*), namely Śiva.

According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *harit* refers to a eunuch or grass; it is used in three genders for color, and in the feminine for the directions. It is a marvel that even a person who has taken refuge [in worldly life] should become swollen with prosperity—that is, corpulent through wealth. In reality, however, one who is smeared (*upacita*) with ashes (*bhūti*) and is without a loincloth (*sakaupīna* means "with a loincloth," so *asakaupīna* means "without a loincloth") would be a sky-clad ascetic. The sense is that, by the principle of "according to one's resolve" (*yathākratu*), one who worships as a sky-clad ascetic will indeed become a sky-clad ascetic, attaining identity with Him.

"‘Bhūti’ [is used] in the sense of an elephant’s ornament, birth, prosperity, and ashes; ‘upacita’ [is used] in the sense of smeared and increased," according to the *Ratnamālā*. "‘Bhūti’ [is used] in the sense of ashes and prosperity; ‘upacita’ may mean smeared or abundant, and it is of common gender," according to the *Medinī*. Here, there is a mutual interpenetration (*ekavācakānupraveśa*) of two figures of word and meaning: the *yamaka* and the *samālaṃkāra*.
Just as you might think you will attain lordship over men by worshipping common deities, O fool, so too should you strive; for I believe you will indeed attain lordship over men.

This is the humorous remark of a person of mature intellect directed toward a certain simpleton who, disregarding the Lord Śrīnivāsa—the bestower of all fruits—seeks sovereign empire through the worship of ordinary deities. "O simpleton! You think that by the worship—that is, the adoration—of ordinary deities, meaning deities other than the Lord, you will attain the status of a lord of men, that is, universal sovereignty; the sense is that you believe, 'I shall attain it.'"

This transposition of persons (*puruṣavyatyaya*) is for the purpose of indicating derision, as in the example, "Come, I think you will eat rice," and so forth. Accordingly, the *sūtra* states: "And in derision, when *manye* is used as an accompanying word, the first person is used for the verb *man*, and it is treated as singular. [The text continues: "manyadhā..."

The meaning of that [rule] is: "In that verbal root which has a prefix (upasarga) as its original form (prakṛti), the middle voice (madhyama-puruṣa) shall occur; however, for the root *man*, the first person (uttama-puruṣa) shall occur, provided it expresses a single object. You should strive accordingly. "O fool!"—this repeated address highlights an excess of mockery. "You will attain, you shall obtain, the status of a lord of men"—this is what I think, I know; such is the sense. But the inner intention (*hārda-abhiprāya*) is that the word *arenareśvaratām* is a compound.

The meaning is that you will obtain a lordship over men (*nareśvaratā*) devoid of the letter *r*—that is, a perishable lordship (*naśvaratā*). If you, O Blessed One, were to resort to an indifferent goddess, then where could true lordship over men be found? Rather, it would be nothing but perishability; this is the intended sense. Here, the pun (*śleṣa*) in the phrase "arenareśvaratām" is a constituent part of a specific figure of speech, namely *samālaṃkāra*, and this constitutes a *saṃkara* (commingling) with the *yamaka* (chiasmus), as they enter into a single expressive word.
Just as I,
having been seized by old age and other afflictions, bow down to You with manifest devotion while bewildered, O Hari, may old age not enter me again as I shine in Your supreme abode.

O Hare! Seized by old age and the like—the word "and the like" (ādi) including conception, birth, and so forth—I [pray]: I shall bow to You, the one who has dispelled *māyā* (the term *māyā* here signifying *prakṛti*, according to the Śruti: "Know that *māyā* is indeed *prakṛti*"), meaning the one who brings about the complete cessation of the bondage of *prakṛti*; I shall take refuge in You with manifest devotion (*āvirbhaktiḥ*), meaning with devotion having become manifest. Having thus prayed for the means, he now prays for the fruit:
[I shall behold] You shining in Your supreme abode, manifesting by virtue of being beyond the control of karma.

The scriptural text, "He becomes his own sovereign" (*sa svarāḍ bhavati*), is here kept in mind. May old age—by which is implied rebirth in a womb and so forth—never again enter me. The sense is that this cycle of birth, old age, death, and so on, rooted in the bondage of *prakṛti*, ceases precisely upon the surrender of the self to You. Here, it should be noted that the meaning of the second half-verse is caused by the meaning of the first half-verse; thus, there is the figure of speech *kāvyaliṅga*. Furthermore, this is integrated with a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraviṣṭa*) consisting of the verbal ornament of *citra* (punning) formed by five syllables in the second and fourth quarters that proceed both forward and backward (*anulomapratiloma*).
I worship that Brahman who is ever-eager for glory, compassionate, and desirous of the person who prostrates at his feet; who is full of faith, unwearied, and possesses auspicious sleep.

"Faithful" (śraddhāluḥ) means free from sloth; "I am one who desires auspicious sleep," which signifies being wakeful for the performance of the world's welfare. Here, because the state of desiring Śrī is the cause for compassion, and that [compassion] is the cause for the desire to grasp those who fall at his feet, there is a "garlanded" *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of causal indication). Furthermore, since this [garlanded *kāvyaliṅga*] is itself the cause for [attaining] devotion (*bhajana*), there is another *kāvyaliṅga*. This is combined with *vṛttyanuprāsa* (alliteration of syllables) within a single expressive word.

One should observe a particular artistic charm (vicchitti-viśeṣa) in that all the examples from the grammatical rule *spṛhi-gṛhi-pati-dayi-nidrā-tandrā-śraddhābhya āluc* have been arranged according to the specific method of the *Ratnāvalī*, with their sequential order disregarded.

Just as this [sweet] has extended its devotion to Your speech—the jewel of the Lord of Serpents (Śrī Śaṅkarācārya)—therefore it is called *phāṇita* (molasses); it is a transformation of sugar-candy (*khaṇḍa*), and not from any other cause. 2226.

O beloved of the jewel of the Serpent Hill (Phaṇigiri)! Since this particular *khaṇḍavikāra* has established—meaning fashioned—a bond of affection, trust, and friendship with your speech (*phaṇiti*), therefore this *khaṇḍavikāra* (a specific kind of sugar-candy) is designated by the word *phāṇita*. It is not for any other reason. The meaning is that because it possesses a bond of affection with speech (*phaṇiti*), it is called "related to that" (*phaṇita*). From the word *phaṇiti*, by applying the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule *tasyedam* ("belonging to that"), and then eliding the vowel *i* according to the rule *yasyeti ca*, [the form *phaṇita* is derived]. *Note:* The commentary explains the etymological derivation of the term *phāṇita* from *phaṇiti* (speech), linking the confectionery to the goddess's eloquence through a pun. The grammatical process involves the application of the *aṇ* suffix and the subsequent elision of the final vowel and its following consonant (*yasyeti ca*). The resulting form *phaṇita* is then used as a synonym for *phāṇita* (molasses/sugar-candy). The text identifies *khaṇḍavikāra* specifically as a type of *khaṇḍaśarkarā* (crystallized sugar). The commentary concludes by stating that the name is based on this metaphorical connection to the goddess's speech, rather than any other cause. The phrase *ādi* at the end likely indicates that this is the beginning of a further grammatical or exegetical discussion.

The meaning is that the form *phāṇita* was not uttered [by him] through etymologies such as "it becomes thickened" (*vṛddhau*) or "it is made into a syrup" (*phāṇyate*), meaning it attains a liquid state. Here, the figure of speech is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) in the form of a metaphor (*rūpaka*) in the phrase "the jewel of the mountain of Phaṇi"; the *nirukti* (etymological play) in the phrase "he did not utter *phāṇita*"; and the *apahnuti* (concealment) in the sense that this is not due to any other cause—all these are blended with *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), and they enter into a single expressive word along with the *vṛttyanuprāsa* (alliteration).
When even these five aforementioned ornaments, which take the form of the Man-Lion (Narasimha), are combined within a single verse, there is an excellence of beauty. For example:

"Adorned with her natural beauty, cherished by trees, possessing bracelets as bright as a multitude of beautiful rubies, and bearing a crest-jewel like the serpent-king supporting the mountain, does she not shine like the Earth, marked with a tilaka? (2227)

"Tarūpalālyā" means a row (*āli*) of trees (*taru*) and stones (*upala*), possessing a beautiful luster (*svābhā*). Alternatively, "svābhātarūpalālyā" is a single compound word ending in the nominative singular; it refers to that form which shines intensely (*suṣṭhu ābhātam*), being manifest through ornaments such as those worn on the head, the ears, the arms, and bracelets—though not actually adorned, it appears as if adorned, and thus is called "form" (*rūpa*).

Thus has this particular beauty been characterized. By that [beauty], she is "lālyā," meaning she is to be cherished. She is one whose "kaṭaka" (slopes or bracelets) are "paṭu" (sharp or resonant), "ajarjhara" (not jingling), and possess "surucira-kuruvinda-vṛnda" (clusters of very beautiful kuruvindas); that is to say, clusters of mustā (mustard seeds), padmarāga (rubies), and kuruvindas. Regarding the term *kuruvinda*, the *Ratnamālā* states: "Kuruvindas are rubies, vermilion, mirrors, and mustaka (ginger-grass). Regarding the term *kaṭaka*, the *Viśvakośa* states: "'Kaṭaka' refers to a bracelet, a mountain slope, a capital city, and a hip."

The Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa) is the mountain; Hari alone is the sapphire (harimaṇi), or rather, the sapphire is Indra-nīla and Hari himself is the gem. By that [gem], she shines as if marked with a tilaka, or as if a tilaka has been fashioned [upon her].
This applies both to the counter-example (*pratyukti*) and to the simile (*upamāna*), as well as to the expressions of dejection (*viṣāda*) and poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
The particle *nu* should be understood as serving to fill the meter (*pādapūraṇa*), as indicating inquiry (*jijñāsā*), or as a conjunction (*samuccaya*).

This is the remainder [of the analysis]. Here, there is a commingling (*saṃkara*) of the subordinate and the principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) between the pun (*śleṣa*)—beginning with "lālya" and so on—and the hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) rooted therein. And by that [hyperbole], the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the rising [mountain] as being marked by a sapphire-tilaka is itself raised up, being pregnant with a metaphorical identification (*samāsokti*) consisting of the superimposition of the behavior of a heroine upon the earth that supports the mountain of the Lord of Serpents. Thus, because the poetic fancy and the metaphorical identification are equally supported by the aforementioned hyperbole rooted in the pun, they possess an excellence of beauty that is mutually dependent and simultaneous.

Because both exist, there is equal prominence. This *saṃkara* (commixture) occurs only when the poet’s creative effort (*saṃrambha*) is directed toward this much alone. If, however, the effort lies in the simile (*upamā*) "Is she one who has applied a tilaka?", then, because the comparison of the heroine to the Earth—the supporter of the mountain that is the Lord of Serpents—is implied, there is the figure of speech *ekadeśavivartinī upamā* (simile existing in part). Since this is commixed with the subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) rooted in *śleṣa* (paronomasia), there is a *saṃdehasaṃkara* (commixture based on doubt) between these two.

In the phrase *harimaṇinā*, since the compound can be formed in two ways—as *hariḥ eva harimaṇiḥ* (Hari himself is the emerald) or *hariḥ maṇir iva* (Hari is like an emerald)—there is a further "blending by doubt" (*saṃdehasaṃkara*) between the figures of metaphor (*rūpaka*) and simile (*upamā*). In the phrase *surucirakuruvindabṛndapaṭukaṭaka*, there is a "blending by mutual entry into a single expressive word" (*ekavācakānupraveśasaṃkara*) between the paronomasia-based hyperbole (*śleṣamūlātiśayokti*) and alliteration (*anuprāsa*).

Thus, in the verse beginning with "kalitatilaka," the wise should discern that five figures of speech are combined here: the combination (*saṃkara*) of *utprekṣā* and alliteration (*anuprāsa*) based on the term "harimaṇi," the combination (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of the alliterations occurring in the first and second halves of the verse, and so forth. Furthermore, this manner of combining five figures of speech in a single place has been elucidated by us in certain verses from the *Lakṣmīsahasra*, the *Ratnaprakāśikā*, and the *Haṃsasaṃdeśa*.
In some cases, even from the commingling of various figures of speech, a particular strikingness arises. For example:

"In the houses of the wealthy, children gather up the diamonds fallen there—diamonds softened by the rays of the emeralds set in the courtyards—mistaking them for *jāmbava* fruits; that is the beauty of the grace of Lakṣmī’s sidelong glances. (2228)
In the houses of the wealthy and illustrious— the singular number being used with the intention of denoting the class— [the pearls] had fallen,
having slipped away due to neglect, and were gathered in the courtyards because of the levelness of the ground.

The meaning is that those which are spread out like emeralds are shaped like planks. By their rays (*ghṛṇi*), which are smooth, glossy—that is, dark—children, playing, [mistake] diamonds (*vajra*) and sapphires for *jāmbava* fruits, thinking "these are jambū fruits" due to delusion; [the form] *jāmbava* is derived from *jambū* with the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of a product (*vikāra*), as in the rule "from *jambū*. Amara states: "The fruit of the *jambū* is called *jambū*, *jambu*, or *jāmbava* (feminine). *Jāmbava* is thus a derivative (*vaikārika*) [term]. *Jambū* is feminine, while *jambu* and *jāmbava* are neuter. *Phale jambvā jambū strī jambu jāmbavam* (Amara).

The phrase "they glean" (*uñchanti*), meaning they gather one by one, possesses the feminine gender through the power of the word *kaṭākṣa* ("glance") which is being predicated. The "glory of the glance" (*kaṭākṣa-śrī*) belongs to Ramā, the divine queen of Śrīnivāsa; it is indeed the Lakṣmī of her glance. In this context, the description of the abundance and prosperity of those who possess *śrī* (fortune/glory) constitutes the poetic figure known as *udātta*.

In the verse "harimaṇighṛṇimasṛṇāni," there is the figure of speech *tadguṇa* (the quality of one thing being transferred to another), and in that same context, there is the figure of speech *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason) based on the object which serves as the cause for the illusion to be described later; thus, there is a *saṃkara* (commingling) of these two through their mutual entry into a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*). In the phrase "jāmbavadhiyā," there is the figure of speech *bhrāntimat* (illusion). Furthermore, the figure of speech *udātta* (the sublime) is rendered beautiful by those two; therefore, there is a *saṃkara* between them and it [the *udātta*] by way of the relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*).

Thus, the description of the non-difference between the cause of the splendor of the magnificent mansion and the cause of the splendor of Lakṣmī’s sidelong glance is the figure of speech *hetu* (Poetic Cause). And this [figure] culminates in the limitless excellence of the splendor of Lakṣmī’s sidelong glance. If the poet’s effort is directed toward this much alone, then the final rest lies in the figure of *hetu*, adorned by the previously established figure of *udātta*.

If the intent is to praise the excellence of the beauty of Ramā’s sidelong glance by means of an irrelevant effect—namely, the bestowing of boundless sovereignty—as an answer to the question, "What is the nature of the splendor of the sidelong glance of Ramā, who is worthy of description?", then there is a resting place in the figure of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Praise of the Irrelevant) based on the effect (*kārya*). However, if the intention is that the effect itself is also worthy of description, then the resting place is in *prastutāṅkura* (The Sprout of the Relevant). Since no specific determination can be made here, there is a commixture (*saṃkara*) based on doubt (*saṃdeha*).

Furthermore, there is a commingling (*saṃkara*) through mutual interpenetration (*ekavācakānupraveśa*) between the figure of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) and the figure of *udātta* (the noble), insofar as the description of the splendor of the illustrious palace constitutes a statement of connection where no connection exists. There is also a commingling through mutual interpenetration between the figure of *hetu* (cause)—which culminates in the excellence of boundless generosity—and the figure of *atyukti* (exaggeration), which consists in the description of marvelous and unreal generosity. [This leads to] the *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) rooted therein...

There is a commingling (*saṃkara*) through the coalescence (*ekavācakānupraveśa*) of the figure of praise (*praśaṃsālaṃkāra*) or the figure of the "sprout of the subject" (*prastutāṅkurālaṃkāra*) with the figure of the "magnificent" (*udāttālaṃkāra*), which consists of the description of glorious wealth and prosperity; for Dīkṣita himself has stated that the word "vācaka" (expressive) refers merely to that which conveys meaning, and is thus common to both denotative and suggestive functions.

Likewise, there is a combination of equal prominence (*samaprādhānya-saṃkara*) among these three types of *saṃkara* involving a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*): namely, the two figures of *udātta* and *atiśayokti*; the two figures of *hetu* and *atyukti*; and either *vyajyodātta*, *aprastutapraśaṃsā*, or *aprastutāṅkura*. For among these, there is no mutual subservience (*aṅgatva*) of one to the others.

Now, one might object: since the figure *udātta*—which consists of the description of the abundance of prosperity—and the figure *atiśayokti*—which consists of the description of a relationship where none exists—both enter into a single expressive word (*ekavācaka*), and since their subservience to the *hetu* (poetic cause) as a source of beauty for that figure is active, how can there be a "commingling" (*saṃkara*) of these three figures with equal prominence? For it must be said that it is the figure *udātta* itself, by virtue of its being the description of the abundance of prosperity, which acts as the subordinate element (*aṅga*) by imparting charm to the figure *hetu*.

In this case, there is no utility even for the commingling (*saṃkara*) of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), because it is appropriate that the three [figures] possess equal prominence. Thus, in this verse, there is a commingling of all four types of commingling as applicable. To explain: there is a commingling by way of the relation of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) between the commingling of the Sublime (*udātta*) and its Quality (*tadguṇa*), and a commingling by way of the relation of principal and subordinate between the commingling of Illusion (*bhrāntimat*) and the Sublime (*udātta*).

Likewise, those of sharp intellect should discern that there is a "blending by the relation of principal and subordinate" (*aṅgāṅgibhāva-saṃkara*) between the figure *bhrāntimat* (error) and *udātta* (the noble), as well as a "blending by doubt" (*saṃdeha-saṃkara*) between *udātta* as the subordinate and figures such as *hetu* (cause). Blendings of this kind, occurring in the previously shown examples of semantic figures (*arthālaṃkāra*) and in the examples of verbal figures (*śabdālaṃkāra*) that will be presented hereafter, should be identified by wise scholars proficient in the science of poetics; however, for fear of excessive prolixity, I shall desist from further elaboration.
The designation "Śrī" at the end of the work is for the purpose of ultimate auspiciousness; thus, everything is consistent.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, the section on the figure of speech *saṅkara* (commixture), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the section on verbal figures of speech (*śabdālaṅkārasara*).
Thus have the figures of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*) been described according to my understanding.
Now, the figures of speech based on sound (śabdālaṃkāras) will be examined in order, by way of a mere indication.

Although the author of the *Prakāśa* and others have placed the verbal ornaments (*śabdālaṃkāra*) before the semantic ornaments (*arthālaṃkāra*), treating them as more venerable because they reside in words that are themselves more venerable, the author of the *Kāvyānuśāsana*, however, states: "Ornaments are indeed of two kinds: verbal ornaments and semantic ornaments. Since the word functions with reference to the meaning, the semantic ornaments alone are illustrated first."

For this very reason, Daṇḍin and others have described the figures of sense (arthālaṃkāra) first due to their superior excellence, while the figures of sound (śabdālaṃkāra) were described subsequently as being of secondary importance. Therefore, following the opinion of the author of the *Kāvyānuśāsana* and others, we describe the figures of sound immediately after the description of the figures of sense.
Alliteration (varṇānuprāsa) is said to be the similarity of mere consonants.

That similarity of consonants which exists despite a dissimilarity of vowels is *varṇānuprāsa* (alliteration). The term "only" (*mātra*) is included to exclude *yamaka* (rhyme), since similarity of consonants also occurs in *yamaka*. Therefore, because *yamaka* will be defined as consisting of the similarity of both vowels and consonants, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to it. The word "phoneme" (*varṇa*) is specified in the definition to prevent the over-extension of this definition to *lāṭānuprāsa*, which consists of the similarity of both vowels and consonants.

Thus, they say that because *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration of words) lacks the quality of alliteration of phonemes (*varṇānuprāsa*), it is not considered a primary instance [of the figure], and therefore the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in that case does not constitute a fault. Anuprāsa is an excellent arrangement (*nyāsa*) that follows the *rasas* and other aesthetic elements. As it has been said: "That which is an excellent arrangement of phonemes (*varṇa*) following the *rasas* and other elements is indeed *anuprāsa*."
This [alliteration] is of two kinds, distinguished by its occurrence within a single word (cchekavṛtti) and its occurrence as a sequence of syllables (anuprāsa).

This alliteration (varṇānuprāsa) is of two kinds: chekānuprāsa and vṛttyanuprāsa. Chekas are the learned; the alliteration favored by them is called chekānuprāsa. Vṛtti is the operation directed toward rasa based on specific phonemes, which is to say, a particular mode of composition; they call the alliteration that relies upon this "vṛttyanuprāsa."
Chekānuprāsa: They call that chekānuprāsa where there is a single instance of similarity between two consonants.
That which is a simultaneous similarity between two consonants is called *c hekānuprāsa* (alliteration).

May he attain that divine, auspicious, and immeasurable dark splendor which is eternally present within the heart, which dwells upon the mountain of the serpent, and whose form shatters the pride of Kandarpa.

In the first half of this verse, there is a single instance of similarity between *na* and *ta*, *ṅa* and *ga*, and *va* and *ya*; and in the second half, there is a single instance of similarity between *na* and *da*, as well as *ra* and *pa*.
And thus:
"The moon, its body dimmed by the radiance of the dawn..."
It assumed the pale hue of the cheeks of women emaciated by longing.

This is according to the opinion of the author of the *Prakāśa* and others, who—by providing examples of *chekānuprāsa*—accept that *chekānuprāsa* consists in the repetition of two consonants capable of tolerating an interval. However, in the opinion of Vidyānātha and others, the definition is as follows:
"When a repetition of pairs of consonants is performed without any interval, this is called *chekānuprāsa*."

The meaning is that *chekānuprāsa* (rhyme) consists in the repetition of two consonant clusters without being separated by another consonant; therefore, there is no fault even if there is an intervention by a vowel.

Just as the God of gods is superior to the gods, and Rāma is greater than the pleasure-gardens of his own chest, so too is He to be meditated upon— He who is the ornament of the serpent, the mountain, the earth, and the tresses of the Goddess.
Here, in all four quarters, because pairs of consonants recur without any intervening separation, there is *che kānuprāsa* (alliteration).
If there is a repetition of sounds that transgresses the restriction on number—
whether involving one, two, three, or more syllables— it is called *vṛttyanuprāsa* (alliteration).

In this context, since a single consonant repeated only once lacks variety, it follows by implication that its repetition must occur more than once; however, for two consonants, the repetition occurs only once. Otherwise, it would constitute *chekānuprāsa*. There is no contradiction even if there is non-repetition when there is an intervention [by other sounds]. For three or more consonants, the repetition—whether once or repeatedly, with or without intervention—is to be understood accordingly. By the word "vṛtti," the Vaidarbhī and other styles are intended; they say that alliteration characterized by such a style is called *vṛttyanuprāsa*.
The earth of the mountain king, turned dark by the mass of radiance spreading from the emerald that destroys the demon Mura, rests as if draped in a cloak of blue cloth.
A certain goddess of great majesty, whose creeper-like necklace of lovely gems delights the serpent-bearing mountain (Śeṣa), now emerges for the joy of the worlds. 2232.

O Goddess, whose eyes are noble and possess a luster that steals away the pride of the soft lotus, may my mind remain fixed upon Your own body, which is eager to utterly conquer the intoxicating force of the clouds.

In the second verse, the meaning is that the earth (*mahī*), the ground, is the support for those of great majesty; the construction is "some deity. In the third, *madarabhasaḥ* means the impetuosity of intoxication; the sense is "in one who is impetuous—that is, full of exuberance—in conquering it. According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The word *rabhasa* denotes both speed and joy. In these three verses, there is *vṛttyanuprāsa* (alliteration of style) due to the repetition of one, two, or three syllables as appropriate. Here, as well as in the preceding [verses], similarity of vowels is incidental.
It will be explained later that the similarity of both vowels and consonants is the defining factor of *yamaka* (rhyme).
Now, as for *lāṭānuprāsa*:
that repetition of words and meanings which differs only in its intended sense (*tātparya*) is called *śābdalāṭānuprāsa* by those who know the nature of poetry.

Having thus explained alliteration (*anuprāsa*) pertaining to individual phonemes (*varṇa*), he now defines alliteration pertaining to words (*śabda*) consisting of a collection of phonemes: "That which is merely a difference in intention (*tātparya*)," and so forth. That repetition of word and meaning which consists merely in a difference of intention—that word, being a collection of phonemes, and its relation to it, is called *śābda*; because it is dear to the people of Lāṭa, it is termed *lāṭānuprāsa* by those learned in poetry. Here, the term "meaning" (*artha*) is included to exclude *yamaka*, since mere repetition of sound exists in *yamaka* as well.

In the case of *yamaka* (rhyme), because there is a difference in meaning, that is not a case of tautology (*paunaruktya*). Since mere tautology of word and meaning is common to defects such as "the use of already-stated words" (*kathitapadatva*), it should be understood that the qualification "distinct only in its intended meaning" (*tātparyamātrabhinnā*) is employed [to exclude those defects].
It is threefold: in the repetition of a sentence, the repetition of a word, and the repetition of a name.

That is *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration of the Lat country). It is threefold: repetition of words consisting of nominal stems (*subanta*), repetition of words consisting of verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*), and repetition of nouns (*prātipadika*). Among these, the first is as follows:

"O Hari, if you are pleased with us through the practice of the duties of the castes and stages of life, what [need have we] for it? If you are not pleased, what [need have we] for the practice of the duties of the castes and stages of life? (2234)

Here, in the first half-verse, there is disregard for the practice of the duties of caste and stage of life once the fruit in the form of the Lord’s grace has been attained; in the second half-verse, there is disregard when such a fruit has not been attained. Thus, due to this difference in intended meaning (*tātparya*), the repetition of the sentence constitutes *lāṭānuprāsa* (rhyme based on regional expression).
Just as poison may become nectar for him whose mind is unswerving toward Mādhava, so too nectar may become poison for him whose mind falters toward Mādhava.
In whose heart Hari dances, for him the Kali age becomes the Kṛta age; alas! in whose mind Śauri does not reside, for him the Kali age becomes the Kṛta age.

In the first verse, the meaning is that for one whose mind is unswerving in the abode of Śrīnivāsa, even poison becomes nectar—as was the case with Prahlāda—whereas for one whose mind has wavered, even nectar becomes poison. In the second verse, there is *lāṭānuprāsa* (rhyme based on word-repetition) through the repetition of the sentence with a shift in intended meaning: for one who is intent upon meditation on Śrīnivāsa, even the Kali age is the Kṛta age; for another, even the Kṛta age is the Kali age.
The Kali age becomes the Kṛta age for him, and his Kṛta age becomes the Kali age,
in whose heart Govinda resides and in whose mind Acyuta dwells.

Thus, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is established as the authority here. Although in these two verses it is appropriate that the first halves of both stanzas possess primacy because they state the subjects (*uddeśya*), while the second halves possess subordination because they state the predicates (*vidheya*), there is nevertheless a fault in the latter half [of the second verse] consisting of an "unclarified predicate" (*avimṛṣṭavidheyāṃśa*), in the form of a reversal in the presentation of subject and predicate. Nevertheless, since such a flaw does not obscure the comprehension when it is not brought to mind, this example was cited by the ancient masters such as the author of the *Prakāśa* and others; for that reason, we have cited it as well.
The second [verse] is as follows:
"For those men who gaze incessantly and who meditate upon that Lord of Serpents, his eye is their eye and his very birth is their birth. (2237)

In this instance, there is a difference in intended meaning (*tātparya-bheda*) characterized by the excellence of both the second eye and the word "birth. Now, one might object: "In the figure of speech called *ananvaya* (non-comparison), such as 'The moon is beautiful like the moon,' since the repetition of both word and meaning is possible, why should it not be considered *lāṭānuprāsa*? This is true; however, although the definition of *ananvaya* consists merely in the repetition of meaning, nevertheless, because of the risk of the fault of "departure from the established order" (*paryāya-prakrama-doṣa*) when there is a lack of uniformity between the initial mention and its subsequent reference, the repetition of the word is an incidental requirement.

In this case, however, the repetition of both [the word and its meaning] is indeed necessary; thus, because the objects [of comparison] differ, there is no contradiction whatsoever. As it has been said: "In *ananvaya* (self-comparison), the identity of words occurs incidentally due to propriety; but in this *lāṭānuprāsa* (regional alliteration), it is the direct cause."

Thus they say. Now, one might object: "Even so, since the eye and other senses—which are already established by this very *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration)—are here enjoined as being 'the state of being an eye' (*cakṣuṣṭva*) and so forth through a difference in intended meaning (*tātparya*), let there not be the figure of speech called *vidhi* (enjoinment). If you say this, we reply: no. For in cases such as "You are the body of Rāma," where there is an absence of repetition of word and meaning, the figure of *vidhi* is indispensable; therefore, even here, since the two figures coexist by virtue of the sense, it is more appropriate to speak of their *saṃkara* (commixture) as a case of "mutual entry into a single expressive word" (*ekavācakānupraveśa*).
Or rather,
that deity who is so exceedingly noble exists upon the peak of the serpent-mountain; for any person who has been brought even once to the remembrance of that deity— (2238)
When there is identity of compounds, or when a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) occurs in both compound and non-compound forms, or when a noun is repeated in three ways, it is called *lāṭānuprāsa*.

When there is repetition of a noun or a nominal stem (prātipadika) within a single compound, or between different compounds, or between a compound and a non-compound, Lāṭānuprāsa is produced; it thus results in three varieties.

May that Supreme Goddess— who is as cool as the nectar-rayed moon, who is the support of the snowy mountains, who is the limit of compassion, and who is the boundary of ancient words— protect me incessantly.

"Boundless in the object of compassion" means that there is no limit, or that the boundary is non-existent; it signifies that the boundary of compassion has been transcended. Alternatively, "dayāyāḥ sīmā" may mean the limit or end of compassion. Regarding the repetition in "amṛtāmṛta": in one compound, the nominal stem "amṛta" is used; in another compound, "śiśira" is used; and in the case of "dayā sīmā sīmā," there is a repetition of both the compound and the non-compound forms.
Thus, alliteration (lāṭānuprāsa) is said to be of five kinds.

Five types of *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration) have been described: one occurs when a sentence is repeated; another when a word is repeated; a third when a name is repeated within a single compound; a fourth when a name is repeated in different compounds; and a fifth when a name is repeated across both a compound and a non-compound. An example is as follows:

"The splendor of the rays of the white-rayed moon [the sun], the fame of the mountain that bears the form of the sun, and the Goddess of Fortune—O Puruṣa, even that Lakṣmī belongs to you alone and to no other."
This is in accordance with the views of the authors of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* and others who have cited such examples.

In this regard, it must be considered that since both the words "hand" (*kara*) and "word" (*śabda*) rest solely upon their own literal denotations and lack any other-directedness, there is no difference in their intended meaning (*tātparya*), for that [literal sense] alone is the very life-force of such intentionality.

Therefore, this is merely a case of alliteration (*anuprāsa*). Nor should it be argued that even though words such as *kara* (hand) rest in their own primary meanings when used independently, they nevertheless possess a different intended meaning (*tātparya*) within a compound because they abandon their own meaning and function for the sake of another, subordinate meaning; for there is an absence of the necessary conditions for figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Here too, since the word *kara* is subordinate due to its being part of a compound whose primary referent is the meaning of the other member, it remains merely subordinate and there is no sublation of its primary meaning, as it rests precisely in its own sense.

Indeed, there is no identity between the state of being subordinate (*guṇībhāva*) and the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*). For while the subordination of a primary meaning occurs only in relation to something else, sublation is the failure of the word to rest in its own primary meaning; thus, there is a great difference between the two. Furthermore, there is no purpose whatsoever for *lakṣaṇā* (indication) here, so [the objection] is merely a case of redundancy. By this, the author of the *Sarvasva*, who claims that in the verse "closing those eyes which are like lotus petals," there is *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration), is also refuted;
they argue that because the word *abjapatra* is not redundant, such [alleged repetition] is difficult to establish.
Now, if syllables that are either meaningless, or having distinct meanings, or both meaningful and meaningless,
are repeated in succession, that constitutes *yamaka* (chiasmus).
Just as the entire, expansive, and abundant land of the Lord of Serpents, full of lakes and lakes, produces joy for Śauri and incessantly leads away the misfortune of men to cessation; 2240.

In this context, *yamaka* (rhyme) is that repetition of syllables—whether they are meaningless, as in *sarasāsarasā-kalā* where *rasāsa-* and so forth are meaningless; or whether they possess different meanings due to the presence of meaning, as in *vipulāvipule*; or whether they are sometimes meaningful and sometimes devoid of meaning, as in *janayati nayati*—that occurs according to their sequence.

In the case of *sarasāsarasā-kalā*, there is no over-extension (*avyāpti*) because the repeated syllables *rasāsa* lack meaning, and thus there is an absence of both "having different meanings" and "being meaningful and meaningless"; therefore, it was stated that they are "or meaningless. In the case of *vipulāvipulā*, regarding the repeated [syllables]...

Regarding the term *vipulā*: since there is an absence of both meaningfulness and meaninglessness among its constituent phonemes (*varṇa*), there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*). Therefore, it is stated that they are "either having distinct meanings" (*bhinnārthakāḥ*). In the expression *janayati nayati*, the second occurrence of the word *nayati* is meaningful; thus, it lacks meaninglessness, yet it does not have a distinct meaning [from the first], because the first *nayati* is meaningless. Consequently, there would be an over-narrow definition in that case as well. Therefore, it is stated that they are "either meaningful or meaningless" (*sārthakānarthakāś ca*).

In cases such as *kapiḥ* and *pikaḥ*, since there is a repetition of phonemes (*varṇa*) that possess distinct meanings, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of these being considered *yamaka*. Therefore, it is stated [in the definition] "in sequence" (*kramāt*). The meaning is that they must be repeated in the very same sequence in which they were first recited; thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to such cases. The plural number in the word *varṇāḥ* ("phonemes") is not intended to be restrictive.

Consequently, [the definition applies to] such verses as: "Be victorious, O you who are saluted by the world (*bhava*), O you whose specific fear has been born from the destruction of the sons of Diti! O Murāri, you who are the jewel among the women of the earth, the supporters of the serpent-mountains, and the enjoyer of the remnants! (2241)

In this case, there is no loss of the quality of *yamaka* (rhyme). [The compound] *ditijanīnām* refers to the multitude (*jātam*) born of the *ditijās*, i.e., the Daityas; he by whom that particular fear arising from them has been *ditaḥ*—that is, severed—is addressed as such. According to Amara, "dita, chita, and vṛkṇa" all mean "severed. Nor should it be argued that the definition is thus not followed, for some maintain that *yamaka* is the repetition of syllables within any one of the three aforementioned modes; others hold that *yamaka* is the repetition of words with different meanings but identical sounds.

Others hold that since the distinction regarding the identity of meaning is indistinguishable across syllables—whether they are meaningless, have different meanings, or are meaningful yet devoid of semantic content—there is no lack of universal applicability (ananugama).
That [composition] is of four kinds, according to the application of a verse, a half-verse, a quarter-verse, or a portion thereof.
That *yamaka*, occurring in the repetition of a verse, the repetition of a half-verse, the repetition of a quarter-verse, and the repetition of a part of a quarter-verse, is thus fourfold.
In that regard, an example of the *ślokāvṛtti* (repetition of a verse) is as follows:

"May Govinda, who instantly bestows what is desired—He who possesses a vast interior shimmering with mandāra flowers upon His lofty central stage, and who is the support of the greatness of that mountain [Govardhana]—grant his wish. (2242)

Sadyoga attained that mountain, the support of great majesty, which possesses a lofty middle ground and a vast, expansive breast shimmering with the waves of the Kāmandā river, bestowing his desired goal.

The word division (*padaccheda*) is as follows: *uttuṅgamadhyavanikāmandārollāsisuvipulakroḍaṃ taṃ acalaṃ ahiṃ ādhāraṃ sadyaḥ govindaṃ ādadhataṃ iṣṭam | uttuṅgaṃ adhyavani kāmaṃ dārollāsisuvipulokroḍaṃ taṃ acalamahimādhāraṃ sadyogaḥ avindaṃ ādadhataṃ iṣṭam*. [He saw] that mountain, the support of the earth, which immediately bore the beloved Govinda; [he saw] him who possesses a very vast lap shining with the gentle breeze from the forest situated upon its high slopes, and who is the foundation of the greatness of the immovable one. In the phrase *uttuṅgāyām*: "In that [place] where there are lofty *punnāga* trees"—according to Amara, "in *punnāga*, the words *puruṣa* and *tuṅga* [are used]. [Note: The commentary clarifies the double entendre (*śleṣa*). The first part describes the mountain bearing Govinda. The second part describes a yogi (*sadyogaḥ*) finding (*avindan*) the desired state: he who has reached the high ground (*adhyavani*), whose desire (*kāma*) is fulfilled, whose vast chest (*kroḍa*) shines with the gift (*dāra*) of joy, and who is established in the greatness of the immovable.]

"In the middle of the Madhyavanikā" means in the midst of the forest. Regarding the "Mandāras," they are Pārijāta trees; as Amarasimha states: "The nimba tree is called Pāribhadra, while the Mandāra is the Pārijātaka. That [place] is one where the Earth-goddess (Bhūdevī) is "exceedingly expansive" (*suvipula*), meaning she is beautifully and broadly manifest, being embraced by her—referring to the Primeval Boar (*Kroḍa*) who is situated therein. This is because the Lord, in the form of the Primeval Boar, manifested on Śeṣādri.

Regarding the phrase "‘Kroḍo bhūdāra’ ityapi," Amara [includes these] among the synonyms for Varāha. The grammatical construction is: "him, the well-known serpent, the mountain" (ahiṃ acalam), meaning Śeṣādri. Since it is well-established in the Purāṇas that Śeṣa himself descended as a mountain, he is referred to by way of identity. "Ādhāram" means the support or dwelling place; the sense is that he was making [the mountain] his residence, or dwelling there. "Iṣṭam" means the object of unsurpassed affection, based on the scriptural statement: "For the wise man is exceedingly dear" (*Bhagavad Gītā* 7.17). The root *iṣ* (in the sense of "desire") takes the suffix *kta* in the passive sense. Alternatively, "iṣṭam" means "worshipped by all"; here the suffix *kta* is applied to the root *yaj* (to sacrifice/worship).
The word *iṣṭa* may mean "hoped for" (*āśaṃsita*) or "worshipped" (*pūjita*), and when used as a masculine adjective it means "beloved" (*preyasi*).
As a neuter noun, it refers to the "seven-threaded [sacrificial cord]" (*saptatantu*), to a "purificatory rite" (*saṃskāra*), or to a "sacrificial act" (*kratukarman*).

Thus says the *Medinī* lexicon. "Uttaṅgam" means exceedingly lofty by virtue of all its qualities. "Adhyavani" means upon the earth; this is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of a locative case. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "bearing the mountain Himavat as its support upon the earth. "Kāmam" means sufficiently. "Dharmiṇyā lakṣmyā" means with his lawful consort, Lakṣmī. "Ullāsi" means shining or manifesting. "Suvipulam" means extremely vast. "Kroḍam" means the space between the arms (the chest). Thus, the meaning is: one whose broad chest is embraced by Lakṣmī.

To that Govinda, Śrīnivāsa—who is renowned for his multitude of auspicious qualities such as being the cause of the universe known through the Vedānta; who is the substratum of immovable, stable majesty; who is desired and sought after by those who have taken refuge in Him; and who nourishes or sustains the sacrifice performed by the sacrificers—there is an abundance of the name "Govinda" on Śeṣādri, as the name conveys the highest degree of His good character and, according to the scriptural statement, "When [the world] cried out 'Govinda!'," it is understood to signify an excess of affection toward the Blessed One.

Because he is thus celebrated by people, he is designated by the word "Govinda. Being one whose yoga—meaning meditation—is excellent (san), he is so described; [thereby] I immediately found (avindam) him as my refuge, I chose him. This is the first person singular form of the root *vid* in the imperfect tense.
Half-rotation (*ardhāvṛtti*) is as follows:
"O Śubhadāmodara, O radiant one, conquer! Protect me, O you who possess a firm lower lip and delight the distressed. (Śubha dāmodara bhāsura jaya mā pāhi sthirādharāmodīn) || 2244 ||

The word division is: *śubhadāmaḥ*, *adarabhāsurajaya*, *māpa*, *ahisthirādharāmodin*, *śubhadāmodara*, *bhāsura*, *jaya*, *mām*, *pāhi*, *sthirādharāmodin*. *Śubhadāmaḥ*: O giver of auspiciousness. *Adarabhāsurajaya*: O Conqueror (*jaya*) of the Asuras who possess non-meager (*adara*) splendor (*bhāsura*). *Māpa*: Protect me (*mām pāhi*). *Ahisthirādharāmodin*: O You who delight (*āmodin*) the stable (*sthira*) lower lip (*adhara*) of Ahi (the serpent). *Śubhadāmodara*: O Auspicious Dāmodara. *Bhāsura*: O Radiant One. *Jaya*: O Victorious One. *Mām pāhi*: Protect me. *Sthirādharāmodin*: O You who delight the firm lower lip. Thus is the analysis of the words. *Adarabhāḥ* means those Asuras of no small (*analpa*) brilliance; *jaya* means he who conquers them.

The suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule *pacādyac*. "Victory over them" means victory over the Daityas of no small prowess; the vocative of that is "O Adarabhāsurajaya! (O you whose victory is radiant and unsurpassed!). "Ahisthirādhara" refers to Śeṣādri (the serpent-mountain); "āmodin" means gladdening. You are of the nature of auspiciousness, according to the saying, "the most auspicious among all auspicious things. O Dāmodara, O Radiant One, whose essential nature is self-luminous! You are gladdened by the lower lip (*adhara*)—that is, the nectar—of Sthirā, the Goddess Earth. Alternatively, "Sthirādhara" means the Supporter of the Earth (*Dharaṇidhara*), as in the phrases "O Acyuta, Supporter of the Earth, Holder of the Conch and Discus," and "O Supporter of the Earth, instruct my mind."

The following point should be noted here: for this very reason, [the word] *āmodin* means "possessing an exceedingly captivating fragrance. The sense is that because the Earth Goddess naturally possesses fragrance, she is eternally endowed with it;
as it is said: "The term *parimala* refers to a scent produced by crushing that is enchanting to people;
*āmoda*, however, is that which is exceedingly captivating."

Thus says Amara. Alternatively, because of the scriptural statement, "He who possesses all fragrances and all tastes," the meaning is "possessing all divine fragrances. O Lord of Śrī! You, whose auspicious garland (dāmā) is Vaijayantī, be victorious—this is the first person singular imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *ji*. According to Amara, "dāma" is not used in the masculine for "a bond"; since the word *dāma* is feminine, the suffix *ṅīp* is prohibited by the rule "manaḥ," but the suffix *ḍāp* is applied by the rule "ḍābubhābhyāmanyatarasyām. Thus, the compound is a *bahuvrīhi*. [And finally: O Bhā! Protect me, that is, preserve me.
Or, for example:
"Speak that supreme lotus, nurtured by your speech, which has arisen on the peak of Mount Vedagiri; speak, O best of men, that which has been proclaimed upon the head of the mountain. (2245)

The analysis of the verse is as follows: "O Lord, speak that supreme lotus which has surpassed the moon; it has arisen on the peak of the mountain of the Vedas, O Knower of Men. By means of his face (*vadanena*), he has surpassed (*abhibhāvitaḥ*)—that is, brought into subjection or eclipsed—the lotus-born moon (*abjaḥ*). In this act of eclipsing, the Blessed One possesses the status of the *prayojaka-kartṛ* (the instigating agent), while the face possesses the status of the *prayojya-kartṛ* (the instrument or subordinate agent).

On the summit of Mount Añjanavedagiri—that mountain which is both "Añjana" and "Veda," known as Añjana and Veda—the [Lord] arose, having manifested. He is he by whom the lotus was brought into being and produced within his navel.

"Upon the navel of the Unborn, one [thing] is fixed, in which this entire world is supported"—so says the Śruti. On the "Veda-mountain," that is, on speech in the form of the Śruti, at its summit, meaning in the Vedānta; it is "uttered" (udita), spoken—this is the past passive participle (*kta*) of the root *vad* used in the passive sense—as in the Śruti: "Him, who is known through the Upaniṣads. O people! It is the supreme (*parama*), in the sense of being most excellent (*para*).

"Speak, speak the most excellent word! Proclaim to the people that the Blessed One, who has manifested on Mount Añjana, is the Supreme Brahman—the cause of the entire universe—by virtue of being the navel-lotus from which the Creator and the Source of all beings arose. This is the proclamation addressed to the people.
Just as no other means indeed experience joy from your surrender (*prapadana*), so too only those who have surrendered and offer praise experience joy, and not other means. || 2246 ||

The word division is as follows: *prapadanataḥ tava na anye avākalayante mudam nanu upāyāḥ prapadanataḥ stavanāni eva akalayan te mudam na nu upāyāḥ*. The word *nanu* is used as an address (*āmantraṇa*). O Lord! From *prapadanataḥ*, meaning "from taking refuge" (*śaraṇavaraṇāt*), the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *ādi* (Pāṇini 5.4.44). Other means (*anye upāyāḥ*)—namely, other instruments such as sacrifice, charity, austerity, fasting, and so forth—do not bring about (*avākalayante*), nor do they produce (*avākalpayante*), Your joy or delight.

The suffix *laṭ* follows the root *kalayati* preceded by the prefix *ava-*. *Te* means "of you. *Prapade* means "at the tips of the feet"; as Amara states: "the tip of the foot is *prapada*. *Nataḥ* means "having become one who has sought refuge. *Akalayam* means "I composed" or "I fashioned," referring to hymns—that is, praises alone; this is the first person singular of the *laṅ* (imperfect) following the root *kalayati*. *Mudam* means "joy" or "affection"—the sense being that [joy] resulting from that praise. The word *nu* is used for inquiry; as Amara states: "*nu* is used in inquiry and in alternative."

"Did you not approach with means? [I say] you certainly did approach," using the *laṅ* (imperfect) middle person from the root *yā* preceded by either *upa-aṅ* or *upa*. "For 'one who loves praise' (*stavapriya*) is indeed your name"—this is the intended meaning. In the second half-verse, regarding the phrase *prapadanataḥ stavanāni*, there is the elision of the *visarga* according to the rule: "The elision of *visarga* before *kharpara* (a sibilant followed by a consonant) or *śari* (a sibilant) should be stated. In the word *akalayante*, there is the optional substitution of the *parasavarṇa* for the *anusvāra* according to the rule: "The *parasavarṇa* is optional at the end of a word.
Here, Viṣṇu, who is without origin (*ayoni*), was praised with these excellent words.
May the Lord Janārdana, honored by this sacrifice of speech, be pleased with me.

Such authoritative sources (*pramāṇa*) as these should be consulted. These two verses—namely, the *vṛttyardhavṛtti-yamaka* and the *mahāyamaka*—are designated by the names *samudgaka* and *mahāyamaka* respectively by Rudraṭa and others. As it is said:
"When half [of a verse] is repeated, it produces a *yamaka* called *samudgaka*;
but when the entire verse is repeated, it is a *mahāyamaka*."

Just as Lakṣmī shines forth from you, who are protected by the essence of fresh clouds; what other Lakṣmī could there be for you, who are without end, since you are illuminated by that which is not without essence? || 2247 ||

In the first half [of the verse], the division is: "O *avitah* (Protector), *lakṣmīḥ* (fortune) shines for you, who are illuminated by the essence of fresh clouds (*navatoyadasārabhāsitāt*). But in the second half, the division is: "And what fortune (*kā lakṣmīḥ*) is there for you, O *anavataḥ* (one who does not protect), since you are illuminated by that which is without essence (*asārabhāsitāt*)? O *avitah*—from the root *avi*, meaning "to protect," with the suffix *tṛc*—O Protector!
For it is said: "Indeed, there is no capacity to protect except for Hari, the Lord of All."

Thus it is said. "Navatoyada" refers to the clouds of the rainy season; their "sāra" is the most excellent [cloud], and its "bhā" is its luster. From that which is "asita," meaning dark blue—or alternatively, from that which is dark like the "sārabhā" (supreme radiance) of the new cloud—or even from that which is darker than even that [radiance]—from you, O Lord, "lakṣmī" shines forth. The sense is that she appears with a heightened brilliance, like lightning situated in the midst of a dark blue cloud. Or else, "lakṣmī" refers to the prosperity of people, [which shines] from your presence.

The sense is that the attainment of prosperity for the worlds shines forth from you alone. From you, Śarva—who is *anavataḥ* (devoid of protection) in times of distress, who provides no refuge, and who does not please others through his nature as a destroyer—even *lakṣmī*, that is, *śrī* or even the mere report of wealth—what is there? The sense is that no prosperity at all is accomplished for people; therefore, what [prosperity] could possibly exist?
To the question "Why?", he says "yad" (because). Here, the word "this" (*ayam*) is to be supplied as the subject.

That which is essence-less, devoid of substance, or inferior is merely "ash-spoken" (bhasita), like the speech of crows, Rākṣasas, and the like—the suffix *aṇ* being used here in its own sense (*svārthika*). From such [speech], one becomes "protected" (*avita*), "pleased" (*prīta*), or "satisfied" (*tṛpta*). This is derived from the roots *ava-* meaning "to please" or *tṛp-* meaning "to satisfy," with the suffix *kta* in the active sense (*kartari*). The underlying thought is: how could the attainment of prosperity by people possibly result from one who is incapable of protection, who is satisfied merely with an abundance of ashes, and who is not a protector of all—unlike the Blessed Lord Śrīnivāsa, who is the abode of Fortune?

Just as one who has taken refuge at the feet of the illustrious Śobhita, though very lowly, becomes a great benefactor; so too the Lord of Śrī (Viṣṇu), ever resorting to the prosperity of Abhitassadā, makes even the most humble a great doer.

The word division is as follows: *śrīśobhitaḥ*, *saḥ*, *dāsam*, *padam*, *śritam*, *bahukaraḥ*, *ati-hīnam*, *api*, *śrīśaḥ*, *abhitaḥ*, *sadā*, *saṃpadam*, *śritam*, *bahu*, *karoti*, *hi*, *inam*, *api*. [He is] "adorned with glory" (*śrīśobhitaḥ*); [he is] "the Lord of Glory" (*śrīśaḥ*). He is "possessed of many hands" (*bahukaraḥ*)—that is to say, he possesses four hands suitable for bestowing the four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*) in accordance with his own abundance. The sense is that he is resplendent with the glory of the sixfold political virtues (*ṣāḍguṇya*). Indeed, the Lord of Glory (*śrīśaḥ*), who is adorned with splendor, always bestows abundant prosperity upon even one who has taken refuge at his feet—a servant (*dāsa*) who is exceedingly lowly (*ati-hīnaḥ*)—and he likewise bestows much [prosperity] upon even a lord (*inaḥ*) who has taken refuge in his presence on all sides (*abhitaḥ*). Thus, he makes even the lowly great, and indeed, he makes even a lord great.

He, the Lord Śrīnivāsa—the Blessed One renowned in all the Upaniṣads as the Sovereign of All—bestows abundant and vast prosperity upon his servant, that conscious being who is his own subordinate part, even if he be exceedingly lowly or exceedingly destitute; the word "even" (api) here indicates a contrast. He grants this to one who has taken refuge in his feet—that is, who has sought shelter—and does so "abhitaḥ," meaning in every place and at all times.

It is not merely this; rather, it also makes [him] a lord (*ina*), that is, a master (*prabhu*). According to Amara, "the word *ina* refers to the sun and to a master. Here, the particle *api* functions as a conjunction (*samuccaye*), and *hi* indicates well-known fact (*prasiddhau*).

Just as the leader of the gods (Indra) becomes possessed of splendor when freed from the thunderbolt (pavi) by his grace within his own abode, so too does one become possessed of a splendor free from distress (tāpa-viyukta-śrī) through grace while sporting (devane) in one's own abode. || 2249 ||

"In her own abode, the leader of the gods, joined with the thunderbolt, becomes Śrī through grace; in her own abode, during play, she becomes one whose beauty is free from distress through grace"—this is the word-division (*cheda*). She whose own (*nija*)—meaning eternal (*nitya*)—abode (*dhāma*), that is, splendor (*tejas*) or power (*prabhāva*), is [such] is *nijadhāmni*. The vocative form is *he nijadhāmni*! The suffix *ṅīp* is optional here according to the rule *ana upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām*. Amara states: "In the sense of one's own, the word *nija* is always used in the three genders; *gṛha*, *geha*, *tviṣ*, and *prabhāva* are synonyms for *dhāma*."

The *Medinī* lexicon states: “*Nija* means one’s own (*svīya*) and eternal (*nitya*). O Śrī! "From your favor" (*bhavatyanugrahāt*)—here the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of all case endings. Regarding the form *bhavatyanugrahaḥ*, there is no masculine conversion (*puṃvadbhāva*) of the word *bhavatī*; this is because the author of the *Bhāṣya* maintains that "masculine conversion occurs only in compound formations (*vṛtti*) for pronouns," and because the commencement of the *Vārttika* rule "*ṭhakchasośca*" indicates that this [rule] is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). Thus, the feminine form is retained.

And this has been explained by us more thoroughly in our *Haṃsasandeśarasāsvādinī* under the verse beginning with "by your good fortune, living... Indra, the leader of the gods, is "armed with the thunderbolt" (*pavimuktaḥ*), meaning accompanied by the *vajra*; as Amara states: "The *kuliśa*, the *bhidura*, and the *pavi* [are synonyms for the thunderbolt]. By this, his heroism and steadfastness are manifested. Therefore, he is one who, by virtue of such favor, "is not slain"—meaning not harmed—by the fierce (*ugraiḥ*) and cruel beings, such as the Daityas.

Therefore, in his own abode, his own place—namely, in heaven (tridiva), which is characterized by sporting, playing, shining, or rejoicing—he becomes one whose glory is free from affliction; that is, he is one whose prosperity (śrī) is devoid of the miseries such as those pertaining to the self (ādhyātmika) and so forth. Here, the narrative of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa should be consulted. All these examples of half-verse repetition (ardhāvṛtti-yamaka) will also serve as examples of the "cow's urine" pattern (gomūtrikābandha) to be described later.

Now, the classification of *yamaka* based on the repetition of quarters: when there is repetition starting from the beginning of the first quarter in the second and subsequent quarters, there are nine varieties.

When the first quarter is repeated in the second, third, and fourth quarters respectively, there are three varieties; when it is repeated simultaneously [in all three], there is one. Thus, there are four varieties based on the repetition of the first quarter. Similarly, when the second quarter is repeated in the third and fourth quarters respectively, there are two [varieties].

There is one variety based on the repetition of the third foot in the fourth foot; thus, there are seven pure varieties based on the repetition of feet. Likewise, there is one variety based on the repetition of the first foot in the second and the third foot in the fourth; and similarly, there is another variety based on the repetition of the first foot in the fourth, the second foot in the fourth, and the second foot in the third. Thus, including these two mixed varieties, nine varieties based on the repetition of feet are obtained in total. This is merely illustrative.

Just as four varieties were stated for the repetition of the first quarter in the second and subsequent quarters—both sequentially and simultaneously—it should be understood that other three varieties are also possible when the first quarter is repeated in the second and third, the second and fourth, and the third and fourth quarters respectively. Likewise, just as there are two varieties when the second quarter is repeated in the third and fourth quarters sequentially, another variety is also possible when it is repeated in both simultaneously. This is how it should be considered.
Now, the classification of *yamaka* (rhyme) based on partial repetition of quarters:
if, in a two-part division of the quarters, the first parts and so forth of the first [quarter] are repeated in the second parts and so forth of the subsequent quarters, there would be ten varieties.
If the first and subsequent final parts were to reside within the second and subsequent final parts,
even then, these same tenfold divisions would certainly exist.
Thus, when divided into two parts, there would be twenty varieties;
when divided into three parts, it should be understood that there are thirty, following this sequence.

Regarding the division of the quarters into two parts, there are four varieties when the first part of the first quarter is repeated sequentially or simultaneously in the first parts of the second and subsequent quarters. There are two varieties when the first part of the second quarter is repeated sequentially in the first parts of the third and fourth quarters. There is one variety when the first part of the first quarter is repeated in the first part of the fourth quarter; likewise, [there is another] when the first part of the first quarter is repeated in the first part of the fourth quarter and the first part of the second quarter [is repeated] in the third.

Furthermore, there is another variety when there is a repetition of the first half-portion of the quarters; likewise, according to the principle of repeating the halves, there is yet another variety when the first half-portion of the first quarter is repeated in the first half-portion of the third quarter, and the first half-portion of the second quarter is repeated in the first half-portion of the fourth quarter. These and others constitute the ten varieties based on the repetition of portions.

If it is asked, "Why are those various sub-varieties not also stated according to the principle of verse-repetition (*ślokāvṛtti*), just as they are according to the principle of half-verse repetition (*ardhāvṛtti*)?"—it should be understood that sub-varieties based on the repetition of parts within a different verse are not mentioned because they lack a specific aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*). In this very same way, there are ten sub-varieties based on the repetition of the final part. Thus, when the quarters (*pāda*) are divided in two ways, there are twenty varieties; when divided in three ways, thirty; and when divided in four ways, there are forty varieties, and so forth, which should be inferred accordingly.
In this manner, the pure varieties have been described.
Now, the varieties of mixed [alliteration]:
likewise, those beginning with the final and ending with the initial, those beginning with the middle and ending with the initial,
those beginning with the final and ending with the middle, those beginning with the middle and ending with the final, and the combinations of these.

When the final portion of the first foot and so forth is rhymed with the initial portion of the second foot and so forth, then it is called *antyādi* (final-initial), based on adopting an etymological derivation meaning "the final is rhymed at the beginning. When the initial portion of the first foot is rhymed with the final portion of the second foot, then it is called *ādyanta* (initial-final), meaning "the initial is rhymed at the end. Similarly, when the middle portion of the first foot and so forth is rhymed with the initial portion of the second foot and so forth, it is *madhyādi* (middle-initial). Likewise, when the initial portion is rhymed with the middle portion, it is *ādimadhyaga* (initial-middle).

Thus, when the final portion of one quarter is restrained (*yamana*) by the middle portion [of another], it is called *antya-madhyaga*; when the middle portion of one quarter is restrained by the final portion [of another], it is called *madhya-antya*. It should be noted that when these occur together, they constitute a combination (*samuccaya*). In this way, the varieties based on the mutual dependence of portions within one quarter upon the portions of other quarters have been demonstrated. Now, the varieties based on the mutual dependence of portions within a single quarter are shown; when the initial, middle, and final portions within each individual quarter—fixed and possessing a fixed sequence—are restrained, there are one hundred such varieties.

However, when the arrangement of the initial, medial, and final portions within each individual quarter-verse occurs both in a fixed order and in an unfixed order, then hundreds of various types become possible. Since these subdivisions of *yamaka* (rhyme) have become like throat-tumors to the beauty of poetry (*kāvyalakṣmī*), they do not merit detailed elaboration; therefore, only a mere indication is provided here as an illustration.
For that person whose mind is composed who would serve this crest-jewel of the mountain, what state would that person of composed mind not attain? (2250)

That person, that human being, who—possessing a concentrated mind and a focused heart—should serve the jewel upon the crest of the serpent-mountain (Śeṣa), for that person [Viṣṇu], renowned as "the bestower of all fruits," will grant everything. The term *māhitamanāḥ* means one whose mind is beneficial (*hita*) and dear (*priya*) to *Māyā*, that is, to Śrī; by this, both the presence of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) and single-minded devotion in practicing what is pleasing to Him are expressed. What fruit would the Lord not bestow? The sense is: "What is unattainable when the Lord, the abode of Śrī, is pleased? as it has been said.
O Sage, just as a man, having ascended a mountain of jewels, takes from it gems according to his capacity,
so too does one obtain desires from Kṛṣṇa in accordance with their merit.
Such passages as these should also be considered here.
Just as this entire flood of my sins has been destroyed by you, O Hari, who are like a dark cloud upon the mountain of serpents, so too shall it be destroyed by you, O Lord.

The word division is "nāśam itaḥ abhavat amunā" in the first quarter, and "na aśamitaḥ bhavadamunāḥ" in the third quarter. O Hari! The word "idam" (this) contains the intention of [Your] power to remove the misfortunes of those who have taken refuge in You. By "amunā" (by this one)—that is, by You, who are the intended object for the offering of the self—the instrumental case is used in the sense of cause. "Mama akhiladuritaughānām" means of all the multitudes of my past sins; this is also an elliptical expression including future sins committed through negligence.

"Nāśam" means destruction; this is also an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for non-attachment. "Itaḥ prāptaḥ" [is derived from] the root *iṇ* with the suffix *kta* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). The past tense designation (*bhūta-nirdeśa*) is employed with the intention of treating the subsequent non-attachment as already established. "Bhavat" refers to *saṃsāra* itself; "damunāḥ" means fire (*agni*), as in Amara's lexicon: "The seven-rayed one is *damunāḥ*. The word "bhavat" is also to be supplied here [to complete the compound]. "Aśamitaḥ" means that which will not cease; it will not be extinguished (*anirvāpita*). This is derived from the root *bhū* with the future suffix *luṭ*.

The epithet "phaṇiśailanīlajalada" (like a dark cloud over the serpent-mountain) intends to convey the capacity to extinguish the fire of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). The underlying meaning is that once my past and future sins have been destroyed and I am embraced by you, the torment of *saṃsāra* shall never again arise.

O Acyuta, for those who have taken refuge at Your feet, there will surely be respect and reverence; yet for others, there will surely be disrespect and lack of regard. Who indeed could have any doubt about this? 2252.

O Acyuta! That person who possesses no regard (*ādṛti*)—that is, no respect or honor—for the service and hospitality of those devotees who have taken refuge at your feet, shall indeed become one whose regard is for what is improper; that is, he shall become one whose regard is fixed upon unwholesome and censurable actions. Alternatively, the third quarter of the verse may be read as a single compound word: *bhavitā-asatkṛtyādṛtiḥ*.

He is one who lacks respect for the duty—that is, the conduct—of the virtuous knowers of Brahman who exist within the state of transmigratory existence; thus he is "one who disregards duty" (*asatkṛtyādṛti*). Alternatively, he is one who has no regard for an improper or unworthy ritual act or deity.

According to Amara, *kṛtyā* refers to both a ritual act and a deity. Thus, he will become one who possesses such disregard (*ādṛti*). The sense is that such is the fate of those who are averse to the worship of the Lord (*bhāgavata*). Alternatively, *asatkṛttyāḥ* means a hide (*kṛtti*)—such as that of a dog—which is "unworthy" (*asatī*) of touch and so forth (Amara: *ajinaṃ carma kṛttiḥ strī*). He will become a leather bag (*dṛti*) for that [hide]. The sense is that a man devoid of respect for the service of the Lord is merely like a leather pouch and not truly conscious. In these three verses, there is a recurrence of the first quarter in the third quarter.
Just as the protection of the world is performed by the Lord on Vṛṣācala, surely even a bull, with a mere fraction of his power, would be able to accomplish this.

"Is he not our Lord?"—the analysis of the verse is as follows: "Is he not our Lord (īśā), and is he not also the Bull (vṛṣā) even by a fraction (leśena)? [The word *īśā*] is the third case singular ending in *-ā*, meaning "Lord," as in the Vedic passage "Īśā vāsyam idaṃ sarvam" ("By the Lord all this is to be pervaded"). The meaning is "O Master. As for the protection of the world (*bhuvanāvanam*)—that is, the preservation of the universe—which is being performed, is Śarva (Śiva) capable (*īśānaḥ*) of accomplishing this protection of the world? And is Vāsava (Indra) also [capable], even by a fraction (*vṛṣā ca nu*)? According to Amara, "nu" is used in the sense of inquiry or option.

Indeed, not even in the slightest degree could anyone else prevail [over him], for the word *nanu* is used here as an emphatic particle—Amara states: “*Nanu* is used in questions, emphasis, permission, conciliation, and address.
O one of great wisdom, no one other than Hari, the Lord of All, who is established in the maintenance [of the world], possesses the capacity for protection.

Thus, the capacity for protection has been stated; the sense is that the scriptural passages—“He is neither existent nor non-existent, but Śiva alone” and “Indra, through his powers of illusion, appears in many forms”—which serve as the basis for the doubt regarding causality, cannot apply to both Śiva and Indra (Śatamakha).

Just as a man who is desirous of prosperity becomes one who lacks the welfare of being free from Dāmodara; so too a man who is not desirous of prosperity becomes one who always possesses the welfare of being free from joy (āmoda).

A man who is *bhūṣṇu* (desirous of prosperity) and *vardhiṣṇu* (desirous of growth) becomes more excellent (*śreyān*)—that is, more praiseworthy—by means of being "devoted to Dāmodara" (*dāmodarahita*). The word *dāmodarahita* is formed with the fourth case according to the rule *hitayoge ca*; the compound is formed by the rule *caturthī tadartha* and so forth. His state is *dāmodarahitatā*, and by that he becomes more excellent. Furthermore, a man who is *abhūṣṇu* (not desirous of prosperity), if he is devoid of *sadāmoda*—meaning *sat* (good) and *āmoda* (joy), thus "excellent joy"—then by reason of that lack, or separation, he becomes *aśreyān*, one for whom excellence (*śreyaḥ*) does not exist. Note that the suffix *kap* is not applied here because of the rule *īyasaśca* regarding the *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Just as one who would address you, O Acyuta, even with the mere word "Antaryāmin," attains that very glory, he does not enter [into the state of being merely] the mere word "Antaryāmin. (2255)

O Acyuta! The sense is that even one who would utter the mere word "Antaryāmin" (the Inner Ruler) with reference to You—let him not understand its actual meaning—he attains that prosperity (*śrī*) and wealth. That prosperity is such that neither the mere sound of the word "fear" (*īti*) nor the mere sound of the word "disturbance" (*viplava*) should enter within it, much less its actual meaning. The underlying idea is that even one who employs the mere word "Antaryāmin" with respect to You attains a state of fearlessness, whether it be worldly or hereafter.

According to Amarasimha, "īti" refers to both "ḍimba" and "pravāsa. "Ḍimba" means "viplava" (disturbance or calamity), as that same author has taught: "ḍimba, ḍamara, and viplava [are synonyms]. "Īti" is defined by that same authority in the same way.
Just as one who is skilled in increasing [the wealth] of the Lord of Śrī (Viṣṇu), whose abode is the mountain of serpents and whose growth is limitless,
becomes a lord of the earth who is unskilled in increasing his own store of fortune (or, a king who is devoid of the treasure of prosperity). || 2256 ||

The word division is as follows: *śrīśe avadhirahitavardhane nipuṇaḥ śrīśevadhiḥ ahitavardhane 'nipuṇaḥ*. This refers to that Person whose nature is such that its expansion (*vardhana*) is "unlimited" (*avadhirahita*), meaning infinite; that is to say, the Supreme Brahman, which is unsurpassedly vast in both its essential form and its qualities. Alternatively, the sense is that it is so called because of its expansion during the Trivikrama incarnation, wherein it grew without restriction. It is "skilled" (*nipuṇaḥ*) in that [expansion], and is the "treasure-store of prosperity" (*śrīśevadhiḥ*). Furthermore, it is "not skilled" (*'nipuṇaḥ*) in the increase of those who are "unfriendly" (*ahita*), namely enemies. Thus, he is the Lord of Śrī, who is expert in the boundless growth of his own nature and the storehouse of all auspiciousness, yet incapable of increasing the prosperity of his adversaries.

"Increasing without limit," or "in one who is increasing. According to the *Medinī*, "vardhana" means increase, while "vardhiṣṇu" means one who increases; and according to the *Amara-kośa*, "vardhiṣṇu" is synonymous with "vardhana. "Skilled in [worship] at the abode of the serpent-mountain, Śrīśa, Śrīnivāsa"—the meaning is that he is solely intent upon His worship, just as in expressions such as "skilled toward his mother.
