The locative case is used in connection with the word "nipuṇa" when "worship" (*arcā*) is implied, according to the rule: "The locative is used after 'sādhu' and 'nipuṇa' when worship is meant, provided 'apratēḥ' [is not present]."

That man becomes a lord of the earth—a king—who is a treasure-trove (*śevadhi*) of prosperity and wealth (according to Amara: *nidhirnā śevadhiḥ*), and who is skillful and adept in the matter of increasing or cutting down his enemies. Here, in the four verses beginning with "That which is performed for the protection of the world," there is a repetition of the second quarter in the fourth quarter. Furthermore, when there is a repetition of the first quarter in the third quarter, it is the *yamaka* known as *saṃdaṃśa*.

Rudraṭa states that when the second [verse] occurs for the fourth time in the rotation, it is the *yamaka* named *saṃdaṣṭaka*. Accordingly, his definition is as follows: "By the alternating repetition of other [verses] together with the first quarter-verse, the *yamakas* known as *mukha*, *saṃdaṃśa*, and *āvṛtti* arise in succession."

The meaning is as follows: when there is a repetition of the second foot by means of the first foot, it is the *yamaka* named "mouth" (*mukha*). When there is a repetition of the third foot by means of that [second], it is the *yamaka* named "tongs" (*saṃdaṃśa*). When there is a repetition of the fourth foot by means of that [third], it is the *yamaka* named "repetition" (*āvṛtti*). This is the sense.
Furthermore, through the repetition of each of the latter two feet by means of the second, the *yamakas* known as "womb" (*garbha*) and "biting" (*saṃdaṣṭaka*) are produced. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that when there is a repetition of the second [pāda] within the third and fourth pādas at the end, these two types of *yamaka* are named "womb-biting" (*garbhasaṃdaṣṭaka*). We did not provide examples here for the repetition of the second and fourth pādas by means of the first and third pādas, because such a structure is not possible among the *āryāvṛtta* meters, out of fear of violating our own formal proposition.
Now, a mere indication of the varieties of *yamaka* occurring at the quarters of the verse is illustrated:

"O you who wear a garland of forest flowers (*vanamālī*), go to that mountain where the one who wears a garland of *nīpa* trees (*nīpāvanamālī*) dwells among yogis; for he who stands here as the wearer of the forest-garland (*vanamālī*)—him, who has not licked the lip of the Daughter of the Ocean (*avanamālīḍhābdhijādharam*), I approach. (2257)

On that mountain Śeṣācala, there is a *nīpāvana*—a grove (*avana*) that protects (*rakṣaka*) *nīpas*, *kadambas*, *bandhūkas*, and *nīlāśokas*; or a grove of *kadamba-bandhūka-nīlāśokas*; or a grove of all these various species of trees. We have stated more than once that "in masculine compounds, having multiple meanings is not a fault. According to the *Viśva-kośa*: "The word *nīpa* refers to the *kadamba*, the *bandhūka*, and also the *nīlāśoka* tree. The term *vana* means a forest (*vipina*), and it *ālīyata*, meaning it embraced or was situated [there].
The construction is: "the line (*ālī*) or row (*paṅkti*) of *yogins* and *munis* also *ālīyata*. Here, on this mountain, is the one who wears a garland of forests (*vanamālī*).
The wise know the garland hanging down to the feet as the *vanamālā*;
that five-colored garland of the wielder of the mace is indeed the *vaijayantī*.

Adorned with the garland named Vaijayantī, whose characteristics have been described in such passages as these, there dwells that Supreme Person. I go for refuge, O friend, to that Śrīnivāsa—He who is *avana*, the protector of all without qualification; He who has tasted the lip of the Daughter of the Ocean (Lakṣmī) while in the *ālīḍha* posture; and He who has tasted the lip of Ramā. Alternatively, the construction may be "O friend, I go for refuge to that *avana*," meaning "I choose Him as my protector. Herein lies a specific feature: the four-syllable segment *vanamālī* from the first quarter-verse is repeated within the segments of the second and third quarters, and there is also a repetition of five syllables between the first and third quarters.

This host of misfortunes, which was exceedingly dear to me and never departed from me, has been seized by you and brought to the state of destruction while you were bearing that sense of "mine-ness. || 2258 ||

"O Acyuta! 'Tāvat' means in its entirety. The sense is: 'They have been utterly disregarded, not accepted, and transcended by me who has taken refuge in you. 'Duritāli' means the entire multitude of sins. 'Mamatām' means affection, the thought 'this is mine. By You, who carry [this affection] and who remove the fever of saṃsāra, [I] have been carried away; this implies Your capacity for forgiving my transgressions. 'Bhavatā kṣamāpadam' means I have been brought to, or made the object of, Your forgiveness."

By this arrangement, the meaning expressed in the verse—“destroying [the karma] not accepted [by us], and the fragment of that which has already begun”—is thus summarized. Here, the three-syllable sequence *mama te* at the beginning of the first quarter is repeated only in the initial portions of the second and third quarters, but not in the initial portion of the fourth quarter. Furthermore, another form of *yamaka* (rhyme) should be noted here.

O Moon of the Mahī mountain, you who praise [the Lord], I consider your own conduct here to be blessed, since you lead this man—who is full of devotion, entirely auspicious, and possessed of a beautiful nature—toward Him. 2259.

O Lord of the moon-like mountain Ahiśikhara! I consider the person who praises your life-story to be blessed, for you lead this fortunate man to a state that is entirely auspicious, wholesome, and conducive to well-being—according to Amara, *bhāvuka*, *bhavika*, and *bhavya* all mean "auspicious. Therefore, I deem him blessed; such is the construction of the verse. Here, there is a repetition (*āvṛtti*) of the first part of the first quarter-verse with the beginning of the second, and of the first part of the third quarter-verse with the beginning of the fourth.
O Śauri, those who have not performed acts of reverence anywhere, or whose pillows are not treated with respect, these very ones, filled with breath, shall surely become pillows for the unrighteous.

By those people who, somewhere or other, offered hospitality—that is, respect—with that hospitality; it should be noted that the doubling of the letter *t* (in *satkṛtyā*) is according to the rule *anaci ca*, for the sake of not violating the requirements of the *yamaka* (rhyme). *Prasevikāḥ* means excellent services; the suffix *ṇvul* is applied to the root *sev* according to the rule *dhātvarthanirdeśe ṇvul vaktavyaḥ*, and the meaning of the root is "serving."

These people are not truly alive; though they possess breath and breathe, they are devoid of virtue and are wicked, unworthy even of touch. They are surely nothing more than leather bellows (*bhastrikā*) for skins such as those of dogs and donkeys—*kṛtti* meaning the hide of a dog, donkey, or similar animal, and *prasevikā* meaning a bellows. As Amara states: "A *bhastrā* is a leather bellows. Devoid of service to the Blessed One, they are merely bellows that produce nothing but breath. Here, the meaning of the *Bhāgavata* verse beginning with "Do not trees live? And do not bellows breathe? should be reflected upon.
In this passage, there is a repetition of the first parts of the second and fourth quarters.
O jewel of the Yadu dynasty, that man who would not have great devotion for the nectar of your stories would surely lack such devotion even after conducting a thorough investigation. (2261)

O jewel of the Yadu dynasty! That man who possesses great *ādṛti*—meaning one for whom there is great respect (*mahatī ādṛtiḥ*) for the nectar of your stories—if he were not [to exist], that is, if such a man did not exist upon thorough investigation, then the word "naḥ" should be split as "na syāt" (he would not be). He, that man, would be "naḥ syāt"—that is, he would be merely a "mahādṛti," a large leather bag; he would be equal to it. From our perspective, he would be nothing more than a mere leather pouch and not a conscious being; this is the intended meaning.

Here, there is a repetition of the final portions of the second and fourth quarters; for the *Medinī* lexicon states, "The word *dṛti* means a leather bag or a fish," and there is also the usage: "Water [flows] from a leather bag as if from the feet."

O Lord of the mountain that supports the serpents, you are the Lord of the worlds, yet you are not merely the Lord of Bhavānī; even Brahmā is the Lord of Bhavānī, but as for me, I am your servant, O Lord of Bhavānī.

O Lord of the mountain of hooded serpents! You alone are the Lord and Master of the worlds. [The term] *bhavānīśa* means that Rudra is not the Lord (*īśa*) for us; nor is Brahmā the Lord. Why is this? To this he says: *bhavānīśa*. This means one who is not the master (*anīśa*)—that is, not independent—of *bhava*, which is worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), being helplessly subject to the bonds of transmigration. As the Śruti states: "Bewildered, he grieves through lack of mastery" (*anīśayā śocati muhyamānaḥ*). Therefore, because Rudra and the others are dependent upon worldly existence, the sense is: "I am desirous of liberation from the bonds of *bhava*."

*Īśaḥ*: This word ending in the genitive case (*īśasya*) is derived from the root *īṣ* (to rule). Its meaning is "of the Lord of all," by virtue of being free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), as supported by such scriptural passages as: "When he beholds the other, the Lord who is worshipped... and "The two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Non-Lord. The sense is: "Of you, who—according to the teaching 'I am the deliverer of them from the ocean of death and worldly existence'—are lifting up those who bow before you from the ocean of rebirth. *Kiṅkaraḥ*: "May I become a servant. This is the first person singular imperative (*loṭ*).

The sense is this: following the maxim, "I am myself bound; how indeed could I be the liberator of another?", I—being myself bewildered by the bondage of worldly existence—shall disregard inference, scripture, and other means, and instead accept servitude unto You alone, who possess the most wonderful power to utterly shake off the bonds of all the fetters of transmigratory existence. In this regard, authorities such as the verse beginning with "From Brahma down to a blade of grass" (*ā brahmastambaparyantā*) should also be considered. Here, the final four syllables of the first quarter, *bhavānīśa*, are repeated at the end of each of the second through fourth quarters.

Just as one who, through his own inherent nature alone, intensely worships the infinite Lord of Vaṣācala during the state of dissolution— He who is the infinite Peace (Śama)— alas, he does not perceive [the world], yet he attains that infinite Peace. 2263.

In the state of dissolution (*pralaya*), together with *svadhā*, that is, with Lakṣmī. The word *eva* (indeed) is displaced and connects with what follows. According to the Purāṇic statement, "O *svadhā*, you are the creator of the worlds," the word *svadhā* denotes Lakṣmī. Furthermore, in the Mahābhārata, in the dialogue between Śrī and Vāsava, it is stated by Śrī herself: "I am indeed *svāhā* and *svadhā*. [He is] breathing intensely and infinitely—"That One breathed, windless, by means of *svadhā*"—according to the Śruti. And in the Mahābhārata:
"Having placed within myself all beings, both moving and unmoving..."
O best of the twice-born, I shall dwell alone together with knowledge.

Thus, the word *vidyā* refers to Lakṣmī, as stated in such passages as, "O Goddess, you are the knowledge of the Self (*ātmavidyā*). Alternatively, according to the principle expressed in, "By her he [Viṣṇu] and that righteous-souled one lived even for a moment," the phrase "by *svadhā* it breathed" intends to convey dependence through love. Or else, based on the etymology "that which is placed (*dhīyate*) in itself (*sva-*)"—the word *svadhā* refers to its own existence. Or, *svadhā* is simply the capacity to sustain the universe belonging to itself.

And likewise, in the section on "The Best" (*Śreṣṭha-ādhikaraṇa*), the Commentary states: "But the phrase *ānīd avātam* does not refer to the breathing of the individual soul (*jīva*) as the best; rather, it declares the existence of the one Supreme Brahman alone. And the Teacher [Śaṅkara] says in the *Catuḥślokī-bhāṣya*: "What is intended here is the state of having an existence that is not dependent on anything else. By this, its status as the cause of the world is stated, because it is heard in the scripture [Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.5], "But the Cause is to be meditated upon," that He alone is the object of worship.

The meaning is that the Supreme Brahman alone—Ananta, who is devoid of the three kinds of limitations, the Lord of Vṛṣācala, residing on the Veṅkaṭādri mountain in the form of an image—is the one whom a person worships. The sense is that he beholds Him as the Lord, who is difficult to perceive due to His extreme majesty and who torments the evildoers; for it is said, "I am the master of other men, but certainly not of the Vaiṣṇavas. He does not look upon Śamana (Yama); for Amarasimha states, "Śamana, Yamarāḍ, and Yama [are synonyms].
Those whose minds have been placed even once here upon the lotus-feet of Kṛṣṇa, being enamored of His qualities—
Having performed atonement for their misdeeds, they do not see Yama or his noose-bearing minions even in their dreams.

The intended meaning is based on such statements from the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata* and other sources. Nevertheless, there is an apparent contradiction in the phrase "he finds (vindate) that Śamana (Yama)," for Śamana is Yama, the god of death. The resolution, however, comes through the word-splitting (*cheda*): *śam-anaṃ*, meaning "the infinite" (*anantam*). The sense is that it is the infinite, undivided, auspicious (*śam*) bliss—the bliss of experiencing the Supreme Brahman—precisely because that [Brahman] alone is infinite. Thus, he "finds" (attains) it. Here too, the final portion of the first quarter-verse is repeated in the subsequent quarters.

Just as that stream of the nectar of your fame consumes the sin of men through austerity, it likewise drinks [the thirst] of those men; furthermore, O Acyuta, it accomplishes devotion toward you, and you in turn accomplish that devotion.

O Acyuta! That multitude of men who, by means of austerity such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts, *adhayati*—that is, consumes, subdues, or overcomes—*agham*, meaning sin (*pāpam*); [the form *adhas* is derived from the neuter indeclinable *adhas* with the suffix *ṇa* in the sense of the superlative, resulting in the elision of the *ṭi* vowel]; that multitude of men drinks (*dhayati*) the nectar of your feet (*tvatpādatīrthasudhām*). [The root *dheṭ* means "to drink," used here in the present tense (*laṭ*) in the active voice (*kartari*). He states the fruit of this: *atha*—then, they accomplish (*sādhayati*), that is, bring to completion, devotion (*bhaktim*) toward you.

And you, being thus worshipped, also "sādhayati" that multitude of men; the meaning is that you make them firm (*bāḍham*) and make them virtuous (*sādhum*). From the word *bāḍha*, when the suffix *ṇic* is applied and the status of *iṣṭhavad-bhāva* occurs, there is the substitution of *sādha* according to the rule "antikabāḍhayornedasādhau. In the second case, from the word *sādhu*, when the suffix *ṇic* is applied and the status of *iṣṭhavad-bhāva* occurs, there is the elision of the *ṭi* (the *u*); such is the difference.

O Giver of Boons, O Hara, just as the elephant removes its own burden, so do Your feet remove my great sins; yet that [removal] is rendered futile, O Śrīpati, because those two feet of Yours were not meditated upon by me for even a single day.

O Hari! Here, one should remember the saying: “Hari removes sins. He who drives away (*nudati*) or casts off (*kṣipati*) evil (*agham*), suffering, or calamity is *aghanud*; this is the vocative case of that term. Your two feet (*caraṇau*) remove my sin (*duritam*). On whatever day (*yadah*), where the accusative case is used to denote continuous duration, if those two aforementioned feet of yours are not meditated upon within the small lotus of the heart (*dahare hṛdayapuṇḍarīke*), that day is in vain, devoid of purpose. In this regard, the meaning of the statement, “even for a moment or an instant (*yanmuhūrtaṃ kṣaṇaṃ vāpi*”), should be remembered.
O Bhavānī, if you do not bestow knowledge upon a living being, then that knowledge does not arise for him; his karmas do not cease, and he is unable to strive to meditate upon you, O delight of Ramā.

"Vinoda" means that which dispels [distress]. "Ramāvinoda" is the dispeller of Ramā; this is its vocative form. Alternatively, it means "for the sake of the dispelling of Ramā," based on the identity of cause and effect. The meaning is: "O Śrīnivāsa! If you, sir, do not show *dayā* (compassion) toward a living being (*jantu*), then—using the root *day* in the present tense (*laṭ*) with the genitive case to express the remaining relation of the object according to the rule *adhīgarthadaya*—the sense is that for this living being, knowledge would not be conducive to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). [Otherwise,] it does not arise; [it is] from the root *ay* in the present tense (*laṭ*).

The phrase "he, your honor" (*sa bhavān*) is connected with "of this" (*asya*). [The meaning is: he does not impel—that is, he does not cause to cease—the actions of this living being (*jantu*), which are of the nature of sin. This is derived from the root *nud* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the present tense (*laṭ*). Alternatively, the word "this" (*ayam*) is to be supplied; the construction would then be: "this living being does not impel his own actions. The underlying sense is that as long as sinful action has not been exhausted, knowledge does not arise. For the Smṛti states: "Knowledge arises for men through the destruction of sinful action."

Therefore, for that reason stated above, I strive—that is, I make an effort—to meditate upon you; this is the first person singular present indicative form of the root *yat*. Since your grace is the primary cause for the arising of knowledge preceded by the destruction of sins, the essential meaning is: "I am making an effort to worship you in order to bring that about."
May that Brahman, who is free from fear, who has made his abode within the lotus of the heart, and who is the beloved of the women of Vraja, now adorn my heart without delay.

That whose navel-lotus is so described—meaning that by which Brahmā, the creator, was fashioned—is [the Lord]. Within the heart, that is, in the interior of the chest, she has made her abode; thus she is "kutani-ketanā. She is "abhīḥ," a *pañcamī-bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "she from whom fear (bhīḥ) is non-existent" (*avidyamānā bhīryasyāḥ sā*). Thus, she is the remover of the fear of those who have taken refuge in her. Alternatively, it may be analyzed as a *ṣaṣṭhī-bahuvrīhi*.

The sense is this: even when those who have committed full offenses and rely upon armies approach, the Goddess of the World—the Lord who wields the rod of punishment—does not fear them; for she makes him realize, "Who in this world is truly innocent? Thus, she is "fearless. That [Lord] in whom resides such a Kamalā (the fearless one) is so described. By these two epithets, his transcendence (*paratva*) is expressed.

May that Supreme Brahman—the one who is *abhīka*, meaning "desirous" (as Amara states: *kamraḥ kāmayitābhīkaḥ*; and as stated in the rule *anukābhikābhīkaḥ kamitari*: the suffix *kan* is applied to the root *abhī* in the sense of "one who desires")—who is ever-desirous of the women of Vraja, the cowherd wives; may He, acting as the agent, adorn—that is, thoroughly purify—my heart, my mind, which is the object. By this, His accessibility (*saulabhya*) is expressed. May that [Brahman] grace my mind.

Now, it is sufficient; it is enough. The meaning is: "When the heart dwells fearlessly and without dread in the Blessed One, the Supreme Brahman, whence can there be even a report of fear for me? This is according to the Śruti: "For when he finds fearless support in that which is invisible, bodiless, inexpressible, and without abode, then he becomes one who has attained fearlessness. Herein lies the distinction: the five consonants accompanied by vowels found at the end of the first quarter are repeated in the final portions of the other quarters.

You always abide in association with Śrī; for that which was formerly ever-present is indeed the Reality (tattva). He who knows you thus—“He abides in the state of being a servant (dāsa) and a benefactor (hita)—he is indeed the Reality. 2268.

O Blessed One! You always abide together with Śrī; thus, the meaning of the word "Śrīmat" is stated as "one who possesses eternal union with Śrī. "That One breathed, windless, by its own inherent power (svadhayā)."

Having stated this, he declares that very [Brahman] to be the cause of the world with the words "yat" (that which). This world, consisting of the conscious and the unconscious, was indeed (*hi*) existing prior to creation. The word-order is "tat tvam" (that thou art); "hi" is used for emphasis. This particle is displaced and connects both with what precedes and what follows. That which is well-known from all the Upaniṣads—namely, "sat," the Existent, denotable by the word "sat," which is Brahman itself—was indeed the Existent; this world had that as its cause and was of that very nature.

*Āsa* is an indeclinable (avyaya) resembling a verbal form (*tiṅanta*) which has the sense of "became" (*babhūva*). Alternatively, it means "shone" (*didīpe*), being the perfect tense (*liṭ*) of the root *as*, which signifies shining. Thus, the construction is either "That Brahman is you alone" or "You alone are that. This recalls the meaning of the causal statement (*kāraṇavākya*): "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sadeva somyedamagra āsīt*). In this way, it is stated that the Lord of Śrī alone is the cause of the universe, and no other.

Such as You are, You attain (ayasi)—the form *ayasi* being derived from the root *idh* (as in *iṭa kiṭa*) in the present tense—the state of being beneficial to those who are Your subordinates (*dāsa*), that is, to those who are subsidiary (*śeṣabhūta*) according to the principle stated as "one's own self is indeed subordinate to the Supreme Self," and You attain the state of being the perfected means (*siddhopāyatva*). The construction is as follows: that person who always knows You thus—as the Lord of Śrī, the cause of the universe, and the perfected means—he alone truly knows the reality (*tattva*), namely the essential nature of both the individual self (*ātman*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

The distinction from previous examples is that there is a repetition of the six syllables—including both vowels and consonants—located at the final portion of the first quarter, within the final portions of the other quarters. In the fourth line, regarding the word *sadā* in the phrase *yaḥ sadā*, one must accept the retention of the visarga (*visarga eva*) according to the rule *vā śari*; it is not to be changed to the letter *sa* by the rule *visarjanīyasya saḥ*, for that would result in a violation of the established structure of the alliteration (*yamaka*) involving uncombined *sa*-sounds.

Cross over to auspiciousness; O son of Gaṅgā, I shall sing of you here, whose form bends the Gaṅgā. May the son of Gaṅgā, whose limbs are graced by Lakṣmī, be purified; let not the son of Gaṅgā go in vain.

Bestow auspicious speech. I shall sing—that is, I shall sing of—you, in whom Bhīṣma, the son of Gaṅgā, is bowed down; "gāyāni" is the first person singular imperative form of the root *gai*. Furthermore, O Brahman, the singing, the chanting, and especially the dancing of Viṣṇu must be performed by those of the Brāhmaṇa caste as a daily duty (*nityakarman*).

This is the meaning according to the statement of Śaunaka. O Lakṣmīsubhagāṅga—O Śrīnivāsa, whose form is auspiciously beautiful—may this cow, which is speech, become purified through the chanting of Your names; such is the intention. For it is said by Śaunaka himself:
"When [devotees] dance before the Lord of Śrī with the clapping of hands and other gestures, the birds of great sins residing within the body are driven away."

Thus [it is said]. Here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "by *saṃsphoṭana* and so forth," singing (*gāna*) is also included, because it was that very subject introduced in the preceding verse. "Singing in vain"—that is, singing devoid of Your praise—let us not even utter.
O best of men! No other singing, such as singing in vernacular dialects (*bhāṣā-gāna*), should be performed by a Brāhmaṇa except for the song of Hari; therefore, sin has been committed by you."

The sense is that this is because singing other than the *Bhagavadgītā* is prohibited. Here, the distinction is that the final three-syllable portion of the first quarter-verse is repeated in the other quarters.

Just as I have declared Your greatness in the Vedānta, so too do I declare my own [greatness] in the Vedānta—within Your own boundless majesty, which outshines even the most difficult-to-conquer existence through compassion for me. 2270.

I know Your greatness through words at the end of [all] speech—the greatness of You who are renowned in the Vedānta—according to the Vedic revelation: "From whence words turn back. To You, the source of the universe, the all-pervading Lord, I have given myself; that is, I have surrendered my own self, or rather, I have offered it as being Yours alone. The meaning is: I have performed the act of self-surrender unto You. In this world where existence (bhava) is difficult to overcome—meaning the cycle of saṃsāra which is hard to dispel by other means except for taking refuge at Your feet—I have sought refuge in Your feet.

"In *saṃsāre* (in the world) is the meaning. In the word *adānte*, the expression *‘aśānto dāntaḥ’* (the undisciplined is disciplined) serves to manifest one's own wretchedness through the absence of self-restraint (*dama*). [The command] "have compassion for me" (*mayi karuṇaya*) is formed by adding the causal suffix *ṇic* to the root *karuṇā* according to the rule *tatkaroti*. In the word *adānte*, the *parasavarṇa* (substitution of the following sound) occurs by the rule *vā padāntasya*. The *yamaka* (rhyme) is as before.

O friend of Kamalā, having set my heart’s delight upon your service, I offer myself as your very slave; my mind clings to you, whose face resembles the moon and who are indifferent to the state of those who do not know how to bow.

This is the speech of the poet who desires to take refuge in the Blessed One. O Friend of Kamalā! This is the meaning of the word *śrīmat*. By this, it is indicated that the object of self-surrender is specifically He who is distinguished by *Śrī*. "Having found delight in Your service (*dāsye*)," that is, in the act of *kaiṅkarya*; by this, the meaning of the word ending in the dative case within the aforementioned section of the mantra of seeking refuge is indicated. The sense is: "I shall offer myself alone to You" (*te*), meaning I shall entrust the burden of protecting my own self to You.

By this, the meaning of "I take refuge" has been stated. Here, he provides the reason with the words "avidita-": "In you, whose indifference toward those who are humble is unknown (or unperceived), my mind therefore clings to you. The epithet *indulasadāsye* ("with a face shining like the moon") serves to manifest the Lord's gracious benevolence. The specific feature here is that the final two-syllable portion of the first quarter is repeated in the final portions of all four quarters.
Or likewise:

He who, having restrained every sense-organ here in this world, does not ever take refuge in Narasakha—the great ornament of the bride of the Vedas—would indeed seek refuge in Bhava, the source of calamities.

That man who, having restrained the entire instrument—the meaning being all the sense organs—in whatever manner is appropriate, and having withdrawn them from their objects, possesses the Veda itself as his bride.

The meaning of "her great ornament" is the crest-jewel. "He attains Narasakha (the friend of men), Nārāyaṇa, as refuge"—that is, as a protector or as a means; the sense is that he chose Him as either his protector or his means. That person shall never resort to *bhava*, meaning *saṃsāra* (worldly existence), which is the refuge or dwelling place of calamities and the birthplace of all misfortunes. The underlying thought is: for one who has entrusted the burden of protection to the Blessed Lord, where could there ever be an entry into the path of worldly transmigration?

It is understood that one who has gone for refuge to the Blessed One, Śarva, shall never resort to Bhava as a refuge—that is, shall never serve him as a protector in times of calamity. Here, there is *yamaka* (rhyme) at the end of both the first and second halves [of the verse].
Now, an example of middle-portion *yamaka*:

"O you whose eyes are like lotuses (*jalajāyatekṣaṇa*), let there be salutation to that Raghu-born one (*raghujāya*) from whom nothing ever arises in vain (*yanmudhā kadācidapi*). May the multitudes of people (*janavrajā*) strive to accomplish this very thing. (2273)

O lotus-eyed one! By this, his extreme benevolence toward those who have sought refuge is revealed. By describing him as born of the Raghu dynasty—being preeminent in the duty of granting protection to those seeking refuge—it is illuminated that he too is consecrated by such a vow. For this very reason, there is the expression: "To Rāghava, the refuge of all the worlds. To you, salutations (*namaḥ*). This self-surrender, expressed in the words "Quickly present me [to him]," is indeed described as: "Having performed a salutation to him, one should offer self-surrender."

"May it be so. To the question "What is gained by that?", he says: "That which is offered as salutation never becomes *mudhā*—that is, it never becomes useless; the sense is that it invariably bears fruit. The idea is that one's own performed self-surrender (*ātmanivedana*) is precisely what should be practiced by all. This is expressed through the words beginning with "janaiḥ" (by people), according to the principle: "May Lord Hari bestow upon all beings without exception the perfection that is free from birth, old age, and the like."

All the multitudes of people, including common folk, critics, and holy men alike—let them all strive (the optative *liṅ* in the sense of a prayer) to perform this very offering of themselves to the Blessed One; let them exert themselves. What is the use of other means whose purposes are subject to deviation?

The sense is this: let them all resort to this one fruit alone, because it possesses supreme authority, because he himself vowed, "I grant fearlessness to all beings; this is my vow," and because it is the preeminent bearer that bestows every desired fruit. Here, the three syllables *jā-y-ate*, located in the middle of the first quarter, are echoed in the middle of the other quarters; thus, this is a *madhyayamaka* (middle rhyme).

Just as a lake on your mountain, O Lord whose essence is the nectar of the earth, shines with its activity endowed with fragrant white lotuses and cranes, possessing cool waters and abounding in rasa, so too does she shine. 2274.

"O beloved of the Earth-goddess Rasā!"—this address is intended to convey that He is her lover, since the Śruti states: "The goddess Mahī, the wife of Viṣṇu, Mādhavī, the beloved of Mādhava. Alternatively, it may mean "O best of mountains," referring to your mountain, Śeṣācala. Regarding "of you": it means on your mountain, Śeṣācala.

The lake—Svāmipuṣkariṇī—shines, its existence (vṛtti) being never devoid of *visāra* fish, *sārasa* birds known as *puṣkara*, *saugandhika* lilies, *kahlāra* white lotuses, and *sārasa* cranes; it is exceedingly cool (*suśītā*), like the essence (*sāra*) or stable portion of camphor (*ghanasāra*), and it is full of flavor (*sarasā*), meaning it abounds with the sweet taste of water.

In this instance, because the pair of syllables "sārasāre," which form a *yamaka* in the middle portion of the first quarter, are repeated in the middle portions of the second and subsequent quarters, it is a specific type of *madhyayamaka*; this is its distinction from the preceding variety.
Or rather:

O Lord, you who are the foremost in battle, come with great speed—your armlets jingling as you move at every step upon hearing the roar of the fray—and become our refuge, O you whose elephants are terrified by the absence of the enemy's clamor.

The word *śaraṇa* means *raṇa*, which signifies sound; that is to say, a cry for protection. As Amara states in his lexicons on miscellaneous meanings: "In the sense of ringing, *raṇa* [is used]," and "In the sense of noise, *raṇa*. Medinī also states: "*Raṇa* is masculine in the sense of a corner or a sound, and both masculine and neuter in the sense of battle. At the very moment of hearing that [cry], he arrived with great speed—such that his bracelets (*kaṭaka*), meaning armlets, were jingling or sounding against his feet; the implication is that he reached the presence of the lordly elephant seized by the crocodile.

O Lord, foremost in battle and leader of the war, become my refuge! You who have caused the agitation of fear—trembling with ever-increasing waves—to cease, you by whom that agitation has been removed; O you by whom the great elephant, though struck down in particular by the attack of crocodiles, has been made to tremble and turn back; O you who have rendered the elephant free from such agitation! (Note: *Raṇaraṇaka* refers to the agitation of fear; *nīraṇaraṇaka* means one from whom that agitation has been removed; *vicakita* means specifically struck or repelled; *vāraṇa* refers to the lordly elephant; the vocative *nīraṇaraṇakitavicakitavāraṇa* thus addresses the one who has caused the great elephant to lose its agitation and turn back.)

The sense is: "Just as for the lordly elephant, may you likewise dispel my state of trembling with fear and grant me protection. Here too, as before, there is a *yamaka* (repetition) of the middle portion of the word "raṇaraṇa" across all four quarters.
This glorious abode of Vāsudeva should be resorted to by all people for the sake of every kind of prosperity; for what prosperity is there that could not be attained from it?

This entire abundance of prosperity, seen as bestowing bliss upon the world, is to be attained and acquired by all people from the Lord Śrīnivāsa himself. Or, the word *avāsādayitum* may be split as *kā vā sā yā avāsādayitum*. Therefore, from that Śrīnivāsa, whatever prosperity there is cannot be *avāsādayituṃ*—meaning to obtain (the causative suffix *ṇic* being used in its own sense)—or rather, it cannot be made to be attained (*āsādayituṃ*) by him, Śrīnivāsa, for the sake of bringing it to those who have taken refuge in him.

The meaning is that such prosperity as this is unparalleled; indeed, no such prosperity exists. Here, in the third quarter, the middle section—characterized by the repetition of two vowels separated by a single consonant—is repeated in the same manner as it appeared in the first quarter. Thus, there is a specific aesthetic distinction (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) from the previously cited example of middle *yamaka* consisting of the repetition of two non-separate syllables.

Thus indeed he triumphs, the wearer of the lord of serpents, who is inherently purifying and the refuge for those who recite prayers; where the giving of gifts, penance, and recitation of prayers by men becomes purifying for the gods.

The meaning of *avana* is going, moving, or attaining; it is derived from the root *ava*, which signifies motion, with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). [Alternatively], he who protects (*pāti*) the gods (*divijān*) is the "protector of the gods" (*divijapa*), the Lord of the Gods, the Blessed One; for him, *avana* means pleasing or gratification. This is derived from the root *ava* in the sense of gratifying, with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*). The rest is clear. Here, the distinction is that while the syllable-cluster *japāvana* occurs in the second quarter of the verse separated by other letters, it is repeated in the fourth quarter in the same manner.
O Lord of Mountains, he whose mind is filled with an abundance of goodness becomes a supreme being; indeed, by your glance, that mountain-born one has become a most excellent being. 2278.

O Lord of the Mountain-Kings! That person whose mind becomes "possessed of exceedingly abundant darkness"—the sense being that it becomes excessively dark even before the expansion of Your side-long glance—such a man, by Your very sight, [becomes one who realizes] "that which is *sattva* is the Lord Hari."

The sense is: "by your glance," referring to you who are said to consist of *sattva*. "Bahulam" means that in which there is abundance of existence (*sattā*), goodness (*sādhutā*), or excellence (*praśastatā*); it is so described accordingly. Alternatively, "bahvī lasattā" refers to the state of shining (*lasattā*), namely union with the Blessed One; in that state, the word "bhūbhṛt" is to be split [as follows]: being a "bearer of the earth" (*bhūbhṛt*)—that is, a king—he "acts with vigor" (*ojāyate*). The particle "hi" is used for emphasis. He shines forth through the manifestation of the quality of *sattva*.

"In that context, *sattva* is illuminating and free from affliction because of its purity"—thus the illuminating nature of the *sattva* quality is indeed proclaimed. Here, the middle portion of the first half-verse is repeated in the middle portion of the second half-verse. Furthermore, this specific feature is that it is a variety of the *vipulā* sub-type of the *āryā* meter.
That meter in which a quarter-verse consists of two halves, each having three initial *gaṇas* [of three syllables] followed by a long syllable (*guru*),
is called *vipulā* by the serpent Piṅgala.
Thus, from the definition.
I shall not bow to that mistress of the Lord of Mahīśaila, whose majesty cannot be measured; for she is easily bowed down to by everyone, yet for me, there will be no fear of Yama beyond this life.

The meaning is that her *vaibhava*—her majesty—is not capable of being measured (*meya*), as she cannot be grasped by the mind; according to the verse, "Even your beloved Lord is not able to measure the extent of your majesty, which is like his own self," it is unbounded even for the Blessed One. I shall bow to—that is, I shall go for refuge to—that Queen of the Lord of Serpents and Mountains. To the question, "How can you, being so ignorant, bow to her? he replies: "For" (*hi*)—"this [ignorance] is one whose restraint is unknown"; such is the sense.

The meaning is that [the Goddess] is easily accessible (*sunamā*)—that is, capable of being approached with ease—by every living being, whether ignorant or omniscient; the sense is that she is the refuge of all, regardless of the distinction between the vulgar and the discerning or out of any parsimony. Thus, the construction is: "Therefore, I shall go for refuge. Furthermore, after taking refuge in her from this point forward, there will be no fear of Yama for me; the sense is based on such statements as, "I am the Lord of others who have not sought refuge in Madhusūdana, but certainly not of the Vaiṣṇavas," for she is inseparable from the Blessed One.

In this instance, there is the variety [of *āvṛtti*] consisting in the repetition of the name of the poet, "nameyam," with identical form in both the final and initial portions of each of the four quarters.
Just as in the world,

one who bears the same name as another may be honored by that other through a pure lunar orb, so may the Lord of the Immortals, who possesses a name identical to his own, favor me with that very name.

The meaning is that she is one whose name is honored as equal to what is esteemed in the world; or, she is one whose name is incomparable (asamāna), or one whose name is equal to the orb of the moon (sudhāṃśubimba).

The word *samānanā* is derived from the root *nī* (to lead) with the prefix *sam-ā-* and the suffix *lyuṅ* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), meaning "she who leads and sustains the entire world equally. According to Amara, *samam sarvam* means "all things equally. May that *Mā*—the Goddess Śrī—*juṣatām*, may she attend upon me. By the two words *mā* and *juṣatām*, the Vedic mantra *śrīrmā devī juṣatām* ("May the Goddess Śrī attend upon me") is recognized. She is the one whom *amarādhināthaḥ* (the Lord of the Immortals), Indra, *samānanāma*, properly bowed down to—that is, sought refuge in. Here too, as before, there is a *yamaka* (rhyme/paronomasia);
the distinction from the previous example is that there is a repetition of five syllables.
I would not flee in fear from this one, nor would I flee from Yama upon seeing him, were it not for the Lord who is the son of Vinatā (Garuḍa), who grants me freedom from fear.

"Having perceived Yama, the son of Kadrū, as a venomous serpent in the form of Yama—this being a *vyastarūpaka* (a distributed metaphor)—one should not flee from this terrifying one; rather, one must indeed flee [to him]. That Lord who grants fearlessness to those who have sought refuge is Vainateya; that Lord, accompanied by Vainateya, is the Blessed One (*bhagavān*). The construction is: 'If it were not so—that is, if he were not the Lord together with Vainateya—then I would not flee,' which implies 'I shall certainly flee. Here, the final portion of the first quarter-verse, consisting of five syllables, is repeated at the beginning of the second quarter-verse."

Likewise, in the second half as well, there is a repetition of five syllables in a different order; this is the distinction from the previous [half]. The same applies further on. In the phrase *savainateyaḥ*, the retention of the *visarjanīya* (the visarga) for the *visarjanīya*—by the rule *vā śari*—must be accepted in order to avoid the dissimilarity (*avairūpya*) of the *yamaka*.
Just as you lead one to the realm of Yama, that living being indeed partakes of the realm of Yama; but whomsoever you cause to go to the supreme state,
he shall be freed from the calamities of saṃsāra.

That living being whom you lead to *asālokya*—where *sālokya* is the state of being with the world, and *asālokya* is the absence of that, meaning the absence of light, which is to say, the state of not being an object of Your glance—that being shall attain *yamasālokya*, the state of being in the same world as Yama. But he whom You cause to go to the supreme, divine abode (*paramapada*) shall become *apada*—meaning a place that is no longer a place, or rather, beyond the scope [of worldly existence]—so that he shall never again experience the afflictions of *saṃsṛti*, the calamities of saṃsāra.

O Mother, just as you indeed protect those who bow down to Śauri out of great humility—even from great humility—so too do you protect those who are dear to Him; are you not His beloved? Or rather, what is the wonder in this? (2283)

"O Mother! Is it not so? By *bahulāghavataḥ*—that is, by extreme lightness; the suffix *tasi* is used here in all its case-senses (*sārvavibhaktikas-tasi*). The sense is: 'by excessive fickleness of mind. Even those who possess *bahulāghava*—meaning those for whom there is much (*bahu*) sin (*agha*) or evil—are protected by you, the beloved of Śauri, when they are bowed down in surrender (*natān* = *śaraṇāgatān*). Alas! The protection even of the sinful is truly wonderful; this is the intended meaning. She herself provides the resolution with the word "Or rather" (*athavā*).

"Are you a Rakshasi, or perhaps Kākāsura, or even Rāvaṇa? [She replies: "I am *dayitā*. [The word *dayitā* is derived from the root *day* (to pity) with the suffix *kta* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), or alternatively, it means "one toward whom compassion has arisen," formed with the suffix *itac* according to the rule for words beginning with *tārakā*. This is clear from both the *Pādma Purāṇa* and the *Rāmāyaṇa*. Therefore, the intended meaning is: "What wonder is there in protecting those who are humble, even if they are sinners? This is a *yamaka* (rhyme) just as before; the only difference is the repetition of six syllables.
May that Divine One be victorious, who constantly and entirely possesses all divine powers— ever more exalted, ever more vast, and profoundly unfailing— and who likewise bestows prosperity.

Divine, bringing great wonder, exceedingly—meaning utterly—unassailable (ahatīḥ), that is, unimpeded; very easy to cross (sutarāḥ), most auspicious, vast, or venerable; and intensely non-false, that is, not superimposed—bearing all these powers in their entirety. O King, that other great form of Hari, which is both the form of the universe and yet different from it, is that wherein all these powers are established.

This is what should be understood here. Likewise, [the phrase] "bestowing prosperity" (*śriyam*)—meaning all forms of abundance culminating in the sovereignty of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa-aiśvarya*)—is to be supplied with the words "upon those who have taken refuge. May the Divine (*daivam*), that is, the Supreme Brahman, be victorious. Here too, as before, there is a *yamaka* (rhyme). The distinction, however, is that there is a repetition of six syllables in the first half-verse and five syllables in the second half-verse. Furthermore, a specific artistic effect (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) should be observed in the second half-verse, wherein the consonants of the *tavarga* group are repeated in their respective order.

O heart, enter that Śrīvatsa which captivates the heart, which possesses all-enchanting sweetness; O heart, know that Supreme Lord who is beyond all objects of desire and who is the ultimate Remainder.

In Him who possesses the Śrīvatsa—a specific mark named after that—captivating the heart and enchanting the mind; in Him upon whose chest (vatse) dwells Śrī, and who possesses a sweetness and love dear to all hearts (*sarvahṛdya-mādhurya-prema*); [as Amara states: *svādu-priyau tu madhurau*]; in Him who is the leader (*dhurye*) of Māyā—that is, the Beloved of Śrī—O Heart! enter (*viśa*), having gone beyond doubt (*gataviśayam*), meaning with great confidence.

The locative case is used here with the intention of expressing the predominance (*adhikaraṇatva*) of the action. The construction is: "In Him—whom you know as Śrīvallabha, the Sovereign (*śeṣin*), the unconditional Sovereign of all—you enter.

Here, there is a specific variety of poetic artistry (*vaicitrya*) compared to previous examples: the three syllables (along with their vowels and consonants) situated at the end of the first quarter recur at the beginning of the second quarter; likewise, those at the end of the second quarter recur at the beginning of the third; those at its end recur at the beginning of the fourth; and finally, those situated at the end of the fourth quarter—the word *hṛdaya*—recur at the very beginning of the first quarter. Thus, there is a repetition (*āvṛtti*) of the final portion of each quarter at the start of the next.

O Lord who reclines upon the serpent Śeṣa, you who are praised by those dwelling in the sky (the gods), you sport with Mandāra flowers on Mount Kailāsa— which is frequented by Śiva and abounds in Mandāras— just as you sport with the perfected ones on the mountain of the perfected ones (Meru).

O Lord who bestows prosperity upon those who bow and prostrate! O You who lie upon the serpent-king Śeṣa, O wielder of the discus and conch! On the mountain of the Serpent (Śrīparvata), which is enriched with Mandāra and Pāribhadra trees, which is worthy of being served by Śiva and frequented by Hari, You sport together with Your consorts while being praised by the gods dwelling there. In the phrase "samandāraiḥ," the substitution of the following sound (parasavarṇa) occurs according to the rule *vā padāntasya*. Here too, as in the previous verse, the *antyādiyamaka* (rhyme at the end and beginning of the line) should be observed.
Daṇḍin, however, calls this "interlocking *yamaka*," as stated in the *Kāvyādarśa*: "The position for interlocking *yamaka* is at the end of one [foot] and the beginning of two."

The people of this world, whose strength lies in the essence of the Ālīḍha posture and who strive for the essence of the Nabhāratara [the Unsurpassed], having abandoned the essence of the mass of darkness, would not be distressed by existence through the essence of the Bhārata [the Great Epic]. || 2287 ||

O Blessed One! [The phrase] *ālīḍhabhāratarasā* means that the *bhāratī*—the speech pertaining to the land of Bhārata—has resorted to [Thee], or rather, that the earth (*rasā*) has been produced by the land of Bhārata; the meaning is that it was generated within the land of Bhārata. This expression is used because, as stated in the *Bhāgavata* and other texts, all human goals (*puruṣārtha*) are easily accessible to those born in the land of Bhārata. *Bhavajjanatā* refers to the multitude of people belonging to Thee. Alternatively, the construction may be joined as: "the multitude of Thy people (*bhavajjanatā*) has resorted to the essence of the land of Bhārata (*ālīḍhabhāratarasa*)."

She by whom the essence of the *Bhārata*—the glorious *Mahābhārata*, its most delicious and quintessential meaning, namely the taking of refuge as the core significance of the final verse—has been tasted (*ālīḍha*) and savored (*āsvādita*). Therefore, she is "one for whom there is no means [other than] the essence of the *Bhārata*" (*nabhāratarasādhanā*). That is to say, she possesses no means other than that which consists of devotion—the exceedingly weighty means (*sādhana*) for accomplishing the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*). The negative particle *na-* is used here in a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

The meaning is that, having obtained the minor means characterized by taking refuge, she disregarded the more weighty means consisting of devotion; this results in the sense that she was intent solely on independent *prapatti*. For this very reason, she was both free from pride and possessed of an assembly.

The term *vitamassabhā* refers to that non-material, divine abode established by such scriptural passages as, "I enter the assembly hall and the dwelling of Prajāpati, which is of solar hue and beyond darkness" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 8.4.1). According to the *Medinīkośa*, "assembly" (*sabhā*) may denote a social gathering, a council, or even a gambling hall. "Delight" (*rata*) in that [abode] refers to the play experienced by the liberated, as recorded in the tradition: "eating, playing, and rejoicing" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.3.22). Here, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) derived from the root *ram*.

She whose *rasa*—that is, her passion—is directed toward Him is thus described; the sense is that she experiences the sovereignty of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). She would not be distressed by the weight of *bhava*, meaning the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), due to its momentum; for the *Amara-kośa* states: "The synonyms for speed are *raṃhas*, *taras*, *rayas*, and *syadas*. The sense is that she hears and remembers such [liberation] as being from which there is no return.

Here, between the first and second halves [of the verse], there occurs a repetition of the five syllables *bhārataraseti*—separated by the single letter *na* and appearing in the same form—which constitutes two instances of *antādyayamaka* (end-beginning yamaka) as well as *saṃdaṣṭayamaka* (clenched yamaka). This should be understood because the yamaka is "clenched" in the middle by the two side-portions of the yamaka, as if by a pair of tongs.

O Hayānana, would I not indeed set foot in the house of a wealthy man out of a craving for wealth? Yet, having been granted such great prosperity by you, what more could I possibly ask for, even if it were of immense magnitude? (2288)

O Hayānana, O Hayagrīva! Out of a desire for wealth (*dhanehayā*), would I not—indeed, I would certainly not—set my foot in the abode of those who possess censurable wealth, because they have bestowed their riches upon unworthy recipients? The suffix *ṭhan* is used here in the sense of censure (*nindā*) following the word *dhana*. Alternatively, the suffix *ini* may be applied to the word *dhana* in the same sense, with the addition of the suffix *kan* to express contempt (*kutsā*). The repetition of "not" (*na na*) serves as an intensifier (*vīpsā*). In this context, the intensification is employed to indicate either fear or a solemn vow (*pratijñā*). As it is said: "It is used in a vow, in praise, in lamentation, and also in a threat."
In both fear and wonder, repetition is indeed an ornament.

Thus [it is said]. Even though there is a distaste for placing one's foot at the door of an ordinary wealthy man, what fault is there in begging from a most noble great king and the like? To this, he says "by you," etc. "One by whom greatness—splendor—is given by you" means one who possesses divine splendor resulting from the extraordinary and eternal sovereignty obtained through your glance; such is the sense. "I am very great"—meaning worthy of honor by the whole world due to my great generosity—"if I were to beg even that Karṇa, the son of the Sun (Bhānusūnu), who is devoid of wealth, for his wealth, why indeed would I not ask for such a person? What other self-styled generous man could there be? Such is the sense.
Here too, as before, there is a *yamaka* (rhyme), the distinction being that the two halves—the first and the second—are of different forms.

O Blessed One, as long as there is any sense of "I" (ahaṃtā) directed toward the placement [of the feet], or toward the feet of the Lord of Mountains who is the King of Serpents—alas, that "I-ness" destroys me; may I never again resort to such "I-ness. (2289)

O Blessed One! As long as the placement of Your feet—Your two lotuses—extends upon the ground of the forest region of Ahīndragiri, may that egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), which causes the loss of my true nature, not strike me—that is, destroy me (from the root *han*, in the periphrastic future). "May it strike" (*hantā*) expresses the joy born from contemplating a great future gain. May I never again resort to—that is, experience—that egoism, even after the subsequent placement of Your feet upon the forested ground of Śeṣaśaila. [The verb] *bhajate* is used in the potential mood (*liṅ*) to express possibility.

Here, in the first and third quarters, there is a *yamaka* characterized by the repetition of two vowels and consonants in the middle portion; this same *yamaka* form is repeated in the initial portion of the second and fourth quarters. Thus, it should be understood as a specific type of *madhyādyayamaka* (repetition at the middle and beginning) and also as a *saṃdaṃśayamaka* (enclosing *yamaka*).
O Mukunda, by you I am to be gladdened; indeed, I am to be made joyful by you, through whom I shall not have to seek any other protector, since my entire burden has been entrusted to you.

"O Mukunda, O bestower of the ground of liberation! [The remainder of the sentence is: 'by you, to me'—this is the sense; that is, knowledge concerning You. It must be given by You alone, by means of which knowledge I may rejoice, attaining the bliss of union with You, according to [the Lord's words]: 'I give that yoga of discernment by which they come unto Me.'"

The sense is: "Because [he] is a singer. To the objection that one should instead petition some other person for this purpose, he says: "What?"—that is, whom else but you would I petition? Or rather, what should I not petition? That is, what object could I possibly request from another who is incapable of granting the knowledge I desire? The sense is that the desired object cannot be obtained from anyone else. To the question of why such a vow is made, he says: "I petition," and so forth.

The sense is this: since I have entrusted the burden of my own self to You, the Lord and Sovereign of all—how could it be possible for me to seek protection from another when the burden of my own preservation has been placed in Your hands? As it has been said: "A person should never pray to Viṣṇu for any fruit other than devotion to His feet and knowledge; by praying for anything else, one certainly perishes."

Thus: here, the middle portion of the first quarter is repeated at the beginning of the second quarter; and the middle portion of the third quarter is repeated at the beginning of the fourth quarter. This is the *madhyādi-yamaka* (middle-beginning yamaka) and a variety of *saṃdaṃśa-yamaka* (sandwich yamaka).
The mountain peak shines with joyful throngs of women, and it also gleams with joyful herds of elephants that have emerged from their dwellings and possess expansive, uplifted trunks.

By the elephants (ibhaiḥ)—that is, by the tuskers—accompanied by their mates (sapramadaiḥ), along with their females (sastrīkaiḥ), and full of joy (saharṣaiḥ); [as Amara states: "gaṇḍaka" refers to the rhinoceros (khaḍga) or the elephant (khaḍgin)]; those whose temples (gaṇḍāḥ) or frontal globes (karaṭāḥ) are accompanied by rut-fluid (pramadāḥ = *prakṛṣṭa-dāna-udaka*) are "sapramadagaṇḍakāḥ," the suffix *kap* being applied according to the rule "śeṣādvibhāṣā"; by those who have torn (ditāni) or cut asunder the *sārasa* lotuses (padmāni)—meaning by those who agitate the lotuses; [as Amara states: "dita" means "chita" (cut)]; by such elephants.

The forest mountain shines with *sairibhas*—wild buffaloes—whose essence and strength have arisen vast and truly so, having increased beyond measure; or, [it may be interpreted as] "by those vast ones whose essence has arisen. Here, because of the repetition of the initial portion of the first and third quarters and the middle portion of the second and fourth quarters, there is a single variety of *saṃdaṃśa-yamaka* (enclosing alliteration), consisting of both the beginning and the middle.

Thus, the varieties of *yamaka* (rhyme) involving parts situated in one foot with reference to parts in another foot have been illustrated merely by way of direction. Now, the varieties involving mutual reference between parts situated within the same foot are illustrated merely by way of direction. For example:
"May this wife of Śauri protect you from misfortune—she who was born from the ocean of nectar, whose splendor is unblemished, who is to be sung, and who is not to be disregarded by the wise. (2292)

The construction of the sentence is as follows: "May this wife of Śauri—the daughter of the ocean of nectar, who is shadowless yet the abode of shadows, who is lovely, who is praised by the wise, who is beyond censure by anyone, and who is irreproachable—protect us from calamity."

May that Mother of the World, who resembles a beautiful lotus, whose beloved is the Lord of Beasts and the Lord of Serpents, and whose majesty is such that she is meditated upon by the immortals— may she protect us with her auspiciousness.

The auspicious lotus of that [Lord] has dawned; "kalya" means the break of day, the beginning of morning (according to Amara). She is the Mother of the World, whose auspiciousness is to be meditated upon by the immortals, who possesses such glory, whose sovereignty transcends the reach of speech and mind, and who is the beloved of the Lord of Śeṣādri—the sovereign of both the lions and the serpents. May she protect us—this is the construction of the verse.
Just as [the gods] bowed to Skanda,
the lord of the hosts who acts for the sake of the gods, so may I find refuge at the lotus-feet of Nandīṣṭasuta, which are filled with bliss.
Regarding the phrase "in the assault upon the host of the Daityas who were like gods," it refers to the defeat [of those Daityas] by the more powerful Īśāna; the rest is easy to understand.

May we find in our hearts a most intense longing for Mukunda— the finder of the cows, the root of the host of enemies, the root of the tree of the world, the one who is exceedingly gentle yet not mild, and whose tusks are like the peaks of Mount Kailāsa.

The construction is as follows: "May we find delight—that is, intense attachment—in our hearts toward Mukunda, who is the root of the tree of the universe (arida-vasya kande), who is the cloud (jalade), who is the non-stump (akanda) that serves as the foundation, and who possesses teeth as praiseworthy as jasmine buds (kundeḍyarade), being most skillful (amande) and [like] jasmine (kunde). [This is according to the *Medinīkośa*: "Akanda refers to the suraṇa tuber, the root of a crop, and also a water-cloud. May we find such devotion toward him.

May he who bestows pure intellect, who bestows the destruction of all doubts, who bestows [victory] over the Asuras, who protects unshakable prosperity, and who is the protector of the one whose lip is a lotus— may he protect me.

"Avadātām" means pure; "dātaḥ" means by whom all doubt has been cut (chinna). This is derived from the root *do* in the sense of "cutting" (*avakhaṇḍane*), with the suffix *kta* in the passive sense; as Amara states: "kṛttaṃ dātam. "Dhiyaṃ dātā" means the giver of wisdom, according to the Gītā: "I give that yoga of wisdom" (*dadāmi buddhiyogaṃ tam*). The word *avadāta* denotes purity. Regarding the form *dātā*, since it ends in the suffix *tṛn*, its use with [the word *avadātām*] is governed by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṝnām*, which prohibits the genitive case. By this suffix *tṛn*, the Lord's habitual nature (*tācchīlyam*) of bestowing wisdom is illuminated.

This is because [the suffix] is prescribed in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*) by the rule *ākvestacchīla* (Pāṇini 3.2.134). He is the giver and the cutter of the Asuras; [the form] *dyat* takes the suffix *tṛc*. There is a compound with a genitive of relation (*śaiṣika-ṣaṣṭhī*). He is the protector (*pātā*), that is, the guardian, of *śrī*, meaning prosperity, which is "unfallen" (*anipātāṃ*); by the force of the epithet, it is understood that he is the Lord Śrīnivāsa, the protector of the lip of Kamalā—that is, Śrī—the ordainer of the tasting of the nectar of Rāmā’s lower lip. "He will protect me" (*māṃ pātā*); this is the periphrastic future (*luṭ*) of the root *pā*. This applies throughout the five verses here as well.

The repetition occurs at the end of the initial portion of each quarter-verse; however, in the final [quarter], the initial portion of the first quarter is repeated in its own final portion, and the beginnings and ends of the second and third quarters are repeated. Thus, the specific distinction is that the initial portion of the third quarter is repeated in its own final portion, and the beginnings and ends of the fourth quarter are repeated.
Now, the various types of mixed *yamaka* are illustrated by way of a mere indication:

"Beholding Rāma in the assembly—him who was extending [his power] over the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*) and gladdening the gods who partake of sacrifices (*kratubhuj*), while he himself was one whose power was equal to that of Mitra—the Rāvaṇa, though possessing great energy, had his own energy subdued. (2297)

Bringing an end to the bodies—the flesh-eating corpses—of those who eat flesh, he delights and satisfies the gods who partake of the sacrificial offerings, even as this flesh-eater acts as their adversary.

Beholding Rāma in the assembly—that is, in the conflict—even Rāvaṇa, who was renowned for being invincible, became one whose *ojas* (vitality) was diminished; that is, he whose *ojas*, meaning power or brilliance, was thus reduced, and consequently, he whose *ojas*, meaning radiance, was pacified or brought to stillness. (The word "became" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. According to Amara, "Ojas [denotes] power and radiance. Here, the final portion of the first quarter-verse, *tanvantam*, merges with the initial portion of the second quarter-verse, *samitau*.

The final portion of the third quarter is repeated at the beginning of the fourth quarter; furthermore, there is a repetition of the words *tanvantaṃ* and *mitaujāḥ* in the second and fourth quarters respectively—thus, there is a combination (*saṃkara*) [of these figures].

Just as I shall cross the ocean of existence, O Mother, so shall I be carried across by Your sidelong glance; indeed, how else could my ultimate liberation come to pass? For it will surely come to be.

"I shall cross over, I will cross over, the ocean of existence (*bhavābdhi*)," from the root *tṛ* meaning "to swim or to cross," in the periphrastic future (*luṭ*). To the question "How will you cross? he replies: "O Mother! [I shall do so] by means of Your side-glance (*apāṅgaka*), that is, Your sidelong look. The sense is that You are renowned as the one who "causes one to cross the ocean of saṃsāra. It has been said in the *Amara-kośa*: "A boat is called *nau*, *taraṇi*, or *tari* in the feminine. It has been reached (*itā*) [by me]. The sense is: "When Your side-glance serves as a boat, how could I not cross the ocean of existence?"

"From this point forward, how indeed will my state of being in *saṃsāra* come to be? It will come to be. [This is the form] from the root *bhū* with the suffix *luṭ*. Even though the reason was previously presented as to why it would not be so, he now presents another reason for the sake of strengthening that argument: "For (*hi*) liberation (*niḥśreyasa*), which is *mokṣa*, will come to be (*saṃbhavitā*), i.e., will occur. Here, because the first part of each of the two pairs of quarters does not recur in their latter parts, this is a *yamaka* (rhyme) based on the mutual dependence of parts within a single quarter.

The repetition of the initial portions of the first and third quarters in the initial portions of the second and fourth quarters constitutes a *yamaka* here that is intermingled with respect to the parts of different quarters; this should be understood in the same way in what follows as well.

Just as the consumer of honey [the bee] now [removes] the sorrow with honey, so too has my distress within my heart been dispelled by you—who possess auspicious gains—through your most divine conduct, which is like honey. 2299.
The word division is *śucam adhunā*. The construction is: "by you who have become [present] in the heart," meaning by you who abide in the heart.

If, however, that Supreme Brahman—the compassionate one who takes pity on the heart—were not to manifest upon this earth, then no person in the world would ever arise, rolling about in the state of being subject to worldly existence.

If that compassionate Supreme Brahman, who is merciful toward the virtuous, were not to manifest on this earth in a physical form—should He not descend upon Venkatachala and other such places within this worldly existence—then [all would be lost].

The sense is that this person, falling and rolling about due to a tendency to fall, would not be filled with joy (*samut*) in this world—that is, he would find no bliss whatsoever in this universe. Here, the shadow of the meaning of the Śruti, "For who indeed could breathe, who could live, if this Ākāśa were not bliss? has been followed. In this verse, there is a repetition (*āvṛtti*) of the vowels and consonants *na-sa-mu-d-bha-ve* located in the middle of the first quarter in the middle portion of the third quarter.
Furthermore, between the second and fourth quarters, there is a specific type of *yamaka* (rhyme) in the form: *dayālu dayālu tayālu tayālu*.

Take refuge in the feet of the Blessed One, which remove humiliation for those who seek them and bring about the removal of humiliation; do not, however, resort to the abode of the miserly, which is a hell for the miserly.

O people! Take refuge in the feet of the Blessed One, which ward off all humiliation and remove the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) hereafter—according to the manner stated in the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata*: "I am that which should always be meditated upon as the remover of humiliation, the destroyer of humiliation, and the granter of desires.
As for the miserly person, he causes suffering to himself, his religious duties, and his wife and children;
he who, out of greed, [neglects] his parents and brothers is known as a miser (*kadarya*).

Those who possess the characteristics thus described are "kṛpaṇas" (miserly); they are both "kutsita" (despised) and "arya" (masters), hence "kadaryas. Their "aryas" are either masters or Vaiśyas—the word "arya" being correct by virtue of the grammatical rule "aryassvāmivaiśyoḥ. As Amara states: "The word 'arya' may mean a master or a Vaiśya. Furthermore, the substitution of "kad" for the word "ku" occurs according to the rule "koḥ kattatpuruṣe'ci. Do not resort to "nilaya" (abode), which is a "vyastarūpaka" (distributive metaphor) for "niraya" (hell).
The sense is: do not serve the homes of despised kings or wealthy Vaiśyas, which, due to the desire for wealth, are equivalent to hell.
I always perceive that infinite Śrī through her entire form, yet she perceives me through a single part; now, by her exceeding speed, she swiftly destroys my sin.

"I always perceive her with my entire being as immeasurable; he perceives her with a single part as measured. "By that power, she who is exceedingly swift now swiftly shakes away sin—that is Śrī. This is the word-division (*cheda*). "Her" means the well-known one; "with an entire part" means immeasurable, yet known as measured—meaning she is known through a majesty that cannot be delimited by any scripture.

That splendor (*śrī*) which I, though reduced to the state of a servant, always perceive and meditate upon—she is so described because she possesses a *rasa* (essence) of compassion that has been attained with extreme speed (*atitarasā*), that is, continuously (*sātatyena*). Regarding the word *atitā*, it is derived from the root *ata* in the sense of "continuous movement" (*sātatyagamana*), with the suffix *kta* used in the passive sense. The meaning is: being one whose compassion never ceases. Furthermore, she is *atitarasādhu*; that is, by him who is exceedingly excellent (*mahāśreṣṭha*).

In the context of its grammatical function (*vṛtti*), the word *ati* denotes a substance (*dravyavacana*). Therefore, there is no application here of the suffix *ām*, which is prescribed for the intensification of non-substances by the rule "after an indeclinable ending in *ghat*, *ām* is used for the intensification of a non-substance" (*avyayaghādāmvadravyaprakarṣe*). *Tarasā* means with speed; that is, with limitless velocity. *Adhunā* means this very day; it shakes—that is, causes to tremble—the evil (*agha*), meaning sin. The sense is that for me who meditates upon Śrī as characterized by the aforementioned attributes, the destruction of prior sins and the non-clinging of future sins occur immediately.

Daṇḍin, however, declared that when there is a repetition from the end backward starting with the quarter-verse (pāda), it is "pratilomayamaka" (reverse-order yamaka). Accordingly, its definition is as follows: "A repetition occurring in reverse order across the quarter-verse, the half-verse, or the entire verse is known as 'pratiloma' because it is a reverse-order yamaka."

Thus [it is said]. Where the second quarter is produced by the reverse repetition of the first quarter, the second half-verse by the reverse repetition of the first half-verse, and another verse by the reverse repetition of a single verse, that is the meaning of *pratilomayamaka* (reverse palindrome-yamaka). Others say this is a variety of *anulomapratiloma-citra* (direct-and-reverse ornament). This is also seen when there is reverse repetition of the sub-divisions of a quarter. In this regard—

Since it was promised that examples would be shown by means of specific exclusions, and since it is difficult to achieve the reversal of a full *pāda* because those [exclusions] do not consist of an even number of syllables, the reversal of the half-verse (*ardhaśloka*) portion of the *pāda* is demonstrated.
In that regard, an example of the reverse repetition of each quarter-verse (*pādabhāga*) is as follows:

"O Rāma, who dwells in the light of fame, whose essence is known as the abode of nectar, who stands in the state free from darkness, and who is the bee to the forest-garland of the world—oh, by you, such as this, has the grace of the Supreme Man been attained! (2303)

O you whose disposition and intention are full of aesthetic essence (rasa)—O Līlāmānava, you who have assumed a human form by your own will, O Rāma! You, who are known by your fame as "Rasa" according to the Vedic text "He is indeed Rasa," meaning one whose nature consists of bliss, abide in the place that is free from darkness, in the supreme ether (parama-vyoman).

By you, who are such as this, a line—a succession—of forest garlands, that is, of the splendors of the groves, has been attained. Oh, how wonderful it is that one residing in an extraordinary, divine abode should reach the ordinary Daṇḍaka forest; such is the intended meaning. Herein lies a specific type of *yamaka* (rhyme) consisting of five vowels and consonants in the first and third quarters of the verse, arranged in reverse order.

O Hari, while the power of the Kali age (Tiṣya) prevails, it will produce an eye that brings reproach; yet there is no other way for men to remove their misfortune than by the recitation of your names.

O Hari! Producing—that is, leading people onto the wrong path—a censurable and blameworthy course of conduct (ayana); [this occurs] during the Kali age, for "Tiṣya is Puṣya and [it denotes] the Kali age," according to Amara. Only the Vibhava [incarnation] will prevail—meaning it will attain dominance. The sense is that in this age there is no opportunity for the performance of means such as sacrifice, charity, or austerity. If one asks, "In that case, how is one delivered from fault? [the author] says: "Hari removes sins," as has been previously declared.

The meaning is that there is no other way or means for removing—the dispelling of—the calamities of men, which consist of the repeated recollection of those very misfortunes, because of the traditional enumeration of names. The chanting of Your name alone is the means for crossing over calamity. As it is said: "In the Kali age, a storehouse of defects, there is indeed one great virtue:
by the mere chanting of Kṛṣṇa's name, one is released from bondage and goes to the Supreme."

Thus it is said. Here, it should be understood that at the end of the first and third quarters, there is a transposition of two syllables separated by one intervening syllable, whereas in the second and fourth quarters, there is a transposition of four syllables without any intervening space.
The repetition of the half-verse in reverse order is as follows:

"May that wife—who is exceedingly free from sin, who is the hope of her beloved, who brings great delight to the people, who is the mistress of the forest, who possesses a peaceful form, who is the source of fear for enemies, and who is abundant in compassion—shine forth. (2305)

The word division is as follows: *sābhāyāt*, *anaghatarā*, *kāntāśā*, *atīva*, *janavarāmodā*, *dāmorāḥ*, *vanajavatī*, *śāntākārā*, *ārātaghanadayā*, *bhāsā*. *Anaghatarā*: One who is most free from sin (*apahatapāpmā*). *Kāntāśā*: She whose hope (*āśā*)—meaning desire or longing—is fixed upon the Beloved (*kānta*), that is, the Blessed Lord; the sense is that she is characterized by unsurpassed love directed toward the Lord. Alternatively, *āśaḥ* means pervasion (*vyāpti*), derived from the root *aśū* (to pervade) with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state. *Sābhāyāt*: From her own splendor (*ābhā*). *Atīva*: Exceedingly. *Janavarāmodā*: One who brings supreme delight (*āmoda*) to people (*jana*). *Dāmorāḥ*: Of the wicked ones (*dāma*). *Vanajavatī*: Possessing lotuses (*vana-ja*). *Śāntākārā*: Of peaceful appearance (*ākāra*). *Ārātaghanadayā*: With intense (*ghana*) compassion (*dayā*) directed toward those who have approached (*ārāta*). *Bhāsā*: By [her] radiance (*bhāsā*). [The full phrase is: "By her radiance, which is exceedingly free from sin, whose hope is fixed on the Beloved, which brings supreme delight to people, which belongs to the wicked, which possesses lotuses, which is of peaceful appearance, and which has intense compassion for those who have approached. (Note: The term *dāmorāḥ* appears to be used here in a specific, perhaps archaic or dialectal, sense; it may intend to signify those who are bound or subdued, or it could be a corruption/variant of *damorāḥ* meaning "tamed" or "subdued," though the provided text suggests a connection to the wicked. *Vanajavatī*: Possessing lotuses. *Śāntākārā*: Of peaceful form. *Ārātaghanadayā*: With thick, near-at-hand mercy. *Bhāsā*: By the light. Thus is the analysis of the words. *Anaghatarā* means one whose sins have been destroyed. *Kāntāśā* means she whose desire is for the Beloved—the Lord; the implication is that she is endowed with incomparable affection for the Lord. Or else, *āśaḥ* is pervasion, from the root *aśū* (to pervade), in the sense of a state of being.

She whose hope (*āśā*) is like the hope of her beloved; for it is said: "O Mother, the world of moving and unmoving beings is pervaded by you and Viṣṇu. She who excessively (*atīva*), that is, to an extreme degree, gladdens (*āmodā*) the best of men (*janavarāṇām*); [the word *āmodā*] is derived from the root *mud* with the prefix *ā-* and the suffix *ac*. Alternatively, she whose joy (*āmoda*) is excellent (*vara*) among people—meaning she possesses unsurpassed affection (*varāmodā*). Or else, she who gladdens (*āmodā*) through excellent boons (*varaiḥ*) according to the various desires of those who know [her], thus she is *jānanāṃ varāmodā*. She upon whose chest (*ura*) lies a garland (*dāma*) of flowers (*dāma*), thus she is *dāmorāḥ*.

Dāmorā; for this very reason, her name is "Mahāmālāvibhūṣaṇā" (Adorned with a Great Garland). The suffix *kap* does not apply according to the rule "uraḥprabhṛtibhyaḥ kap," because the application of compound-final suffixes (*samāsāntavidhi*) is not universal. Thus, there is the usage by Murāri: "āpūryamāṇorasam" (with a chest being filled). She is called *vanajavatī*, meaning she possesses a *vanaja*—that is, a lotus (*abja*); the sense is that she is a *padminī*. This is supported by such authorities as: "O *padminī*, who stands upon a lotus, who loves the lotus, and who holds a lotus in your hand."

She by whom sin or suffering is pacified for those who have taken refuge is Śāntākā. According to the Viśva lexicon: "Akaṃ means both sin and suffering. She whose intense compassion (ghana-dayā) has been fully grasped (ārātā) is Ārātaghanadayā; [the root] rā, meaning 'to take,' takes the suffix kta in the passive sense. She is she whose compassion is dense and thick; the meaning is that she is the well-known Śrī. By her splendor (bhāsā), that is, by her power—according to the Medinī lexicon: "Bhāḥ means both power and light"—may she shine forth (bhāyāt).
