Regarding the phrase *sā bhāyāt*, in the reading *mā bhāyāt*, the word division is *mā bhāyāt*. Regarding the phrase *dayābhāsā* at the end of the fourth quarter, in the reading *dayābhāmā*, the word division is either *ārāta-ghana-dayā-bhāmā* or *ārāta-ghana-dayā-abhā-mā*. The meaning of *ārāta-ghana-dayā* has already been stated. In the second alternative, however, the analysis is: *ārāte* (O Thou who art near), *ātte* (taken up), *ghane* (dense); and *dayā* and *ābhā* (splendor) are *dayābhe*; she whose [these] are [her attributes] is *mā*—this is the substantive, meaning Lakṣmī.
*Mā* means "may she shine toward me," that is to say, "may she manifest herself and be present within me."
The reverse order of the verse is as follows:
*Jyājñā damanayorāmatārā janitā bhuvi tāne vaitāne sārasavanodāsā nadīvibhavagatimānā bhānayanasarasāvanasādā.* (2306)

The one whose name signifies a future state free from the defects of despondency and the constant flow of worldly existence; the knower of knowledge, the most excellent, the one to whom the immortals bow, the giver, the mother, and indeed the leader of her own Lord.

The word-by-word analysis of the two verses is as follows: *vaitāne*, *bhuvi*, *janitā*, *mā*, *tārārāmadamanayoḥ*, *ājñā*, *mānātigavibhavanadī*, *dāsāvanasārasarasanayanābhā*, *bhānāyanasarasarasā*, *anavasādā*, *ādīnavabhavigatināmā*, *jñā*, *jyāyaḥ*, *namadamarā*, *rātā*, *mātā*, *nijavibhunā*, *itā*, *vai*. *Vaitāne* means in the ritual connected with the sacrificial canopy (*vitāna*); the sense is: at the time of ploughing the ground for the sacrifice.

"Born on earth"—this is the subject qualified by "Śrī. She whose command is to be applied to the subduer of Tārā’s Rāma; that is, Tārā’s Rāma is Vālī, and the one who subdued (damana) him, the punisher, is the Lord Dāśarathi (Rāma). She is she whose command (ājñā)—that is, her edict—is to be applied (yojyā) to him, for it is well known in the *Śrīrāmāyaṇa* that she follows his commands. She is a river of boundless majesty; that is, she is the river of a splendor (vibhava) that transcends measure (mānātiga), meaning it exceeds all limits (velātīta) and serves as its source.

Although the nature of the manifestation as water is not explicitly depicted through the description of the Blessed One in the form of a river, it is nevertheless understood; thus, this is a specific type of partial metaphor (*ekadeśavivarti-rūpaka*). For this very reason, she is recited in the *Sahasranāma* (Thousand Names) as "the carrier of great manifestation" (*mahāvibhavavāhinī*). She is described as one whose splendor of eyes (*nayanābhā*)—which are beautiful (*sarasā*), compassionate (*sadayā*), and essential (*sārā*, i.e., supreme) for the protection (*avane*) of her servants (*dāsānām*, i.e., attendants)—is so characterized.

"Bhānāyanasarasarasā" means "charming by means of that necklace (sara) which is the path (ayana)—that is, the locus—of light (bhāna), derived from the root *bhā* in the sense of 'shining' with the suffix *lyuṭ*. "Anavasādā" means "one in whom there is no dejection (avasāda)," that is, no emaciation.

*Ādīnavabhavigatināmā*: *ādīnava* refers to affliction (*kleśa*), according to Amara’s lexicon which states, "ādīnava and āsrava [denote] affliction. It is the *gati* (course) of *bhavins* (beings)—that is, transmigrating beings—characterized by affliction; *gati* is derived from the root *gam* with the suffix *ktin* in the passive sense, meaning that which is reached. Thus, the intended meaning is: she whose name is to be kept in mind by transmigrating people defiled by the threefold suffering. *Jñā* means knowing; it signifies the Omniscient One. For this very reason, they recite her among her names as "Sarvajñā Kamalaprabhā" (The All-Knowing One, Lotus-Radiance). *Jyāyaḥ* (superior) connects with what follows later.

"Namadamara-namantāmarāḥ" refers to those immortals (amarāḥ) who bow down (namantaḥ) [to her]. She is thus described. "Nijavibhunā" means by her own beloved Lord; "itā" means joined with or endowed with. "Jyāyaḥ" means the highest good, that is to say, most praiseworthy sovereignty (aiśvaryam). From the word *praśasya*, when the suffix *īyasun* is added, there is the substitution of *jya* according to the rule "jya ca. "Rātā" means she will give; this is from the root *rā* in the sense of giving, in the periphrastic future (*luṭ*). "Vai" is used for emphasis or well-known fact. Thus, the example of Yamaka has been illustrated.
Now, that which appears as a tautology (punaruktavad-ābhāsa) is what appears as a tautology where there is no repetition in meaning, though it may be so in substance;
this "appearance of tautology" pertains to the domain of nouns and verbs.

Where a meaning appears as if it were a repetition—appearing slightly disconnected at first glance, yet in reality and from the perspective of ultimate truth, becoming something entirely different at the time of syntactic connection—that is the figure of speech named *punaruktavadābhāsa* (appearance of repetition). This is of two kinds: that which relies on nouns (*nāma*) and that which relies on verbs (*ākhyāta*). Although this belongs to the category of semantic figures (*arthālaṅkāra*), its definition is stated here in the context of verbal figures (*śabdālaṅkāra*) because it relies upon the repetition of words. An example of that which relies on a noun is as follows: [Example omitted per instructions]

May I constantly direct my devotion toward that ineffable deity, who possesses the stability of the serpent-bearing mountain, whose splendor is like that of the sun, the friend of the moon, and whose broad chest is dense with precious jewels. 2308.

The serpent-bearing mountain is the king of serpents; that very mountain is the "Acala" (the immovable). He whose stability rests upon that [mountain] is the sun, possessed of heat (*ghṛṇin*); he is the friend of that [sun], and thus his radiance is equal to it. A source of that radiance is the "maṇiratna," the best of gems—according to Amara, "ratna" may also mean the best of its own kind. With that [radiance], his chest is thick. Here, by employing synonyms such as *dharaṇibhṛt* for *acala*, there appears at first a tautology; however, since through the aforementioned connection this results in a different sense, this is the figure of speech known as *punaruktavadābhāsa* (the semblance of tautology), which relies on the basis of words.
An example based on the verbal root (ākhyāta):
"O Lord whose radiance is like that of the sun, Lakṣmī shines, gleams, and resplends upon You;
indeed, O Blessed One, O ornament of the earth and the mountains, she is beloved by You and dwells under Your protection. (2309)

"O Lord whose radiance is like that of the sun, O ornament of the serpent-hill and the earth! Indeed, [the word] *te* in *te tava kamalā* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) functioning as a substitute for a case-ending, similar to how *te* is used in the phrase *lakṣmīpate te 'nghriyugam*. It is not the substitute *te* prescribed by the rule *yuṣmadasmador dvyekayoḥ te me* (Pāṇini 8.1.20). This is because the vocative *dinanāthasadṛkprakāśa*, being treated as non-existent according to the rule *āmantritaṃ pūrvam avidyamānavat* (Pāṇini 8.1.72), does not stand at the beginning of a sentence (*pādādi*); and since the substitute *te* occurs after such a [non-existent] word, the rule *padasya padāt* (Pāṇini 8.1.16) applies."

Because of the rule "anudāttaṃ sarvamapādādau" (everything [following a vocative] is unaccented except at the beginning of a verse-quarter), since this is prescribed only for cases not at the beginning of a quarter, the phrase *te kamalet* establishes the well-known fact of Viṣṇu’s eternal and fixed subservience to his consort—as seen in such passages as *sadā tavaivocitayā tava śriyā* ("always by your own Śrī, who is worthy of you") and *viṣṇoḥ śrīranapāyinī* ("the Śrī of Viṣṇu is inseparable")—in the same way as in the example *sadā tavaivocitayā tava śriyā*. [The word *kamalet*] shines, sports, appears, manifests, prevails, is powerful, is desired, is dear, exists, and resplends in You.

In this context, among the verbs *dīvyati*, *bhāti*, *virājati*, and *prakāśate*, as well as *īṣṭe* and *prabhavati*, there is an appearance of tautology because they initially seem to have the same meaning, like other finite verbs; however, as established by the method explained, their meanings resolve differently at the time of syntactic connection (*anvaya*). Thus, it should be understood that this is "resemblance to tautology" (*punaruktavad-ābhāsa*) based on finite verbs. According to the view of the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, however, this [figure] is twofold: residing solely in the word (*śabdaikaniṣṭha*) and residing in both word and meaning (*śabdārthadvayastha*).
That which resides solely in the word is further divided into two types by the distinction between *sabhaṅga* (with word-break) and *abhaṅga* (without word-break).

Furthermore, this *punaruktavadābhāsa* (the semblance of repetition) is of two kinds: that which rests on the word alone (*śabdamātra-samāśraya*), and that which rests on both the word and its meaning (*śabdārtha-ubhaya-samāśraya*). Of these, the first—resting on the word alone—is twofold: with a break in the compound (*sabhaṅga*) and without a break (*abhaṅga*). Among these, an example of *punaruktavadābhāsa* resting solely on the word with a break in the compound (*sabhaṅga-śabdaikagocara*) is as follows:
"O Hari, through my devotion (*sneha*), I have long been smeared with egoism (*ahaṃkṛta-mati*).

O Unborn One (*aja*), how indeed could Your abode, which is honored in many ways, be difficult for me to attain? (2310) [In this verse, the words *sneha*, *ahaṃkṛta*, and *aja* are used with double meanings: *sneha* as "affection" and "oil"; *ahaṃkṛta* as "egoism" and "made of copper"; and *aja* as "Unborn" and "goat."]

O Hara! protect me! Out of affection (*sneha*)—that is, love (*prema*)—toward You, I have been smeared (*digdha*) with substances such as oil for a long time, for many ages. [The phrase] "bahudhā mahitaṃ te aja" is to be analyzed as follows: O Aja! O Blessed One, how indeed could Your supreme abode, which is honored (*mahita*)—worshipped—in many ways (*bahudhā*), that is, in manifold manners, be difficult to attain? The meaning is that for one in whom such devotion toward You has arisen, it would be easily attained.

In the verses "atrāvalipto’haṃkṛtaḥ" and "ityatra bahudhāmahitaṃ tejaḥsthānam," the words *avalipta* and *ahaṃkṛta*, as well as *dhāma* and *tejaḥ*, appear to have the same meaning; however, because these pairs are composed of distinct meanings through word-splitting (*padabhaṅga*) according to the method described, this constitutes the figure of speech known as *punaruktavadābhāsa* (semblance of tautology) with a break (*sabhaṅga*).

O Acyuta, your lineage shines forth as one that is unbroken—praised by Vākpati, Guru, Saumya, and Budha—and is a treasury of auspiciousness for Bhauma; it possesses supreme magnanimity that removes the dullness of the son of the Sun (Śani). 2311.

O Acyuta! Your devotee, who is the object of your grace, shines forth as one praised by the masters of speech, the eloquent, the preceptors, the most excellent, the gentle, the non-cruel, and those who are wise and learned; he is the repository—the very foundation—of that auspiciousness which belongs to the earth (Bhauma), and his supreme magnanimity surpasses even that which causes the dullness (mandatā) of Karṇa, the son of the Sun (Bhānusuta). Thus it is said.

In this regard, it should be understood that, according to the method described, the appearance of a single meaning—namely, Bṛhaspati, Rauhiṇeya, Aṅgāraka, and Śanaiścara—in the pairs of words *vākpati* and *guru*, *saumya* and *budha*, *bhauma* and *maṅgala*, and *bhānusuta* and *manda*, is based on non-compounded (*abhaṅga*) words.
As an example based on both word and meaning:
"O Abode of Śrī, may you cause Lakṣmī—who has limbs of molten gold, whose beautiful mass of hair resembles thick rain-clouds, and who possesses noble and great radiance—to dwell in my family. (2312)

She whose limbs possess a beautiful complexion like refined gold or beaten gold is "Hiraṇyavarṇā," according to the Śruti. She whose hair-arrangement is as lovely as a dense, thick rain-cloud—meaning it is of the same lineage or similar to it—is "Rucirakacabandhā. She is "Udārā," meaning generous or munificent, according to the Śruti: "Devajuṣṭāmudārām" (cherished by the gods, the noble one). Amara states: "Udāra refers to a donor or something great. She is "Mahatī," meaning venerable, based on the etymology: that which is honored (*māhyate*) or worshipped (*pūjyate*).

O Śrīnivāsa! Dwell in my lineage, my progeny, and my home—that Lakṣmī whose radiance is a pre-eminent light. By this, the Vedic mantra "Dwell in my lineage, O Śrī" is recognized. Here, the quality of being based on sound (*śabdāśrayatva*) arises because the words *suvarṇa*, *ghana-prabhā*, and *udārā* are incapable of being synonymous substitutes for one another.

It should be understood that the pun (*punaruktavadābhāsa*) rests on both word and meaning because the words *tapanīya-jalada-lakṣmī-mahatī-śabda* and *gāṅgeya-mudira-kamala-pūjya-ādi* are capable of supporting multiple meanings through their respective alternative senses.
Now, that which appears like a corrupt word (apaśabda) but ceases upon the knowledge of its correctness— wherein there is the cognition of a corrupt word—
is called the figure of speech "Appearance as a Corrupt Word" (apaśabdavadābhāsa).
I shall go for refuge to that Lord, the Self-born Śambhu, the sovereign of Ramā, by whose glories the world is pervaded like the ocean.

The construction is as follows: "I shall go for refuge to Him—the self-existent (svayaṃbhuvam), whose fame has pervaded the world so that it, becoming white and pale, acts like the ocean of milk (payonidhīyati)—using the suffix *kyac* according to the rule 'upamānādācāre' [Pāṇini 3.1.10]—to Śambhuva, the ground of bliss, the Lord (īśam), the Sovereign of all (sarveśvaram), and Ramādhibhuvam, the beloved of Śrī."

In this context, because of the co-occurrence of the word *hariṇa* ending in the nominative case with the word *yasya* ending in the genitive case, it appears as a non-word (*apaśabda*) due to its appearance as if it were ending in the genitive—just like *kariṇaḥ*; because of the division of *payonidhīyate* into *payaḥ* and *nidhīyate*, it appears as such due to the use of the root *dhā* preceded by *ni* in the parasmaipada for the object—just like *vraje'yam* in *vrajeyam* where it is divided into *vraje* and *ayam* and the root *vraj* is used in the ātmanepada; and because of its possession of the *uvaṅ* substitution, it appears as such—just like *svayaṃbhuvam* in *śambhuvam*.
Thus, it possesses the quality of "appearing as a non-word" (*apaśabdavadābhāsatva*).
Just as the illustrious Lord on the Vṛṣādri mountain is capable of granting the desires of those who seek him, he is likewise exceedingly capable of bestowing misfortune upon his adversaries.

In the first half [of the verse], "kalpati" means it acts like the *kalpataru* (wish-fulfilling tree); in the second half, "kalpati" means the *kalpa* (aeon) acts like the *pralaya* (dissolution). According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *kalpa* refers to dissolution, logic, scripture, the day of Brahmā, and ritual injunction; it also refers to the celestial tree and alternative. If it is a suffix (*pratyaya*), it has the same meaning. Here, because the form "kalpati" appears as if it were in the *parasmaipada* (active voice) despite being derived from the root *klṛp*, it has the appearance of a grammatical error (*apaśabda*), since that root is invariably *ātmanepada* (middle voice).
Now, as for the appearance of indeclinables (*avyayābhāsa*):
when words ending in nominal suffixes (*sup*) or verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), which have distinct meanings,
are combined together such that they appear as if they were indeclinables, those who know [the art] call that by the name *citra*.

Just as the slayer of the demon Bala, having become manifold through his own power, is known by many names; so too has he been attained—who is beyond all faults, who is the auspicious day itself, and who is ever intent upon removing both what is timely and what is untimely.

The word *sadvāḥ* means "one who possesses doors" (*dvāraiḥ saha vartate*), ending in the letter *r*. Regarding the word *enaḥ*: it signifies sin or evil; as Amara states, "sin, evil, impurity, and crookedness are synonyms. The meaning is: that which has ignorance, attachment, aversion, and so forth as its cause—namely, demerit (*pāpa*). A "destroyer" (*hantā*) of that is one who dispels it; the meaning is: one who is preeminent in removing the root sins, both past and future, of his own worshippers. Intending to state the reason for this, he says "much" (*bahu*).

He is called *bahudhāḥ* because he holds, maintains, and nourishes the manifold universe (*viśvam*) in many ways through his nature as both conscious and unconscious; this word ends in *-ā* just like *viśvapāḥ*. Furthermore, he is called by the name *bhūyasvadhāmavān*, meaning one whose natural power (*svadhāma*)—which, according to Amara, refers to "home, body, luster, and majesty"—is exceedingly great (*bhūyas*). He is thus described because he possesses such a name due to his being the sustainer, the nourisher, and the possessor of supreme majesty.

The sense is that [the Lord] is the destroyer who strikes down all evils along with their very roots. For this very reason, He is "beyond defects" (doṣātītaḥ), meaning He has transcended all defects; the compound is formed according to the rule "the second [case-ending] is used in the sense of 'resorted to,' 'transcended,' etc. One should here keep in mind the meaning of such scriptural passages as, "He has risen above all evils; He is free from sin" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.7).

Alternatively, "names"—that is, the names of gods, humans, and so forth—which are numerous, possess their own inherent powers (*svadhāman*), possess various bodies, or possess various forms—belong to Him; by the word "in manifold ways" His nature as the Self is shown, while by this [subsequent phrase] it is demonstrated that He assumes those respective names and forms through entering into those respective bodies preceded by the differentiation of name and form (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*). He is *sudivā* because He shines excellently; He is innate (*svābhāvika*).

The meaning is that he shines forth by virtue of possessing auspicious qualities such as omniscience and bliss. Even though he has entered into the bodies of various gods and others, this [verse] illuminates the fact that he remains untouched by the defects produced by those [bodies]. This was formulated in the Sūtra: "If it be argued that there would be the attainment of enjoyment [of suffering], no, because of the difference in nature. By me, Śrī. Here, the word *yaḥ* (who) is to be supplied, as is seen from the appearance of *saḥ* (he) later on. *Āsa* means "shone"; it is the perfect tense (*liṭ*) of the root *ās*, which signifies shining.

The sense is that the Blessed One, who is endowed with natural and limitless luster, shines forth preeminently with the splendor of a jewel set in gold. He is "intent upon protecting" (udyata) the world—meaning he is ever-exerted for its preservation, as it is said: "Indeed, there is no capacity for protection except for Hari, the Lord of All. That Blessed One, possessing the aforementioned qualities, was "attained" (prāpi) by me; the sense is that he was reached by me, who am his subordinate (śeṣabhūta). This is derived from the root *āp* preceded by *pra*, in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*), in the *luṅ* tense, with the *ciṇ* suffix.

In this verse, there is the appearance of a series of indeclinables (*avyaya*), such as *sat*, *vā*, *re*, *no*, *hanta*, *ā*, *bahuthā*, *bhūyas*, *svadhā*, *āmavat*, *na*, *amā*, *doṣā*, *atītaḥ*, *sudinā*, *samayāsamayā*, *ava*, *naḥ*, *ut*, and *yataḥ*. It should be understood that *samayāsamayā* is the appearance of an indeclinable repeated twice.
Now, regarding the "semblance of a finite verb" (*tiṅantavadābhāsa*): where there is an appearance of finite verbs through words that have entered into another meaning,
that is considered by experts in poetry to be the "picture-verse resembling a finite verb" (*tiṅantavadābhāsacitra*).

O remover of existence, O bringer of victory, [remove] the sins of one who wallows in the world of becoming; O ocean of love, if you were not present within the mind, there would be no other power for me.

The term *bhavatāpahara* is a vocative addressing Him who removes the torment of worldly existence. *Jayāvaha* means one who bestows excellence upon those who take refuge in Him. *Premā* refers to His state of being beloved; the compound *premādadherniratiśayapriya* means "one who is supremely dear to the ocean of love. [The word] *priya*...

For by him [the Knower] it is sung: "I am indeed exceedingly [the Knower]. For me—who am wallowing in various forms within *bhava*, that is, in the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), or in a forest fire (*dava*), or in a wilderness (*kāntāra*)—[O Lord], remove his sins. This is the ellipsis for "mine. The form *nirākuru* is the second person singular present imperative of the root *as* belonging to the *divādi* class. To the question "Why do you persist in binding me alone? he replies with the words beginning "prabhavitā": "Other than you (*bhavataḥ*), there is no other (*itaro'nyaḥ*) sovereign (*prabhavitā*); that is to say, no one else is the lord (*prabhuḥ*) or capable in the act of removing sin."

The word "mama" (of mine) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sense]. "Cetastaḥ": *citta* (mind) with the suffix *tasi*, which is used for all case-endings (*sārvavibhaktika*). "Na vāti" means it does not go. This is derived from the root *vā* (to go), belonging to the first class (*ādādika*), in the present tense (*laṭ*). The meaning is: no one other than You, who is pre-eminent in removing sins, enters the range of my mind. The underlying thought is based on such scriptural statements as: "Hari removes sins even when remembered by those of wicked minds. Therefore, the meaning is: "You alone must dispel my sins.

Here, because there is an appearance of finite verbs (*tiṅanta*) through a sequence of words having other meanings, this is a novel type of *citram* (poetic figure/picture) called *tiṅantavad-ābhāsa*, discovered by us.

"O Bhava, take away my sins; O Hara, bring [them] to an end! May there be love for him who rolls about in the dust; may you, the powerful one, be the protector and deliverer of the ignorant. In this verse, nineteen finite verbal forms appear; thus, it should be observed with careful attention.
Now, regarding the variegated rules for vowels, places of articulation, consonants, and so forth—
since the rule governing vowels, places of articulation, and consonants is indeed difficult,
this one beginning with four [syllables] has been taught; hereafter, the easier ones will be shown.

Among the difficult poetic compositions (*duṣkaracitra*), this rule regarding vowels (*svara*), places of articulation (*sthāna*), and consonants (*vyañjana*) is now demonstrated, beginning with fourfold [combinations]. Here, "vowels" refers to *a* and the others, the *ac* letters; "places of articulation" refers to the locations such as the throat (*kaṇṭha*) and so forth, as stated in the rule "the throat is the place for *a*, *ku*-series sounds, and *visarjanīya*"; and "consonants" refers to the *hal* letters. The restriction (*niyama*) concerning these, which was declared by former authorities to be difficult to perform, is shown here starting from fourfold combinations. By the phrase "starting from four," it is meant that four varieties are being demonstrated according to their forms of four, three, two, and one.
But another [type], beginning with five [syllables] and so on, is easy to perform because it can be accomplished without excessive effort; therefore, its examples should be inferred accordingly.
In this regard, first, a wonderful example of the restriction to four vowels is illustrated:

"O Lotus-eyed One, through meditation upon your feet, desire, delusion, and even excessive greed dissolve away; whether it be worldly enjoyment, spiritual discipline, or liberation, all may be attained through your sidelong glance. (2328)
Here, only four vowels—namely *a*, *ā*, *i*, and *o*—are fixed.

May she—who is a moon to the night-lotuses of good fortune, a sky for the stars of the stability of Lakṣmī, and a sinless boat across the ocean of worldly existence—shine upon the earth for our welfare. 2329.

*Glauḥ* is the moon; stability (*sthairya*) and powers (*prabhāva*) are themselves the stars (*tārāḥ*), the *tārakāḥ*, and their sky (*dyauḥ*). *Padmā* is Lakṣmī. Here, these four vowels alone—*a*, *ā*, *ai*, and *au*—are fixed.

May she who dwells on the Nāga mountain, according to the rule of the three vowels, always protect me from the misfortunes of existence—she who bestows fortune, modesty, wisdom, splendor, fame, and love, while taking away all calamities. (2330)

She whose abode is the Naga mountain (Girivraja) and who dwells on the Śeṣa mountain; *hīḥ* is shame regarding what should not be done; *dhīḥ* is wisdom; *śrīḥ* is splendor; *kīrtiḥ* is fame; *prītiḥ* is affection for those who seek refuge—she possesses these in their multiplicity due to the diversity of their objects. *Dadhatī* means nourishing; *ītīḥ* refers to calamities, as Amara states: "The word *ītiḥ* denotes a riot or a plague. *Harantī* means removing. The construction is: may *Śrī*, the Goddess of Fortune, protect us from the ruin of existence—that is, from the misfortune that is the nature of *saṃsāra*. Here, there are only three vowels: *a*, *ā*, and *ī*.

O bestower of boons, O slayer of Mura, just as you are constantly praised by sages seeking liberation and indeed even by those seeking worldly enjoyment, so do you grant every single thing desired by them. 2331.
In this regard, these three vowels alone—*a*, *i*, and *u*—are strung together.
The rule of the two vowels is as follows:

in the Veda, in that which is to be known, in that which is to be meditated upon, in the immeasurable, in the beloved, in the actionless, in the imperishable; in that which is to be sung, in the unconquerable, in the God, in the Lord of Gods, in the one worthy of praise—my eye delighted in the Imperishable.

In every Veda—that is, in each individual Veda; in that which is to be known (*vedya*), i.e., that which is to be understood; in that which is to be meditated upon (*dhyeya*), i.e., that which is to be contemplated; in the immeasurable (*ameya*)—in the manner described by such passages as "from which words turn back"—that which is beyond the limitation of speech and the other senses, or that which is not within the scope of the three types of determination (*pariccheda*); in the beloved (*priya*), the object of unsurpassed affection; in the actionless (*akriya*)—in the manner described by such passages as "actionless and partless"—that which is not subject to karma; in the indestructible (*akṣeya*)—that which is not capable of being destroyed (*kṣetuṃ yogyaḥ kṣeyaḥ*), and thus *akṣeya*; in Him. This is a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) to the rule regarding the forms *kṣayya* and *jayya*.

This is an illustration of the absence of all modifications of existence (*bhāvavikāra*). "In that which is fit to be sung" (*geye*) means in that which is worthy of being chanted. "Unconquerable" (*ajeya*) means that which is not capable of being conquered; in Him. This too is indeed a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) to the aforementioned sūtra. "By the lords of gods" (*deveśaiḥ*), such as Brahmā and others, "to be praised" (*īḍye*) means worthy of hymn. "In the Lord, the Blessed One Śrīnivāsa," my eye—my vision—"rejoiced" (*reme*) means it took delight; the sense is that it became one-pointed in constant meditation upon Him.

In this context, the use of the perfect tense (*liṭ*) in "reme" indicates a state of remoteness resulting from his own being overwhelmed by joy; here, there is a restriction to these two vowels alone, namely *i* and *e*.

O Lotus-eyed One, O Giver of Boons, O Destroyer of the Enemies of Others, for me—whose every impurity has been destroyed by taking refuge at Your feet—the wondrous power of the restriction of Your single voice removes the exhaustion of wandering upon the path of the forest fire of worldly existence. 2333.

"O Destroyer of fear"—that is, the dispeller or destroyer of the terror caused by external enemies such as desire and the like; this is the vocative address. Herein, there is the composition of only a single short vowel, the letter *a*.

Now, the restriction of positions: therein, the restriction of four positions is as follows: "In the world of the mountains of vision and hearing, which sustains the movement of the Lord, there is the conduct of the wise, which is the ground of policy, discipline, splendor, fortitude, and majesty, and which maintains the stability of the Vedas and the law-books. (2334)

"Dṛṣṭiśruti" means one who hears with his eyes; "cakṣuśśravas" (the serpent) is he, and that which is the mountain is the Śeṣa-giri—this is the meaning. The "vibhu" (lord) of that is Śrīnivāsa; the "nutisṛtibhṛt" is one who bears the path of praise, that is, a hymn. Such a person on earth possesses both "dhī" (intellect) and "vṛtta" (conduct); these two are "dhīvṛtte. Since he has both "śobhane" (excellent) "sudhīvṛtte," the suffix *ini* is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), meaning he is one whose intellect and conduct are excellent. Thus, the meaning is: one of noble understanding and noble behavior.

He is the ground and the refuge of policy (nīti), method (naya), discipline (vinīti), humility (vinaya), splendor (dyuti), brilliance (tejas), fortitude (dhṛti), steadfastness (dhairya), prosperity (vibhūti), and sovereignty (aiśvarya). He knows the established order (sthiti) and the boundaries (maryādā) of both the Vedas (śruti) and the Dharmaśāstras (smṛti); thus he is "one who knows the stability of Śruti and Smṛti" (śrutismṛtisthitivit). According to Amarasimha, "maryādā," "dhāraṇā," and "sthiti" are synonyms. The word "he is" (bhavati) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

In this instance, the composition is formed solely by letters of the palatal (*tālavya*), retroflex (*mūrdhanya*), dental (*dantya*), and labial (*oṣṭhya*) classes; however, since it is said that "nasality is their additional quality," one should understand that there is no violation of the rule regarding place of articulation (*sthāna*) here, as the intention is merely to specify the dental nature of the letter *na*. This is also a *niṣkaṇṭhya-varṇa-citra* (a poetic figure consisting of non-guttural sounds). Furthermore, in this case, only these five vowels were employed: *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, and *ṛ*.

Although we have stated that the composition using only five vowels is not particularly difficult to achieve and is therefore not a marvel, nevertheless, it should be understood that when the placement of the phonemes is restricted, the restriction of the vowels follows as a necessary consequence, and thus even that is indeed marvelous.

O daughter of the glorious ocean, wonderful and joined with the celestial river, you who are vast, meditated upon by sages, the remainder, and the sovereign—may you take great delight in your beloved on this mountain.

The construction of the verse is as follows: "O you who are meditated upon by sages! O daughter of Śrīsindhu! O sovereign! O expansive one! O increased one! O wonderful one! O variegated one! O you who are joined with the celestial river! O you who are endowed with the Ākāśagaṅgā! O you who reside on the mountain Śeṣa, the Śeṣādri! You attain—along with your beloved Śrīnivāsa—an exalted, unsurpassed love and joy. This verse is composed of letters excluding those produced in the throat (*niṣkaṇṭhya-varṇa-grathita*). Here, "throat-sounds" (*kaṇṭhya*) refers exclusively to those produced solely in the throat; therefore, there is no fault even though the sounds *e* and *ai* (produced in the throat and palate) and the sound *o* (produced in the throat and lips) are present.

May the Lord of Ramā protect me—he whose sharp arrows and quiver are skilled at agitating the hosts of Rākṣasas, whose eyes are beautiful, and who destroys the rising power of the enemies of the gods.

He whose eyes are beautiful is *svakṣaḥ*; the suffix *ṭac* is applied at the end of the compound according to the rule *bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ*. As for the prohibition [of the suffix] by the rule *na pūjanāt*, it is restricted in the authoritative treatise (*ākara*) as applying only prior to the rule *bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ*. Here, the composition is made up exclusively of dentals (*tālavya*), and the restriction to five vowels is a secondary feature (*ānuṣaṅgika*).

"O mind, abandon your fickleness; ascend the five-weaponed god [Kāmadeva], who possesses a somewhat unshakable majesty, whose garment is lifted by the lord of the chamberlains [the wind], and who is the deity of the mountain [Himālaya].
(2337) Here, only the guttural, palatal, dental, and labial sounds have been employed. This very type is designated as "nirmūrdhanya" (devoid of retroflex sounds).

O Speech, serve that indescribable majesty which sports upon the ridges of the vast and lofty Veṅkaṭagiri, which possesses the charm of a lovely necklace, and which alone removes the heavy burden of fear arising from worldly existence. 2338.

O Bhavabhava, [I bow to] Him whose neck-ornament is captivating and beautiful, possessing the luster of a necklace, and who sports upon the slopes of that mountain Veṅkaṭa, which is vast and expansive with its peaks.

"O Speech (gīḥ), serve—that is, describe in detail—the very attributes of that Supreme Brahman alone, who is determined as a 'glory' (vaibhava) and who is the remover of the burden of fear; for He is the remover of the burden of fear arising from worldly existence (bhava). In this verse, the composition is made exclusively with letters produced in the throat (kaṇṭhya), the palate (tālavya), the roof of the mouth (mūrdhanya), and the lips (oṣṭhya). This is precisely what constitutes the "Dentally Excluded" (nirdantyacitra) figure.

Here, there is a prohibition against the use of purely dental sounds; therefore, it should be understood that there is no fault even if the letter *va*, which is produced at both the teeth and the lips, is present.

Just as one might seek refuge in some indescribable protector— the beautiful luster of the crest-jewel of the Lord of the Gods atop the peak of the mountain whose crown is the serpent-king, and who is the refuge for the most lovely of women— so too do I seek refuge at the outset.

The meaning is: "I accept as my refuge—that is, as my means (upāya)—a certain Person who is a protector, who is most delightful to the heart, and whose chest is a shelter, that is, a house for the heart."
The word *śaraṇa* belongs to the house-protector (*gṛharakṣitṛ*) in its conventional sense;
however, it is now employed here as a term that expresses solely the meaning of a means (*upāya*).
Thus it is stated in the Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā; in every respect, this [mantra] is to be pronounced without the dental *n*.

May she who is the Mother of the worlds, whose heart-dwelling is the Lord of the universe, who is expert in removing the suffering of people, whose eyes are as expansive as lotus petals, and who is the daughter of the ocean—may she, the joy of those who have taken refuge in her, bestow victory upon us. 2340.

In this [work], there is a composition consisting exclusively of sounds produced by the throat, palate, roof of the mouth, and teeth; this very fact is called "without labials" (*niroṣṭhya*). Here, the specific artistic charm (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) lies in the fact that only these five vowels—*a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, and *ṛ*—are employed.

Victory to you, O Lord who dwells in the sky-like expanse of the dense forest of the golden mountain, whose body is ever-expanding; O conqueror of the world’s sins, O cloud of compassion for the heavy burdened, O destroyer of hell, O rain-cloud that extinguishes the fire of the elephant's [Lord Gaṇeśa’s] tusk! 2341.

O you who dwell in the dense forest (*gahana*) of shining, radiant trees on the slopes of the golden mountain Vṛṣādri; O you who are constantly saluted by the sky-dwellers, the inhabitants of heaven; O giver of victory that is stainless (*anagha*) and free from suffering for the worlds; O cloud (*jalada*) for the fire of fear (*dara*) that is the elephant (*gaja*).

"O destroyer of hell, O enemy of hell, victory! Attain excellence! Here too, only the guttural (*kaṇṭhya*), palatal (*tālavya*), and retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) consonants are strung together. This [verse] consists of eight *niroṣṭhya* (labial-less) syllables, has a single vowel, and is entirely light; thus it is a specific variety of *vicchitti* (poetic charm) distinct from the previous one.

Adorned by the serpent Śeṣa, possessing auspicious attire, delighted by the hymns of the Lord of Speech (Brahmā), and the ornament of the hearts of women—she is that primordial deity who is both the remainder and the non-remainder of all.

She whose heart-ornament is the maiden Lakṣmī—she is this primordial deity (Ādidevatā). She to whom all [beings] without exception are subordinate (śeṣa), being her subordinates (śeṣabhūta)—she is she. Here, with reference to Śrīnivāsa, his status as the Lord of all without exception is enjoined. This is a *citram* (puzzle) verse lacking the nasalized (nāsikya) letter.

Thus has the rule regarding the phonemes in four positions been shown. Now, the rule regarding the phonemes in three positions is illustrated as follows: "Because of her boundless beauty and because of her ultimate tranquility, she who is an ocean of compassion, bestowed by the Lord of the Golden Mountain (Śiva), shines in the world, adorned with shimmering golden girdles. (2343)

The construction is as follows: "She who is beloved due to the infinity of her loveliness, who is most peaceful, who is charming and delightful, who is an ocean of compassion, who is adorned with a shining golden girdle, and who is the beloved of the Lord of the Golden Mountain (Meru)—she is victorious in the world. This is composed solely of guttural, palatal, and dental sounds; thus, it is a poetic figure characterized by the absence of labial and retroflex sounds (*niroṣṭhyamūrdhanyacitram*).

In this case as well, it should be understood that in the previously cited *niṣkaṇṭhya* verse "dṛṣṭiśrutibhūbhṛdvibhu," the letter *na* [in the word *nakha*] does not violate the rule regarding the restriction of place (sthāna), because there is merely an intention to express the dental nature of *na* and the palatal nature of the two *i*s. Otherwise, it would be an example solely of the restriction of the four places of articulation for the letters. Here, the restriction of three vowels—namely *a*, *ā*, and *i*—is also further established.

May there be victory for the Lord of the Mountain of the Sky (Viṣṇu), who bestows all desired objects, who has shattered the Daityas, whose fame is like the full moon, and whose radiance is cherished by the rows of water-laden clouds.

"Victory be to Śrīnivāsa, the Lord of Khagācala, whose fame is like the full moon and who possesses the glory of the complete moon"—this is the construction [of the verse]. Here, there is an invocation for the victory of the Blessed One, similar to [the verse] "Victory to you, O Lotus-eyed One. However, this is an example of the *śuddha-tristhāna-varṇa-niyama* (restriction of letters to three positions) because it is not interspersed with nasal sounds (*nāsikya*); this is its distinction from the previous example.
The rule regarding the phonemes in two positions is as follows:

"O Mahābhūmā (Great Earth), who removes the sins of those like me, who destroys the portion of arms that resemble the coils of serpents, who dispels the luster of the sun and moon, and who possesses the splendor of the sky-eating serpents upon the surface of the earth."

*Bhāmā* refers to Satyabhāmā; *bhāma* means anger (from the root *bhām*, "to be angry," with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state). According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *bhāma* denotes anger, the sun, and radiance. That which removes (*apohyate*) or dispels (*apanīyate*) this anger is *bhāmābhāmāpoha*. Those two [faces] possess a luster (*ābhā*) whose fullness (*ābhoga*)—meaning its complete expansion—is like that of a serpent’s body (*bhoga*).

"Bhoga-abhoga-ābha-bāhu-bhāk" means one who possesses arms resembling the coils of a serpent (*bhoga*). "Bhū-bhāga-makha-bhuj-aga-bhāk" means one who causes the portion of the earth (*bhū-bhāga*)—that is, a region of the ground—to serve the tree of the sacrifice (*makha-bhuj-aga*), namely the celestial tree (*svardruma*). This is derived from the root *bhaj* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) followed by the suffix *kvip*. The meaning is that he brought the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpataru*) to the earth. Alternatively, from the root *bhaj* in the sense of "bestowing" (*viśrāṇana*) belonging to the *curādigaṇa*, with the suffix *kvip*: the meaning is that he bestowed the wish-fulfilling tree upon the world of mortals. For this very reason, it is said that he is the dispeller of the luster of Bhāmā (*bhāmā-bhāmā-poha*).

Therefore, the Blessed One—the Great-Earthed One (Mahābhūmā) of vast majesty, the destroyer of evil (Aghahā), the slayer of the demon Aghāsura, the delighter of the Yadus, and the remover of my sins—is the one who takes away my misfortunes; this is the understood sense. Here, the composition is based solely on guttural and labial phonemes; thus, it is wonderful in being devoid of palatals, cerebrals, and dentals. Furthermore, as before, the letters *ma* and *ṅa* consist only of guttural and labial sounds, and the restriction of vowels is also reinforced here, as there are only five vowels: *a*, *ā*, *u*, *ū*, and *ā*.
The restriction of syllables to a single position is as follows:
*kākāghahā’ṅkagāṅkaḥ khagāṅkagāgāgagāhakaḥ khagagaḥ | aṅkāgāṅkāṅkāṅkagakaṅkakakaṅkākahā khagāṅkāṅkaḥ* || 2346 ||

*Kākāghahā*: He who destroys (*han*) the evil (*agham*)—that is, the suffering—of the crow (*kākasya*), the messenger of Indra (*aindrervāyasasya*); thus he is so called. *Aṅkagāṅkaḥ*: He whose chest (*aṅkaḥ*, meaning "bosom") goes to (*gacchati*) the mark (*aṅkam*) known as Śrīvatsa; that is to say, he whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa. The commentary (*kośa*) for this will be cited immediately below. *Khagāṅkagāgāgagāhakaḥ*: *Khagāḥ* refers to the sky-dwellers (the gods); those who go near (*aṅkagāḥ*) him are those who approach him, meaning he is exceedingly lofty (*atyunnata*). Thus described is *agāgaḥ*, which is the mountain of the serpents (*phaṇigiri*). As the *Ratnamālā* states: "The words *aga* and *naga* refer to a serpent, the navel, a tree, and a mountain."

Hemacandra also states: "The word *agā* [is used] for a tree, a mountain, a reptile, and the sun. Thus, *khagaṅkagāgāgaḥ* means one who goes (*aga*) to the moon (*khagaṅka*), that is, one who has entered the highest mountain, Śeṣācala (the mountain of Śeṣa); the suffix *ṇvul* is applied to the root *gāh* (to enter). Alternatively, it means one who goes by means of a bird (*khaga*).

*Khagagaḥ* means "he whose vehicle is Tārkṣya" (i.e., Garuḍa). The suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *gam* according to the Vārttika rule: "It should be stated that [the suffix] is seen elsewhere as well. Alternatively, he is *khagagaḥ* because he goes to the sky-dweller (the sun), meaning he resides within the solar orb, based on such scriptural passages (*śruti*) as, "He who is within the sun. He is *aṅkāgaḥ* because he does not go to a numerical count (*aṅka*), meaning he is beyond numbering (*asaṃkhyāka*). This refers to the sequence: *aṅkāga-aṅkāṅka-aṅkāṅka-aṅkaga-kaṅka-kaṅkāka-hāṅka*, which does not reach a finite number.

Alternatively, *aṅkāgaḥ* means that which does not go to *aṅka*, i.e., a stain; thus, it means "spotless. Or, *aṅka* refers to a "wager" or "spectacle," such as a marvelous battle (*citrayuddha*); that which goes to the vicinity (*aṅka*) of that place is *aṅkāṅkagaḥ*. Alternatively, *aṅka* means "offense"; that which does not go to that is *aṅkāgaḥ*, meaning "faultless. Thus, the term *aṅkāṅkagaḥ* is a *karmadhāraya* compound with two qualifying words. Such a one is *kaṅkakaḥ*, a vulture—meaning Jaṭāyu.

His *kaṅkākahā* is *kaṅka*, meaning Yama; he is so called because he destroys (*han*) the *aka*—that is, the suffering (*duḥkha*)—caused by him. This is derived from the root *han* with the suffix *kvip*. The sense is that by the Blessed One’s granting of a divine abode—as expressed in such passages as "the destination of those devoted to sacrifice"—the pain of traveling to the realm of Yama has been forcibly seized and cast away. [Lexical note: *Aka* means suffering or sin; *aṅka* means ornament, metaphor, mark, a spot in a variegated battle, a portion of a drama, a place, a lap, proximity, or a fault.

Thus says Hemacandra. *Khagāṅkāṅka* means that which is the mark (*aṅka*) of the sky (*kha*). "Sky" refers to the supreme ether (*paramavyoman*), and one who goes there is a "sky-goer" (*khaga*). This refers to the specific abode named Śrī Vaikuṇṭha, described in such passages as "the divine, undecaying, and immeasurable place. The meaning is that [the Lord] is its mark—that is, its ornament (*ābharaṇabhūta*).

The essential purport here is this: the Blessed Lord, whose vehicle is Tārkṣya, who dwells in the supreme ether (paramavyoman), and who bears the Śrīvatsa on His chest, having descended in the form of Rāma to remove the calamity of the demon Kāka and to bestow the highest beatitude upon Jaṭāyu, now resides on Śeṣādri in the form of an image (arcātman). By His dwelling in the supreme ether and so forth, His transcendence (paratva) is manifested; by His abiding in the form of His divine manifestation (vibhava-rūpa), His accessibility (saulabhya) is manifested; and by His abiding in the form of an image, His unsurpassed nature (niratiśayatva) is likewise manifested.
In this [verse], the composition of the poem is made solely with guttural vowels and consonants; they say that this poetic figure (*citram*) is difficult to achieve.
Now, the rule of color (varṇaniyama).
Among these, an example of a multicolored verse not belonging to the five groups is as follows, from my own *Prapannānanda-stuti*:

"She who dwells in the abode of the lotus, whose lovely laughter steals the light of the cool-rayed moon, who reclines upon a couch graced by excellent swans, that graceful Śrī has embraced [the Lord] with her head. (2347)

A loud laugh is a laugh with [open] lips; that Fortune (Śrī) took refuge upon his head—that is, she resorted to him. Here, due to the absence of letters belonging to the *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa* groups, only letters such as *ya* and others were employed. This very example is a figure of speech consisting of non-consonantal (*asparśa*) letters.

O Hare, who steals the wealth of Vāsava, who brings under control the most excellent of Asuras and destroys their valor; O Lord who sports together with Śrī, accompanied by the circle of cowherds—may you protect us. 2348.

O Hara! O Hari, who sports with Śrī! You who are the subduer of the best of Asuras, Bāṇāsura—the one who casts away (asyati) that foremost of Asuras who was himself under the control of the best of boons granted by Śambhu, namely the sacrifice (sava) of Vāsava’s master (Indra); you who are the companion of the circle of cowherds; protect me yourself, without requiring any service performed by me. This too is a *pañcavargīya* citra, as before.

May that indescribable splendor of the Lord of the World—variegated with infinite stops and sibilants, possessing the luster of the golden river [the Gaṅgā], and dense with majesty—grant me the intelligence of the wise, so that I may not fall into the proximity of those who are intoxicated by pride. 2349.

May Śrī—the one whose ground is firm, whose majesty is dense, who possesses the splendor of the Lord of the World, and who is beloved by the Sovereign of All—grant me intelligence. May I not go near the feet, the vicinity of the feet, or the presence of those who are excessively intoxicated, whether they be gods or men. The sense is: "May she so bestow upon me intelligence that I may not approach those who consider themselves masters of the ill-behaved. Here, only the consonants (sparśas), beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*, have been employed.

However, there is no fixed rule that the semivowels (antasthā) must be *y* and so forth, nor that the sibilants (ūṣman) must be *ś* and so forth; rather, the restriction on consonants is that only these specific ones are employed. Likewise, one should also observe the restriction on vowels, which are fixed as being only three: the letter *a*, the letter *ā*, and the letter *i*.
An example of the restriction to letters belonging to a single varga is as follows:

"O Lord, who are the source of the destruction of the miserable and the helpless, who are the treasury of manifold bliss, and who are not of recent origin—bow down to that Lord! (dhānādānādhīne dīnānāthādhidhūnananidāne | nānānandanidhāne nāthe'nadhunātane natiṃ nāthe ||)

By the gift of *dhānā* (parched grains) and *pṛthuka-taṇḍula* (flattened rice), [I offer salutation] to the Lord, the Ancient Person (*purāṇapuruṣa*), who is the master (*adhīna*)—that is, dependent upon Kucela; who is the cause (*nidāna*) for the shaking off (*dhūnana*) of the mental anguish (*ādhi*) of the wretched (*dīna*), the helpless, and those devoid of any other refuge; and who is the inexhaustible treasure (*nidhāna*) of manifold joys (*nānānanda*) that are practiced in a sequence of hundredfold increase. I pray for refuge (*nati*) in that Master (*nātha*). The use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in "I pray" (*āśāse*) is according to the rule "the root *nāth* is used in the sense of a blessing.
Here, the composition is constructed solely with letters belonging to the dental class (*tavargīya*).
Just as our Lord, the infinite leader of us who are leaderless, now [acts], so may He dispel that wretchedness of ours; therefore, may He gladden these prostrate ones by the gift of wisdom.

The Lord, the Sovereign of the World, the infinite Blessed One who is our leader—our guide for those of us who are protectorless and bereft of any other refuge—may He now, at this very moment, shake off that ineffable wretchedness; that is to say, may He uproot it so that it never arises again.

Thereafter, may He gladden and satisfy us, these who are bowed before Him, by the gift of wisdom, through the bestowal of the yoga of intellect as stated in the words, "I grant that yoga of wisdom. Here too, there is a restriction to the use of only the *ta*-class consonants (*tavarga*).

O Mother, whose luster is like the light of the sun; O Mother, who dispels the fear of me who am overwhelmed by the sins of worldly existence; O Mother, whose ground is like the orb of the rising sun; O Mother, who possesses a splendor that overcomes all fear! 2352.

*Bhūbhūpāpābhibhū* refers to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva; he is so called because he overcomes (*abhibhavati*) *bhūbhūpāpa*, which means either *bhūbhū* (one who is born on earth) who is a sinner—the most wicked son of Bhīma, Naraka—or else those born on earth (*bhūbhuvaḥ*) who are sinners, such as Pralamba, Baka, Cāṇūra, Kaṃsa, Śiśupāla, and others. His *bhāme* means his two wives.

The waters of sin are like [ordinary] water; those who are sinful are the "lokas. He whose reflection is the sun-disk (papī-bimba) is the "papī"; she whose greatness (bhūmā) consists of such [sinners] is addressed here as "papībhūme" (O you whose greatness is such). By this, her similarity to the beloved is indicated, for it is said: "She always possesses the qualities of that [beloved]. The feminine suffix *ḍāp* is applied according to the rule "ḍābubhābhyāmanyatarasyām. From the root *pā* (to protect), the form "papīḥ" is derived by adding the suffix *ī* and doubling the root, according to the rule "yāpoḥ kiddve ca"; thus, grammarians state, "papīḥ is the sun."

"Bhīmā" means extremely fierce, the radiance or power (*prabhāva*) of the wicked; as the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *bhās* denotes power and brilliance. She is the "ground" (*bhūmi*), that is, the substratum of that [power]. The vocative form is "O Sītā, you who are the ground of that [power]. The sense is: she is the locus of divine majesty that strikes fear into enemy hosts, as is well known from such passages as "She was consumed by the splendor of Sītā's luster; even the flame of fire could not have done that. Alternatively, there is a word-split as *abhīmā*, meaning "favorable" (*anugrā*); [as in the prayer] "Be gracious (*śīto bhava*)."

The meaning is: "the ground (bhūmi) of that gentle radiance (bhā)," which, according to the manner stated in the passage beginning with "No one does not commit an offense," refers to the gracious power (prabhāva) toward those who have taken refuge. "O Mother!"—this is the ellipsis. Being such as to possess a luster (ābhā) like that of the constellation Bhā (Bharaṇī), you thus became *abābhāḥ*, meaning you shone intensely (*abhāḥ*). This is from the root *bhā* in its yaṅluk form, in the imperfect tense (*laṅ*). Here, the composition is formed exclusively with letters of the labial class (*pavarga*).

I bow to that one who possesses diverse faces, whose mind is not uplifted, who is free from pride, and who is the refuge for those with various faces—He who is indeed the nameless, the nameless-faced, the nameless, the nameless-minded, the nameless-prideful, and the nameless-nameless. 2353.

The word division is as follows: *nāmānanāni*, *nāma*, *āmanāni*, *māminīnanāmāni*, *nūnam*, *ananunnamanamanāḥ*, *namāmi*, *nānā*, *ananānamanam*, *enam*, *iti*. Those whose *mānana* (reverence) is non-existent (*avidyamāna*) are called *nāmānanāni*; however, [the names here] are not so, meaning they are exceedingly worthy of reverence (*atimātramānanīya*). *Mā* is Lakṣmī; *māninī* is her [wife]; *ina* is her lord, meaning Śrīnivāsa. His *nāmāni* (names) are indeed (*nūnam*), that is, certainly, *āmanāni* (to be practiced or repeated). *Ananunnamanamanāḥ*: one whose mind (*manas*) is neither excessively elevated (*nunna*) nor depressed (*nata*). *Nānā*: in various ways. *Ananānamanam*: that which is not bowed down by sin (*ana* = sin). *Enam*: him [the Lord]. Thus is the analysis of the words.

From the root *mnā* preceded by the prefix *ā*, the substitution *man* occurs according to the rule "pā-ghrā-dhmā... and so forth. This is the first person singular of the imperative (*loṭ*). The sense is: "May I repeatedly chant the names of Śrīnivāsa. He whose mind is *anunnamana*—that is, not elevated—is one who is not haughty; this is the meaning. Hence, Amara states: "Pride (*māna*) is the elevation of the mind. *Ananāmana* means *anana*, which signifies that which causes life or brings about revival. He to whom such a bowing—that is, prostration—belongs is [the object of the verse].
Even a single well-performed prostration made to Kṛṣṇa is equal to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of ten horse-sacrifices.
One who has performed ten horse-sacrifices returns to birth again, but one who bows to Kṛṣṇa does not return for the sake of further existence.

Based on such authoritative evidence, I bow down to this Śrīnivāsa in many ways—that is, in manifold manners. The sense is that there is certainly no room for doubt whatsoever in this matter. This [verse] is composed with two consonants joined by a nasal.
Just as I,
who am free from pride, bow down to the one whose name is not known by various sages, who is beyond thought and mind, and who is the measure of the immeasurable—
I truly worship Him, the Mother of the world, who is free from the conceit of "mine," and whom I approach with reverence.

She whose name is the "life-giver" (*anana*)—the repeated chanting of the names of those various and many sages who are the best of ascetics (*maunīnāṃ muniśreṣṭhānām*). She is called *mānā* because she is honored (*mānyate*) by Umā (Gaurī) in her mind; here the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), according to the rule "also when not denoting an agent, provided it is a technical term" (*akartari ca kārake saṃjñāyām*). They say that the restriction "provided it is a technical term" is merely illustrative. Furthermore, although ending in *ghañ*, this word is variable in gender (*bhedyaliṅga*), for the *Liṅgānuśāsana* states: "But when following words such as 'object' (*karman*), even a word ending in *ghañ* takes the gender of the substantive."

Alternatively, *māna* means "honoring" (derived from the root *mān* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state). She who possesses such honoring of me (*umā-manas-māna*) is so described; her I honor—that is, I seek refuge in her, Śrī. May I certainly not go to—meaning, may I never attain—*amānanā*, which is devoid of worship, or *amā*, which is misfortune (*alakṣmī*). The sense is that immediately after choosing refuge in Lakṣmī, misfortune surely perishes. The meaning of the Vedic verse, "I seek refuge in her whose wheels are lotuses; may misfortune perish for me; I choose you," is reflected here.
This too, as before, contains exactly two consonants.

O you who are bowed down, extend that protection which has been spread out for those who bow; O Leader, do not abandon the lowly, but protect those who are uplifted and those who have reached the end of suffering, O Infinite One.

May the Infinite One (Ananta), the Father (Tāta) of the Effulgent One (Atanu), the Leader (Netā), lead these very ones—us, who are his followers—to the thinning of the fatigue of those who are bowed down, and to the attenuation [of their suffering].

[The word division is as follows: *tāntim*, *tatām*, *natānām*, *tanutām*, *netā*, *tanotu*, *tān*, *etān*, *netā*, *naḥ*, *atanutaḥ*, *tātaḥ*, *anītīn*, *nantṝn*, *nitāntataḥ*, *anantaḥ*. *Explanation:* "Fatigue" (*tānti*) means exhaustion; "extended" (*tatām*) means widespread. "Of those who are bowed down" (*natānām*). "To the thinning" (*tanutām*) means to the state of being diminished. "The Leader" (*netā*) means one who causes to reach; [the suffix] *tṛn* is used here. Precisely for this reason, there is no genitive case governed by a *kṛt* suffix. "The Father of Atanu" (*atanos tātaḥ*) means the progenitor. "The Leader" (*netā*) means the Lord. "The Infinite One" (*anantaḥ*) refers to the Blessed One. "Those who bow" (*nantṝn*) refers to those who have come for refuge. "These very ones" (*etān tān*) refers to us. The meaning is: "We, who have said 'We are to be protected by you,' are yours"—that is, we are your own.

"Anītīn" means those for whom calamity (*īti*), that is, suffering (*pīḍā*), does not exist—meaning those whose affliction caused by the association with ignorance has ceased. "Tanotu" means "may he extend" or "may he perform. Here, because two consonants belonging to the same class (*ekavargīya*) are joined together, this is a "double-consonant figure" (*dvivyañjanacitra*), which possesses a distinction from the previous example.

Just as the support of the mountains that hold the clouds which hold the streams [of rain], so was he worshipped— the one who holds the burden of wisdom, the supporter of the earth, and the sustainer of the stream from Rādhā’s lips.

The meaning is that he is "cool" because he is constantly moistened by the downpours of water from the clouds—that is, the streams of rain from the incessant, thick, and heavy clouds—and thus he is celebrated in the divine compositions. He is the one whose support or locus is that mountain which is both a "supporter of the earth" (dharādhara)—referring to Śeṣa—and a "mountain" (dharādhara); thus, the sense is that he dwells upon the mountain of Śeṣa, characterized by the aforementioned attributes.

*Rādhādharadhārādhāḥ*: one who drinks (*dhā*) the streams (*dhārāḥ*) of the nectar of Rādhā’s lower lip (*adharasya adhararasasya*). [The suffix] *kvip* is applied to the root *dheṭ* (to drink). *Dhīraḥ*: steadfast, possessing fortitude "like Himavat through his stability," according to the stated manner; the meaning is "of the *dhīras*, i.e., yogis whose minds are restrained from sense objects. For the Pātañjala Sūtra states: "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. *Dhurandharaḥ*: one who takes upon himself the burden of protecting them.

For it is recited among His names: "Yoga, the leader of those who know yoga. Alternatively, according to the manner stated in such passages as "Clearly He is the Great Yogin, the eternal Supreme Self," the meaning is that He is the Lord of yogins. *Arādhi* means "was worshipped"; "by us" is the ellipsis. The suffix *ciṇ* is used in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense for the passive (*karmaṇi*) of the root *rādh*. Here too, the composition is achieved solely through two consonants, as before; furthermore, there is a specific type of *yamaka* (rhyme/parallelism) in the first half-verse, which constitutes its distinction.
Just as [the following verse]:

"The one who has destroyed the poverty of those whose enemies have been destroyed, whose chests are free from fear, who has shattered the cities of his foes, and who is not poor—[that Lord] has rent asunder the heart of the enemy, which was fierce, difficult to behold, hollow, and full of distress. (2357)
The division of the verse is as follows: *dur-ari-dara-dārida-radoḥ uro-ararodāra-dāra-dāridrī raudrāri-dur-dara-udara-dara-dāra-durodarādara adāri*. [This refers to] the fierce one (*raudra*).

He who is fierce; he who is the enemy and adversary, Hiraṇyakaśipu; he who is *durdara*, impossible to pierce or shatter; he who is the *udaradara*, the cavity of the belly (for *adara* means "fear" or "cavity," according to Amara: *adaro'striyāṃ bhaye śvabhre*). He for whom the *dāra*—the act of splitting or tearing—is the *durodara*, whether as a game of dice or a wager, and who possesses *ādara* (respect) for that; or else, he who is *adara* (fearless) toward him. Or rather, *raudrāridurdarodaradaradāre durodaraḥ* refers to a gambler or a daring person (*dyūtakāraḥ*, *sāhasikaḥ*); this is his address.

*Durōdara*: According to Amara, *durōdara* refers to a gambler, a stake, or gambling itself. *Urorarara*: *uraḥ* (chest) is like an *araram* (door-panel); thus, *uro'raram*. He whose *dārāḥ* (wives) possess that which is *udārāḥ*—meaning they possess the nobility (*audārya*) described in the Śruti as "the noble prosperity cherished by the gods in this world"—is addressed here. The meaning is: one whose chest, broad as a door-panel, is the abode of Śrī (Goddess Lakṣmī).

"Duraridaradau" means those two which grant fear (*dara*)—that is, terror—to wicked enemies (*dur-ari-śātrava*). He whose arms (*doṣau*) are thus described as "duraridaradau" (the discus and conch); [this is] the vocative case of such a person. [The Amarakośa states: "Bhuja, bāhu, praveṣṭa, and doḥ [are synonyms for arm]. O bearer of the conch and discus! O Blessed One!—this is the meaning. "Dāridrī" refers to poverty (*dāridryam*); because [the word *daridra*] belongs to the class of words beginning with *brāhmaṇa*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied, and due to the presence of the letter *ṣ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added according to the rule "ṣid-gaurādibhyaḥ. [Thus,] she has destroyed (*adāri*) poverty.

The sense is that for me, who takes refuge in You, Śrīnivāsa, all forms of wretchedness—such as the lack of devotion, detachment, and the wealth of knowledge—have been rent asunder; or rather, it has burst open of its own accord. This is derived from the root *dṛ* (to tear), used in the passive or reflexive voice (*karmakartṛ*) with the *luṅ* suffix and the *ciṇ* affix.

Just as the mountain-dwelling elephants following the path of the sky, those whose gait follows song, who are free from sin, and who are not serpents—do they not indeed lead us, O Lord, by means of various mountains, serpents, faces, and mountains, toward the state of non-attachment? 2358.

The word-division is: *gaganaganaga anugānāṃ gānānuganāga go'nana anāgaḥ nānānaganāgānananāganagena āninaḥ nu naḥ nanu gāḥ*. *Anugānām* means "of the followers," that is, of those who have taken refuge [in you]. *Gaganaganaga* refers to the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpaśākhin*).

"O you whose serpents—those with hoods—follow the songs, following the melody of the flute played by yourself! This address is based on the saying: "A child knows, a beast knows, and a serpent knows the essence of song. [The name] *Gānānuga* means "one whose followers are the songs. *Gavānana* means "the life-sustainer of cows (dhenu). *Anāgas* means "one whose sins are destroyed"; according to Amara, *āgas* refers to sin or offense. *Nanu* is used here as a gentle form of address.

O Lord of the Mountain of Serpents (Nāganaga)—that is, Śrīnivāsa, the master of Śeṣādri, the sustainer (ānana) of various and manifold mountains (nagāḥ), trees (taravaḥ), serpents (nāgāḥ), and elephants (gajāḥ)—you have, by the process described in the verse, "He who, entering within, revives this speech of mine which was dormant by His own splendor," brought to life (āninat) our words (gāḥ) consisting of praise. This is the meaning of the second person singular imperfect (luṅ) of the causative form of the root *an* (to breathe/live).
The word "nu" is used here as a particle of emphasis. The distinction in the three cited verses is that they are composed with two consonants belonging to different vargas (classes).
A single consonant is variegated, just as:

"nūnaṃ no nānenānenā nenena nonena | nānainonunnānāṃ nānainenānanī na no nanu nauḥ ||" (2359) Indeed, for us, it is not by this [one], nor by that [other], nor by this one, nor by that one; for those who are not pushed away by various [factors], there is no boat, nor is there a boat for us, alas! Not by this one, nor by that one, nor by this one, nor by that one. Indeed, for us, it is not so. Nor is there a boat for the two of us. || 2359 ||

The word-division (*padaccheda*) is as follows: *nūnaṃ*, *no*, *na*, *anena*, *anenāḥ*, *nā*, *inena*, *nonena*, *nānainonunnānām*, *nānā*, *enena*, *ananī*, *na*, *naḥ*, *nanu*, *nauḥ*. *Nonena*: not deficient (*ūna*), thus "nona"; by him, [thus] "nonena. This means: by the most excellent one. *Anena inena svāminā bhagavatā hetubhūtena*: by this Lord, the Blessed One, acting as the cause; *nā kaścid api pumān*: no man at all; *anenāḥ*: one whose sin (*enaḥ*) is non-existent (*avidyamāna*); *no iti na*: "not [is he] 'no' [sinless]"—that is not so. Rather, he is indeed sinless (*anenā eva*). The word *nūnam* is used for an extreme degree of certainty regarding the matter already stated. *Nānainonunnānām*: of those who have not been driven away (*nunna*) by various (*nānā*) sins (*ainaḥ*). *Nānā*: in various ways. *Enena*: by this [Lord]. *Ananī*: one who is without end (*ani*). *Na naḥ*: "not us"—that is not so. *Nanu nauḥ*: "surely our boat"—that is not so. (The sense is that we are not merely saved from the flood, but are made sinless by the Lord.)

And by this Blessed One, we—who have been driven away, cast off by those various kinds of sinful transgressions (*enāṃsi*)—have been provided with a boat (*nauḥ*), that is to say, the means of crossing over; [the word *enan* is used here as a substitute for *etena* in the sense of a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), according to the rule *advitīyā ṭaussvenaḥ*; and the word *nānā* takes the instrumental case according to the rule *pṛthagvinā nānābhiḥ*; as Amara states: *pṛthagvināntareṇarte hirunānā ca varjane*]. It is a boat that leads us across, meaning the equipment for our deliverance.

"Not indeed; not at all. The word *nanu* is used here for emphasis. Since every person is liberated from sin by this Blessed Lord Śrīnivāsa, the sense is that, apart from him, there is certainly no one else who can carry us across the ocean of worldly existence—us who are overwhelmed by various kinds of evil deeds. In this verse, the poetic composition is formed using only a single negative particle (*na*).
Just as:
"O you who are playful, restless, charming, sweet-voiced, and full of grace; O you whose play is ever-moving, who are radiant and delightful, who are beautiful and full of sport! (2360)

*Līlālolelālīlālīlalaḥ*: She who fondles the friend *ilā*—that is, the Earth—who is *lolā*, meaning attached or devoted, to *līlās*, that is, playful diversions; thus she is *līlālolelālīlālinī*. Furthermore, she is the *ālī*, a row or series, of *ilās*, which here means words; the masculine form is applied according to the rule "puṃvat karmadhāraye" (the first member of a karmadhāraya compound takes the masculine gender). Thus: *līlālolelālīlālīlālī*.

He is called *lala* because he sports (*lalati*) with her; from the root *laḍ* (meaning "to sport") with the suffix *ac*. The meaning is: one who sports with the series of playful words of his friend the Earth, who is attached to his play. Alternatively, *alilīlālāḥ*: *ali* means a bee; its *līlā* is its grace, which is to say, its splendor. He is so called because he takes (*lāti*) or assumes that [splendor]. As in the verse, "Your pair of eyes bears the grace of blue lotuses," the meaning is that his radiance is similar to theirs. The suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *lā* (meaning "to take").

*Lolollolelālaṃlīlālālaḥ*: She in whom there are *lolāḥ* (fickle), *cañcalāḥ* (restless), and *ullolāḥ* (surging) great waves; she is thus *lolollolā*. And she is *ilā*; for Amara states: "The words *ilā*, *jala*, *bhū*, *go*, and *vāk* all mean earth, water, and speech. Thus, it refers to the waters of the great ocean at the time of universal dissolution (*pralaya-mahodadhi-jala*). *Alaṃlīḥ*: That which completely dissolves (*alam līyate*) is *alaṃlīḥ*. From the root *lī* (to adhere/to dissolve), belonging to the *divādi* class, the suffix *kvip* is applied. She is that *ilā*—either the Earth or the Vedic Speech—and her *lā* is the taking up (*ādāna*); for it is said: "*La* [is used] for Indra, but *lā* is used for giving and also for grasping. Thus, the compound means: He who is the one who takes up the Earth (or the Veda) that completely dissolves within the waters of the great ocean at the end of the world.

According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The root *lī* [is used] in the sense of clinging (*śleṣaṇa*) and in the sense of being fickle (*capala*). From that [root], one who "plays" (*alati*) is an *ala*. The meaning is "sufficient" (*paryāpta*). This is derived from the verbal root *ala*—meaning "ornamentation," "sufficiency," and "prevention"—with the suffix *pacādyac*. The meaning is: he who uplifts the earth submerged in the great ocean, or the Vedic speech. He "played" (*lalāla*), "shone forth" (*vilalāsa*). This is from the root *lala*, meaning "sport" (*vilāsa*), in the perfect tense (*liṭ*). *Lolāla*: *Lolā* means Lakṣmī. According to the *Medinī*: "The word *lolā* may be used as an adjective for both genders; it means 'greedy,' 'fickle,' or it is feminine when referring to the tongue or a lotus. And according to the *Hemacandra*: "*Lolā* [is used] for the tongue and for Śrī (Lakṣmī)."

The word *ala* means "that which adorns" or "beautifies"; it is derived from the aforementioned root with the suffix *pacādyac*. Thus, *lolāla* means "the ornament of the fickle one" (*lolāyā alaḥ*). Alternatively, *lolāla* means "he who sports with the fickle one" (*lolāṃ lalati*), formed with the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of the object. Or again, *lolāla* means "he who dissolves into the fickle one" (*lolāyāṃ lināti*), using the root *lī* in the sense of "adhering," with the suffix *ḍa* according to the rule "it is seen after other roots as well" (*anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*) following the *krayyādi* group. Or else, *lā* means "she who dissolves" (*lināti*); thus, *lolāla* is "he in whom the fickle one (*lolā*) is the *lā*. In every case, the meaning is simply "the Beloved of Śrī. The construction is *lalāla*.

Here, the poetic composition is formed with the letter *la* alone; therefore, this is a one-syllable figure (*ekākṣara-citra*) consisting of no letters from the five classes of consonants (*apañcavargīya-varṇa*).

May that abode, which is variegated by the regulation of the seven musical notes, which possesses a weightless gravity in the union with Māninī, which destroys the enemies of the enemy of the mountain-dweller (Śiva), which has cast out pride from the Vedas, and which bestows wealth upon me who am near it— may that abode [grant] the destruction of my sins.

The thought "May she not be Lakṣmī" [is held by] the proud bride; through union with her, his greatness (garimā)—meaning his weight or dignity—is peerless (nissama), that is, incomparable. The sense is that such majesty belongs to him precisely because he is the beloved of Śrī. He is called *aridāriṇī* because he tears apart (dārin) his enemies; and he is *sāri-gada*, meaning one who possesses the *sāri*—that is, the discus (*ari*)—along with the mace *Kaumodakī*.

*Nigamāpasāridamadam*: He who bestows punishment (*dama*) or restraint upon those such as Madhu and Kaiṭabha, who are *apasārin*—that is, thieves or plunderers (*apahartṛ*) of the *nigama*, the Veda. *Dhanī*: One who possesses wealth; *dāsadhani* means "one whose wealth consists of servants," implying that his servants are not distinct from his wealth. The sense is that his servants, like his wealth, are to be protected. *Dhāma*: Splendor or luster.

The meaning is "the Supreme Brahman. [He] has cast away my sins: this is from the root *asu* (in the sense of "casting") belonging to the *divādi* class, in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense. Here, the composition of the verse is made using only the syllables *sa*, *ri*, *ga*, *ma*, *pa*, *dha*, and *ni*, which represent the seven notes well-known in the science of music (*saṃgītaśāstra*). It should be noted that in the circles of singers, it is well known that the notes *ṛṣabha* and *ṣaḍja* are pronounced by the syllables *ri* and *sa* respectively, while the note *dhaivata* is pronounced by both the syllables *dha* and *da*; thus, the weaving together of both *da* and *dha* is to be understood here.

As it is said by me myself in the *Raṅgarājavilāsa*: "O Mādhava, do not ever set foot in my abode! O Gadādhara, always bestow that [peace] upon me! O Pāpa (Sin), speak words of praise! Do not, O Māmadari (O Mother of Māda), treat me as a slave! (2362)

This verse, rendered by the lute (vīṇā), is spoken by Lakṣmī upon suspecting that the Lord Raṅgarāja has returned from the festival of his hunting excursion accompanied by another woman. Thus: *dadhaḥ* means "one who holds" (*dadhāti*). *Gadārin* refers to the mace and the discus—Kaumodakī and Sudarśana; hence, it means "O bearer of the mace and the discus. This is its vocative form. "In my abode, in my home, do not, do not place your foot (*padaṃ mā mādhāḥ*); do not set it down. The repetition of "do not" (*mā*) is due to the agitation of her anger.

In the *luṅ* (aorist) following the root *dhāñ* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, there is a prohibition of the augment *aṭ* due to the rule "na māṅyoge" (Pāṇini 6.4.74). To the question "Whence comes such anger?", he replies with the words beginning with "āsa. The sense is: "That and that wicked woman was my co-wife. She does not mention her name out of intolerance. She was the "locus"—that is, the recipient—of your speech, which was a formal proclamation (*nigada*). Her very conversation was dear to you; the sense is: "Do not address me with that woman, do not converse with her. This word is *mā*, not the prohibitive particle *māṅ*; therefore, there is no *luṅ*.

Fearing that he might entreat her with flatteries such as "You alone are truly my beloved," she addresses him with excessive anger as "Madarimāninī-dāsa" (the slave of the woman who considers herself superior to me). The meaning is: "the servant of the woman who is my rival. Here too, as before, only the seven musical notes—sa, ri, ga, ma, pa, dha, ni—are employed as phonemes.

"Immediately after I have departed," said Śrī in anger; and as if imitating those words devoid of essence, the lute delighted the King of the Stage with its collections of notes, exceedingly beautiful.

One should recognize that as "variegated" (citra) where there is no repetition of phonemes— such as *ka*, *kha*, and so forth— and thus it consists of non-repeated syllables. This is the variegated [type].
O rogue mind, come always to the cow who is like the peak of Mount Ṛṣabha— crushing with her excessive compassion, filled with the brilliance of vital energy, and ever-prosperous.

The word *atha* signifies auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). As Amarasimha states: "The word *atha* [is used] in the senses of auspiciousness, immediate succession, commencement, inquiry, and totality. This indeclinable (*avyaya*) is listed both at the beginning [of the list of particles] and among the vowels. Consequently, its status as an indeclinable is established even when it functions as a substantive denoting auspiciousness. For this very reason, Śrī Harṣa [wrote]:
"Then, having lifted the golden jars upon the interior of the altar-platform, which was beautiful with its fourfold splendor..."
Then, according to family custom, the group of matrons bathed that daughter of the lord of the earth.

Thus [it is said]. For here, the meaning of "atha snapayāṃbabhūva" is "he performed an auspicious bath. The particle "atha," by its very nature, is auspicious, like the sound of a drum. Nor should it be asked why, in this verse of Śrīharṣa, the meaning of "atha" might not simply be "immediacy" (anantarya).

Because two instances of the word *atha* are heard [in the verse], it must necessarily be stated that the *atha* occurring in the first half has the sense of "immediacy" (*ānantarya*), while the *atha* occurring in the second half has the sense of "auspiciousness" (*maṅgala*); otherwise, the fault of tautology (*paunaruktya*) would be unavoidable. Let this suffice for now. Now, as for the auspicious one: the meaning is "the Blessed Lady who is like a crest-jewel (*āpīḍa*) upon the peak (*kūṭa*), the summit, of that Ṛṣabhācala, the Vṛṣādri mountain. This is the substantive (*viśeṣya*).

*Atighṛṇā* means excessive compassion (*ghṛṇā*), that is, unsurpassed mercy (*karuṇā*). That itself is a *jharī*, meaning a stream or flow; by that [stream]. *Bāḍhe* means "excellent" or "highly praised," according to Amara’s lexicon: "The word *bāḍham* is used for 'excessive' and 'highly praised'. *Avaḥ* refers to one who protects (*avati*) the cows—meaning either the milch-cows (*dhenūnām*) or the Vedic words (*vedavācām*)—or the earth (*goḥ bhuvaḥ*) and heaven (*divaḥ*). [He is] always prosperous (*sadā ṛddhe*), that is, possessed of abundance.

O mind, you rogue, you scoundrel! Go—go to Śrīnivāsa for refuge. [The word] *ojas* refers to splendor; [the compound] *ojaskhacchāya* means that whose shadow (*chāyā*) is in the sky (*kha*), that is, in the expanse of space, meaning one who is dark as the vault of heaven. According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The word *chāyā* is used for lack of sunlight, beauty, reflection, and the wife of the Sun.
