And Hemacandra states: "The word *chāyā* is used for a row and a reflection. The locative case is used here because the action of going is intended to have the object as its locus. The meaning is: "Go to Śrīnivāsa for shelter."

In this regard, it has been stated that the consonant (*vyañjana*) is not repeated; thus, this is the poetic figure named *apunaruktavyañjana* (non-repetition of consonants). It should be noted that even when there is a repetition of vowels (*ac*), there is no repetition of consonants.

Now, I praise the beautiful and doubt-free one, who is a masterpiece of both refined Sanskrit and Prakrit; whose abode is the mountain of the best of serpents (Śeṣa); whose arms are the ocean of the flow of sweetness; and who is a mass of jewels of excellent qualities. 2365.

I meditate upon Him who dwells on the mountain that supports the earth, who is a necklace of jewels bearing a lovely mass of great rays, who is far removed from the multitude of qualities to be abandoned, whose qualities are to be sung, and who is accompanied by His retinue.

I meditate upon Him whose gentle smile is like a cluster of jasmine flowers, whose limbs shine with the delicate beauty of blue lotus petals, who dwells on the coiled mountain (Śeṣa), and who is radiant with the playful grace of Lakṣmī. 2367.
In these three verses as well, the forms of the words are identical in both the Sanskrit and Prākrit languages; thus, this is *samasaṃskṛtaprākṛta* (equal Sanskrit-Prākrit).
Now, variegated [colors] such as lotuses and so forth,
having assumed the form of a lotus and so forth, are cited as "variegation" (citra).

If it is asked, "How can this be a verbal ornament (*śabdālaṃkāra*), since the form of the lotus and so forth resides in the lines and sub-lines [of the script]?"—the answer is true. However, they say that this designation as a verbal ornament is merely figurative (*aupacārikī*), because there is a metaphorical attribution (*adhyavasāya*) of the forms—which actually reside in the lines that indicate the phonemes—to the phonemes themselves which are to be inferred.
In that regard, if there should be a single sixteen-petaled lotus where every syllable is separated by one [empty space],
that sixteen-petaled lotus has its phonemes joined to the pericarp.
If a single type of syllable is composed such that it is separated by another single syllable and joined at the pericarp, that sixteen-petaled lotus is called a *citra* (variegated) pattern.

She who is as white as a star, the embodiment of glory, the bestower of wealth, the one who grants success, and who is ever-smiling; she who is to be propitiated by kings, who is near at hand, vast, and whose hands hold the earth and the ocean.

*Tārā* (the Savior); *tarakā* (the Star); she who possesses a fair form and a fair complexion (*gaurākṛti-gauravarṇā*). She whose wealth (*rāḥ*)—meaning power or prosperity—is perfected and established (*rāddha-siddha-rāḥ*). She whose face is smiling (*smerā*), meaning with a laughing countenance. She who is to be propitiated by kings (*rājabhir-ārādhyā*). She whose support (*ādhāraḥ*)—meaning her locus or foundation—is the vast (*sphāraḥ*) and extensive (*viśālaḥ*) Śeṣa, the King of Serpents (*ahīrādharaḥ*), who is himself the mine (*ākaraḥ*), meaning the most excellent or the source of manifestation. According to Amara: "The word *irā* may mean earth, speech, liquor, or water. According to Medinī: "The word *ākara* is said to refer to a collection, a place of origin, or something excellent."

That well-known Śrī, Lakṣmī, quickly—that is, immediately—bestows (rāti) riches (rāyaḥ), wealth; [the root] *rā* means "to give. This very same composition is both a *dvicatuṣkabandha* and a *gomūtrikā*. As for its definition: "That which consists of internal and external circles, moving through as many squares as there are, and joined with eight corners—that the wise know as *dvicatuṣka*."
If, in that [verse], the syllables are interlaced with odd-numbered syllables or even-numbered syllables,
then this very [pattern] attains the renown of *gomūtrikā*.

Thus it is said. This is what is meant: having drawn two intersecting four-sided wheels (caturaracakras), one facing the cardinal directions and the other facing the intermediate directions, and having drawn two concentric circular lines (maṇḍalarekhā) both outside and inside them, and having divided each of these into eight compartments, one should write the unjoined syllables of the first half in the outer circle and the unjoined syllables of the second half in the inner circle; then, one should write the eight joined syllables of the two halves within the eight corners formed between the two circles.

Thus, because it is distinguished by having two sets of four corners, it is designated as "dvicatuṣka. This is a *gomūtrikā* (cow’s urine pattern) composed of even syllables arranged in direct order (*anuloma*). Here, the contact with the mandala is preceded by the contact with the corners. Likewise, there will also be a *gomūtrikā* when composed of odd syllables; however, the distinction to be understood is that in that case, the contact with the corners is preceded by the contact with the mandala.
Just as a young woman— unsteady and trembling with the playful sport of swinging on a mountain of serpents,
possessing beauty, crossing the shore, wearing a garland, and being entirely devoid of impropriety— [is so described]. (2369)

She was intent (*lolā*)—that is, devoted—to the sport of swinging (*dolālīlā*), the act of swaying, upon the earth (*ilāyām*, i.e., *dharāyām*) of the mountain of Śeṣa (*vyālādriḥ*). She was immovable (*acalā*), her heart steady; she was the "immovable girl" (*acalā-bālā*), meaning the daughter of the Earth. This is the subject (*viśeṣya*). She is "possessing beauty" (*śrīlā*), meaning beautiful. The suffix *lac* is used here in the sense of possession according to the rule for words beginning with *sidhma*. As Amara states: "One who possesses *lakṣmī* (fortune) is *lakṣmaṇaḥ* or *śrīlaḥ*. She is one by whom all (*akhilāni*) improper (*aślīlāni*) and inauspicious things (*khilāni*, i.e., destroyed) have been removed. She gives (*lāti*) to me (*me*) a garland of speech (*ilāmālām*) that has transcended limits (*avelām*)—meaning a garland of words resembling a flower-garland. Such is the construction.

We bow to that Name which is the abode, dark as the sky, the object of desire, the path to security, and capable of all; which possesses the splendor of the stability of love, the ground of the earth, and is free from fatigue.

Like the sky, it is dark blue, as vast as one might desire. It is "fit for the sequence of welfare"—that is, suitable for the orderly progression of well-being, meaning it brings about security. It possesses the "splendor of the stability of love," meaning it has the excellence of constancy in affection. It is the "unwearied abode of abundance"—the dwelling place of all-pervasive power; this is an elliptical expression implying its remoteness from all qualities to be abandoned. Its "radiance" (dhāma) is its splendor; the sense is that it is the abode of Śrī.

We pay homage; we bow down. *Nāma* is used here in the sense of assent, wonder, or remembrance. Alternatively, [the compound] *vyomaśyāmaṃ dhāma* means "the dark-blue radiance," the abode of Śrī, which is *aklamaṃ*—that is, for the sake of the absence of the exhaustion of worldly existence (*bhava*). The term *aklamaṃ* is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) according to the rule *arthābhāve’vyayībhāvaḥ*, as seen in examples such as *niṣpratyūham upāsmahe*. The fourth case ending takes the form *am* by the rule *nāvyayībhāvādatom tvapañcamyāḥ*. The construction is: "We pay homage—that is, we worship—in a manner that is sufficient and complete. The suffix *kyac* is applied to the word *namaḥ* in the sense of worship according to the rule *namo-varivas-citraṅaḥ kyac*.

The first person singular of the imperative (loṭ) follows that [suffix]. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *nāma* is used in the sense of anger, acceptance, wonder, and also remembrance. Even if the reading were *kṣemakramakṣamandhāma*, there would be no break in the poetic figure (*citrabhaṅga*). In that case, it would mean: "the abode (*dhāma*), that is, the place, which is sufficient (*kṣama*) for the course of security (*kṣemakrama*)."

The meaning is that it is a state which brings about security (*kṣema*). Here, in cases such as *śyāmaṃ kāmaṃ* and so forth, one should understand that the *parasavarṇa* (the following sound) for the *anusvāra* occurs everywhere by virtue of the rule *vā padāntasya*. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the intended poetic figure (*citra*) being ruined. Although poets accept the assumption of non-distinction between those with and without the *bindu*, and between those with and without the *visarga*—as in the case of *sabindukābindukayoḥ* and *savisargāvisargayoḥ*—nevertheless, as long as the power of one's intellect persists, it is better not to resort to such forced efforts. This is what should be kept in mind.
In these two verses as well, figures such as the *padma* (lotus) and others are to be observed, just as in the verse previously cited beginning with "tārāgaure" (O you who are fair as a star).
Now, regarding the *gomūtrikā*:
when the syllables of two half-verses are identical at intervals of one,
the wise who know poetic figures call that the figure known as *gomūtrikā*.

When there is a single uniformity—that is, an identical form—separated by one intervening syllable between the first and second halves of a verse respectively, those who know the art of *citraprabandha* (ornamental poetry) call such a composition, formed by the shape of a cow’s urine as it moves, *gomūtrikā*. It is called *gomūtrikā* because it is like a cow’s urine (*gomūtra*). [The suffix] *kan* is applied according to the rule *ive pratikṛtau*, and then the feminine suffix *ṭāp*; subsequently, the substitution of *i* for *a* occurs according to the rule *pratyayasthāt*.

May he who is as fond of sporting upon the surface of the mountain of the Lord of Serpents as he is pure by virtue of his lineage praised by the net of the lords of yogis grant us well-being; may he bestow upon us auspicious fruit.

The meaning is that Śrīnivāsa—who is eager for sport upon the ground of Bhogīśvaraśaila (the mountain of the Lord of Serpents)—may grant us well-being. He is "pure," meaning gracious, through the multitudes of hymns, that is, collections of praises, offered by the host of Yogīśvaras. May this Śrīnivāsa not bestow, that is, not nourish, "bad fruit" (kuphalam), meaning evil results, upon us. This is a *gomūtrikā* (cow’s urine) pattern composed of pairs of syllables. The method of its extraction has already been demonstrated on the occasion of describing the sixteen-petaled lotus.
This very verse also takes the form of a threefold *gomūtrikā* according to the method previously demonstrated; the same applies to the following verses as well.

May He whose abode is the summit of the serpent-mountain, whose eyes are like fresh lotuses, and whose chest is adorned with a shimmering jewel—may He, who grants liberation from the cycle of worldly existence, ever protect me. 2372.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: "May that Blessed One—who possesses a chest-garland (*urohāra*) whose mass upon the breast is shimmering, trembling, and moving because of the *tarala* jewel—protect me always from misfortune. This too is indeed a *gomūtrikā* composed with linked pairs of syllables (*yugmākṣara-śliṣṭa*). Here, too, the method of writing the diagram follows the manner previously demonstrated.

O Mādhava, Your conduct, which destroys sin and shatters worldly existence, lies far beyond the reach of words. O Śauri, protect me, Your follower, who am trembling with fear caused by enemies and distressed by the heat of worldly existence.

"From the heat of existence"—that is, from the torment of *saṃsāra*—it is "shaken," meaning its mind is unsettled; "beset by enemies"—meaning one who is terrified by the six internal enemies such as desire (*kāma*) and the rest. [The phrase] "make me your follower" is made known by this: "Make me your servant. "Protect me"—that is, guard me. This is an *ayugmākṣara-śliṣṭa-gomūtrikā* (an interwoven cow's urine pattern with uneven syllables). As for the extraction [of the hidden verse], it is as follows:

"May [the Lord] whose form is equal to the Mind-born (Kāmadeva), who is the Lord of the entire world, whose splendor shines upon the bow, who is compassionate, swift, and fierce in conquering his enemies—may He take hold of my heart. (2374)

The analysis of the compound is as follows: *arijayaviṣaye* means "in the intense and sharp domain of the conquest of enemies"; *ānaṃ* means "that which brings [life]," and *jagadujjīvayitṛ* means "the reviver of the world"; thus, *manasijasamānarūpe* refers to one whose form (*rūpa*) is equal to that of the mind-born (Kāma), being both a reviver of the world and possessing a form similar to the mind-born. Alternatively, *mānaṃ* is derived from the root *mān* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (accusative) according to the rule *akartari ca kārake*; such is the *rūpa*, and that which exists together with it is *samānarūpa*. Thus, the analysis is *manasija iva samānarūpam*, meaning "one whose form is equally worthy of honor (*mānanīya*) like that of the mind-born (Kāma). The sense is: in him whose form is comparable to that of Kandarpa.

However, the analysis of the compound is not "that which has a common form" (*samānaṃ rūpaṃ yasya*). For if that were the case, the word *samāna* would undergo the substitution *sa-* by the rule *jyotirjanapadādibhyaḥ*. Alternatively, the suffix *rūpap* is added to the word *samāna* in the sense of praise; thus the analysis is "an excellent similarity" (*praśastaṃ samānaṃ samānarūpam*). The meaning is "in the two excellent similarities of the Mind-born [Cupid]," that is, in those two whose beauty is equal to his.

The meaning is as follows: *bhāvaḥ* refers to one whose bow (*cāpa*) is *lasamānam*, that is, of a nature to gleam (*lasanaśīlam*). The suffix *cānaś* is applied to the root *las*. As Māgha says: "His fresh silken garment was gleaming" (*lasamānanavāṃśukaḥ*). The construction is: "May it quickly (*laghu*) and swiftly (*kṣipram*) cling (*lagatāt*) to the heart. This verse also takes the form of an *ayugmākṣara-śliṣṭa-gomūtrikā* (a rhymed cow's urine pattern with uneven syllables).

This "Necklace Arrangement" (hārabandha), which bears the auspicious mark of Śrī Lakṣmī, provides fearlessness by taking refuge in the dense splendor of the clouds; it is the gem upon the earth that supports the mountain Śeṣa, spoken by the virtuous and meditated upon by the pure-minded.

O heart, take refuge in Śrīnivāsa—the one whose ornaments are the goddess Lakṣmī and the Śrīvatsa mark; who possesses the dense luster of a rain-cloud in the monsoon season; who is meditated upon and worshipped by sages of purified inner hearts; who is proclaimed by the Vedas as the possessor of infinite auspicious qualities; and who is the jewel-like gem of the earth supported by the serpent Śeṣa. The *uddhāra* (extraction) of this verse is formed according to the *gavākṣabandha* (window-pattern) ciphered with the poet’s name: śrīḥ lakṣmīḥ lakṣma śrīvatsaśca alaṅkriye alaṃkārau yasya tam | ghanāghanaghanaśriyaḥ prāvṛṣeṇyajaladasāndrarucaḥ bhayadaṃ tāto'pi nīlamiti yāvat| pūtaiḥ śuddhāntaḥkaraṇaiḥ munibhiḥ dhyātaṃ upāsitam | guṇī anantakalyāṇaguṇākara iti bhaṇitaṃ śrutibhiḥ pratipāditaṃ śeṣadharādharadharāyāḥ maṇiṃ ratnabhūtaṃ śrīnivāsaṃ he cetaḥ hṛdaya śraya āśrayasva || (Note: The extraction of the poet's name from the *gavākṣabandha* follows the specific rules of that poetic figure.)

I meditate upon Hari, the ornament of the Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa), who is to be contemplated, and who has manifested the brilliance of a jewel shining forth from his severed head as it was being heated; he is the one who bestows honor upon those who bow before him.

I meditate upon Hari—the ornament of the Hill of Serpents (Śeṣācala), who is honored by those who bow before him, and whose broad chest bears the Kaustubha jewel; that jewel which is described as being "skilled in destroying the pride of the luster of the sun," meaning it cuts off or shatters the expansion and manifestation of the radiance emerging from the hot-rayed sun.
[The diagrammatic description is as follows: "There should be nine squares one above the other in the middle, and likewise there should be nine squares across the middle."
On both sides of these two, seven, five, and three squares shall be produced respectively in due order.
The wise one should draw lines of equal measure both horizontally and vertically; beginning from the central grid at the head of the path, he should proceed to draw them.
One, three, five, seven, then nine, seven, five,
three, and one— these are the syllables of the verse, arranged in horizontal succession.

The extraction of the names of poets, works, and so forth intended for oneself is desired by means of the syllables situated in the upper, middle, and lower lines, joined together in their respective order.
This simple poetic arrangement known as *gavākṣa* (the window) is esteemed by poets.

Here, in the upper and middle sections, the name of the poet and other details—such as "this is the work of the noble poet Kṛṣṇa"—are extracted. They also call this very same arrangement *rathabandha* (the chariot-arrangement).

We praise the stainless cause of the worlds, whose chest is illuminated by noble jewels, who is worthy of honor, who sports on the king of mountains, the Phani-giri, and whose praises are sung by Kinnaras. 2377.
In this [work], within the chapters on the superior and middling varieties, there is the extraction of the title of the poem: "This is the *Alaṃkāramaṇihāra*.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, the Chapter on Verbal Figures of Speech (*śabdālaṃkārasara*), in the *Alaṃkāramaṇihāra*.

The venerable Śrī Kṛṣṇabrahmatantraparakāla, the most excellent of ascetics, completed this work—which he composed while still partially engaged in the life of a householder—for the pleasure of the Lord Śrī Śiva. (2378)
*Apūri apūrayat*: this is the third person singular aorist (*luṅ*) in the active voice (*kartari*) of the root *pṛ*, derived from the rule "dīpa-jana-budha-pūra" which prescribes the *ciṇ* suffix.

May the illustrious Lord Śrīnātha—the lord of the mountain-crested king of serpents, whose fame is worthy of those who have transcended pride and reached the heights of the supreme scriptures—be pleased by this work composed by himself. 2379.
O Lord, although I know that my hymn of praise is unworthy of You, please forgive all this audacity of mine as if it were the act of a child. (2380)

That even the Vedas, though their course is exceedingly unimpeded, turn back of their own accord [from Your praise], while even one of limited intellect attempts Your hymn—this is merely the manifestation of my own restlessness. (2381)

O Lord, may the Goddess of Poetry—possessing a delicate form and complexion, adorned with ornaments, and having beautiful hands and feet—come to you as her lover, and may she shine forth through my words. 2382.

The phrase *sukumārākṛtivarṇā* means that in which the syllables (*varṇa*) are composed of letters (*akṣara*) of tender form, that is to say, fashioned from soft syllables accompanied by *anusvāra*. In the alternative sense, it means that whose form and color are delicate. *Surucikaracaraṇā* refers to that in which the quarters (*caraṇa*)—meaning the lines of the verse—are most delicious to savor; in the other sense, it means that whose hands and feet (*caraṇa*) possess beautiful luster (*suruci*). *Maduditā* means uttered by me, or born from me. May the glory of poetry (*kavitāśrī*), the fortune of composition, shine forth and rejoice!

Blessed is my poetry alone; what other such work could be sought here in this world? For it is like the daughter of the ocean whom the Lord of the Serpent Hill (Śrīraṅgam) cherishes as venerable and heart-pleasing. 2383.

The construction is as follows: he extends [his fame] to her who is venerable and worshipful like the daughter of the ocean; who is distinct from Māyā and Śrī; who is another [form] of her [the first]; who is a virtuous wife (satī); who is dear to the heart; who dwells upon the chest; and who is beloved of the heart.
Whether he praises or whether he censures this work upon hearing it, may we experience not even a mustard-seed’s measure of either joy or resentment, for our intellect is dull. (2384)
For a composition that is too elaborate is indeed difficult for one of dull intellect to perceive, just as a lamp that is excessively brilliant is for one with diseased eyes.

In this world, an unfortunate person never finds anywhere a well-composed poem—smoothed by a series of straight, pure, and excellent qualities, uniform from beginning to end—just as one does not find a fine garment.
Even more than this, whoever would take pleasure in even a single verse of one with tender intellect—who here could do him greater harm than he who acts with malice toward such a poet? (2387)

Who is the man with pure intellect—meaning one whose mind is clear due to being free from the turbidity of envy and the like—who would find fault even with a single verse, rather than five, six, two, or three? For what man could possibly do harm to this author-poet, compared to that man who finds offense even in this single verse—that is, who acts with envy? The sense is: what injury could there be greater than envy?
For he by whom this composition will be difficult to perceive, it will indeed be difficult for him to perceive; but for him by whom it is easy to perceive, it will be easy—of this there is no doubt.

"Duṣṭā" means corrupted by defects such as lack of discrimination (*aviveka*) and envy (*asūyā*); "prekṣā" refers to the intellect (*mati*), according to Amara’s lexicon: *prekṣā upalabdhiḥ cit saṃvit*. "Duṣprekṣaḥ" means difficult to look upon, that is, impossible to perceive. This is derived from the root *īkṣ* with the suffix *khal* according to the rule *īṣaddussuṣu kṛchrākṛchrārtheṣu khal*. The same applies to the term "suprekṣa" which follows.

May those few who have not yet acquired even a trace of the fragrance of poetry never venture into the restless activity of discriminating between merit and fault regarding the words of a poet, which abound with profound meanings. (2389)
For the wise alone recognize the fragrance of the words of a living poet, never others; indeed, a needle cannot be grasped by stones situated upon every mountain peak.

Let this composition—which is cherished upon the heads of those who know the very essence of eloquent poetry—never even set foot at the forefront of those who are far removed from tasting its fragrance; for it is like a fresh, tender garland of flowers, fit to be worn on the head and fondled in the hands of the wise, yet never in the hands of a monkey.

Who indeed, even among the foremost of connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor, would desire to chew everywhere the harsh poetry of a bad poet—harder than sand and more insipid than a mere drop of juice, both within and without? (2392)
Though extremely hard at first glance, the poetry of mature poets, when tasted, consists of dense particles of flavor; it will surely be equal to candied sugar.

Though unexamined it is sweet, yet when examined, the poetry of a true poet appears most delicious to the connoisseur because of its profound internal essence, like the fruit of the plantain tree. (2394)

"Unseparated" means not examined, not investigated, and having its outer skin not peeled away; "separated" means examined, investigated, and having its outer skin peeled away. Because it is "dense with essence," it consists solely of essence. The rest is easy to understand.
Through correct discernment, it reveals the collection of qualities once they have been purified; otherwise, like a mass of cotton, a web of poetry will never manifest even a trace of quality. (2395)

By means of discernment—that is, by investigation; in another sense, by separating [the essence] from the seed-cotton—the poem reveals its own nature as having become clear, purified, and having correctly grasped its meaning. Like cotton-wool, it manifests the web of poetry, which is a collection of qualities such as excellence of diction, and which is like a continuous thread.
Like fresh butter that is smooth, white, and consistent with the palate, may this most excellent new poem attain great sweetness for those who possess the faculty of aesthetic appreciation. 2396.
"With sugar" means with candied sugar (*śarkarā sitā*, according to Amara); [it is for] those who know flavors—the connoisseurs—and for the tongues.

When a composition possesses abundant qualities, a connoisseur of rasa generally does not count its defects; for one who relishes the most sweet taste of nectar, does he ever think of it as being vomited by a scorpion? 2397.
One who seeks out qualities discards even the slightest fault here without hesitation; whereas a man who tastes the flavor of a mango discards its skin from afar to savor the juice.

Crushing the lotus of the eloquent poet’s speech with the claws of his mouth—the lion that is the intoxicated sophist—the poet shall obtain fragrance from non-harsh investigation, just as a gentle breeze finds scent [from the crushed flower]. (2399)
Through gentle reflection, most straightforward inquiry, and a soft touch, [one attains] fragrance, joy, and perfume.
Neither antiquity nor novelty is the cause of beauty; O you who are free from envy, accept this work solely on account of its merits, for it is the merit alone that makes one excellent.
"Upādhvam" means "you have approached" (upāsīḍhvam). It is the second person plural imperative of the root *ās* preceded by the prefix *upa*. The elision of the *s* is according to the rule "dhi ca."
"Only ancient poetry is sweet, not the new"—so say the preeminent masters of composition. Let this not enter your hearts; for how could even something brand-new not be sweet, like honey? (2401)
Whether it be old or new, whatever composition possesses merit should be accepted by the wise; whether a jewel arises on another continent or right here, the wise do not fail to take it up. (2402)

He who, repeatedly resorting to these ornaments, would perfect his own intellect—how could that man of perfected intellect and river-eroding wisdom ever wish to look upon the compositions of others? (2403)

The skillful person who, having relied upon and attained these ornaments—these poetic figures (*alaṃkṛti*) described in this extensive treatise, which are also understood as "adornments" (*bhūṣaṇa*)—attains his own intellect.

The word *labhām* also suggests [the sense of "attaining"]. The term *prasādhayati* means "adorns. The word *alam* also suggests one whose intellect is capable of reaching the shore [of understanding], who knows the entire essence of the aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*) contained within the composition, and who is capable of discerning what is appropriate and inappropriate. The word *kṛtī* means "skilled"; it also suggests that he regards other compositions—which are essentially worthless—as mere "other women" (*itaravadhū*). The phrase *kathaṃ lulokiṣate* means "he does not even wish to look at them, much less see them. For this very reason, the figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*) here is *samāsokti* (condensed expression).

Let those who have mastered only a single science rejoice—or perhaps not—upon seeing my work here and there; but alas, those who are expert in the cultivation of all such sciences will certainly rejoice. For generally, their envy arises from the power of fate; were it not for that, what need would there be [to praise] the glorious Hayagrīva, the conqueror, the treasury of virtues, and the seat of all knowledge?

May that primordial goddess—who sports in knowledge, whose seat is charming, who has a horse-like face, who has shaken off all faults, who is dear to the heart, who is established within the heart, and who is to be attained by the wise—be propitious.

May that Abode protect us—the Abode which, having established Brahmā in the lotus of its navel, sent forth even the Vedas to him so that they might ward off the calamities arising from Madhu and Kaiṭabha; and which is honored by the foremost of ascetics, the venerable Nigamāntadeśika and others, who are steadfast in their departure upon the path of the five-fold daily rites (pañcakāla).

May that Supreme Goddess, whose speech has long been held in reverence by the ancient masters—such as the jewel-like teacher Śrī Brahma-tantra, the preceptor of the Upanishads—and which now dwells within the assembly of the supreme ascetic Parakāla, bestow auspiciousness upon us; she who is the Mistress of Speech and whose face is like the ocean. 2407.

Having heard the wonderful *Śrīmadbhāṣya*, Śāradā praised it with her head bowed; she then bestowed her own image, together with the Lord of Yogis (Śaṅkara), upon her own pedestal under the name "Bhāṣyakāra" (the Commentator). This very image of the Goddess of Speech, whose worship was established by the Lord of Yogis, Kurukeśa, Āgamānta, Ārya, and others, now remains as the object of worship in the temple of Kalimathana, the preeminent seat of the Brahma-veda (Atharva-veda).

May that Hayavadana deity—who is the stainless self of knowledge and bliss; who is known as the wind-storm to the great cotton-wool of the impurities of the Kali age; whose nature transcends all limits; who has chased away all enemies; who has gone to the center of a white lotus; who wears a garland of pure lotuses; who is radiant with a smile like a mass of milk; and who is the object of praise for the King of Kings (Kubera) and others—grant me perfect prosperity.
I bow to that primordial God, whose lotus-feet become smooth with the mass of rays effortlessly streaming forth from the millions of tips of the crowns of the many prostrating gods;

who is worshipped on the crown of the head by the venerable Śrī Rāmānuja, the preceptor of the crest-jewels of the Vedas, the masters of the independent Brahmanical systems, and the teachers of the enemies of the Kali age; and who is ever to be honored and adored.

In a world devoid of light, filled with masses of darkness from those who propound dubious doctrines, the Lord of Śrī commanded him out of great compassion to descend to the earth; may that supreme sage Śrī Rāmānuja, whose very self is the Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa), be victorious—he who composed the *Yogabhāṣya*, a sun that removes all ignorance. 2411.

May this *Śrībhāṣya*, composed by the venerable Yatīndra—the author of the commentary upon which even the author of the Sūtras, Vyāsācārya of world-renowned fame, [relied]—be for our constant and supreme welfare. (2412)

Salutations to this bell, which was formerly offered with a mind bowed in devotion by Padmāsana for the sake of serving the pair of lotus feet of Śeṣādrīśvara; and which, through the resolve of the Lord of Śrī, has arisen from the likeness of Nigamāntadeśika for the purpose of shaking off the various *piśāca*-demons of the Tantras.

May the venerable Śrutyaṃtavidyāguru—who obstructs the movements of his adversaries with a mass of speech that is difficult to determine due to its rivalry with the tinkling of the anklets on the horse-faced [Gaṇeśa] dancing upon the splintering peak of the lion-throne of the tongue; who is the glorious ornament of the most renowned doctrine of the noble Rāmānuja; and who possesses the radiance of the sun—may he eternally bestow auspiciousness upon the worlds. (2414)

May the preeminent teacher Vedāntasūri—the sovereign of all systems, a mass of bliss who is the great stable for the noble horse of the venerable Vāṇī’s feet, whose splendor is a canal for the stream of eloquent speech skilled at extinguishing the distressing heat of worldly existence, and who has removed the stain of doubt from the multitude of conflicting views through his countless compositions—grant us joy. (2415)

May he who was the first illustrious Śrī-Vaṇśaṭhāri, the Lord of Ascetics (Yatipati), whose lotus feet were the source of livelihood for this very Varadaguru of the Śrīvatsa lineage, and who served as his disciple; may that independent master of the Brahmanical system (Brahmatantrasvatantra) be ever victorious—he who is the second incarnation of the Yatipati here on earth, and the second disciple of the Master of Vedānta-sūtras (Vedāntasūri). || 2416 ||

May all these lords of the Yati lineage—the protectors of vast empires, whose faces were graced by the Yadu kings, whose own fame surpassed that of others, who dwell upon Śeṣādri in the city of glorious Mahīśūra, and who are established in the Siddhānta that is the crest-jewel of the Vedas—all of them, independent in the Brahmanical system, may they be renowned throughout the earth. (2417)

He whose feet were worshipped by the lords of Delhi was the third incarnation of the king of the lineage of ascetics; in every divine land, he established the worship and consecration of the Teachers of the Upanishads. Making the holy seat of Śrīmad-Brahmatantra-Uttama-Yatitilaka a treasury of prosperity, he brought forth the science of Nyāsa, which reveals his own greatness through the surrender of the afflicted.

May that lord of ascetics named Parakāla be victorious—he who, possessing renowned and exalted greatness, made the foremost Vaiṣṇavas such as Kṛṣṇa and others, along with their wives, wear the marks of the conch and discus and so forth by the kings of Mahīśūra, who were known from the throne of glorious Karṇāṭa; and likewise, he who composed commentaries on the Bhāṣya and the supreme Drāmiḍopaniṣads.

May the four great lords of ascetics—Śrī Śrīnivāsa, Nigamāntaramaṇi, Vāsudeva, and Rāmānuja—who possess all exalted virtues and who, like the divine manifestations (vyūhas), have assumed bodies for the welfare of the worlds, be victorious!

May the eminent Raṅganātha Yati, the foremost among teachers, who is the abode of the glory of the Vedānta revealed by the Lord of the Bell (Śrī Śaṅkara), and who is adorned with the title of the venerable Brahmatantraparakāla—may these sovereign preceptors of radiant virtues be victorious! 2421.

May our most excellent gurus, whose fame is celebrated throughout the earth, be victorious—they who are intent on establishing the doctrine of the venerable Lord of Ascetics (Śrī Yati-pati), who remove the well-known paths of hypocrisy practiced by those of extremely meager intellect, and who have entrusted the entire burden of protecting the world to Hari, the Lord of Lakṣmī. || 2422 ||

By the grace of the pair of stainless lotus-feet of the foremost of teachers, the conqueror of the Kali age, Śrī Vāsabrahmatantra, who possesses the power to compose various treatises at every step, the lord of ascetics named Parakāla—the first disciple of Śrī Kṛṣṇabrahmatantra—has composed this *Ālaṃkāra-śāstra*, which captivates with the jewels of the excellent qualities of the Lord of Vṛṣādri. 2423.
When five thousand and one years of the Kali age had passed, in the year named Vikārin, the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra* was completed.
This necklace of jewels, renowned for its brilliance, which has been worn by some with longing around their necks, generally spreads their own splendor far and wide. (2425)
May the eternal couple be victorious, along with my own poem, which is possessed of aesthetic flavor, endearing, beautiful, vigorous, composed, pleasing, and adorned with poetic ornaments.

May my poem—rich in aesthetic flavor (*rasavat*), meaning it possesses sentiments such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*); *preyas*, meaning mutually most dear and beautiful; or, in another sense, beautiful through the two figures of speech named *rasavat* and *preyas*; *ūrjasvin*, meaning powerful; and *samāhitapriyaṃkaraṇa*, meaning bringing joy to those who are composed and whose minds are concentrated, that is, to yogis; or, in another sense, bringing joy through the two figures of speech named *ūrjasvin* and *samāhita*; and which is the eternal couple consisting of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa—be victorious!

Let there be some other merit or let there not; her absolute devotion is itself a great merit. O Acyuta, just as Satī was honored by her husband with affection, so may this woman be treated by you with love; that shall be my work.

May the faction of the noble Lakṣmaṇa ever triumph in the world; may the eloquent speech of the preeminent teacher who is the crest-jewel of the Vedas triumph; may the abundant prosperity of the assembly hall of Hayagrīva triumph; and may the eternal glory of Śrīnivāsa on the Hill of Virtue (Vṛṣaśaila) triumph! 2428.

Thus [ends the work] of him who has attained clarity in the knowledge of Brahman through the grace of the compassionate glance of the sovereign ascetic Śrīnivāsa-Brahmatantra-Parakāla, the preceptor who established the path of the glorious Veda, the wandering mendicant of the highest order (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka), the independent master of all systems, the teacher of both Vedāntas, the lion at the throat of the glorious poets and debaters, upon whose pair of lotus feet the entire burden of his soul was placed, and who is the emperor of those who determine the doctrines of the glorious Rāmānuja; by such a one as he... [Śrī...]

Of Śrīnivāsadeśikendra, who has acquired the secret tradition through the grace of Brahma-tantra-parakāla-yatīndra Mahādeśika; of him who has entrusted the burden of his own protection to the lotus feet of that [Mahādeśika]; and of him who, having attained the essence of the nectar of grace from such an eminent great preceptor as Śrīraṅganātha Brahma-tantra-parakāla-muni, was consecrated to the office of the venerable Guru Brahma-tantra-parakāla in the fourth stage of life (turīyāśrama). Śrī...

Of the venerable Śrī Kṛṣṇabrahmatantraparakālayatīndra, the preceptor in the continuous lineage of the sovereign emperor Śrī Kṛṣṇarāja, the lord of the illustrious city of Mahīśūra, who was consecrated to the imperial sovereignty upon the divine jeweled throne of Karṇāṭaka.
Among his works, the treatise on poetics titled *Alaṃkāramaṇihāra* is complete.
Homage to the lineage of the venerable Śrī Brahmatantra Parakāla Gurus.
This composition is finished.
Śrī:
Verses on the Characteristics of the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
May he who dwells upon the mountain of the bull (Śiva) and protects the three worlds be victorious!
The Supreme Brahman is the generous one, whose characteristic mark is the ornament upon his chest.
Where the beauty of similarity between two things shines forth as a manifested comparison, that is *upamā* (simile);
for *upamā* is that charming resemblance which serves to embellish the meaning of a sentence.
That [simile] is declared by those who know the essence of poetic figures to be of two kinds: complete (pūrṇā) and elliptical (luptā).
These [five components] are: the standard of comparison (upamāna), the object of comparison (upameya), the common attribute (dharma), and the signifier (vācaka).
If these four—the object of description, the standard of comparison, the common attribute, and the word of comparison—are employed, that is considered a complete simile (pūrṇopamā).
This applies to both the object of description and the standard of comparison, as well as to the common attribute and the word of comparison.
When one, two, or three [elements] are omitted, there are eight types of elliptical simile (*luptopamā*);
here, [the omissions occur] regarding the word for the quality (*dharma*), the quality itself, and both the quality and its word.
When both the attribute (*varṇya*) and the denoter (*vācaka*) are elided, these are indeed the types of simile where those two are omitted.
When the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is elided, however, that is known as the fifth type, where the *upamāna* is omitted.
The sixth type is called "omission of the denoter and the standard of comparison" by the learned;
another is the "omission of the quality and the standard of comparison," occurring when both the quality and the standard of comparison are elided.
The eighth [type] occurs when the words expressing the object of comparison are omitted;
thus has simile been described according to the method of the *Kuvalayānanda*.
In the opinion of the Easterners, the classification of this simile (upamā) is elaborated as being twofold—
namely, complete (pūrṇā) and elliptical (luptā)— and these two, in turn, are further divided.

The *pūrṇopamā* (full simile) is twofold—verbal (*śrautī*) and objective (*ārthī*)—and each of these exists as threefold: residing in a sentence (*vākyagā*), residing in a compound (*samāsagā*), and residing in a secondary derivative (*taddhitasthā*). These two [types] may also exist separately from one another.
The experts in the scriptures state that when words such as "just like" (*yathā*), which directly express similarity, are employed, it is a *śrautī* (verbal) simile.
Those words such as *sadṛś* (similar) and *nibha* (resembling), which establish similarity by means of an intervening substratum (*dharmī*), possess the *ārthī* [upamā] based on their usage.
It may be of three kinds—omitted in one, omitted in two, or omitted in four;
and it is of one form when omitted in three. Thus, omission is generally eightfold.

When there is the omission of the object (dharma), the standard of comparison (upamāna), or the expressive word (vācaka), it is "omitted in one" (ekaluptā) in three ways; however, it is "omitted in two" (dviluptā) in four ways.

Likewise, when both the attribute and the expressive word are elided; similarly, when the attribute and the object of comparison are elided; likewise, when the object of description and the expressive word are elided; and also when the expressive word and the object of description are elided.
The *triluptā* (omission of all three), however, is of one kind due to the non-omission of the quality (*dharma*) and the denoter (*vācaka*).
Now, the classification beginning with the *dharmaluptā* (omission of the quality) and so forth is demonstrated in sequence.
The *pūrṇopamā* (complete simile) is also twofold: that which is based on direct expression (*śrauti*) and that which is based on implied meaning (*ārthī*), even when the common property is omitted.
Among these, the *śrauti* variety does not occur in the case of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), because the syntactic connection would be lost.
The simile with an elided standard of comparison (*luptopamā*) is of two kinds: that occurring in a sentence (*vākyagā*) and that occurring in a compound (*samāsagā*).
Within a compound, it may have an elided particle of comparison (*vādi-luptā*); furthermore, it occurs in the *karmadhāraya*, the *kyac*-derivative, and the *kyaṅ*-derivative.

In the case of the *ṇamul* suffix, the agentive *ṇin*, the *kvip* suffix, and likewise in *taddhita* derivatives— thus, in these nine ways, this [type of word] should be understood as a "denoter-eraser" (*vācakalopinī*).
However, the elision of the suffix expressing the property (dharmavācaka-luptā) is described in the case of the *kvip* suffix and in compounds (*samāsa*).
But the loss of the standard of comparison occurs in a sentence, in a compound, and in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
In some cases, it is considered that even the expressive word and the object of comparison are elided;
in other cases, there may be an elision of both the expressive word and the object of comparison within a compound itself.
That [compound] in which the case-ending expressing the grammatical relation is elided is a compound with an elided suffix (lupta).
Thus, the eight types of compounds with elided suffixes have been described according to the tradition of the ancients.
When a single object of comparison possesses multiple points of comparison, some discerning scholars call that the "garland simile" (mālopamā).
If each successive object of comparison becomes the standard of comparison for the preceding one,
this is called the "girdle simile" (raśanopamā) by poets.

The figure of speech called *upameyopamā* (reciprocal comparison) occurs when there is a reversal of the roles of the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) between two preceding instances, and this is stated again subsequently.
Non-connection (ananvaya) is that in which one and the same thing serves as both the object of comparison and the standard of comparison.
The *asama* (the peerless) is defined as the total negation of comparison in every respect. The ancients, however, do not consider this to be a distinct figure of speech.
An example is given for the sake of easy understanding of what has been stated in general, by way of defining one part of it; thus,
when their relationship as part and whole has been stated, an illustration is provided.
When the standard of comparison is described as being the object of comparison in turn,
there occurs a disparagement of the subject of description through the acquisition of that which was not previously described— the object of comparison.
That [is *atadguṇa*] when there is disregard for others due to the excellence of the object of description (*varṇya*), which serves as the standard of comparison;
and that is also [the case] when another thing is not fully realized as a standard of comparison because of the excellence of the object of description.
They know the fifth [type], *pratīpa*, to be the purposelessness of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
*Rūpaka* is the coloring of the object (*viṣaya*) by means of the form of the correlate (*viṣayin*).
The wise know that metaphor (rūpaka) is of two kinds, determined by non-difference and by identity.
When there is a superimposition of identity upon a difference, it is called *abhedarūpaka* (metaphor of identity).
That would be *tādrūpyarūpaka* (metaphor of resemblance) if that [superimposition] were of the nature of resemblance (*tādrūpya*).
And that pair [of comparison and superimposition] is threefold, through expressions of superiority, inferiority, or neither.
The description of the superiority of the object being superimposed over its prior state is [the first].

If, in the state being described, there is an excess [of parts], it is "Metaphor of Excess" (adhikābhedarūpaka); if there is a deficiency compared to the prior state, it is "Metaphor of Deficiency" (nyūnābhedarūpaka).
When there is an absence of both superiority and inferiority, it is the *anubhayābheda-rūpaka* (metaphor of non-difference between neither).
Likewise, scholars should infer that there are three varieties even within the *tādṛpya-rūpaka* (metaphor of identity).
In the opinion of the Easterners, the figure of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor) is also defined as being threefold:
that with parts (*sāṅga*), that without parts (*niraṅga*), and the "successive" (*paramparita*).
Thus, *sāvayava-rūpaka* (metaphor with parts) is also of two kinds therein: that which has all things as its object (*samastavastuviṣaya*) and that which manifests in part (*ekadeśavivartin*).
When a collection of figures of speech (rūpaka) whose production is mutually dependent is composed,
that indeed constitutes the "composite" (sāvayava) type.
In the analysis of both the whole and its parts through words,
that [metaphor] which has all things as its object is indeed "with parts" (sāvayava).
If that which is being superimposed is verbal in some cases and conceptual (ārtha) in others,
they know this as *ekadeśavivartin* (partially transformative), which possesses constituent parts (*sāvayava*).
The wise know that to be *niraṅga* (single-limbed) which is the metaphorical representation (*rūpaṇa*) of a single object alone;
according to the opinion of the virtuous, it is of two kinds: the simple (*kevala*) and the garland-like (*mālārūpa*).
If one object is said to be connected with another object by way of the relation of cause and effect, then that is a *paramparita* (transferred) metaphor.
That *paramparita* (successive metaphor) is of two kinds, distinguished by being "joined" (*śliṣṭa*) or "unjoined" (*aśliṣṭa*);
each of these two types may further be of two kinds: simple (*kevala*) or garland-like (*mālikā*).
Thus, in the opinion of the ancients, metaphor (rūpaka) is held to be of eight kinds.
Among these, transference (pariṇāma) occurs where the object of comparison (viṣayin), because it is not applicable to its own context, [is treated] as itself.
It attains the nature of the object; this is declared to be its transformation (pariṇāma).
Ullekha (the figure of multiple description) is that wherein a single object is apprehended in many ways by numerous perceivers,
due to the influence of causes such as personal preference; that they call Ullekha.
The multiplicity of the elements (dhātu) is based on the multiplicity of their objects and so forth; even when the grasper is one, that distinction is likewise accepted.

Recollection (*smṛti*) is that which arises from the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) through the full cognition of similarity; when such recollection is employed, it is called by the wise the ornament named *Smṛti*.
When an illusion,
full of wonder, caused by resemblance,
is not explicitly stated in a composition, that they call "Illusion" (bhrāntimān).
The figure of speech known as *saṃdeha* (doubt) is considered to be a delightful cognition based on similarity,
which is distinct from either probability or certainty.
Apahnuti (concealment) occurs when there is a denial of an intended cognition of identity [between two things], whether that denial is itself the primary subject or merely a subordinate element.
This they call the figure of speech known as Apahnuti (the Concealment) in its general form.
When there is a denial of the nature of the subject at hand, which results in the superimposition of something else,
this pure ornament is called *apahnuti* (concealment).
If that very concealment is preceded by reasoning, it is *hetvapahnuti* (concealment of the cause).
*Paryastāpahnuti* (inverted concealment) occurs where there is a denial of some attribute of that [object].
If that which is to be described is depicted as having the result of superimposing [another quality] upon it,
when there is a suspicion of another [quality], then, for the purpose of warding off such error, this is "the concealment of error" (bhrāntyapahnuti).
When there is a concealment of a fact through the suspicion of something else, it is *tathyāpahnuti* (concealment of truth).
If this concealment is manifested by means of words such as "deceit" (*chala*), "guile" (*chadman*), "resemblance" (*nibha*), or "body," "self," and so forth,
it is indeed *kaitavāpahnuti* (concealment by guile).
Utprekṣā (poetic fancy) is the imagining of one thing as being another due to its connection with the attributes of that other;
it is said to be of three kinds, consisting of the nature of a thing, a cause, or a fruit.
Poetic fancy regarding an object (*vastūtprekṣā*) is considered to be of two kinds, according to whether its locus is expressed or unexpressed.
Fancy regarding a cause (*hetūtprekṣā*) and fancy regarding an effect (*phalotprekṣā*) are distinguished by whether their locus is established or unestablished.
Hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) consists in that where, having swallowed up the subject (*viṣaya*), the object itself (*viṣayin*) is asserted;
those who know the ornaments recognize this as Hyperbole of Metaphor (*rūpakātiśayokti*).
That same [figure], when accompanied by concealment, is called *sāpahnavā* (concealed); it is the same when it contains a concealing metaphor (*apahnutigarbhitā*).
*Bhedakātiśayokti* (hyperbole of distinction) occurs when that which is under discussion is described as something else.
When a connection is described even where no connection exists for the sake of exalting the subject,
those who know the ornaments call that *saṃbandhātiśayokti* (hyperbole of connection).
Even when there is a connection, the absence of connection is declared to be the hyperbole of non-connection (*asaṃbandhātiśayokti*).
When cause and effect exist simultaneously, this [hyperbole] occurs as that which is preceded by a lack of sequence (*akramapūrvikā*).
If an effect is represented as being bound [to its cause] by the mere fact of its attachment to that cause,
that is declared by the skillful to be *capalātiśayokti* (the hyperbole of fickleness).
If there should be a reversal of the sequence between cause and effect,
those who are experts in poetry call that *atyantātiśayokti* (hyperbole of extreme transcendence).
Tulyayogitā (Equal Pairing) occurs where a single attribute is described as being shared by either the subjects alone or by others alone.
That equality of conduct toward both the beneficial and the harmful is considered another [type of *sāmya*];
that statement of equality with those of superior qualities is considered yet another.
The Illuminator (dīpaka) is that in which there is a single common attribute between the subject of description and the object of description.
When there is a repetition of both the word and its meaning, whether combined or separate,
the best of the wise call that *āvṛttidīpaka* (the lamp of repetition), which is said to be of three kinds.
If, in two sentences concluded by a similarity,
a single attribute is employed twice, that is called *prativastūpamā* (simile by parallelism).
The *dṛṣṭānta* (illustrative example):

If there is a comparison between two sentence-meanings (*vākyārtha*) based on properties that have attained the status of being the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), it is designated as an *ārthī dṛṣṭānta*.
If, when two meanings have been presented, their non-difference in meaning is proclaimed,
and it culminates in a comparison, this is *nidarśanā*.
That other [type of simile], which is preceded by the literal meaning of the words, occurs between the standard of comparison (upamāna) and the object of comparison (upameya),
wherein the attribution of the property of one to the other is stated.
If it is argued that there would be the cognition of existence and non-existence through an action, then another illustration [is required].
If some distinction between the standard of comparison and the object compared is stated as a point of contrast,
the wise call that the poetic figure named *vyatireka* (distinction).
When the excellence of the object of comparison is described by virtue of its superior qualities over the standard of comparison, the wise call that *vyatireka* (distinction).
When there is a description of the relationship between two objects— one primary and the other subordinate— connected by the sense of "together," that is known as Sahokti (Simultaneous Description).
Vinokti (the figure of speech "without"):
when the loveliness or even the lack of loveliness of a subject under discussion is described as being [due to] the absence of something else, that is the poetic ornament Vinokti.
"Samāsokti (Abridged Statement) occurs when, due to similarity, the unmentioned subject (aprastuta)— which serves as the differentiator— is implied;
those ancient masters who know the ornaments call this Samāsokti."
*Parikara* (the Pervasive) is a figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*) consisting of an epithet used with a specific intention;
[it is followed by] *parikarāṅkura* (the Sprout of the Pervasive).
If the substantive (viśeṣya) is endowed with significant meaning, it constitutes the "sprout" (aṅkura) of the parikara ornament.
Pun (śleṣa) rests upon both the subject and the non-subject; it relies on multiple meanings.
The first type [of pun] is of eight kinds, based on phoneme, word, gender, language, and case-ending.
And *śleṣa* (punning conjunction) is said to occur through both base and suffix, as well as through words,
wherein a variety of forms assume a single form by virtue of case-endings and the like.
Indeed, it is heard that this is called *varṇaśleṣa* (phonetic pun) by the learned;
whereas that pun which is based on a difference in words is *padaśleṣa* (lexical pun).
The "fusion of genders" (liṅgaśleṣa) is to be understood as the identity of form among words of the feminine, masculine, and neuter genders, whether occurring in short, long, or compound forms.
Pun based on language (bhāṣāśleṣa) arises from the unification of various languages with different meanings;
if there is a punning combination of case-endings and verbal suffixes, it is called pun on inflection (vibhaktiśleṣa).
If two bases (*prakṛti*) possess similarity of form due to the application of unattached suffixes (*atyaya*),
this is *prakṛtiśleṣa* (phonetic punning on the base), which is twofold depending on whether it concerns nominal endings (*supt*) or verbal endings (*tiṅ*).
If there is a similarity of form among many members of a series of bases and suffixes due to their being joined with [other] suffixes, this is called *pratyayaśleṣa* (the pun on suffixes).
That would be a verbal pun (vacanaśleṣa) if the words were to coalesce.

Where there is a description of something irrelevant (aprastuta) that serves as a means of implying the relevant (prastuta), that is called the figure of speech known as Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description). This very ornament is thus defined.

When the effect, the cause, the pervaded, the pervader, or the similar is intended, but another [related] thing is mentioned; likewise when the similar is mentioned for the sake of the similar—thus this [figure of speech] is fivefold.
The "sprout of the relevant" (prastutāṅkura) occurs when the relevant [meaning] is suggested by means of the relevant.
Paryāyokta (periphrasis):
Paryāyokta occurs when that which is intended to be expressed is stated by means of another mode,
whether it be one's own or another's, through a charming pretext.
And when that which is desired is established [indirectly], the wise know that as *paryāyokta* (periphrasis).
If censure is revealed through praise, or if praise is expressed through censure,
the wise call that figure of speech "vyājastuti" (ironical praise).
Praise through censure, or censure through praise, where the expressed and the suggested have different objects, is "Praise by Disguise" (*vyājastuti*);
it is a form of praise where the suggested meaning has a distinct subject matter from the literal one.
Indirect censure (*vyājanindā*), however,
occurs when censure is suggested by means of praise.
That is *ākṣepa* (paraleipsis),
which is a prohibition of one's own statement arising from deliberation;
it is a prohibition that, being sublated, implies some particular excellence.
Others have declared that this *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) has as its subject matter what is yet to be said or what has already been said;
for just as there is a semblance of prohibition (*niṣedhābhāsa*), a semblance of injunction (*vidhyābhāsa*) is also accepted as *ākṣepa*.
That contradiction is [the figure of speech] Contradiction (virodha); it occurs even where there is no actual contradiction, provided there is an appearance of contradiction.
It becomes tenfold through the various relations of universals (jāti) and so forth with themselves and others.
Vibhāvanā (the description of the extraordinary) is the production of an effect even in the absence of its cause;
it is considered to be the arising of an effect despite the incompleteness of its causes.
The third [type of] *vibhāvanā* is the production of an effect even when there is an obstacle;
the fourth *vibhāvanā* would be the production of an effect from what is not its cause.
If the production of an effect is [described as occurring] from its opposite, that is the fifth *vibhāvanā*;
if the emergence of a cause [is described as occurring] from the effect, that is the sixth *vibhāvanā*.
Viśeṣokti (the figure of speech of specific denial):
Viśeṣokti occurs when the effect does not arise even though the cause is fully present.
Impossibility (*asaṃbhava*) is the statement of the inconceivability [of a matter]; it is the impossibility of establishing the intended meaning.
The wise call that ornament *asaṃgati* (incongruity), wherein a contradiction between cause and effect is described as having different substrates.
That which is an action intended for one purpose, yet is performed elsewhere than that;
and that which is an action contrary to what was undertaken by one who had set out to do something else.
The joining together of two things that do not correspond to one another is indeed the "incongruous" (viṣama); likewise,
they know the production of an effect that is dissimilar [to its cause] as the "incongruous."
The attainment of the undesired despite striving for the desired is considered "viṣama" (the uneven).
They know that as *sama* (the Equal) where a corresponding arrangement is described;
that *sama* is also the similarity of the effect with its cause.
Whatever effort is exerted for the sake of accomplishing a desired object,
its accomplishment is said to be impossible without encountering the undesired.
If, for the sake of achieving a desired object for one who seeks it, an action contrary to that [usual means] is performed,
the wise call this effort *vicitrā* (the "extraordinary" ornament).
The *adhika* [figure] consists of describing the contained as greater than its container when the container is large,
or describing the container as greater than the contained when the contained is vast.
The substratum is said to be smaller than the superstratum when it is subtle;
and from that subtle substratum, there arises the subtlety of the superstratum.
They know that mutual bestowal of excellence and mutual adornment of one another constitute *viśeṣa*.
If the supported were described without a support, there would be no distinction [between them].
Where a single object to be supported is described as simultaneously resting upon multiple supports, that too is proclaimed as a specific variety [of the figure].
When, by the mere commencement of some task, another task that is extremely difficult to accomplish is thereby performed,
that too is recognized as a *viśeṣa* (distinction).
When an object that accomplishes a certain effect is shown to accomplish something contrary to it, then this figure of speech known as *vyāghāta* (contradiction) is declared.
When an action that is contrary to an opponent's intended effect is established as being easy to perform, that too is called "contradiction" (vyāghāta).
If each subsequent element were to be invariably connected to each preceding one,
then in a series of objects arranged in a row, there would either be a transposition or it would be a chain.
The *kāraṇamālā* (garland of causes) consists of preceding entities serving as causes for each succeeding one;
this *gumbha* (cluster) is also accepted when the sequence is reversed.
When each preceding term is an adjective for each succeeding term,
or when they call it such when each preceding term is the substantive for each succeeding one, that is then called *ekāvalī* (the single-string necklace).
This is *mālādīpaka*; it would be *mālādīpaka* through its conjunction with *dīpaka* and *ekāvalī*.
This is the essence.
That very [connection] is called "essence" (sāra) by the wise when there is a progressive excellence;
where the relationship of the topics is stated according to their numerical order, following the sequence of their enumeration.
Others have stated the sequence there, in forward order, according to their respective numbers.
Paryāya is that figure of speech where a single object to be placed is described as resting successively upon multiple substrates; this is called the ornament Paryāya.
Successively, within a single substratum, there is also a multiplicity of superstrata.
*Parivṛtti* (exchange) is the substitution of objects by means of equals or unequals; it may also be *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification).

When there is the possibility of multiple attainments for a single [subject], the restriction to one among them is what those who travel the path of poetic figures call *parisaṃkhyā* (enumerative exclusion).

If it is described that there is an option between two contradictory [possibilities], then it is an option; if there is the possibility of both, it is described as an alternative; if there is the attainment of one side, it is described as an option; and if there is the combination of both, it is a conjunction.
If there were simultaneity of objects, their connection would be a mere conjunction (*samuccaya*). [This is] the *kāraka-dīpaka* (illuminator of grammatical factors),
which occurs when successive actions belong to a single grammatical factor.
That which is performed as a combination (gumbhana) would be the kārakadīpaka.
Where the ease with which a certain effect is produced due to the presence of other auxiliary causes is described, there the figure *samādhi* (concentration) is said to occur.
*Pratyanīka* (the counter-array) is defined as the disparagement of a powerful adversary, or of his faction,
or else it is the assistance rendered to one's own opponent.
Poetic presumption (*kāvyārthāpatti*) occurs where another matter follows by way of the "stick-and-cake" maxim (*daṇḍāpūpikayā*);
this is considered poetic presumption by those who know the ornaments of poetry.
If, because of some object sharing a common principle of reasoning, the occurrence of another object is stated,
this is called *kāvyārthāpatti* (poetic presumption).
Poetic Figure of Reason (kāvyaliṅga) is that wherein the justification of the matter to be supported is not touched upon by the relationship of general and particular;
that is called poetic figure of reason.
Arthāntaranyāsa (corroboration) is the support of a particular by means of a general, or of this [general] by that [particular];
they call it arthāntaranyāsa when it is based on similarity or otherwise.
When a general statement is supported by a particular instance,
and that [particular] is in turn supported by another particular, it is called *vikasvara*.
Bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) is the imagining of something as the cause of excellence when it is not actually the cause;
this has been described as bold assertion by the wise, such as the mouth of Jayadeva.
Sambhāvanā is the act of conceiving; it is a conjecture that "if this were so, then that would follow," for the purpose of establishing something else.
If, for the sake of establishing some falsehood, another false object is imagined,
that is declared to be the poetic figure named *mithyādhyavasiti* (false attribution).

When the subject (*dharmī*) has been introduced, the description of its reflection (*tatpratibimba*) therein, without mentioning the actual account of the object to be described (*varṇya*), is considered *lalita* (the graceful).
If the accomplishment of a desired object occurs without effort, it is *praharṣaṇa*; furthermore,
the acquisition of something even greater than the desired object is also *praharṣaṇa*.
When an effort is being made for the accomplishment of a means,
the fortuitous attainment of the actual result itself is called *praharṣaṇa*.
Despair (*viṣādana*) is the attainment of an object contrary to what is desired; that would be despair.
*Ullāsa*.
When the production of qualities or defects in one person by means of the qualities or defects of another is described,
they call that the ornament *ullāsa*.
If those two were not instances of contempt, then that contempt would be an ornament;
[this is] permission.
If that permission is a request for a fault out of eagerness for a virtue,
it is a censure; if it is a fault because of its connection with a virtue, then it is indeed a censure.
If a quality is described as a defect, or a defect as a quality,
the wise call that figure of speech *leśa* (the "trace").
Mudrā consists of words intended for their literal meaning; mudrā is the indication of a hidden meaning.
— *Ratnāvalī*
If there is the setting forth of meanings that are traditionally recited together,
it is known as a *ratnāvalī* (jewel-garland), distinguished by its sequential or non-sequential order.
The quality of that [object] results from the abandonment of one's own quality; the grasping of another's quality is its "becoming that" (tadbhāva). This is the first form (pūrvarūpa).
Furthermore, the re-acquisition of one's own quality is called the "prior form" (pūrvarūpa).
However, those experts in poetic ornaments also declare that when an object, even though transformed, continues to follow its previous state, that too is called *pūrvarūpa*.
*Atadguṇa* (Non-attribution of Quality):
They know *atadguṇa* to be the non-acceptance of the qualities of another that have come together [with it].
*Anuguṇa* (Conformity of Quality).
If there is an enhancement of a previously established quality due to the proximity of another thing possessing a quality of the same kind, that is indeed consistent with the nature of the quality.
If the distinction [between two things] is not perceived due to their similarity, that is *mīlita*;
this occurs when an object is [mistakenly identified] by means of a mark— whether innate or adventitious— that is common to both.
If [an object] is concealed by another object, that is called *mīlita* (the hidden).
If the universal is not perceived because of its similarity to the particular,
it is called a "universal" (sāmānya) due to the intention to express equality of qualities between another [object] and the subject at hand.
Oneness is said to arise from yoga; that is declared to be the universal.
The *unmīlita* (the "unveiling") is known by the learned as the unveiling of the distinction between two things possessing equal qualities.
This is the *viśeṣaka* (the distinguishing feature).
When the dissimilarity between two equal things becomes manifest, there arises a "distinguisher" (viśeṣaka).
An answer may be given to a question concerning elevation, or an answer may be provided to a fixed question.
Wherever an answer is uttered with intentional meaning, it is called *sākūta*.
The *citrottarālaṃkāra* (the ornament of the "wonderful answer") consists of an answer that is both manifest and non-different [from the question],
and it is also accepted as an answer when it is not distinct from another answer.
If a riddle is composed such that it is not distinct from another question, or if it contains another meaning within itself,
some have called that a "wondrous riddle" (*citrapraśna*).
The subtle intention and activity of one who knows the thoughts of others is expressed subtly.
It is well-said.
The intentional action of one who knows the transformation of others is considered "concealed" (pihita).
Vyājokti (Artful Concealment): When there is the concealment of one's true form by means of stating another reason,
it is *gūḍhokti* (Concealed Speech).
Gūḍhokti (the veiled statement) occurs when something intended for one person is spoken to another.
Explicit statement (*vivṛtokti*) is that where a double entendre (*śleṣa*), though hidden, is made explicit by the poet;
this is the technique (*yukti*).
It may be appropriate to deceive others through action in order to protect one's vital point.
Lokokti: This is called *lokokti* if it is an imitation of popular sayings.
Chekokti: [This is called *chekokti* if...]
If worldly speech should contain another meaning within it, it is desired as *chekokti* (pithy or witty speech).
When a statement intended for one purpose is interpreted otherwise by another person—
either through punning (śleṣa) or through intonation (kāku)— that is called *vakrokti* (circuitous speech).
Svabhāvokti (Natural Description):
The description of the inherent nature residing in things such as genus and so forth is called Svabhāvokti. Bhāvika.
The description of a marvelous object, whether past or future, [is called *udāttam*].
That in which things appear as if directly perceived is considered *bhāvika*;
that in which a noble subject matter (*udātta*) is described as being exceedingly prosperous is called *udātta*.
Or else, something indicative of another [character] or a praiseworthy conduct is composed.
Exaggeration (*atyukti*) is held to be the description of extraordinary qualities such as heroism that are not actually true.
Etymology (*nirukti*).
Etymological interpretation (nirukti) is the conceptualization of a different meaning for a name based on its etymological derivation (yoga).
Negation is the description of a negation that has been perceived.
That is a prescriptive rule (vidhi) which is characterized by prescription, wherein that which is already established is indeed prescribed.

If the cause is said to be mentioned together with that which possesses the cause, then the wise have declared the cause and the possessor of the cause to be one. Thus have the learned proclaimed the cause.
Thus, having thoroughly examined the opinions of both ancient and modern scholars according to my own understanding, more than a hundred figures of speech (alaṅkāras) have been defined.
Based upon rasa, bhāva, their semblances (tadābhāsa), and the cessation of emotion (bhāvaśānti),
[the figures] known as Rasavat, Preyas, Ūrjasvin, and Samāhita are established.

Those four exceedingly beautiful varieties of *aparāṅgavyaṅgya* (suggested meaning subordinate to another element) which were previously described by ancient scholars have now attained the status of *alaṃkāra* (poetic figures).
The three [types] of *bhāva* are *udaya* (emergence), *saṃdhi* (union), and *śabalatva* (intermixture).
Thus, seven ornaments have been defined; now others will be described.

The wise call that *rasavat* (the flavorful) which possesses *rasa* (sentiment); they also call it *rasavat* when it occurs in the subordinate elements of *rasa* (*rasāṅga*) or in the subordinate elements of *bhāva* (*bhāvāṅga*).
*Preyas* (the pleasing)... [is as follows].
If the state of being a subordinate element to the aesthetic flavor (rasa) is desired as the "more dear" (preya) aspect of a sentiment (bhāva), [then that is acceptable].
When a semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa), or a semblance of emotion (bhāvābhāsa), attains the status of being a subordinate element to a dominant emotion (bhāva) through its vigor,
then this is called the ornament named Ūrjasvin.
The state of being composed again and again is [the *samāhita*]; however, when it serves as a constituent of an emotional state (*bhāva*), it is an ornament.
The emergence of an emotional state (*bhāvodaya*).
When the emergence of an emotion serves as a constituent part of another emotion, it is considered an "emergence of emotion" (bhāvodaya).
The fusion of emotions (*bhāvasandhi*) is an ornament when it constitutes a limb of an emotion; the fusion of emotions is an ornament [only] within the context of the fusion of emotions.
Emotional complexity (*bhāvaśabalatā*).
When there is a mixture of emotions within a constituent of the emotion, it is called the "mixture of emotions" (bhāvaśābalya).

If the means of valid cognition, such as perception and the rest, were to possess aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*), then other learned scholars would declare that there are eight ornaments of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇālaṅkāra*).
That knowledge which arises from the contact of objects and the sense organs is called perception (*pratyakṣa*); if it is beautiful, it is an ornament.
Inference is defined as the knowledge of the probandum (liṅgin) produced by the mark (liṅga). Analogy...
That cognition which consists in the apprehension of a relationship between a name and the named,
and which has the knowledge of similarity as its instrument, is called analogy (upamāna).
Verbal testimony is that word which is proclaimed as a means of valid cognition;
"word" is said to take the form of the Vedas (śruti), the law codes (smṛti), the epics (itihāsa), and so forth.
Presumption (arthāpatti) is that which is postulated as some other fact because [the observed fact] would otherwise be inexplicable;
the wise call that presumption *arthāpatti*.
Non-perception is the ascertainment of non-existence when there is the non-perception of that which is perceptible;
the wise know this beautiful non-perception to be a supreme ornament.
*Saṃbhava* (Probability) is the determination of a lesser duration based on the existence of something greater.
*Aitihya* (Tradition) is [the knowledge derived from] hearsay.
Where there is a traditional report beginning with "Thus they say" (*itihocuh*) and so forth, whose original speaker is not specified,
and which represents a continuous oral tradition— that is *aitihya*, serving as an ornament.
*Saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling) occurs when all the figures of speech (*alaṃkṛtis*) are combined as far as possible;
for, like worldly things, their beauty is observed to increase through such union.
The status of *alaṃkāra* (poetic figure) shines forth as distinct through the method of Narasiṃha;
therefore, we shall here state its determination according to the opinion of the ancients.
When figures of speech are blended with one another to such an extent that they are like sesame seeds and rice grains, it is called *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture).
The mutual commingling of verbal figures and semantic figures,
as well as that of both together, is considered to be threefold.
Where figures of speech (alaṃkāras) become intermingled with one another like milk and water,
those who know poetry recognize this as *saṅkara* (commixture).
Thus, this [conjunction] occurs through the relationship of part and whole, through equal prominence,
as well as through doubt, and by way of entering into a single expressive word.
The fourfold *saṅkara* (admixture) has been proclaimed by the venerable Appayadīkṣita;
thus, the figures of Nṛsiṃha are considered to be five alaṃkāras.
The commingling by the relation of principal and subordinate:
if a primary figure of speech is sustained by a subordinate figure of speech,
then that is considered a commingling by the relation of principal and subordinate.
When a certain figure of speech, containing within it another figure of speech, emerges with equal prominence,
and this occurs simultaneously with that other figure, it is the "Commixture of Equal Prominence" (samaprādhānyasaṅkara).
Even in the absence of simultaneity, if two figures of speech are elevated by a single [element],
that too is the commixture of equal prominence (samaprādhānya-saṃkara).

When there is a mixture of doubt such that no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is seen to establish either the prover (*sādhaka*) or the refuter (*bādhaka*) when one or the other is to be accepted, that is a "mixture of doubt" (*saṃdehasaṃkara*).
The commingling through the entry into a single expressive word occurs if various figures of speech are cognizable by the same word.
In that case, it is accepted as the commingling through the entry into a single expressive word.
This [conjunction] is proclaimed to be of three kinds, based on the mutual entry (anupraveśa) of two meanings, two words, or both word and meaning into a single expressive unit.
Thus have the ornaments of meaning been described according to my understanding;
now, the ornaments of sound will be described in order, merely by way of illustration.
The repetition of mere phonemes (*vyañjana*) alone is called alliteration (*varṇānuprāsa*).
This is twofold, distinguished as *chekānuprāsa* and *vṛttyanuprāsa*.
Chekānuprāsa (refined alliteration) is defined as the similarity between two consonants occurring once;
it is that uninterrupted sequence of pairs of two consonants.
When such repetition is performed, this is called *chekānuprāsa* (alliteration).
