If there is a repetition of one, two, three, or more syllables, disregarding the restriction on their number, it is called *vṛttyanuprāsa* (alliteration).
Lāṭānuprāsa (alliteration):
That repetition of words and meanings which differs only in intended sense is called Lāṭānuprāsa by those who know poetry; this is verbal alliteration.
That [repetition] is threefold: in the repetition of a sentence, in the repetition of a word, and in the repetition of a name;
it occurs in the unity of a compound, in a secondary derivative (taddhita), and in both compound and non-compound forms.
Furthermore, when there is a repetition of names, it is called *lāṭānuprāsa*;
thus, *lāṭānuprāsa* is said to be of five kinds.
If syllables are repeated in sequence— whether they are meaningless, have different meanings, or possess both meaningful and meaningless aspects— that constitutes *yamaka* (rhyme).
That [repetition] is fourfold by way of repetition of a verse, a half-verse, a quarter-verse, or a part thereof.
When there is repetition of the first quarter and so forth in the second and subsequent quarters, there are nine varieties.
If, in a two-fold division of the quarters,
the first and subsequent [quarters] are repeated in the second and subsequent divisions, there would be ten varieties.
If the first, middle, and final portions were to reside within the second, middle, and final portions respectively,
even then, there would likewise be these same ten divisions.
Thus, in a two-fold division, there would be twenty varieties;
in a three-fold division of quarters, it should be inferred that there are thirty, in due order.
Thus, the last and the first, the first and the last, the middle and the beginning,
that which is both beginning and middle, the last and the middle, and the middle and the last— these are their combinations.
If the initial, middle, and final sections are constrained within each individual quarter-verse and possess a fixed sequence, there are one hundred varieties of that [yamaka].
The "appearance of tautology" (punaruktavadābhāsa) is that which appears as if it were a tautology, though not so in reality;
this appearance of tautology pertains to both nouns and verbs.
This [pun] is of two kinds: that which rests solely on words and that which resides in both words and meaning.
That which relies exclusively on words is further divided into two types by way of the distinction between *sabhanga* (with word-break) and *abhaṅga* (without word-break).

Where the cognition of an incorrect word ceases upon the knowledge of its correct form— just as the appearance of an incorrect word [ceases]— that is declared to be the ornament known as *apaśabdavadābhāsa*.
When words ending in *sup* or *tiṅ* suffixes— which denote distinct meanings— are combined so as to appear like indeclinables (*avyaya*),
that is known by the wise as *citra*, which indeed appears like an indeclinable.
That which appears like a verbal suffix (tiṅanta), where there is an appearance of verbal suffixes through words conveying different meanings,
is considered by experts in poetry to be the "Verbal-Suffix-Like-Illusion" (tiṅantavadābhāsa) figure.
If the syllables belonging to one foot are hidden within other feet, that is the figure known as *gūḍhapāda* (hidden-foot);
it is called such because the fourth and other initial positions are concealed.
If an action or other element, though present, is not clearly perceived due to the skill of the context, the wise recognize that as the "deception of action" (kriyāvañcana).
The "Puzzle of the Concealment of the Seven Case-endings" is that wherein the seven case-endings of a single word alone are concealed;
therein, the concealment of the seven case-endings is called a *citra* (puzzle).
The variety consisting of the rules for vowels, places of articulation, consonants, and so forth—
the rule regarding vowels, places of articulation, and consonants which is indeed difficult to perform—
is taught starting from four [syllables] onwards; hereafter, the easier [rules] will be shown.

One should recognize as *citra* (the "variegated") that which possesses variegated phonemes without repetition, wherein no recurrence of phonemes such as *ka*, *kha*, and so forth is observed; that is the *anāvṛttavarṇaka*.
Various colors, such as those of a lotus and so forth, which have assumed the form of a lotus and so forth, are declared to be "variegated" (citra).
If there should be a single sixteen-petaled lotus in which every syllable is separated by one [empty space],
that sixteen-petaled lotus has its phonemes joined to the pericarp.
Two sets of four squares, situated in the outer and inner mandalas, occupy that many cells.
The wise know that to be possessed of eight corners and having two sets of four [sides].
If, in that [verse], the syllables are interlinked by means of odd-numbered syllables or by even-numbered syllables,
then this alone attains the renown of being "gomūtrikā" (cow’s urine pattern).
When there is a single form for the syllables at intervals of one in the two halves [of a verse],
the wise who know the arts of composition call that the *gomūtrikā* (cow’s urine) figure.
In the gavākṣa-bandha, there should be nine squares stacked one above the other in the center;
likewise, there should also be nine squares extending horizontally in the middle.
On both sides of these two, squares shall be produced in descending order:
seven, five, and likewise three, respectively.
The wise one should draw lines of equal measure both horizontally and vertically; beginning from the square at the head of the central path, he should proceed to draw them.
One, three, five, seven, then nine, seven, five,
three, and one— such are the syllables of the verse, arranged in horizontal sequence.

The extraction of the names of poets, works, and so forth intended for oneself is desired by means of the letters situated in the upper, middle, and lower lines, which are combined in their respective order.
This simple bond, known as gavākṣa, is approved by poets.
The verses defining the characteristics of the *alaṃkāramaṇihāra* are completed.
